OpenClaw 2026.4.11-pre Deep Analysis: Enhanced Multimodal Interaction and Operational Visibility

Apr 12, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw 2026.4.11-pre Changelog Deep Analysis

Section titled “OpenClaw 2026.4.11-pre Changelog Deep Analysis”

Overview

Section titled “Overview”

The OpenClaw 2026.4.11-pre pre-release version focuses on three core directions:

  1. Capability Expansion: Memory, UI, video generation, plugin declarations, etc.
  2. Integration Usability: Experience enhancements for existing integrations like Feishu, Teams, Ollama, OpenAI-compatible
  3. Stability Fixes: Critical path fixes for Codex OAuth, audio transcription, Talk Mode, WhatsApp, ACP streaming output

Overall, this release is not about single major features but continuous convergence around “stronger multimodal interaction, clearer integration boundaries, and reduced internal leakage and configuration friction.”

Key Highlights:

  • 9 feature enhancements covering Dreaming, WebChat, video generation, plugin setup, Teams/Feishu, etc.
  • 12 fixes focusing on Codex OAuth, audio transcription, Talk Mode, ACP/QA leakage control, WhatsApp path consistency
  • Continuation of 2026.4.10 directions in Codex, Active Memory, strict agentic execution, provider classification, and QA systems

Deep Dive into New Features

Section titled “Deep Dive into New Features”

Dreaming/memory-wiki: ChatGPT Import Integration + Imported Insights / Memory Palace Subpages

Section titled “Dreaming/memory-wiki: ChatGPT Import Integration + Imported Insights / Memory Palace Subpages”

Change: Dreaming can now integrate ChatGPT imported content and directly view imported source chats, compiled wiki pages, and full source pages in the UI.

Background: Previously, Dreaming leaned more toward OpenClaw’s endogenous memory flow. External imports were often “black-box入库” for users, making it difficult to verify mapping between import sources, compiled wiki pages, and original materials.

Use Cases: For example, when users import a batch of ChatGPT history conversations, they can confirm which old conversation a particular preference was extracted from, or trace back original evidence when reviewing durable memory in Dreaming.

Considerations: Import capabilities increase memory source complexity. After upgrading, pay attention to import data volume, indexing latency, and privacy boundaries, especially avoiding indiscriminate import of private chats in shared environments.

Future Evolution: Likely to move toward multi-source imports, conflict detection, evidence chain visualization, automatic summary verification, and even converting imported chats directly into claim/evidence review flows.

Control UI/webchat: Structured Rendering of media/reply/voice Directives + [embed …] Tags

Section titled “Control UI/webchat: Structured Rendering of media/reply/voice Directives + [embed …] Tags”

Change: WebChat now renders assistant’s media, reply, and voice directives as structured chat bubbles, adds [embed …] rich output tags, and adds configuration gating for external embed URLs.

Background: These capabilities often existed as text conventions or implicit formats in the past. Users might see semi-structured raw content that wasn’t intuitive and could expose internal protocols.

Use Cases: For example, when agents return voice replies, embed videos, rich media cards, or display structured reply directives as interactive bubbles in the browser instead of confusing text.

Considerations: When upgrading, pay attention to frontend custom rendering, embed whitelists, and CSP/external link security policies. Scripts or tests relying on raw text output may need adjustment.

Tools/video_generate: URL-only Asset Delivery, typed providerOptions, Reference Audio, etc.

Section titled “Tools/video_generate: URL-only Asset Delivery, typed providerOptions, Reference Audio, etc.”

Change: Video generation tool adds URL-only delivery, typed providerOptions, reference audio, asset role hints, adaptive aspect ratios, and higher image input limits.

Background: Common pain points in video generation included overly large files, inconsistent provider parameters, and weak input media role expression, preventing seamless exposure of multiple video vendor capabilities.

Use Cases: For example, having agents generate videos with reference voiceovers, or passing multiple reference images marked as cover/frame/reference, returning only URLs instead of stuffing large generated files directly into memory.

Considerations: After upgrading, check if downstream consumers accept URL-only results and if additional download logic is needed. With providerOptions becoming typed, custom plugins or scripts passing wrong fields may fail earlier.

Feishu: Document Comment Session Enhancement

Section titled “Feishu: Document Comment Session Enhancement”

Change: Improved context parsing, comment reactions, and typing feedback for document comment sessions, making document threads more like instant messaging.

Background: Document comments and IM sessions differ greatly in context structure and interaction feedback. Previously, bots in document comments often behaved like “outsiders” with incomplete context and delayed feedback.

Use Cases: Directly @OpenClaw in Feishu document reviews to explain content, reply to comment threads, or add reactions to indicate processing.

Considerations: Verify comment permissions, reaction API limits, and threading ownership. If enterprise Feishu tightens bot registration methods or agent identity policies, configuration may need synchronization.

Microsoft Teams: Reaction, Reaction Listing, Graph Pagination, Delegated OAuth

Section titled “Microsoft Teams: Reaction, Reaction Listing, Graph Pagination, Delegated OAuth”

Change: Teams adds reaction sending and listing, Graph pagination handling, and delegated OAuth configuration for sending reactions, while retaining application-auth read paths.

Background: Common issues with Teams integration included insufficient write operation capabilities, incomplete pagination, and inconsistent read/write authentication modes, resulting in “can see but can’t send completely.”

Use Cases: For example, bots adding 👍 to messages in Teams groups, reading existing reactions as lightweight signals, or paginating through large channel history for context.

Considerations: Delegated OAuth typically means more complex tenant authorization and token lifecycle management. Confirm administrator consent and scope when upgrading.

Plugins: Manifest Declaration of Activation and Setup Descriptors

Section titled “Plugins: Manifest Declaration of Activation and Setup Descriptors”

Change: Plugin manifests can now declare activation and setup descriptors to describe authentication, pairing, and configuration steps without hardcoding special logic in core.

Background: When plugin onboarding relies on core hardcoding, extensibility suffers, new plugin integration costs increase, and setup processes easily scatter across documentation, code, and UI.

Use Cases: A third-party provider plugin can declare “requires API Key + profile selection + device pairing,” allowing consoles or TUIs to automatically guide users through configuration based on descriptors.

Considerations: Plugin authors need to follow manifest schema changes. Old plugins without these fields should still run but need upgrades to get new setup experiences.

Detailed Analysis of Key Fixes

Section titled “Detailed Analysis of Key Fixes”

OpenAI/Codex OAuth: Fix authorize URL Scope Rewriting Causing invalid_scope

Section titled “OpenAI/Codex OAuth: Fix authorize URL Scope Rewriting Causing invalid_scope”

Change: Stop rewriting upstream authorize URL scopes to prevent new Codex logins from failing with invalid_scope before obtaining authorization codes.

Background: In OAuth flows, if scopes are incorrectly modified, users get stuck in the first half of login, experiencing “why does official login report scope error from the start?”

Use Cases: New deployments or re-logins to Codex provider no longer get blocked by incorrect scopes.

Audio transcription: Disable Pinned DNS Only for OpenAI-compatible Multipart Requests

Section titled “Audio transcription: Disable Pinned DNS Only for OpenAI-compatible Multipart Requests”

Change: Only disable pinned DNS for OpenAI-compatible multipart transcription requests while continuing hostname validation, restoring compatibility for OpenAI, Groq, Mistral transcription.

Background: Strict network security policies conflicted with multipart upload compatibility, potentially causing some transcription requests to fail due to DNS pinning mechanisms.

Use Cases: When users upload audio to OpenAI-compatible STT backends, transcription finally works normally instead of being mistakenly blocked by network protection.

macOS/Talk Mode: No Secondary Switch Required After First Microphone Authorization

Section titled “macOS/Talk Mode: No Secondary Switch Required After First Microphone Authorization”

Change: After first opening Talk Mode and granting microphone permission, the flow continues automatically instead of requiring users to click again.

Background: Typical desktop permission flow issue where UI/logic doesn’t continue after authorization state changes, making users think features are broken.

Use Cases: Smoother first-time Talk Mode activation for new users, especially reducing one blocking step during demos or initial onboarding.

WhatsApp: Default Account Resolution and Reaction Path Fixes

Section titled “WhatsApp: Default Account Resolution and Reaction Path Fixes”

Change: One fix ensures active listener helper correctly uses configured default account when account id isn’t explicitly passed; another fixes react actions using gateway-owned action paths, enabling active listener usage in both private and group chats.

Background: Inconsistent WhatsApp multi-account and listener ownership paths could cause subtle issues like “messages can send but reactions can’t” or “default account incorrectly registered as default.”

Use Cases: In multi-WhatsApp account deployments, default account configurations finally work as expected, and reactions become as stable as message send/poll.

ACP/agents + Codex/QA: Suppress Child Assistant Commentary Leakage and Harness Metadata Exposure

Section titled “ACP/agents + Codex/QA: Suppress Child Assistant Commentary Leakage and Harness Metadata Exposure”

Change: ACP parent flow updates no longer expose commentary-phase child assistant relay text; Codex QA also treats app-server coordination chatter as leakage and adds live leak scenarios.

Background: In multi-agent/ACP orchestration, internal progress chatter easily mixes into user-visible output, affecting experience and potentially exposing internal implementation details.

Use Cases: Users in parent sessions only see outputs they actually need to see, no longer seeing internal chatter from child sessions or harness coordination text.

Summary and Upgrade Recommendations

Section titled “Summary and Upgrade Recommendations”

Upgrade Recommendations

Section titled “Upgrade Recommendations”

  1. Priority Testing Scenarios:

    • If you rely on Codex, WebChat rich media, Teams/Feishu, video generation, Ollama, local Talk Mode, this pre-release is worth testing soon
    • Production environments should use gradual rollout, focusing on OAuth login, WhatsApp reactions, multi-provider video generation, ACP visible output boundaries

  2. Maintainer Focus Areas:

    • Pay attention to QA parity gate, packaging behavior, and timeout strategy changes
    • If internal debugging relies on leaked outputs, switch to dedicated logs or verbose channels after upgrade

Future Trends

Section titled “Future Trends”

  1. Platform Evolution:

    • OpenClaw is transitioning from “strong feature stack” to “strong operations, strong visibility, strong plugin declarative capability platform”
    • Memory line will continue toward external knowledge imports, evidence chains, and Dreaming review consoles

  2. Multimodal Unification:

    • Multimodal tool layer will continue strengthening unified abstraction, but provider capability negotiation will become increasingly important
    • Visible output and internal debug output isolation will become stricter, especially in ACP, Codex, QA

  3. Enterprise Integration Deepening:

    • Integration depth for enterprise collaboration scenarios like Teams, Feishu continues to strengthen
    • Plugin ecosystem moves toward declarative, self-describing direction, reducing integration costs

Competitive Comparison Summary

Section titled “Competitive Comparison Summary”
  • Compared to lightweight frameworks: OpenClaw emphasizes more platformization and enterprise collaboration integration, leading in channel consistency, packaging quality, operational visibility
  • Compared to complex orchestration systems: OpenClaw’s advantage lies in integrated experience and progressive complexity control
  • Compared to minimal implementations: OpenClaw leads significantly in plugin declarations, QA governance, channel consistency, and multimodal provider abstraction, though with higher complexity

This article is based on deep analysis of OpenClaw 2026.4.11-pre official changelog, with technical desensitization applied to content.

New Features (Features)

Section titled “New Features (Features)”

Dreaming/memory-wiki: ChatGPT Import Integration + Imported Insights / Memory Palace Subpages

No obvious breaking changes, but UI and memory review habits will change.

  • Future evolution: Likely to continue toward multi-source imports, conflict detection, evidence chain visualization, automatic summary verification, and even converting imported chats directly into claim/evidence review flows.

Section titled “Control UI/webchat: Structured Rendering of Media/Reply/Voice Directives + [embed …] Tags”
  • Change: WebChat now renders assistant’s media, reply, and voice directives as structured chat bubbles, and adds [embed …] rich output tags, while adding configuration gating for external embed URLs.

  • Historical evolution: 2026.4.8 already strengthened Control UI multilingual and skill panels, 2026.4.10 simplified Dreaming scenario pages. This version continues advancing WebChat from “chat window” toward “rich interactive console.”
  • Competitor comparison: NanoClaw and PicoClaw common approaches are markdown + attachments; Hermes Agent without custom frontends typically doesn’t implement voice/reply directives this natively. OpenClaw now更接近”protocol-driven native agent UI.”
  • Future evolution: Expected to continue adding more complete rich component protocols, such as forms, approval cards, resumable task cards, timeline blocks, etc.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
  • Upgrade recommendation:
    • If you rely on Codex, WebChat rich media, Teams/Feishu, video generation, Ollama, or local Talk Mode, this pre-release is worth testing soon.
    • For production environments,建议先灰度, focusing on verifying OAuth login, WhatsApp reactions, multi-provider video generation, and ACP visible output boundaries.

    • OpenClaw is evolving from “strong feature stack” toward “strong operations, strong visibility, strong plugin declarative capability platform.”

  • Competitor comparison summary:
    • Compared to lightweight frameworks like Hermes Agent, NanoClaw, and Nanobot, OpenClaw is more platform-oriented and enterprise collaboration integrated.
    • Compared to systems like IronClaw that可能强调 complex orchestration, OpenClaw’s advantage lies in channels, packaging, operations, and UI integration.

OpenClaw Active Memory Deep Guide: Making AI Remember Who You Are

Apr 12, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw Active Memory Deep Guide: Making AI Remember Who You Are

Section titled “OpenClaw Active Memory Deep Guide: Making AI Remember Who You Are”

Introduction: Core Pain Points of AI Memory Systems

Section titled “Introduction: Core Pain Points of AI Memory Systems”

Most AI memory systems are passive—either waiting for users to explicitly say “remember this,” or relying on the main model to decide “it’s time to search memory.” This passive model has a fundamental problem: By the time the model realizes it needs to search memory, the optimal timing has often passed.

Memory Failures in Real-World Scenarios

Section titled “Memory Failures in Real-World Scenarios”

Consider these common situations:

  1. Dietary preferences: You mentioned hating cilantro last week, today you ask “what should I eat tonight?” and AI recommends cilantro salad
  2. Travel habits: You prefer window seats, China Eastern Airlines membership, but when asking “help me book a flight,” AI doesn’t know this information
  3. Schedule patterns: You play badminton every Saturday, but when asking “weekend plans?” AI completely forgets this routine

This information is stored in the memory system, but the main model never queries it when generating responses. This is the limitation of traditional memory systems.

What is Active Memory?

Section titled “What is Active Memory?”

Active Memory is a core feature introduced in OpenClaw 2026.4.10, offering a direct and effective solution:

Before the main response is generated, insert a lightweight memory sub-agent to search for relevant memories, inject results into context, then let the main model generate responses based on enhanced context.

Core Design Philosophy

Section titled “Core Design Philosophy”
  1. Active rather than passive: No longer waiting for user prompts or model self-awareness
  2. Lightweight and efficient: Specially optimized memory search agent
  3. Seamless integration: User-unaware, natural experience
  4. Secure and controllable: Strict tool restrictions and timeout mechanisms

Detailed Working Principles

Section titled “Detailed Working Principles”

Technical Architecture

Section titled “Technical Architecture”

Key Design Features

Section titled “Key Design Features”
  1. Blocking execution: Main response waits for memory search to complete, ensuring context integrity
  2. Hard timeout protection: Default 15-second timeout, automatically skips if exceeded, avoiding system hangs
  3. Tool restrictions: Sub-agent can only use memory_search and memory_get tools, preventing unexpected behavior
  4. User-unaware: Memory results injected into hidden system context, users see smarter responses
  5. Memory isolation: Each agent has independent SQLite database, ensuring privacy and security

Practical Application Scenarios

Section titled “Practical Application Scenarios”

Scenario 1: Automatic Personal Preference Recall

Section titled “Scenario 1: Automatic Personal Preference Recall”

Background: User previously mentioned “I like dark themes,” “I use Vim keybindings,” “I hate YAML format.”

Conversation:

  • User: “Help me configure the editor.”
  • Without Active Memory: AI gives generic configuration suggestions
  • With Active Memory: Sub-agent searches preferences, main model directly provides dark theme + Vim keybindings configuration, skipping YAML format

Scenario 2: Long-term Project Context Maintenance

Section titled “Scenario 2: Long-term Project Context Maintenance”

Background: User discussed last week “We’re migrating services from Docker Compose to K8s.”

Conversation:

  • User: “How to modify the deployment script?”
  • Without Active Memory: AI doesn’t know migration background, might ask “What deployment method do you use?”
  • With Active Memory: Sub-agent searches migration context, main model directly provides K8s migration-based solutions

Scenario 3: Multi-agent Cluster Personalization

Section titled “Scenario 3: Multi-agent Cluster Personalization”

Background: System has 17 agents, responsible for development, operations, QA, product, etc.

Advantage: Active Memory enables each agent to remember user preferences and historical decisions related to its domain, rather than starting from scratch each time, achieving true personalized service.

Detailed Configuration Methods

Section titled “Detailed Configuration Methods”

Basic Configuration

Section titled “Basic Configuration”

Add to plugins.entries in openclaw.json:

queryMode — Memory Search Scope

ModeContent SeenLatencyUse Cases
messageOnly latest messageLowest (3-5 seconds)Quick preference recall, lightweight interaction
recentLatest message + recent conversationsMedium (~15 seconds)Recommended starting configuration, balanced

strictConservativeShortAvoid memory interference, exact matching

Other Key Parameters

  • timeoutMs: Memory search timeout, default 15000ms (15 seconds)

Common Issues and Solutions

Section titled “Common Issues and Solutions”

Issue 1: Memory recall too “noisy” (too many irrelevant memories)

Section titled “Issue 1: Memory recall too “noisy” (too many irrelevant memories)”

Solutions:

  1. Lower maxSummaryChars value (e.g., from 220 to 150)
  2. Switch promptStyle to strict or precision-heavy
  3. Optimize memory storage, delete outdated or low-quality memories

Issue 2: Response too slow

Section titled “Issue 2: Response too slow”

Solutions:

  1. Lower queryMode to message (fastest)

Section titled “Issue 3: No memory recall”

1. Progressive Deployment Strategy

Phase One: Single agent testing

Phase Two: Core agent expansion

  • Project context: Tech stack, architecture decisions, team agreements
  • Work habits: Meeting times, communication methods, report formats

Section titled “3. Security and Privacy Considerations”

Isolation strategy:

  • Independent database per agent, avoiding information leakage
  • Encrypted storage for sensitive information
  • Regular security audits

Access control:

  • Only authorized agents can access relevant memories
  • Implement memory access logging
  • Support memory deletion and correction

FeatureTraditional Memory SystemsOpenClaw Active Memory
Trigger methodPassive waitingActive searching

User experienceRequires explicit promptsCompletely unaware

Comparison with Competitive Solutions

Compared to prompt engineering-based memory:

  • More precise memory recall

Compared to external knowledge bases:

  • Lower latency

Future Evolution Directions

Short-term Improvements (2026.Q2)

  1. Intelligent memory filtering: Automatically filter irrelevant memories based on context

Medium-term Planning (2026.Q3-Q4)

  1. Multimodal memory: Support non-text memories like images, audio
  2. Memory relationship graph: Establish relationships between memories
  3. Predictive memory: Predict user needs based on patterns

Long-term Vision (2027+)

Section titled “Long-term Vision (2027+)”
  1. Distributed memory network: Cross-instance memory synchronization
  2. Federated learning memory: Privacy-preserving collective memory optimization
  3. Emotional memory understanding: Understand emotions and intentions behind memories

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

OpenClaw Active Memory represents an important evolution direction for AI memory systems: from passive storage to active service. Through lightweight, efficient, and controllable design, it solves core pain points of traditional memory systems, providing users with truly personalized intelligent interaction experiences.

Core values:

  1. ✅ Active intelligence: AI actively remembers users, not passively waits
  2. ✅ Seamless experience: User-unaware natural interaction
  3. ✅ High controllability: Flexible configuration and tuning options
  4. ✅ Secure and reliable: Strict isolation and protection mechanisms

Action recommendations:

  1. Try immediately: Deploy Active Memory in test environment
  2. Optimize progressively: Start small, gradually tune parameters
  3. Continuous feedback: Collect user feedback, continuously improve experience

Active Memory is not just a technical feature enhancement, but a key step in AI assistants evolving from “tools” to “partners.” It enables AI to truly begin understanding and remembering each unique user, opening a new chapter in personalized intelligent services.

OpenClaw Security Lesson 1: Changing Default Port — From Public Target to Stealth Deployment

Section titled “OpenClaw Security Lesson 1: Changing Default Port — From Public Target to Stealth Deployment”

Introduction: Why Default Ports Are Security Risks?

Section titled “Introduction: Why Default Ports Are Security Risks?”

In cybersecurity, default configurations are often the biggest security vulnerabilities. OpenClaw’s default port 18789 is a classic example. This port number is documented in official documentation, tutorials, and README files, making it a public target for automated scanners.

📊 Real Threat Data

Section titled “📊 Real Threat Data”
  • 330,000+ OpenClaw instances exposed to public internet - According to real-time monitoring site openclaw.allegro.earth
  • Shodan search results: product:"OpenClaw" port:18789 returns thousands of exposed instances
  • Masscan scanning cost: masscan 0.0.0.0/0 -p18789 --rate=10000 can scan the entire internet in hours
  • Public exploit tools: Tools like OpenClaw-PwnKit can directly obtain reverse shells

Step 1: Understanding Risk Principles

Section titled “Step 1: Understanding Risk Principles”

1.1 How Automated Scanning Works

Section titled “1.1 How Automated Scanning Works”

Attackers use automated tools to scan specific ports at extremely low cost:

1.2 Why is Port 18789 So Dangerous?

Section titled “1.2 Why is Port 18789 So Dangerous?”
  1. Public information: Port number explicitly marked in official documentation
  2. Concentrated target: All OpenClaw users share the same port
  3. Low scanning cost: Scanning single port vs full port range
  4. High success rate: Almost everything found is an OpenClaw instance

Step 2: Solution — Changing Default Port

Section titled “Step 2: Solution — Changing Default Port”

2.1 Principles for Choosing New Port

Section titled “2.1 Principles for Choosing New Port”
  1. Range: 20000-65535 (avoid common service ports)
  2. Avoid conflicts: Don’t use 22(SSH), 80(HTTP), 443(HTTPS), 3306(MySQL), etc.
  3. Recommended port: 28800 (easy to remember, low conflict probability)
  4. Randomness: Consider random ports for increased stealth

2.2 Modifying Configuration File

Section titled “2.2 Modifying Configuration File”

Edit OpenClaw configuration file ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json:

Key configuration notes:

  • port: New port number
  • bind: “loopback” restricts listening to local loopback address, avoiding public exposure

  3. Psychological principle: Attackers tend to look for low-hanging fruit

Before modification:

  • Faces hundreds of automated scans daily

After modification:

Changing OpenClaw’s default port is a low-cost, zero-risk, high-return security hardening measure. Through this simple change, you can:

  1. ✅ Immediately reduce 90%+ automated attack risk
  2. ✅ Disappear from public scanning radars
  3. ✅ Increase attacker probing costs
  4. ✅ Lay foundation for subsequent security hardening

Security is not a one-time task, but an ongoing process. Start by changing the default port, then gradually build a complete security protection system.

GBrain: Garry Tan's Opinionated Knowledge Brain for AI Agents

Apr 11, 2026
Vibe Sparking

What happens when a Y Combinator president decides his AI agent isn’t smart enough? He builds it a brain — from scratch.

GBrain is Garry Tan’s open-source knowledge brain system. It started as a simple markdown repo for his OpenClaw agent and grew into a full-blown personal intelligence platform: 10,000+ markdown files, 3,000+ people dossiers, 13 years of calendar data, and a “dream cycle” that enriches the brain while he sleeps.

This isn’t another note-taking app. It’s a compounding knowledge system where every conversation, meeting, and idea makes the agent permanently smarter.

The Core Idea: Compiled Truth + Timeline

Section titled “The Core Idea: Compiled Truth + Timeline”

Every page in GBrain follows a simple but powerful pattern:

  • Above the separator: Compiled truth — your current best understanding, rewritten when evidence changes
  • Below the separator: Timeline — append-only evidence trail that never gets edited

The compiled truth is the answer. The timeline is the proof. This separation is what makes GBrain an intelligence system rather than just a note dump.

The Compounding Loop

Section titled “The Compounding Loop”

This is the key insight that separates GBrain from static note systems:

Every cycle through this loop adds knowledge. Look someone up once, and that lookup lives in the brain forever. A pattern emerges across three meetings — the agent captures it. Generate an original idea in conversation — it goes to your searchable intellectual archive.

An agent without this loop answers from stale context. An agent with it gets smarter every conversation.

Why Markdown? Why Not a Database from the Start?

Section titled “Why Markdown? Why Not a Database from the Start?”

GBrain’s knowledge model is just markdown files in a git repo. No proprietary format. No vendor lock-in. Human-readable, human-editable.

You don’t need Postgres to start. The skills and schema work with any AI agent that can read and write files. At 500 files, grep is fine.

But at 3,000 people pages, 5,800 Apple Notes, and 13 years of calendar data, grep falls apart. That’s when GBrain adds Postgres + pgvector — hybrid search that combines keyword matching for exact names with vector search for semantic meaning, fused via Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF).

The Dream Cycle

Section titled “The Dream Cycle”

Perhaps the most fascinating feature: GBrain’s agent runs a dream cycle while you sleep. It:

  1. Scans every conversation from the day
  2. Enriches missing entities
  3. Fixes broken citations
  4. Consolidates memory

You wake up and the brain is smarter than when you went to sleep. OpenClaw ships this as DREAMS.md. It’s the agent equivalent of how human memory consolidates during sleep.

How Search Actually Works

Section titled “How Search Actually Works”

GBrain’s search is a multi-stage pipeline:

  1. Multi-query expansion (Claude Haiku) — generates alternative phrasings
  2. Parallel search — vector (HNSW cosine) + keyword (tsvector)
  3. RRF Fusion — score = sum(1/(60 + rank))
  4. 4-Layer Dedup — best chunk per page, cosine similarity > 0.85, type diversity cap, per-page chunk cap
  5. Stale alerts — flags when compiled truth is older than latest timeline

Why both? Keyword search alone misses conceptual matches — “ignore conventional wisdom” won’t find “The Bus Ticket Theory of Genius.” Vector search alone misses exact phrases. RRF gets both right.

Architecture Overview

Section titled “Architecture Overview”

The repo is the system of record. GBrain is the retrieval layer. The agent reads and writes through both. Human always wins — you can edit any markdown file directly and gbrain sync picks up the changes.

Real-World Scale

Section titled “Real-World Scale”

These numbers come from Garry’s actual deployment:

ContentScale
Markdown files10,000+
People dossiers3,000+
Calendar events21,000+ (13 years)
Apple Notes5,800+ (since 2009)
Meeting transcripts280+
Original ideas300+
Media pages500+

Storage for ~7,500 pages: about 750MB in Postgres (text + embeddings + indexes). Supabase Pro at $25/month handles it comfortably.

What You Can Ask It

Section titled “What You Can Ask It”

The power shows in cross-referencing queries:

“Who should I invite to dinner who knows both Pedro and Diana?” — Cross-references the social graph across 3,000+ people pages

“What have I said about the relationship between shame and founder performance?” — Searches YOUR thinking, not the internet

“What changed with the Series A since Tuesday?” — Diffs timeline entries across deal and company pages

“Prep me for my meeting with Jordan in 30 minutes” — Pulls dossier, shared history, recent activity, open threads

Fat Skills, Not Application Code

Section titled “Fat Skills, Not Application Code”

GBrain’s intelligence lives in markdown skill files, not code. The CLI provides tools; the skills tell the agent HOW and WHEN to use them:

SkillPurpose
ingestImport meetings, docs, articles with entity propagation
query3-layer search with synthesis and citations
maintainFind contradictions, stale truth, orphans, dead links
enrichEnrich pages from third-party APIs
briefingDaily meeting prep with participant context
migrateUniversal import from Obsidian, Notion, Logseq, etc.

Without the skillpack, your agent has tools but no playbook. With it, the agent knows when to read, when to write, how to enrich, and how to keep the brain alive autonomously.

Getting Started

Section titled “Getting Started”

The beauty of GBrain is that you can start small:

  1. Just markdown: Create a repo with the compiled truth + timeline pattern. Any AI agent that reads files can use it.
  2. Add search: When grep isn’t enough, install GBrain CLI and connect Supabase.
  3. Add skills: Load the skillpack to make your agent autonomous.
  4. Enable the dream cycle: Let the agent consolidate and enrich while you sleep.

Works with OpenClaw, Hermes Agent, Claude Code (via MCP), Cursor, Windsurf — or standalone from the terminal.

The Bigger Picture

Section titled “The Bigger Picture”

GBrain represents a fundamental shift in how we think about AI assistants. Instead of asking “how do I make my AI smarter right now?” it asks “how do I make my AI smarter over time?”

The answer: give it a memory system where every interaction compounds. Not just chat history. Not just RAG over documents. A living, growing, self-maintaining knowledge graph where the agent is both reader and writer.

Vannevar Bush imagined the Memex in 1945 — a device that would store all of a person’s books, records, and communications, mechanically indexed for instant retrieval. Eighty years later, GBrain might be the closest anyone has come to actually building it.

OpenClaw 2026.4.10 Changelog Deep Dive: Native Codex Integration, Active Memory & Local MLX Voice

Apr 11, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Overview

Section titled “Overview”

2026.4.10 is a heavyweight release, shipped on April 11, 2026. It contains 17 new features and 20+ fixes, covering model integration, memory systems, voice, security hardening, and multi-channel fixes.

Three highlights:

  1. Native Codex Integration — OpenAI Codex as a built-in provider, independent from the OpenAI channel
  2. Active Memory Plugin — Automatic memory recall without manual user triggers
  3. Local MLX Voice — macOS Talk Mode supports local MLX voice inference

New Features

Section titled “New Features”

1. Models/Codex — Native Codex Provider

Section titled “1. Models/Codex — Native Codex Provider”
  • What changed: Added built-in Codex provider and plugin-level app-server harness. codex/gpt-* models use Codex-specific authentication, threads, model discovery, and compaction paths. openai/gpt-* retains the original OpenAI provider path.
  • Background: Previously, Codex models reused the OpenAI provider path, unable to leverage Codex’s native OAuth authentication, session thread management, and context compaction capabilities. Mixing two model sets in one provider caused authentication and feature conflicts.
  • Use cases: When configuring codex/gpt-4.1 or codex/gpt-5 as the model, it automatically uses the Codex authentication flow (OAuth) with native threading and compaction. Ideal for long coding sessions.
  • Notes: Requires configuring Codex OAuth scopes; existing openai/gpt-* configurations are unaffected; first use after upgrade requires completing OAuth authorization.
  • Evolution: OpenClaw initially supported only a single OpenAI provider → later added multi-provider architecture (OpenRouter, Anthropic, Ollama, etc.) → this version elevates Codex to a first-class independent provider.
  • Competitive landscape: Most similar products still treat Codex as an OpenAI variant without independent provider separation.
  • Future trends: Subsequent versions are expected to establish independent provider paths for more OpenAI sub-products (e.g., Sora, DALL·E).

2. Memory/Active Memory — Automatic Memory Recall Plugin

Section titled “2. Memory/Active Memory — Automatic Memory Recall Plugin”
  • What changed: Added optional Active Memory plugin that automatically runs a memory sub-agent before the main reply, pulling relevant preferences, context, and historical details. Supports message/recent/full context modes, /verbose real-time inspection, advanced prompt/thinking overrides, and optional transcript persistence.
  • Background: Previously, users had to manually say “remember this” or “search memory” to trigger the memory system. Useful context in daily conversations was being missed, rendering the memory system largely ineffective.
  • Use cases: When a user mentions “I’m going to Tokyo next week” in casual conversation, Active Memory automatically records and recalls it in subsequent conversations. No explicit commands needed. Configuration example: enable the plugin with context: "recent" mode, and the agent automatically queries recent relevant memories before each reply.
  • Notes: Adds latency to each reply (extra sub-agent call); increased token consumption; recommend starting with message mode (lightest) to evaluate before upgrading to full mode. Use /verbose to observe the recall process.
  • Evolution: OpenClaw memory system evolution: manual memory_search → MEMORY.md files → Dreaming (sleep-time memory consolidation) → this version’s Active Memory (real-time auto-recall).
  • Future trends: Active Memory + Dreaming will form a complete “remember-consolidate-recall” loop, with subsequent versions expected to optimize their synergy.

3. macOS/Talk — Local MLX Voice Provider

Section titled “3. macOS/Talk — Local MLX Voice Provider”
  • What changed: Added experimental local MLX voice provider supporting explicit provider selection, local audio playback, interruption handling, and system voice fallback.
  • Background: Talk Mode previously relied on cloud TTS services (e.g., ElevenLabs), suffering from high latency, privacy concerns, and network dependency. Apple Silicon chips on macOS are fully capable of running voice models locally.
  • Use cases: Using Talk Mode offline; privacy-sensitive conversation scenarios; automatic fallback to system voice when network is unstable.
  • Notes: macOS Apple Silicon (M1+) only; experimental feature — voice quality may not match cloud services; requires downloading MLX voice models.
  • Evolution: Talk Mode: cloud TTS only → this version adds local MLX option, evolving toward a hybrid architecture.

4. Tools/Video Generation — Seedance 2.0 Support

Section titled “4. Tools/Video Generation — Seedance 2.0 Support”
  • What changed: Added Seedance 2.0 model reference for the built-in fal provider, submitting duration, resolution, audio, seed and other provider-specific fields.
  • Use cases: Generate videos through OpenClaw using fal’s Seedance 2.0, with control over duration, resolution, audio, and other parameters.
  • Notes: Requires fal API key; video generation is asynchronous and time-consuming.

5. Microsoft Teams — Enhanced Message Actions

Section titled “5. Microsoft Teams — Enhanced Message Actions”
  • What changed: Added pin, unpin, read, react, and list reactions message actions.
  • Use cases: Agents can pin important messages, add emoji reactions, and mark as read.

6. QA/Matrix — Matrix Live Test Channel

Section titled “6. QA/Matrix — Matrix Live Test Channel”
  • What changed: Added live QA test channel based on disposable Matrix homeservers, covering threads, reactions, restarts, and allowlist behavior.
  • Use cases: Automated Matrix channel integration tests in CI/CD pipelines.

7. QA/Telegram — Telegram Live Test Channel

Section titled “7. QA/Telegram — Telegram Live Test Channel”
  • What changed: Added Telegram private group bot-to-bot test channel, hardened artifact handling, maintaining native Telegram command reply threads.

8. QA/Multipass — Virtual Machine Test Runner

Section titled “8. QA/Multipass — Virtual Machine Test Runner”
  • What changed: Added --runner multipass option allowing QA scenarios to run in disposable Linux VMs.

9. CLI/exec-policy — Execution Policy Management Command

Section titled “9. CLI/exec-policy — Execution Policy Management Command”
  • What changed: Added openclaw exec-policy command with show/preset/set subcommands for syncing tools.exec.* configuration with local exec approval files.
  • Use cases: openclaw exec-policy show to view current policy; openclaw exec-policy preset strict to quickly switch to strict mode.

10. Gateway/commands.list RPC

Section titled “10. Gateway/commands.list RPC”
  • What changed: Added commands.list RPC allowing remote gateway clients to discover runtime native commands, text commands, skill commands, and plugin commands.

11. Models/providers — Private Network Endpoint Support

Section titled “11. Models/providers — Private Network Endpoint Support”
  • What changed: Added models.providers.*.request.allowPrivateNetwork configuration allowing trusted self-hosted OpenAI-compatible endpoints.
  • Use cases: Connect to intranet-deployed vLLM, Ollama, and other OpenAI-compatible services.
  • Notes: Limited to model request surface only; does not affect other security policies. Must be enabled per provider.

12. Feishu — AI Agent Registration

Section titled “12. Feishu — AI Agent Registration”
  • What changed: Standardized request User-Agent, registering the bot as an AI Agent.

13. Matrix/Partial Streaming — MSC4357 Live Markers

Section titled “13. Matrix/Partial Streaming — MSC4357 Live Markers”
  • What changed: Added MSC4357 live markers for draft previews, supporting client-side typewriter animation rendering.

14. Control UI/Dreaming — Scene and Diary UI Improvements

Section titled “14. Control UI/Dreaming — Scene and Diary UI Improvements”
  • What changed: Simplified Scene and Diary interfaces, stabilized pending entry sorting.

15. Agents — GPT-5 Strict Execution Contract

Section titled “15. Agents — GPT-5 Strict Execution Contract”
  • What changed: Added optional strict-agentic embedded Pi execution contract where plan-only or filler turns continue executing until hitting a genuine blocker.
  • Use cases: Enable when using GPT-5 series models to ensure the agent keeps working until truly complete or blocked.
  • Notes: Opt-in feature requiring explicit enablement; may increase token consumption.

16. Agents/OpenAI — Codex Tool Compatibility

Section titled “16. Agents/OpenAI — Codex Tool Compatibility”
  • What changed: Added OpenAI/Codex tool schema compatibility and embedded run replay/liveness state.

17. Docs i18n — Documentation Translation Improvements

Section titled “17. Docs i18n — Documentation Translation Improvements”
  • What changed: Chunked translation of source documents, rejection of truncated tag output, recovery from terminated translation sessions.

Fixes

Section titled “Fixes”

1. Browser/Security — Browser Security Hardening (Major)

Section titled “1. Browser/Security — Browser Security Hardening (Major)”
  • What changed: Comprehensive hardening of browser and sandbox navigation defenses: strict SSRF defaults, hostname whitelist, interaction-driven redirects, subframes, CDP discovery, existing sessions, tab operations, noVNC, marker-span sanitization, Docker CDP origin scope enforcement.
  • Notes: ⚠️ May affect existing browser automation scripts after upgrade, especially those accessing intranet addresses.

2. Security/Tools — Tool Security Hardening (Major)

Section titled “9. Gateway/Thread Routing — Thread Routing Fixes”

Section titled “10. Models/Fallback — Model Fallback Stability”

Section titled “11. Agents/BTW — Side-question Feature Fix”
  • What changed: Fixed /btw failure after tool-use turns, cleaned up replayed tool blocks, hidden reasoning, and malformed image payloads.

12. Commands/Targeting — Multi-Agent Command Targeting Fix

Section titled “12. Commands/Targeting — Multi-Agent Command Targeting Fix”

13. iMessage/Self-Chat — Self-Chat Distinction

  • Notes: Default timeout extended to 120s; check custom configurations.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

Upgrade Recommendations

  1. Strongly recommended to upgrade — this version contains numerous security fixes (browser SSRF, tool security); delaying upgrade poses security risks
  2. Considerations:

OpenClaw Active Memory: Making AI Proactively Remember Who You Are

Apr 11, 2026
Vibe Sparking

The Problem

Section titled “The Problem”

Most AI memory systems are passive — they either wait for the user to say “remember this,” or rely on the main model to decide “maybe I should search my memory.” The problem: by the time the model realizes it should check, the best moment has already passed.

For example:

  • You say “what should I eat tonight?” and the AI doesn’t know you mentioned hating cilantro last week — it recommends a cilantro salad
  • You ask “help me book a flight” and the AI doesn’t know you prefer window seats and are an airline loyalty member
  • You say “weekend plans” and the AI doesn’t know you play badminton every Saturday

All this information exists in memory, but the main model simply never looked it up when generating its reply.

Active Memory’s approach is straightforward: before the main reply is generated, insert a lightweight memory sub-agent that searches relevant memories, injects the results into context, then lets the main model reply.

How It Works

Section titled “How It Works”

Key design decisions:

  1. Blocking — the main reply waits for it to complete, not async
  2. Hard timeout — 15 seconds by default; if it times out, it’s skipped without hanging
  3. Sub-agent limited to two tools — memory_search and memory_get only; it can’t go rogue
  4. Invisible to the user — injected as hidden system context; the user just sees a smarter reply
  5. Memory isolation per agent — each agent has its own SQLite database; no cross-contamination

Real-World Scenarios

Section titled “Real-World Scenarios”

Scenario 1: Personal Preferences Surface Automatically

Section titled “Scenario 1: Personal Preferences Surface Automatically”

The user previously mentioned “I like dark themes,” “I use Vim keybindings,” and “I hate YAML.”

Now the user says: “Help me configure my editor.”

Without Active Memory: AI gives generic configuration advice. With Active Memory: sub-agent finds preferences, main model directly provides dark theme + Vim keybinding config, skipping YAML format.

Scenario 2: Long-Term Project Context

Section titled “Scenario 2: Long-Term Project Context”

Last week, the user discussed “we’re migrating services from Docker Compose to K8s.”

Today the user says: “How should I update the deployment scripts?”

Without Active Memory: AI doesn’t know the migration context, might ask “what deployment method are you using?” With Active Memory: sub-agent finds the migration context, main model gives a solution based on the K8s migration.

Scenario 3: Personalization Across Multi-Agent Clusters

Section titled “Scenario 3: Personalization Across Multi-Agent Clusters”

We run 17 agents, each handling different domains (dev, ops, QA, product, etc.). Active Memory lets each agent remember user preferences and historical decisions relevant to its own domain, instead of starting from scratch every time.

Configuration

Section titled “Configuration”

Add to the plugins.entries section of openclaw.json:

Core Parameters

Section titled “Core Parameters”

queryMode — how much conversation the sub-agent sees:

ModeWhat It SeesLatencyBest For
messageLatest message onlyLowest (3-5s)Quick preference recall
recentLatest message + recent turnsMedium (~15s)Recommended starting point
fullFull conversation historyHighest (15s+)Deep context needed

promptStyle — how aggressively the sub-agent returns memories:

  • balanced: General default, recommended starting point
  • strict: Conservative, prefers returning nothing
  • recall-heavy: Aggressive recall, returns soft matches too
  • precision-heavy: Extremely conservative, only exact matches
  • preference-only: Focuses on preferences, habits, tastes
  • contextual: Emphasizes conversation continuity

allowedChatTypes — which chat types activate it:

  • direct: Private chats (recommended default)
  • group: Group chats
  • channel: Channels

Verification

Section titled “Verification”

Method 1: /verbose on

Section titled “Method 1: /verbose on”

Type /verbose on in any conversation session. Subsequent replies will include an Active Memory status line:

  • ok = running normally
  • 842ms = sub-agent duration
  • recent = query mode used
  • 34 chars = summary length injected

Method 2: /active-memory status

Section titled “Method 2: /active-memory status”

Check the Active Memory status for the current session:

Method 3: Gateway Logs

Section titled “Method 3: Gateway Logs”

With logging: true, you can see Active Memory run details in the gateway logs:

Method 4: Memory Health Check

Section titled “Method 4: Memory Health Check”

Verify the underlying memory system is working:

Method 5: Manual A/B Test

Section titled “Method 5: Manual A/B Test”
  1. Store a memory (mention a preference in conversation)
  2. Start a new session, /verbose on
  3. Ask a related but indirect question
  4. Check whether the Active Memory Debug line recalled that memory

Tuning Tips

Section titled “Tuning Tips”
  • Too noisy: Lower maxSummaryChars, or switch to strict / precision-heavy style
  • Too slow: Downgrade queryMode to message, shorten timeoutMs
  • No recall: Verify openclaw memory status --deep is healthy, confirm agent id is in the list
  • Debugging: Temporarily enable persistTranscripts: true to keep sub-agent transcripts (watch for file accumulation)

Our Deployment

Section titled “Our Deployment”
  • Instance: Local machine (OpenClaw 2026.4.10)
  • Scope: All 17 agents
  • Memory isolation: Each agent has its own SQLite database, no cross-contamination

Full Configuration

Section titled “Full Configuration”

Configuration Summary

Section titled “Configuration Summary”
ParameterValueNotes
agentsAll 17Every agent enabled
allowedChatTypesdirectPrivate chats only
queryModerecentLatest message + recent turns
promptStylebalancedGeneral balanced style
timeoutMs1500015-second hard timeout
maxSummaryChars220Summary cap at 220 chars
modelFallbackPolicydefault-remoteUse built-in remote default when no explicit model
persistTranscriptsfalseDon’t keep sub-agent transcripts
loggingtrueDebug logging on (during tuning)

OpenClaw 2026.3.24 Deep Dive: OpenAI Compatibility, Teams Migration, Skills Management UX Overhaul

Apr 9, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw 2026.3.24 Deep Dive: OpenAI Compatibility, Teams Migration, Skills Management UX Overhaul

Section titled “OpenClaw 2026.3.24 Deep Dive: OpenAI Compatibility, Teams Migration, Skills Management UX Overhaul”

Generated: 2026-04-09 10:10 CST
Version: v2026.3.24 (stable)
Publisher: @steipete, 2026-03-29

📌 Version Overview

Section titled “📌 Version Overview”
VersionTypeCore Themes
2026.3.24Stable18 Changes + 16 Fixes, covering OpenAI compatibility, Teams complete refactor, skills management UX overhaul, multi-platform messaging fixes
2026.3.24-beta.2Pre-releaseSubset of 3 Fixes from stable + 1 test isolation fix, serving as RC validation round

All 4 fixes from beta.2 were absorbed into stable (Outbound media, Node 22 floor, CLI/update preflight), with the additional Tests/security audit item being an internal CI fix not listed in the stable changelog.

一、Changes (Feature Updates)

Section titled “一、Changes (Feature Updates)”

1. Gateway/OpenAI compatibility

Section titled “1. Gateway/OpenAI compatibility”

Change: Added /v1/models, /v1/embeddings endpoints, and forward explicit model parameters through /v1/chat/completions and /v1/responses.

Background: OpenClaw’s Gateway exposes an OpenAI-compatible HTTP API, allowing third-party clients (like Cursor, Continue, LibreChat, Dify) to use OpenClaw as an OpenAI proxy. Previously missing /v1/models (for client model enumeration) and /v1/embeddings (essential for RAG pipelines) caused many client integrations to fail or have incomplete functionality.

Usage Examples:

  • You configure a custom OpenAI endpoint in Dify pointing to http://localhost:3000/v1 - previously Dify calling /v1/models would 404, now it can fetch the model list normally
  • LangChain’s OpenAIEmbeddings class sending requests to /v1/embeddings - previously would fail, now OpenClaw can proxy to backend embedding models
  • Specifying "model": "claude-opus-4-6" in /v1/chat/completions request body - previously might be ignored using default model, now correctly forwarded

Notes:

  • /v1/models returns a list based on Gateway-configured providers/models, not OpenAI’s full model catalog
  • /v1/embeddings requires a configured backend embedding model (like text-embedding-3-small), otherwise returns error
  • Model override forwarding means clients can override agent default models - be aware if you have permission controls

Competitive Comparison:

ProductOpenAI CompatibilityModel EnumerationEmbedding Support
OpenClaw✅ Complete✅ New✅ New
LiteLLM✅ Core feature✅✅
LocalAI✅✅✅
Ollama✅ Partial✅✅
TypingMind❌ Frontend onlyN/AN/A

LiteLLM is the benchmark in this space - specifically designed as an OpenAI-compatible proxy. With these endpoints complete, OpenClaw’s positioning as “AI agent platform + API proxy” is more comprehensive.

Future Trends: OpenAI compatibility layer is becoming the de facto standard interface for AI infrastructure. Expect OpenClaw to later add /v1/assistants, /v1/threads (Assistants API compatibility) and Realtime API WebSocket proxying.

2. Agents/tools: /tools visualization improvements

Section titled “2. Agents/tools: /tools visualization improvements”

Change: /tools now shows only tools actually available to the current agent, with compact default view + optional detailed mode; Control UI adds “Available Right Now” section.

Background: Previously /tools listed all registered tools, including those unavailable due to permissions/configuration issues. Users were confused: “Why can I see web_search but can’t use it?” This change separates “registered” from “currently available.”

Usage Examples:

  • You configure an agent with workspaceOnly sandbox - /tools now shows only tools available within the sandbox, not those disabled by policy
  • In Control UI, see the green “Available Right Now” list at a glance, no guessing which tools are currently callable

Notes:

  • Compact view may hide details you need (parameter signatures, etc.), switch to detailed mode when needed
  • If a tool “disappears,” it might be a configuration/permissions issue, not a bug

Competitive Comparison:

  • Copilot Studio / GPTs: Tool list visible in configuration UI, but doesn’t distinguish “available/unavailable” at runtime
  • LangChain Agent: Tools bound at code level, no runtime visualization
  • Semantic Kernel: Has plugin availability checks but no frontend display

OpenClaw’s “runtime tool availability transparency” is leading UX design among similar products.

Future Trends: Tool observability will become increasingly important. Expect future additions like tool call frequency statistics, latency monitoring, failure rate dashboards.

3. Microsoft Teams: Migrate to official SDK + AI UX best practices

Section titled “3. Microsoft Teams: Migrate to official SDK + AI UX best practices”

Change: Migrated from custom Teams integration to official Teams SDK, implementing streaming 1:1 replies, welcome cards, prompt starters, feedback/reflection, informative status updates, typing indicators, and native AI labeling.

Background: Teams as an enterprise collaboration platform has ~320 million monthly active users. Previously OpenClaw’s Teams integration was based on low-level Bot Framework implementation, missing Microsoft’s recommended AI agent UX patterns. Microsoft released Teams AI Library and AI Agent UX Guidelines in 2025, this migration fully aligns with those standards.

Usage Examples:

  • User @mentions OpenClaw in Teams - now sees typing indicator instead of waiting silently
  • Replies appear progressively via streaming, not all at once after full generation
  • First conversation pops up welcome card with preset prompt starters (“Help me summarize today’s emails,” etc.)
  • Message bottom has AI-generated label (native AI labeling), complying with Microsoft’s AI transparency requirements

Notes:

  • Breaking change potential: Migration to official SDK may change Teams channel configuration format, backup config before upgrading
  • Need to re-register/update manifest in Azure Bot Service
  • Streaming replies depend on Teams SSE support, older Teams clients may degrade to regular messages

Competitive Comparison:

  • Microsoft Copilot for Teams: Native integration, but limited functionality (only Q&A, no custom tools)
  • LangChain Teams Bot: Based on Bot Framework, but lacks official SDK’s AI UX optimizations
  • Power Virtual Agents: Low-code bot building, but cannot integrate with OpenClaw’s tool ecosystem

OpenClaw now becomes the only solution in Teams ecosystem with:

  1. Official SDK compliance
  2. Full tool calling capability
  3. Enterprise-grade security sandbox
  4. Multi-model agent routing

Future Trends: Enterprise AI agent platforms are evolving from “chatbots” to “collaborative workflow automation.” Teams as enterprise entry point, OpenClaw’s deep integration will enable more “conversational business process” use cases.

4. Microsoft Teams: Message edit and delete support

Section titled “4. Microsoft Teams: Message edit and delete support”

Change: Added edit and delete support for sent messages, including in-thread fallbacks when no explicit target is provided.

Background: Teams conversations are persistent, but AI agents sometimes generate inaccurate or need-to-correct replies. Previously OpenClaw couldn’t edit or delete sent messages, leaving incorrect information in conversations.

Usage Examples:

  • Agent replies with wrong code snippet, user points out, agent can edit original message to correct
  • Agent sends message containing sensitive information (like API key), can delete immediately
  • In long threads, agent can delete outdated status updates, keeping conversation clean

Notes:

  • Edit/delete permissions limited by Teams API (can only operate on own sent messages)
  • Delete operation irreversible, use cautiously
  • In-thread fallback mechanism: when message target unclear, OpenClaw tries to operate in most recent active thread

Competitive Comparison:

  • Slack: OpenClaw already has full message edit/delete support
  • Discord: Supports edit, delete has restrictions
  • Telegram: Supports edit, delete has permission limits

Future Trends: AI agent “self-correction” capability will become key requirement for enterprise deployment. Especially in compliance-sensitive fields like finance, healthcare, need AI to be able to retract incorrect information.

5. Skills/install metadata: One-click install recipes

Section titled “5. Skills/install metadata: One-click install recipes”

Change: Added one-click install recipes for bundled skills (coding-agent, gh-issues, openai-whisper-api, session-logs, tmux, trello, weather), so CLI and Control UI can prompt installation when dependencies missing.

Background: Many skills require external dependencies (CLI tools, Python packages, system services). Previously users needed to manually read skill documentation, install dependencies one by one, fragmented experience.

Usage Examples:

  • First time using coding-agent skill, OpenClaw detects missing code CLI, prompts: “Need to install Visual Studio Code CLI? Run npm install -g @vscode/code”
  • In Control UI skill card, see “Needs Setup” label, click shows specific installation commands
  • weather skill detects missing OpenWeatherMap API key, guides you to apply on website and save

Notes:

  • Install recipes are suggestive, users can skip or install manually
  • Some dependencies may require system permissions (like apt-get install)
  • Network installation needs proxy/firewall consideration

Competitive Comparison:

  • Homebrew: Complete formula system with dependency resolution
  • npm: package.json declares dependencies, but no runtime detection
  • Docker: Image contains all dependencies, but large size

OpenClaw’s skill dependency management balances between “fully automatic” and “fully manual,” balancing flexibility and usability.

Future Trends: AI agent platform “skill stores” will increasingly resemble app stores, requiring complete dependency management, version compatibility checks, and automatic updates.

6. Control UI/skills: Status filter tabs & detail dialog

Section titled “6. Control UI/skills: Status filter tabs & detail dialog”

Change: Added status filter tabs (All / Ready / Needs Setup / Disabled) with counts; replaced inline skill cards with click-to-detail dialog showing requirements, toggle switch, install action, API key entry, source metadata, and homepage link.

Background: Control UI is OpenClaw’s web management interface. Previous skill list was flat, hard to quickly find available or need-to-setup skills.

Usage Examples:

  • Want to find a usable weather skill, click “Ready” tab, see only configured ones
  • See “Needs Setup: 3,” click in, quickly configure those 3 unready skills
  • In skill detail dialog, directly input API key, click “Save” takes effect immediately
  • Via “Homepage” link jump to skill documentation or GitHub repository

Notes:

  • API key saved takes effect immediately, no restart needed
  • Skill toggle can temporarily disable a skill without uninstalling it
  • Source metadata helps judge skill origin (official bundled, community contributed, custom)

Competitive Comparison:

  • Vercel Integration Marketplace: Similar card UI, with status tags
  • GitHub Actions Marketplace: Search filter + detail page pattern
  • Slack App Directory: Category browsing + installation flow

Future Trends: Control UI is evolving from “configuration panel” to “skill workbench.” Expect future features like skill composition (workflow), skill testing, skill performance monitoring.

7. Slack/interactive replies: Rich reply parity restoration

Section titled “7. Slack/interactive replies: Rich reply parity restoration”

Change: Restored rich reply parity for direct deliveries, auto-render simple trailing Options: lines as buttons/selects, improved Slack interactive setup defaults, and isolated reply controls from plugin interactive handlers.

Background: Slack supports rich interactive components (buttons, select menus, date pickers, etc.). Previously OpenClaw’s Slack integration lost these interactive capabilities in some scenarios (especially direct delivery vs thread replies).

Usage Examples:

  • Agent replies: “Which report would you like to view? Options: Monthly Sales | User Growth | Financial Summary”
  • Before: displayed as plain text
  • Now: automatically renders as three buttons, user clicks and agent receives corresponding choice
  • In DMs can also use full interactive components, not limited to channel replies

Notes:

  • Options: syntax is OpenClaw convention, not Slack native format
  • Button count limited (Slack max 5)
  • Interactive messages have 30-minute timeout

Competitive Comparison:

  • Slack Bolt: Official framework, but requires manually defining interactive components
  • Workflow Builder: Low-code, but cannot integrate AI models
  • Zapier: Rich connectors, but no AI-native interaction

Future Trends: Conversational UI evolving from “Q&A” to “guided conversation.” Rich interactive components significantly reduce user cognitive load, improve task completion rates.

8. CLI/containers: —container and OPENCLAW_CONTAINER

Section titled “8. CLI/containers: —container and OPENCLAW_CONTAINER”

Change: Added --container flag and OPENCLAW_CONTAINER environment variable to run openclaw commands inside a running Docker or Podman OpenClaw container.

Background: OpenClaw supports containerized deployment (Docker/Podman), but previously managing container instances was cumbersome: needed to enter container shell to run openclaw commands.

Usage Examples:

Notes:

  • Requires container runtime supporting exec operations
  • Some commands may be limited by container permissions
  • Network access may be affected by container network configuration

Competitive Comparison:

  • Docker CLI: docker exec is general solution, but need to know container name and command path
  • kubectl exec: Similar functionality in K8s environment
  • Podman: Compatible with Docker CLI

Future Trends: Containerized AI workloads increasingly common. OpenClaw’s container-friendly design reduces operational complexity, especially for multi-instance, multi-tenant deployments.

9. Discord/auto threads: Optional autoThreadName: “generated”

Section titled “9. Discord/auto threads: Optional autoThreadName: “generated””

Change: Added optional autoThreadName: "generated" naming so new auto-created threads can be asynchronously renamed to concise LLM-generated titles while keeping existing message-based naming as default.

Background: Discord supports auto-creating threads for bot replies, but thread titles usually taken from first message, can be long or not descriptive.

Usage Examples:

  • User asks in #general: “Help me analyze last month’s sales data and generate visualizations”
  • OpenClaw auto-creates thread, title initially “Help me analyze last month’s sales data and generate visualizations”
  • Asynchronously, LLM generates more concise title: “2026-02 Sales Data Analysis & Visualization”
  • Thread renamed, easier to identify in sidebar

Notes:

  • Renaming asynchronous, may have few seconds delay
  • Requires Discord’s Manage Threads permission
  • Generated title length limited by Discord (100 characters)

Competitive Comparison:

  • GitHub Copilot in Discord: No automatic thread management
  • Midjourney Discord bot: Creates thread per job, but fixed titles
  • Slack threads: No auto-renaming functionality

Future Trends: AI-assisted information organization becoming standard for collaboration platforms. Automatic categorization, tagging, summarization, renaming significantly improves information retrieval efficiency.

10. Plugins/hooks: Add before_dispatch

Section titled “10. Plugins/hooks: Add before_dispatch”

Change: Added before_dispatch hook with canonical inbound metadata, and route handled replies through normal final delivery path, preserving TTS and routed delivery semantics.

Background: Plugin system is OpenClaw’s extension mechanism. Previously plugins processing replies might bypass normal delivery pipeline, causing TTS (text-to-speech) failure, message routing errors, etc.

Usage Examples:

  • You write a plugin that modifies agent replies before sending
  • Previously: plugin might break TTS delivery to WhatsApp voice messages
  • Now: before_dispatch hook ensures TTS pipeline preserved
  • Plugin can inspect/modify replies while maintaining all delivery semantics

Notes:

  • Hook receives canonical metadata (channel, provider, surface, chat_type)
  • Must return modified message or null to continue
  • Critical for plugins that need to maintain cross-platform compatibility

Competitive Comparison:

  • LangChain callbacks: Similar hook system, but focused on LLM calls not message delivery
  • Semantic Kernel plugins: Have pre/post hooks but not delivery-aware
  • Bot Framework middleware: Similar concept but platform-specific

Future Trends: Plugin ecosystems need standardized lifecycle hooks. before_dispatch establishes clear boundary between “message processing” and “message delivery,” enabling more sophisticated plugin architectures.

11. Control UI/agents: Expandable file rows with markdown preview

Section titled “11. Control UI/agents: Expandable file rows with markdown preview”

Change: Convert agent workspace file rows to expandable <details> with lazy-loaded inline markdown preview, and add comprehensive .sidebar-markdown styles for headings, lists, code blocks, tables, blockquotes, and details/summary elements.

Background: Control UI’s agent workspace shows files (SOUL.md, USER.md, etc.). Previously needed to open each file in separate dialog, couldn’t quickly preview content.

Usage Examples:

  • Browse agent’s workspace, click ▶️ next to SOUL.md, expands showing first few paragraphs
  • Markdown rendered with proper styling: headings, code blocks, tables all formatted
  • Can collapse/expand without page reload
  • Lazy loading: only loads content when expanded, saves bandwidth

Notes:

  • Large files truncated in
