Shipping a Full CI/CD Pipeline Through OpenClaw Chat: 10 Iterations, 9 Bugs, One Green Run

Apr 8, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Intro

Section titled “Intro”

This post documents a complete CI/CD deployment flow driven through the OpenClaw chat interface. No manually opening a terminal, no hand-editing YAML, and no clicking through GitHub Actions pages to debug jobs. Nearly everything happened in chat, using natural language to drive OpenClaw through the work.

The project was openclaw Manager (ocm), a multi-instance OpenClaw cluster management tool that includes:

  • A cross-platform CLI for 5 targets
  • An Electron Desktop app for macOS, Windows, and Linux
  • A containerized Server + Web stack
  • An Astro website deployed to Cloudflare Pages

The target was simple: run git tag v0.1.0 && git push origin v0.1.0, then let automation handle cross-platform builds, packaging, Docker pushes, and GitHub Release publishing.

Round 1: Generate the Release Workflow

Section titled “Round 1: Generate the Release Workflow”

OpenClaw first inspected package.json, electron-builder.yml, and the Dockerfile to understand the project layout, then generated a complete GitHub Actions workflow in one pass.

The core jobs looked like this:

The distribution model was also clean:

  • Desktop users get the Desktop app, which bundles server, web, and CLI pieces
  • Command-line users get CLI binaries
  • Self-hosted users get a Docker image

After that, OpenClaw committed the workflow, pushed the branch, created a tag, triggered CI, and even created a cron monitor to report status every two minutes.

Round 2: All Desktop Builds Fail

Section titled “Round 2: All Desktop Builds Fail”

In the first run, the CLI and Docker jobs passed quickly, but all three Desktop builds failed.

The logs exposed two classic packaging issues:

  1. apps/desktop/package.json was missing description and author
  2. The Electron version was declared as ^33.0.0 instead of a fixed version, which broke electron-builder’s version detection

The fixes were straightforward:

  • Add description and author
  • Pin electron and electron-builder to exact versions

This was not really a product bug. It was a packaging metadata problem surfacing in CI.

Round 3: Bun and electron-builder Fight Each Other

Section titled “Round 3: Bun and electron-builder Fight Each Other”

Once the desktop bundle step passed, electron-builder failed again while installing production dependencies. The error was strange at first glance: Node.js was trying to execute the bun binary as if it were JavaScript.

The root cause was that electron-builder detected bun in PATH and incorrectly tried to use it during dependency installation.

The fix was small but important:

  1. Remove bun from PATH before the electron-builder step
  2. Make sure a web build failure would not block desktop packaging

Example:

Round 4: npm Does Not Understand workspace:*

Section titled “Round 4: npm Does Not Understand workspace:*”

After bun was removed, electron-builder fell back to npm, which immediately hit another issue:

This is a familiar monorepo trap. workspace:* is fine for bun or pnpm, but npm does not understand it.

More importantly, those dependencies had already been bundled earlier, so electron-builder did not need to reinstall them at all.

The final fix had two parts:

  1. Add npmRebuild: false to electron-builder.yml
  2. Remove unnecessary dependencies from the desktop package manifest

Rounds 5 and 6: electron-builder Edge Cases

Section titled “Rounds 5 and 6: electron-builder Edge Cases”

The next two issues were both very typical electron-builder traps.

1. Missing repository metadata

Section titled “1. Missing repository metadata”

electron-builder could not infer repository information from .git/config, so the repository field had to be added explicitly in package.json:

2. The publish: never semantic trap

Section titled “2. The publish: never semantic trap”

Writing publish: never inside electron-builder.yml looks reasonable, but electron-builder interprets it like a publisher name and tries to load a non-existent electron-publisher-never module.

The correct approach is not a config change. It is a CLI flag:

Small detail, big time sink.

Round 7: Everything Builds, but Release Still Fails

Section titled “Round 7: Everything Builds, but Release Still Fails”

At this stage, all build jobs passed for the first time:

  • build-cli ✅
  • build-docker ✅
  • build-desktop-mac ✅
  • build-desktop-win ✅
  • build-desktop-linux ✅

But the release job still failed because artifact downloads timed out. The reason was simple: desktop artifacts were too large, and downloading everything in one shot was unreliable.

The fix was to download artifacts one by one rather than in a single bulk step.

Not flashy, just more resilient.

Round 8: Cross-Repo GitHub Release Returns 404

Section titled “Round 8: Cross-Repo GitHub Release Returns 404”

Once builds and artifact downloads were working, another subtle problem surfaced:

  • gh release create --repo other/repo returned 404
  • GH_TOKEN had already been set

The real issue was token precedence. Inside GitHub Actions, the gh CLI prefers GITHUB_TOKEN, and that default token only has access to the current repository.

The effective fix was to override both variables in the job environment:

This turned out to be one of the most important lessons in the whole pipeline.

Round 10: Fully Green

Section titled “Round 10: Fully Green”

After 10 iterations, the workflow finally went fully green:

The final outputs included:

  • A public GitHub Release page
  • CLI binaries for 5 platforms
  • Desktop installers for macOS, Windows, and Linux
  • Docker images at ghcr.io/vs-openclaw/ocm-server
  • A SHA256SUMS.txt checksum file

In total, 9 bugs were fixed along the way:

  1. Missing metadata in package.json
  2. Unpinned Electron version
  3. Bun conflicting with electron-builder
  4. npm not supporting workspace:*
  5. Missing repository metadata
  6. Incorrect use of publish: never
  7. Artifact bulk download timeout
  8. GITHUB_TOKEN taking precedence over GH_TOKEN
  9. Intermittent Linux AppImage 502 failures requiring release-job fault tolerance

What OpenClaw Actually Saved

Section titled “What OpenClaw Actually Saved”

The biggest win here was not “AI can write YAML.” It was how much shorter the debug loop became:

  • pull logs
  • identify root cause
  • patch code or workflow
  • commit and push
  • re-trigger CI
  • monitor progress via cron

Doing that manually means constant window switching, copying logs around, searching errors, editing files, and triggering jobs again. Over 10 iterations, that operational overhead adds up fast.

Inside OpenClaw, those steps can be chained together in conversation, which makes the whole loop faster and harder to break.

Key Takeaways

Section titled “Key Takeaways”

The most valuable lessons from this run were:

  1. Bun monorepos plus electron-builder are a risky combination. Handle npm compatibility and rebuild behavior early.
  2. GitHub Actions token precedence is surprisingly tricky. For cross-repo releases, override both GH_TOKEN and GITHUB_TOKEN.
  3. electron-builder YAML config and CLI flags are not always semantically equivalent, especially around publish: never.
  4. Release jobs should be fault tolerant. One flaky platform should not block the whole release pipeline.
  5. Chat-driven agents are a strong fit for CI debugging, because they compress the loop of reading logs, analyzing, patching, and retrying.

One-Line Summary

Section titled “One-Line Summary”

Four hours, 10 CI rounds, 9 bugs, zero manual terminal work, and a fully working cross-platform release pipeline.

If you are already using OpenClaw, one of the best ways to push it beyond demos is to bring it into real delivery workflows. CI/CD, with its fast feedback loops and repetitive iteration, is exactly the kind of environment where an agent can pull real weight.

Guide to Enabling OpenClaw Dreaming (Experimental)

Apr 6, 2026
Vibe Sparking

What Is Dreaming

Section titled “What Is Dreaming”

Dreaming is the background memory consolidation system built into OpenClaw’s memory-core plugin. It mimics how human sleep consolidates memories — automatically promoting high-frequency, high-relevance short-term memories into persistent long-term memory (written to MEMORY.md).

The feature is disabled by default and must be enabled manually.

The Three Phases of Dreaming

Section titled “The Three Phases of Dreaming”

Each sweep executes three phases in order:

PhasePurposeWrites to MEMORY.md
LightIngests recent short-term memory signals, deduplicates and stages candidate entries❌
REMExtracts thematic and reflective signals, providing enhanced scoring for the Deep phase❌
DeepWeighted scoring, promotes qualifying candidates to MEMORY.md✅

Deep Phase Scoring Weights

Section titled “Deep Phase Scoring Weights”
SignalWeightDescription
Frequency0.24Short-term signal accumulation count
Relevance0.30Average retrieval quality
Query diversity0.15Number of distinct queries/day contexts that triggered the signal
Recency0.15Time-decay freshness
Consolidation0.10Cross-day recurrence strength
Conceptual richness0.06Concept tag density

Promotion thresholds: minScore >= 0.8, minRecallCount >= 3, minUniqueQueries >= 3

Dreaming Output Files

Section titled “Dreaming Output Files”
  • Machine state: memory/.dreams/ (recall store, phase signals, ingestion checkpoints, locks)
  • Human-readable: DREAMS.md (or existing dreams.md), containing phase summaries and a Dream Diary
  • Phase reports (optional): memory/dreaming/<phase>/YYYY-MM-DD.md
  • Long-term memory: Only the Deep phase writes to MEMORY.md

How to Enable It

Section titled “How to Enable It”

1. Edit openclaw.json

Section titled “1. Edit openclaw.json”

Add the memory-core configuration under plugins.entries:

memory-core is a built-in plugin — no installation needed, just declare it in your config.

To modify via command line:

2. Restart the Gateway

Section titled “2. Restart the Gateway”

3. Verify

Section titled “3. Verify”

After restarting, memory-core will automatically create a cron job to schedule dreaming sweeps. Confirm via cron list:

You should see a job named “Memory Dreaming Promotion” with these defaults:

  • Schedule: 0 3 * * * (daily at UTC 03:00)
  • Session Target: main session
  • Payload: systemEvent
  • Wake Mode: next-heartbeat

Optional Configuration

Section titled “Optional Configuration”

Adjusting Sweep Frequency

Section titled “Adjusting Sweep Frequency”

frequency accepts a standard cron expression; the default is 0 3 * * *.

Configuration Reference

Section titled “Configuration Reference”
SettingDefaultDescription
dreaming.enabledfalseWhether to enable dreaming
dreaming.frequency0 3 * * *Sweep schedule (cron expression)

Promotion thresholds (minScore, minRecallCount, minUniqueQueries) are managed internally by memory-core and cannot currently be adjusted via configuration.

Hands-On Walkthrough

Section titled “Hands-On Walkthrough”

This setup was completed entirely within an OpenClaw agent’s main session:

  1. Confirmed the current config had no memory-core entry under plugins.entries
  2. Used a Python script to inject memory-core.config.dreaming.enabled: true into the config file
  3. Ran openclaw gateway restart — service restarted successfully
  4. Verified via cron list that memory-core automatically created the “Memory Dreaming Promotion” cron job
  5. Confirmed job parameters: 0 3 * * *, main session, systemEvent

The entire process took about 2 minutes with no additional plugins to install.

OpenClaw 2026.4.5 Deep Dive: From Agent Runtime to a Multimodal Agent OS

Apr 6, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw 2026.4.5 Detailed Release Analysis

Section titled “OpenClaw 2026.4.5 Detailed Release Analysis”

Version: v2026.4.5 (3e72c03)
Released: 2026-04-06
Scale: 114 commits since the previous release

Overall Verdict

Section titled “Overall Verdict”

OpenClaw 2026.4.5 is not a routine patch release—it is a clear platform leap.

If 2026.4.2 focused on redrawing core/plugin boundaries, restoring the Task Flow substrate, and tightening transport/exec/approval safety, then 2026.4.5 shifts center of gravity toward:

  • Productized media generation (video + music as built-in tools)
  • Productized memory systems (Dreaming: configurable, observable, recoverable)
  • Deeper CLI/ACP/Claude/OpenAI runtime integration
  • Prompt caching as real infrastructure
  • Control UI, mobile approvals, and multilingual UX as first-class entry points
  • Continued fail-closed hardening across pairing, auth, plugins, SSRF, and allowlists

OpenClaw 2026.4.5 pushes the project from “a powerful agent runtime” toward “a full multimodal agent OS with an operational control plane.”

Breaking Changes

Section titled “Breaking Changes”

Legacy Config Aliases Removed

Section titled “Legacy Config Aliases Removed”

Old public config aliases are cleaned up:

  • talk.voiceId / talk.apiKey
  • agents.*.sandbox.perSession
  • browser.ssrfPolicy.allowPrivateNetwork
  • hooks.internal.handlers
  • channel/group/room allow toggles

Loading remains backward-compatible, and openclaw doctor --fix helps migrate. But template repos, scripts, and docs referencing old field names should be updated.

Theme A: Multimodal Generation Era

Section titled “Theme A: Multimodal Generation Era”

Native video_generate

Section titled “Native video_generate”

Agents can now generate videos through configured providers and return media directly in replies. Use cases: marketing assets, product demos, animated explainers.

Native music_generate

Section titled “Native music_generate”

Built-in music generation with Google Lyria, MiniMax, and Comfy workflow support. Includes async task tracking and follow-up delivery. Unsupported optional hints now produce warnings instead of hard failures—very practical for multi-provider compatibility.

ComfyUI Workflow Plugin

Section titled “ComfyUI Workflow Plugin”

A bundled comfy plugin supports local ComfyUI, Comfy Cloud, image/video/music generation, prompt injection, reference images, live tests, and output download. This is OpenClaw building a unified media layer.

Expanded Providers

Section titled “Expanded Providers”

New support for Qwen, Fireworks, StepFun, MiniMax TTS, Ollama Web Search, MiniMax Search, plus stronger Bedrock/Mantle handling. OpenClaw is increasingly a provider federation runtime.

Theme B: Memory Evolves from Recall to “Dreaming”

Section titled “Theme B: Memory Evolves from Recall to “Dreaming””

The experimental memory/dreaming system receives a major expansion:

  • Weighted short-term recall promotion
  • /dreaming command and Dreams UI
  • Three-stage pipeline: light → deep → REM
  • Independent schedules and recovery behavior per stage
  • Aging controls: recencyHalfLifeDays, maxAgeDays
  • Multilingual conceptual tagging
  • Replay-safe deep promotion
  • Top-level dreams.md trail
  • Better chunking of daily notes into coherent units

The core problem being solved: most memory systems either remember too much (context pollution) or too little (no long-term value). Dreaming makes memory promotion configurable, observable, recoverable, and explainable—a cognition pipeline under engineering control.

Theme C: Prompt Caching Becomes Infrastructure

Section titled “Theme C: Prompt Caching Becomes Infrastructure”

A large batch of improvements includes:

  • Deterministic MCP tool ordering
  • Normalized system-prompt fingerprints
  • Whitespace/line-ending normalization
  • Boundary-aware cache shaping for Codex Responses and Anthropic Vertex
  • HEARTBEAT.md moved outside stable prefix boundary
  • openclaw status --verbose cache diagnostics
  • Visible cacheRead/cacheWrite in transcript fallback

Prompt caching only works when it is stable. Tiny formatting drift can break cache hits. OpenClaw now treats this as core performance infrastructure.

Theme D: Deeper Runtime Integration

Section titled “Theme D: Deeper Runtime Integration”

Claude CLI via Loopback MCP Bridge

Section titled “Claude CLI via Loopback MCP Bridge”

Background Claude CLI runs now access OpenClaw tools through a loopback MCP bridge with stdin + streaming JSON. Paired with extensive security hardening: env cleanup, settings source control, permission fail-safes, session reuse fixes.

ACPX Runtime Embedded

Section titled “ACPX Runtime Embedded”

ACP runtime pulled into the bundled acpx plugin—no more external CLI hop. Better session binding, lower overhead.

OpenAI/GPT/Codex Tuning

Section titled “OpenAI/GPT/Codex Tuning”

Provider-specific behavioral tuning: lower verbosity, retry for “plans without action” turns, preserved reasoning.effort: "none", stricter schema compatibility, commentary buffered until final_answer.

Theme E: Control UI & Approvals Mature

Section titled “Theme E: Control UI & Approvals Mature”
  • Multilingual Control UI (zh-CN, zh-TW, pt-BR, de, es, ja, ko, fr, tr, id, pl, uk)
  • Skills panel with integrated ClawHub search/install
  • iOS APNs exec approvals + in-app modal
  • Matrix native approval prompts
  • Per-session thinking-level picker on chat and mobile

Control UI is becoming a primary surface, not a sidecar.

Theme F: Context Governance

Section titled “Theme F: Context Governance”

New contextVisibility setting: all / allowlist / allowlist_quote. Controls whose quoted or fetched context enters the model—important for group chats and semi-public collaboration.

Theme G: Transport Overrides Unified

Section titled “Theme G: Transport Overrides Unified”

OpenAI, Anthropic, Google, and compatible providers now share support for headers, auth, proxy, and TLS overrides. Powerful for enterprise proxies and audit requirements.

Theme H: Runtimes Pulled In-Process

Section titled “Theme H: Runtimes Pulled In-Process”

Lobster workflows now run in-process instead of spawning external CLI. Same direction as ACPX and Claude integration: fewer hops, lower overhead, tighter host control.

Key Fixes

Section titled “Key Fixes”

Security (fail-closed continues)

Section titled “Security (fail-closed continues)”

Plugin-only tool allowlists preserved, owner-only /allowlist, fail-closed hooks, earlier SSRF redirect blocking, tighter plugin trust boundaries, marketplace symlink escape prevention, tool-call marker suppression in outbound text.

Reply & Commentary Leaks

Section titled “Reply & Commentary Leaks”

Commentary buffered until final answer, no accidental reasoning previews, reply tags no longer leak, no duplicate final blocks.

Channel Quality

Section titled “Channel Quality”

Targeted fixes across Telegram, Discord, Slack, WhatsApp, Matrix, and Teams covering reply handling, media paths, approvals, reactions, voice, reconnection.

Gateway & OS Integration

Section titled “Gateway & OS Integration”

macOS launchd restart ownership, Windows task scheduler fixes, stale lock/PID detection, bounded websocket shutdown, startup progress display.

Compared with 2026.4.2

Section titled “Compared with 2026.4.2”
2026.4.22026.4.5
Plugin-owned boundariesMedia generation first-class
Task Flow substrateDreaming memory productized
Exec/transport tighteningPrompt caching engineered
Deeper runtime integration
UI/approvals matured
Security hardening continued

The trajectory: strengthen foundations first, then build heavier capabilities on top.

Upgrade Advice for Operators

Section titled “Upgrade Advice for Operators”
  1. Run openclaw doctor --fix and diff config templates
  2. Decide which instances get music/video generation
  3. Start Dreaming low-frequency with verbose logging
  4. Regression test Claude CLI / ACPX / Lobster flows
  5. Monitor prompt cache via openclaw status --verbose
  6. Revisit pairing/device auth/approval assumptions
  7. Test gateway restart paths on each OS

Conclusion

Section titled “Conclusion”

OpenClaw 2026.4.5 is another major step from agent runtime platform toward a multimodal, memorable, governable, operationally mature agent OS.

OpenClaw Billing Proxy: Route Requests Through Your Claude Code Subscription

Apr 6, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Background

Section titled “Background”

On April 4, 2026, Anthropic revoked subscription billing for third-party tools. Since then, all OpenClaw API requests are billed to Extra Usage — even if you already have a Claude Max or Pro subscription.

openclaw-billing-proxy was built for exactly this: a local HTTP proxy that sits between OpenClaw and the Anthropic API, routing your requests back through subscription billing.

Zero cost increase. Full OpenClaw functionality. No code changes to OpenClaw.

How It Works

Section titled “How It Works”

The proxy performs bidirectional request/response processing:

Outbound (Request to API)

Section titled “Outbound (Request to API)”
  1. Billing Header Injection — Injects an 84-character Claude Code billing identifier into the system prompt
  2. Token Swap — Replaces OpenClaw’s auth token with your Claude Code OAuth token
  3. Keyword Sanitization — Replaces trigger phrases that Anthropic’s streaming classifier detects (8 default patterns)

Inbound (Response to openclaw)

Section titled “Inbound (Response to openclaw)”
  1. Reverse Mapping — Restores sanitized tool names, file paths, and identifiers back to their original forms so OpenClaw works normally

The result: Anthropic sees a “Claude Code” request while OpenClaw sees its own tool names and paths.

Prerequisites

Section titled “Prerequisites”
  • Node.js 18+
  • Claude Max or Pro subscription
  • Claude Code CLI installed and authenticated
  • OpenClaw installed and running

Installing Claude Code CLI

Section titled “Installing Claude Code CLI”

Authenticate:

Verify:

Quick Start

Section titled “Quick Start”

Configuration

Section titled “Configuration”

The config.json file (generated by setup or created manually):

Replacement Rules

Section titled “Replacement Rules”
  • replacements — Outbound: each [find, replace] pair performs raw string replacement on the request body before forwarding to the API
  • reverseMap — Inbound: each [sanitized, original] pair restores terms in the response before returning to OpenClaw

⚠️ Important: Use space-free replacements for lowercase openclaw. Replacing it with a term containing spaces breaks filesystem paths.

Adding New Patterns

Section titled “Adding New Patterns”

If your OpenClaw version has new sessions_* tools, add them to both replacements and reverseMap.

Running as a Service

Section titled “Running as a Service”

Linux (systemd)

Section titled “Linux (systemd)”

PM2

Section titled “PM2”

Token Refresh

Section titled “Token Refresh”

Claude Code’s OAuth token expires roughly every 24 hours. The proxy reads the token fresh from disk on each request.

Refresh methods:

  • Easiest: Open Claude Code CLI briefly — it auto-refreshes on startup
  • Automated: Set up a cron to run claude -p "ping" --max-turns 1 --no-session-persistence daily

Health Check

Section titled “Health Check”

Returns token status, request count, uptime, subscription type, and pattern counts.

How Anthropic’s Detection Works

Section titled “How Anthropic’s Detection Works”

Anthropic uses two mechanisms to detect third-party tools:

  1. Billing Header — The API checks the system prompt for x-anthropic-billing-header. Without it, OAuth requests go to Extra Usage
  2. Streaming Classifier — Scans requests for specific trigger phrases:
    • OpenClaw (platform name, case insensitive)
    • sessions_spawn, sessions_list, sessions_history, send_to_task, sessions_yield, sessions_yield_interrupt, sessions_store (session management tools)
    • HEARTBEAT_OK (heartbeat acknowledgment identifier)
    • running on + platform name (self-declaration phrase)

Not detected: Assistant names, workspace filenames (AGENTS.md, SOUL.md), config paths, plugin names, non-session tool names (exec, cron, etc.).

Why Reverse Mapping Matters

Section titled “Why Reverse Mapping Matters”

Without reverse mapping, the model sees sanitized paths in its context but the actual filesystem uses original paths. Reverse mapping ensures:

  • Tool names match OpenClaw’s tool registry
  • File paths match the actual filesystem
  • Session management commands use correct identifiers

Common Issues

Section titled “Common Issues”

”Could not find credentials file”

Section titled “”Could not find credentials file””
  • Run claude auth login to authenticate
  • On Mac, the file may be at ~/.claude/credentials.json (no dot prefix)
  • If file is empty, run claude -p "test" --max-turns 1 to force a write

Proxy Returns 400

Section titled “Proxy Returns 400”
  • The API rejected the request due to unsanitized trigger terms
  • Run node setup.js to auto-detect tools, or manually add patterns

Token Expired

Section titled “Token Expired”
  • Open Claude Code CLI briefly to auto-refresh
  • Or run: claude -p "ping" --max-turns 1 --no-session-persistence

Tool Execution Fails / Wrong Paths

Section titled “Tool Execution Fails / Wrong Paths”
  • Ensure every replacements entry has a matching reverseMap entry
  • Use space-free replacement terms

Rollback

Section titled “Rollback”

Change baseUrl back to https://api.anthropic.com in openclaw.json and restart the gateway. Enable Extra Usage in your Claude settings if needed.

Disclaimer

Section titled “Disclaimer”

This is an unofficial workaround. Anthropic may change their detection at any time. Use at your own risk. This proxy does not modify OpenClaw or Claude Code — it is a transparent HTTP middleman.

OpenClaw Local Upgrade to 2026.4.5 — Troubleshooting Notes

Apr 6, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw Local Upgrade to 2026.4.5 — Troubleshooting Notes

Section titled “OpenClaw Local Upgrade to 2026.4.5 — Troubleshooting Notes”

Date: 2026-04-06
Upgrade: 2026.4.2 → 2026.4.5

The Problem

Section titled “The Problem”

After running openclaw update, openclaw -v in the shell still showed the old version 2026.4.2.

Root Cause

Section titled “Root Cause”

Two separate OpenClaw installations existed on the machine:

PathVersionSource
/opt/homebrew/bin/openclaw2026.4.5 ✅Homebrew npm global
~/.asdf/installs/nodejs/24.9.0/bin/openclaw2026.4.2 ❌asdf Node.js 24.9.0 npm global

openclaw update only updated the Homebrew copy. Since asdf has higher PATH priority, which openclaw pointed to the stale version.

Solution

Section titled “Solution”

  1. Remove the stale asdf binary:

    After this, which openclaw correctly resolved to /opt/homebrew/bin/openclaw (2026.4.5).

  2. Kill a lingering npm install process: A previous attempt to update the asdf copy via npm install -g openclaw@latest was consuming 1.1 GB of memory without completing — killed manually.

Post-Upgrade Issue: Legacy Config Key

Section titled “Post-Upgrade Issue: Legacy Config Key”

Restarting the gateway produced an error:

Cause: Version 2026.4.5 renamed the allow field to enabled in Discord channel config. Old configs were no longer compatible.

Fix: Running openclaw doctor --fix automatically migrated the config.

Lessons Learned

Section titled “Lessons Learned”
  1. Watch PATH priority with multiple Node managers — asdf, nvm, and Homebrew may each have their own OpenClaw install; openclaw update won’t update all copies.
  2. Check which openclaw before upgrading — make sure you’re updating the binary that actually runs.
  3. Run openclaw doctor after upgrades — new versions may introduce config schema changes.
  4. Consolidate to a single install source — remove duplicates to avoid version confusion. This machine now uses /opt/homebrew/bin/openclaw exclusively.

ClawHub CLI in Practice: Installation, Login, Publishing, and Versioning

Section titled “ClawHub CLI in Practice: Installation, Login, Publishing, and Versioning”

Date: 2026-04-05

Today I walked through the full ClawHub CLI workflow end to end:

  • installed clawhub with bun
  • confirmed that the CLI supports skill publishing
  • logged in with an API token
  • published skill-vetter-guide to ClawHub
  • verified that 1.0.0 already existed from a web upload, then published 1.1.0 through the CLI

1. The short version

Section titled “1. The short version”

OpenClaw CLI does not publish skills

Section titled “OpenClaw CLI does not publish skills”

At the moment, openclaw skills is mainly used to:

  • search for skills
  • install skills
  • update skills
  • inspect local skill information

It does not include a publish subcommand.

Publishing to ClawHub uses the separate clawhub CLI

Section titled “Publishing to ClawHub uses the separate clawhub CLI”

In other words:

  • installing / searching / updating local OpenClaw skills → usually openclaw skills
  • publishing to the ClawHub registry → clawhub

These tools operate at different layers:

  • openclaw focuses on the local OpenClaw workflow
  • clawhub focuses on registry operations

ClawHub CLI supports token login and skill publishing

Section titled “ClawHub CLI supports token login and skill publishing”

That was verified in practice here:

  • clawhub login --token <clh_...> works
  • clawhub publish <folder> --version <semver> works

So if you want batch publishing, automation, or headless publishing, the token-based flow is viable.

If clawhub publish points to a real directory but still says:

3. Core ClawHub CLI capabilities

Based on both the help output and this real run, the core CLI capabilities fall into five broad buckets.

1) Authentication and identity

Common commands:

Typical usage:

3) Installation, updating, and sync

Common commands:

Useful when you want to:

There is some overlap with openclaw skills install/update, but the emphasis differs:

4) Publishing and version management

Useful when you want to:

Section titled “4. Where ClawHub CLI fits best”

ClawHub CLI is especially useful when:

  • you publish your own skills
  • you maintain multiple versions

  • you manage both GitHub source and ClawHub distribution together
  • you operate more like a maintainer than a pure end user

That is the key shift:

openclaw skills is mainly for using skills, while clawhub is for publishing and managing them.

Keep token login available as a fallback

Browser OAuth is convenient, but token login is the better long-term option for automation.

This run showed that relative paths can be misleading. The safer default is:

It helps if these line up cleanly:

6. Why this run mattered

Section titled “6. Why this run mattered”

The main value here was not just getting a command to work. It was verifying three larger things:

  3. GitHub + ClawHub dual-track distribution works well

That combination is a strong default for shareable OpenClaw skills:

openclaw skills is for using skills; clawhub is for publishing and managing them.

If you are mainly an end user, openclaw skills will be the more common tool.

Remote Setup: OpenAI Codex CLI + OpenClaw Integration via SSH

Vibe Sparking

No browser on the remote machine? No port forwarding needed. Codex CLI’s Device Auth mode handles OAuth cleanly over SSH. Here is the full walkthrough.

Remote Setup: OpenAI Codex CLI + OpenClaw Integration via SSH

Section titled “Remote Setup: OpenAI Codex CLI + OpenClaw Integration via SSH”

Date: 2026-04-05

Today I set up OpenAI Codex CLI on a remote Mac (connected via Tailscale) and integrated it with OpenClaw:

  • installed Codex CLI remotely over SSH
  • completed OAuth using Device Auth mode
  • added openai-codex/gpt-5.4 to the OpenClaw model configuration
  • configured fallback and restarted the Gateway

The entire process required no browser on the remote machine and no SSH port forwarding.

Goal

Section titled “Goal”

Install OpenAI Codex CLI on a remote OpenClaw instance, complete OAuth authorization, and register openai-codex/gpt-5.4 as an available model in OpenClaw.

1. Install Codex CLI

Section titled “1. Install Codex CLI”

Connect via SSH and install globally with npm:

Verify the installation:

Note: Use bash -l in remote SSH commands to load environment managers like asdf or nvm. Otherwise npm/node may not be found.

2. OAuth Authorization (Device Auth Mode)

Section titled “2. OAuth Authorization (Device Auth Mode)”

Headless remote machines cannot open a browser. Codex provides Device Code Authorization as an alternative that requires no port forwarding.

Prerequisites

Section titled “Prerequisites”

Enable Device Code Authorization in ChatGPT settings first:

  • Go to https://chatgpt.com/settings → Security
  • Find Device code authorization for Codex → turn it on

If this is not enabled, the authorization page will show: “Enable device code authorization for Codex in ChatGPT Security Settings.”

Run the login command

Section titled “Run the login command”

Example output:

On any device with a browser:

  1. Open https://auth.openai.com/codex/device
  2. Enter the one-time code
  3. Sign in to your OpenAI account and authorize

Once authorized, the SSH terminal automatically shows Successfully logged in.

Why not use port forwarding?

Section titled “Why not use port forwarding?”

The default codex login (without --device-auth) starts a local HTTP server (e.g., localhost:1455) to receive the OAuth callback. On a remote machine, that port is not accessible from a local browser without SSH port forwarding.

--device-auth avoids this entirely. It uses the Device Code flow where the browser and CLI communicate through OpenAI’s servers, requiring no direct network connection between them. Always use this mode for remote or headless machines.

3. OpenClaw Model Configuration

Section titled “3. OpenClaw Model Configuration”

Add the following to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json:

Auth Profile

Section titled “Auth Profile”

Model Definition

Section titled “Model Definition”

Add to agents.defaults.models:

Fallback Configuration

Section titled “Fallback Configuration”

Add "openai-codex/gpt-5.4" to the agents.defaults.model.fallbacks array so it serves as a backup when the primary model is unavailable.

4. Restart the Gateway

Section titled “4. Restart the Gateway”

Final Status

Section titled “Final Status”
ComponentStatus
Codex CLIv0.118.0 ✅
OAuthDevice Auth complete ✅
OpenClaw auth profileopenai-codex:default (oauth) ✅
Model configopenai-codex/gpt-5.4 (alias: openai-gpt) ✅
FallbackAdded to fallbacks list ✅
GatewayRestarted ✅

Key Takeaways

Section titled “Key Takeaways”
  1. Use codex login --device-auth for remote OAuth — no port forwarding needed, authorize from any browser on any device
  2. Enable Device Code Authorization in ChatGPT Security Settings first — the auth page will reject the request otherwise
  3. OpenClaw’s openai-codex provider uses oauth mode, relying on the OAuth token stored by Codex CLI in ~/.codex/
  4. Standardize model aliases — use openai-gpt as the alias for openai-codex/gpt-5.4 across all instances for easy switching

Remote Upgrading OpenClaw: A MacBook Pro 2018 Field Guide

Apr 5, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Remote Upgrading OpenClaw: A MacBook Pro 2018 Field Guide

Section titled “Remote Upgrading OpenClaw: A MacBook Pro 2018 Field Guide”

Date: 2026-04-05 Target Host: Legacy MacBook Pro 2018 (connected via Tailscale) Pre-upgrade Version: OpenClaw 2026.4.2 Post-upgrade Version: OpenClaw 2026.4.2 (already latest) Method: Remote execution from management machine via SSH

Background

Section titled “Background”

Our OpenClaw cluster has multiple instances spread across different hosts, managed daily through Tailscale + autossh tunnels. This session covers upgrading the legacy MacBook Pro 2018 via openclaw update, along with plugin updates.

The Pitfall: asdf Environment Loading Over Remote SSH

Section titled “The Pitfall: asdf Environment Loading Over Remote SSH”

The target host uses asdf to manage Node.js versions. When executing commands remotely via SSH, the non-interactive shell doesn’t automatically load the asdf environment, causing openclaw to be unrecognized.

Failed Attempts

Section titled “Failed Attempts”

The Solution

Section titled “The Solution”

Use bash -l (login shell) to let the system automatically load the full shell profile (including asdf initialization):

Key points:

  • -t allocates a PTY (openclaw update has interactive progress bars)
  • bash -l starts a login shell, which reads ~/.bash_profile / ~/.profile where asdf is initialized
  • -c "..." executes the command within the login shell

Lesson learned: When remotely executing commands that depend on version managers like asdf/nvm via SSH, always wrap them with bash -l -c "command".

The Upgrade Process

Section titled “The Upgrade Process”

1. Running openclaw update

Section titled “1. Running openclaw update”

Took approximately 420 seconds (~7 minutes), with most time spent on npm package downloads. The process has three stages:

  1. Updating via package manager (384s) — npm global package update
  2. Running doctor checks (31s) — health checks, all passed
  3. Updating plugins — automatic update of installed npm plugins

Result: Version 2026.4.2 → 2026.4.2 (already latest, no actual version change).

2. Plugin Update Status

Section titled “2. Plugin Update Status”

openclaw update automatically attempts to update all installed plugins:

PluginResultNotes
openclaw-weixin✅ Updated to 2.1.6Normal update, only 2 suspicious patterns (below dangerous threshold)
openclaw-qqbot❌ Blocked by security policy12 dangerous code patterns detected

Why openclaw-qqbot Was Blocked

Section titled “Why openclaw-qqbot Was Blocked”

OpenClaw 2026.4.x has stricter security scanning. The openclaw-qqbot plugin contains patterns flagged as dangerous:

  • Environment variable access + network send (3 occurrences) — Reading env vars and making network requests, flagged as “potential credential exfiltration”
    • Actual purpose: QQ Bot API authentication (appId/appSecret read from env vars and sent to the server)
  • Shell command execution (child_process) (9 occurrences) — System command calls
    • Actual purpose: Audio transcoding (ffmpeg), platform detection, SDK linking scripts, etc.

These are all normal and necessary behaviors for an IM Bot plugin, but automated scanning can’t distinguish intent.

Why openclaw-weixin Doesn’t Require Force Install

Section titled “Why openclaw-weixin Doesn’t Require Force Install”

openclaw-weixin only has 2 suspicious patterns (lower severity), not reaching the dangerous threshold, so it’s not blocked. This reveals:

  • suspicious = warning, doesn’t prevent installation
  • dangerous = blocks installation, requires --dangerously-force-unsafe-install to override

openclaw-qqbot has more child_process calls (audio transcoding, CLI tools, etc.), combined with the env variable + network send pattern, exceeding the dangerous threshold.

3. Force Installing openclaw-qqbot

Section titled “3. Force Installing openclaw-qqbot”

Installation successful, version 1.7.1.

Note: openclaw plugins install won’t automatically overwrite existing plugin directories — you need to manually remove them first.

4. Restarting the Gateway

Section titled “4. Restarting the Gateway”

Output: Restarted LaunchAgent: gui/501/ai.openclaw.gateway

Final State

Section titled “Final State”
ComponentVersionStatus
OpenClaw2026.4.2✅ Latest
openclaw-qqbot1.7.1✅ Force installed
openclaw-weixin2.1.6✅ Normal update
Gateway—✅ Restarted
Doctor checks—✅ All passed

Lessons Learned

Section titled “Lessons Learned”
  1. asdf + SSH = use bash -l -c: Always use a login shell when remotely executing commands that depend on version managers
  2. Remove old plugin directory before reinstalling: openclaw plugins install doesn’t support in-place overwrites
  3. Security scan levels: suspicious (warning) vs dangerous (blocked) — IM Bot plugins easily trigger dangerous due to child_process and env variable + network patterns
  4. openclaw update auto-updates plugins, but plugins blocked by dangerous flags need separate handling with --dangerously-force-unsafe-install
  5. Remote upgrade time is mostly npm downloads (384s / 420s in this case), doctor checks and plugin installs are relatively fast
  6. Config referencing unloaded plugin channels causes CLI to refuse to run — you may need to temporarily remove related channel configs during plugin upgrades

  • openclaw
  • ssh
  • asdf
  • remote-upgrade
  • tailscale

Skill Vetter Guide: Build a Vet-Before-Install Security Workflow for OpenClaw

Apr 5, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Third-party skills are not something you should fear.

But in an agent environment like OpenClaw—where skills can influence file access, command execution, network behavior, and workflow automation—you should absolutely review first and install second.

Why Skill Vetter deserves its own workflow

Section titled “Why Skill Vetter deserves its own workflow”

When people first encounter OpenClaw skills, they often think of them as lightweight prompt packages or convenience wrappers. That is partly true, but not enough.

A skill can shape what an agent reads, writes, executes, and reaches over the network. In practice, installing a third-party skill means giving an agent a new behavioral protocol. If that protocol is unsafe, automation only amplifies the risk.

That is the point of Skill Vetter:

Never install a skill without vetting it first.

Skill Vetter is not a standalone CLI. It is a safety-first review protocol for agents. Before installation, the agent should inspect the full skill, look for red flags, assess permission scope, produce a structured report, and only then decide whether the skill should be installed.

What Skill Vetter actually checks

Section titled “What Skill Vetter actually checks”

You can think of Skill Vetter as a pre-install security reviewer. Instead of trusting a README or a single SKILL.md, it pushes the agent to inspect all files in the skill.

Typical review points include:

  • Whether the source is trustworthy
  • Whether the skill reaches out to unknown external services
  • Whether it reads sensitive directories or private context files
  • Whether it uses risky patterns such as eval, exec, obfuscation, or base64 decode pipelines
  • Whether it requests tokens, credentials, or elevated permissions
  • Whether its file, command, and network access match the principle of least privilege

In other words, Skill Vetter forces three questions before installation:

  1. What does this skill really do?
  2. What permissions does it need?
  3. Are those permissions justified?

Recommended install scope: make it global

Section titled “Recommended install scope: make it global”

If Skill Vetter lives only inside one workspace, it helps only that one agent. A better pattern is to treat it as shared security infrastructure and install it globally:

That gives you three benefits:

  • Multiple OpenClaw agents on the same machine can reuse it
  • Security policy becomes more consistent across sessions
  • Auditing, upgrading, and recurring reviews become easier to manage

A useful mental model is:

Skill typeTypical locationBest for
Built-in OpenClaw skillsOpenClaw installation directoryOfficial bundled capabilities
User-global skills~/.agents/skills/Shared capabilities across agents
Workspace-local skillsProject or workspace directoryNarrow, project-specific behavior

Skill Vetter clearly belongs in the second bucket.

The most practical usage pattern: vet first, install second

Section titled “The most practical usage pattern: vet first, install second”

In day-to-day OpenClaw usage, Skill Vetter is not usually something you invoke as a command. The easiest way to use it is to make the workflow explicit in natural language.

For example:

If you already expect to install it when the review passes, you can say:

The critical thing is not the wording. It is the order.

A practical SOP for every third-party skill installation

Section titled “A practical SOP for every third-party skill installation”

If you want a repeatable standard, this six-step flow is enough for most OpenClaw environments.

1. Verify the source

Section titled “1. Verify the source”

Start by identifying where the skill comes from:

  • Official OpenClaw source
  • ClawHub
  • A GitHub repository
  • A personal or private share

Then check supporting signals: who maintains it, when it was last updated, whether other people use it, and whether its purpose is clearly documented.

Source quality is not everything, but it is a fast way to filter obvious junk.

2. Review every file

Section titled “2. Review every file”

This is the part people most want to skip, and the part they should skip least.

Common red flags include:

  • curl or wget calls to unfamiliar hosts
  • Silent outbound data transfer
  • Reads of ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, ~/.config, or similar sensitive locations
  • Access to files like MEMORY.md, USER.md, SOUL.md, or IDENTITY.md
  • base64 decode pipelines or other masking behavior
  • eval() or exec() paired with external input
  • Modifications outside the intended workspace
  • Hidden dependency installation
  • Requests for sudo or elevated permissions
  • Access to browser cookies, sessions, or credential stores

The rule here is simple:

Review code, not marketing.

A well-written README is not evidence of safety.

3. Assess the permission boundary

Section titled “3. Assess the permission boundary”

After code review, the agent should explicitly describe the capability envelope:

  • Which files does it read?
  • Which files does it write?
  • Which commands does it execute?
  • Does it need network access?
  • Are the network targets aligned with the stated function?
  • Can the permission surface be reduced further?

If a Markdown formatter wants broad access to personal memory files or system configuration, that mismatch is already a warning sign.

4. Assign a risk level

Section titled “4. Assign a risk level”

A simple but useful grading model:

Risk levelMeaningRecommended handling
LOWLocal formatting, text transforms, weather-like low-risk tasksUsually installable after review
MEDIUMFile operations, browser work, third-party API integrationInstall cautiously after full review
HIGHCredentials, system config changes, automated outbound actionsRequire human approval
EXTREMERoot access, security policy tampering, broad privacy accessDo not install by default

This matters because it turns “maybe we should pause” into an actual operating rule.

5. Produce a structured report

Section titled “5. Produce a structured report”

The report should be easy to audit and easy to compare over time. A practical format includes: skill name, source, author, version, metrics, red flags, permissions needed, risk level, verdict, and notes.

A standard layout makes recurring audits dramatically easier.

6. Record the installation

Section titled “6. Record the installation”

Do not leave the result only in chat. After installation, record at least: install date, skill name, source, risk level, review summary, and install path. Typical destinations include memory files or dedicated security audit folders.

This becomes even more valuable when you operate multiple OpenClaw instances.

Which OpenClaw files should be treated as highly sensitive

Section titled “Which OpenClaw files should be treated as highly sensitive”

In local agent workflows, the most overlooked risk is often not a shell command. It is context leakage.

Files that should normally be treated as highly sensitive include:

  • MEMORY.md
  • USER.md
  • SOUL.md
  • IDENTITY.md
  • TOOLS.md
  • openclaw.config.json
  • memory/*.md

These often contain personal context, private preferences, system-specific notes, internal rules, or memory summaries. If a third-party skill tries to read them, that should usually be treated as a high-risk signal.

Three best practices that pay off fast

Section titled “Three best practices that pay off fast”

1. Write the rule into AGENTS.md

Section titled “1. Write the rule into AGENTS.md”

If you only mention this workflow casually, it will drift. A stronger pattern is to add an explicit rule to the agent operating guide. That makes “vet before install” part of the system, not just a habit.

2. Require human confirmation for high-risk cases

Section titled “2. Require human confirmation for high-risk cases”

Pause and ask for approval whenever the skill touches credentials or tokens, outbound messaging or data transfer, system configuration changes, root or elevated permissions, private context files, or network calls to unfamiliar destinations.

Security workflows collapse when too many exceptions become informal.

3. Audit installed skills regularly

Section titled “3. Audit installed skills regularly”

Installation is not the finish line. A skill can be updated, replaced, or tampered with later. A practical cadence is fast recurring checks every four hours and deeper manual reviews weekly or monthly. Keep history instead of overwriting.

Prompt templates worth reusing

Section titled “Prompt templates worth reusing”

Template 1: Review only

Section titled “Template 1: Review only”

Ask the agent to review a skill using the Skill Vetter protocol without installing it. Have it check all files, output a standard report, and end with a clear verdict.

Template 2: Review and auto-install if safe

Section titled “Template 2: Review and auto-install if safe”

Tell the agent you want to install a skill, but it must perform a full vetting first. Only proceed with installation if the risk is LOW. Stop and wait for confirmation if HIGH or EXTREME.

Template 3: Audit all installed third-party skills

Section titled “Template 3: Audit all installed third-party skills”

Request a security audit of all third-party skills under ~/.agents/skills/. Have the agent label each as Normal, Needs Attention, or Problematic, and write the results to an audit file.

A clean operating model for real OpenClaw setups

Section titled “A clean operating model for real OpenClaw setups”

If you are managing multiple OpenClaw agents or instances, a practical rollout looks like this:

  • Install path: ~/.agents/skills/skill-vetter/
  • Policy file: AGENTS.md
  • Long-term records: MEMORY.md or a security audit folder
  • Automation: audit ~/.agents/skills/ every four hours
  • Mandatory pause conditions: credentials, outbound network access, privacy files, or system changes

That combination is light enough to maintain and strong enough to actually change behavior.

Closing thought

Section titled “Closing thought”

If I had to reduce the whole workflow to one line, it would be this:

Review third-party skills before installation, inspect all files, and stop when the risk is high.

In a framework as capable as OpenClaw, that is not overcautious. It is what professionalism looks like.

Tags:
  • OpenClaw
  • Skill Vetter
  • Skills
  • Security Review
  • SOP

Turning the Skill Vetter Guide into a Skill: A Full Practice from Creation to Publishing and Real Use

Apr 5, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Turning the Skill Vetter Guide into a Skill: A Full Practice from Creation to Publishing and Real Use

Section titled “Turning the Skill Vetter Guide into a Skill: A Full Practice from Creation to Publishing and Real Use”

Date: 2026-04-05

Today I did something that feels very OpenClaw in spirit: instead of writing a documentation file just for myself, I took a complete body of material around Skill Vetter installation, configuration, usage, SOPs, workflows, and best practices and packaged it into a skill that other OpenClaw users can directly reuse — skill-vetter-guide.

Repository: https://github.com/vs-agent-skills/skill-vetter-guide

On the surface, this looks like “writing docs.” In reality, it is a layer of reusable operational abstraction: turning procedures that previously lived in chat history, personal experience, and scattered notes into a skill that an OpenClaw agent can recognize, read, execute, and reuse.

This is not “just wrapping one more layer around it.” It lowers friction, improves consistency, and reduces mistakes.

1. The Starting Point: The Documentation Existed, but It Wasn’t Usable Enough

Section titled “1. The Starting Point: The Documentation Existed, but It Wasn’t Usable Enough”

The starting point was simple.

A long-form guide about Skill Vetter already existed. It covered:

  • what Skill Vetter is
  • where it should be installed
  • why third-party skills must be reviewed before installation
  • what to inspect during a review
  • common red flags
  • how to classify risk
  • how to produce a standard vetting report
  • how to run periodic audits
  • how to write “review before install” into AGENTS.md
  • and prompt templates that OpenClaw can directly use

That kind of document is useful for humans, but it has an obvious limitation:

It was still mainly written for people to read, not for agents to directly use.

In other words, the information existed, but the usage flow was still too manual:

  1. Find the document
  2. Read it yourself
  3. Understand it yourself
  4. Copy a prompt block yourself
  5. Adapt it yourself
  6. Send it to another OpenClaw yourself

That flow is not impossible, but it is noisy and easy to distort.

Especially when the goal is not just “something I might refer back to later,” but rather:

  • sharing it with other OpenClaw users
  • letting other agents reuse it consistently
  • lowering the barrier to using Skill Vetter
  • making “vet first, install later” a standard action

At that point, it should not stop at the documentation layer.

It should become a skill.

2. Why Turn SOPs, Workflows, and Best Practices into a Skill

Section titled “2. Why Turn SOPs, Workflows, and Best Practices into a Skill”

This is the core of the whole exercise.

A lot of people write SOPs and end up with a “knowledge article.” But in OpenClaw, the more effective move is often this:

Turn knowledge into a skill, and turn experience into something triggerable.

2.1 A Skill Is Closer to Executable Knowledge Than an Article

Section titled “2.1 A Skill Is Closer to Executable Knowledge Than an Article”

An article explains a problem. A skill intervenes when the problem actually appears.

An article, no matter how complete, is still static. A skill can be matched, loaded, and applied by the agent when a relevant task shows up.

For example:

  • the user says “help me install this third-party skill”
  • the agent recognizes it as a skill-installation task
  • the agent reads skill-vetter-guide
  • it runs the agreed safety review flow first
  • then it decides whether installation is acceptable

At that point, the SOP is no longer “do you remember to use it?” It becomes “will the system use it automatically?”

That is a huge difference.

2.2 A Skill Turns Tacit Experience into Explicit Rules

Section titled “2.2 A Skill Turns Tacit Experience into Explicit Rules”

A lot of best practices normally live only in experienced users’ heads, for example:

  • do not review only SKILL.md; review all files
  • be cautious around curl, wget, and external fetches
  • reading ~/.ssh, ~/.aws, or MEMORY.md is high risk by default
  • eval, exec, and base64 obfuscation deserve special scrutiny
  • HIGH and EXTREME risks require human confirmation
  • keep an audit trail after installation

If these rules exist only in chat, they disappear in context churn. If they exist only in a long article, they are easy to skip.

Once they are written into a skill, though, they become reusable, portable, easy to copy across instances, easy to share for direct use, and capable of forming consistent habits.

That is experience productized.

2.3 Skills Naturally Fit Cross-Instance and Cross-User Sharing

Section titled “2.3 Skills Naturally Fit Cross-Instance and Cross-User Sharing”

One major reality of OpenClaw is that agents and instances are often distributed:

  • different machines
  • different workspaces
  • different agent personas
  • different channels
  • different maintainers

If everyone relies on handwritten SOPs and custom prompt rewrites, the result will eventually be version drift, inconsistent rules, missed reviews, and repeated labor.

Once it becomes a skill, the sharing model becomes much cleaner: one directory, one file structure, one repository, and one format the agent can recognize.

2.4 A Skill Lowers the Barrier to Usage, Not the Bar for Safety

Section titled “2.4 A Skill Lowers the Barrier to Usage, Not the Bar for Safety”

The biggest problem in many safety workflows is not conceptual difficulty. It is procedural fragmentation.

Skill Vetter itself is not mysterious. It is a straightforward safety review logic:

  • inspect the source
  • inspect the code
  • inspect the permissions
  • inspect the risks
  • make a conclusion

Putting those answers into a skill means users no longer have to reconstruct the entire context from scratch every time.

not lowering the standard, but lowering the friction required to enter the standard process.

3. How It Was Built

Section titled “3. How It Was Built”

The process roughly unfolded in four steps: start from a complete guide, reshape it into a skill structure, unify around English first and then add Chinese, and finally publish it so it becomes something truly shareable.

3.1 Start with a Complete Source Guide

Section titled “3.1 Start with a Complete Source Guide”

The first step was to write a sufficiently complete guide for Skill Vetter itself. That source material covered its positioning, recommended install path, pre-install vetting SOP, red-flag checklist, risk grading model, standard report template, audit suggestions, prompt templates, and recommended AGENTS.md rules.

3.2 Convert the Document into a Skill Structure

Section titled “3.2 Convert the Document into a Skill Structure”

The final shape included:

  • SKILL.md
  • references/report-template.md
  • references/audit-template.md
  • references/prompt-templates.md

The main file carries the principles and entry points. The reference files hold details and reusable templates.

3.3 Standardize on English First, Then Add Chinese

Section titled “3.3 Standardize on English First, Then Add Chinese”

To make the material more suitable for public sharing, the content was first normalized into an English-primary version. But English alone would not be enough for a large group of actual OpenClaw users, so a corresponding Chinese version was also added.

3.4 Publish It to GitHub So It Becomes a Real Shared Asset

Section titled “3.4 Publish It to GitHub So It Becomes a Real Shared Asset”

Only after publishing does it stop being “personal material” and become a shared asset. So the work was organized into an independent repository and published here:

https://github.com/vs-agent-skills/skill-vetter-guide

Along the way, the repository setup was also cleaned up: explicit Git identity, SSH key setup, SSH commit signing, and proper organization ownership.

4. What Problem This Skill Actually Solves

Section titled “4. What Problem This Skill Actually Solves”

4.1 It Solves “I Know I Should Review, but I Don’t Know How”

Section titled “4.1 It Solves “I Know I Should Review, but I Don’t Know How””

skill-vetter-guide turns the review process into a template: what files to inspect, what behaviors are dangerous, what counts as high risk, and how to produce a disciplined conclusion.

4.2 It Solves the Repetition of Explaining the Same Workflow Again and Again

Section titled “4.2 It Solves the Repetition of Explaining the Same Workflow Again and Again”

Without the skill, every explanation tends to repeat the same pieces: where to install it, how to use it, how to vet before install, how to write prompts, and how to audit afterward.

4.3 It Solves Inconsistent Standards Across Instances

Section titled “4.3 It Solves Inconsistent Standards Across Instances”

A shared skill helps unify SOPs, risk language, review templates, and audit outputs.

4.4 It Solves the Risk of Keeping Safety Rules Only in Someone’s Head

Section titled “4.4 It Solves the Risk of Keeping Safety Rules Only in Someone’s Head”

Writing them into a skill upgrades safety habits from personal memory into shared capability.

5. Why This Is More Valuable Than Publishing a Tutorial Alone

Section titled “5. Why This Is More Valuable Than Publishing a Tutorial Alone”

If you only publish an article, people get an explanation, a set of recommendations, and some prompt snippets. If you publish a skill, they get structured content, an agent-recognizable entry point, reusable templates, a consistent operating pattern, and a shared repository that can keep evolving.

For an agent-first system like OpenClaw, something the agent can directly use is often more valuable than something thoroughly written for humans.

6. Practical Use Cases: How It Can Be Used Going Forward

Section titled “6. Practical Use Cases: How It Can Be Used Going Forward”

Scenario 1: New Machine Bring-Up

Section titled “Scenario 1: New Machine Bring-Up”

When a fresh OpenClaw instance is being set up, the agent can install Skill Vetter first, read skill-vetter-guide, write “review before install” into AGENTS.md, and configure the audit flow afterward.

Scenario 2: Reviewing a Third-Party Skill

Section titled “Scenario 2: Reviewing a Third-Party Skill”

The next time a new skill appears, there is no need to improvise the language from scratch. Just tell the agent: vet it first, use Skill Vetter, follow the guide.

Scenario 3: Sharing OpenClaw Best Practices with Others

Section titled “Scenario 3: Sharing OpenClaw Best Practices with Others”

If someone asks how to install and manage third-party skills safely in OpenClaw, there is no longer a need for a long explanation. Just hand them the repository:

https://github.com/vs-agent-skills/skill-vetter-guide

Scenario 4: Acting as a Team-Wide Standard

Section titled “Scenario 4: Acting as a Team-Wide Standard”

If multiple people are maintaining OpenClaw within a team, skill-vetter-guide can act as a shared internal standard for what must be reviewed, what must be blocked, what counts as high risk, how reports should be written, and how audit traces should be kept.

7. The Bigger Meaning: Upgrading “Experience Documents” into “Distributable Capability”

Section titled “7. The Bigger Meaning: Upgrading “Experience Documents” into “Distributable Capability””

In OpenClaw, many high-value pieces of operational knowledge should not end as documents. They should end as skills.

This is especially true for SOPs, workflows, best practices, safety rules, audit standards, interaction templates, and operational checklists.

Once they become skills, their value changes from “I know this” into “I can reuse it, others can reuse it, agents can reuse it, and future me can reuse it too.”

8. What Could Come Next

Section titled “8. What Could Come Next”

Natural next steps include adding a stronger README, release notes, examples, and tighter integration with automated audit tasks. The same method can also be generalized into more guide skills for deployment, operations, security, channel configuration, and troubleshooting.

9. Closing Thought

Section titled “9. Closing Thought”

At its core, skill-vetter-guide is a practical optimization: it turns scattered, personal, easy-to-forget operational experience into a skill that is shareable, reusable, portable, and directly readable by agents.

Turning SOPs, workflows, and best practices into a skill is not just about sharing knowledge — it is about sharing a capability that can be used immediately.

That is far more practical than publishing a tutorial alone.

  • OpenClaw
  • Skill
  • Skill Vetter
  • Security
  • Workflow

Auto-Discovering Blog Content with OpenClaw Cron: daily-blog-sharing-check in Practice

Apr 4, 2026
Vibe Sparking

The Problem: Blog Material Scattered Across a Dozen Agents

Section titled “The Problem: Blog Material Scattered Across a Dozen Agents”

When you manage multiple Agents with OpenClaw, they produce a steady stream of technical docs, troubleshooting notes, and analysis reports every day — scattered across different Agent workspaces. Which ones are worth turning into blog posts? Which have already been published? Manually browsing through a dozen directories is painfully inefficient.

daily-blog-sharing-check was designed to solve exactly this: a daily cron job that automatically scans all Agent workspaces for recent changes, cross-references them against published blog content, and generates a structured “shareable content report.”

What It Does

Section titled “What It Does”

Every day at 12:00 noon (Asia/Shanghai), this Cron Job:

  1. Reads openclaw.json to get all Agents and their workspace paths
  2. Lists existing blog articles (Astro project’s src/content/docs/zh-cn/blog/ directory)
  3. Checks Issue records (tracked sharing Issues in engineering/00-issues/)
  4. Dispatches subagents in parallel — one per Agent, each scanning its workspace for changes in the last 3 days
  5. Aggregates a report, saved to memory/blog-sharing-reports/YYYY-MM-DD.md

What the Report Looks Like

Section titled “What the Report Looks Like”

Key value:

  • Sensitivity assessment — flags content containing company/client/IP/credential info as “High,” reminding you to sanitize
  • Deduplication — automatically matches against published articles and existing Issues to avoid redundant work
  • Category suggestions — recommends appropriate blog categories and processing priority

Configuration Details

Section titled “Configuration Details”

Cron Parameters

Section titled “Cron Parameters”
ParameterValue
Namedaily-blog-sharing-check
Schedule0 12 * * * (daily at noon)
TimezoneAsia/Shanghai
Executionisolated (clean session, doesn’t pollute main session)
Timeout600 seconds (10 minutes)
Deliveryannounce to specified channel

Design Decisions

Section titled “Design Decisions”
  1. Isolated session execution — each run starts with a clean context, separate from the main session
  2. Parallel subagents — 12 Agents scanned simultaneously, ~6-7 minutes total (vs 30+ minutes serial)
  3. No sessions_yield — isolated sessions don’t support yield recovery; uses exec sleep + sessions_list polling instead
  4. Persistent results — reports saved to files for historical comparison and trend analysis

Results in Practice

Section titled “Results in Practice”

Since the first run on 2026-04-03:

  • Single scan covers 12 Agents, 23 changed files
  • Automatically identified 14 potential shareable items
  • Accurately excluded 8 already-published duplicates
  • Found 3 high-quality articles ready for immediate publication

Actual output: 6 new blog posts published that day based on the report’s recommendations. Went from “what should I write about?” to “too many options, which one first?”

Reusable Prompt

Section titled “Reusable Prompt”

Here’s the complete Cron Job payload prompt. You can create it in your own OpenClaw via the Cron tool — just modify the paths.

How to Create

Section titled “How to Create”

Tell OpenClaw:

Create a cron job named daily-blog-sharing-check, running daily at noon, timezone Asia/Shanghai, agentId set to your blog management agent.

Or create directly via the Cron tool API with the payload below.

Complete Prompt (Copy & Paste Ready)

Section titled “Complete Prompt (Copy & Paste Ready)”

Adaptation Guide

Section titled “Adaptation Guide”

Replace these placeholders before use:

PlaceholderDescriptionExample
<YOUR_BLOG_AGENT_ID>Your blog management Agent IDvs-sites-astro
<YOUR_BLOG_CONTENT_DIR>Blog content directory~/blog/src/content/
<YOUR_WORKSPACE>Agent workspace path~/.openclaw/workspace

Optional Enhancements

Section titled “Optional Enhancements”
  • Issue tracking: If you manage blog Issues in a directory, add Issue scanning and deduplication logic in Step 3
  • Custom sensitivity: Adjust sensitivity criteria for your context
  • Delivery channel: Configure delivery to WeChat/Telegram/Discord to browse reports on your phone
  • Time window: -mtime -3 can be adjusted to -mtime -7 (weekly) or -mtime -1 (daily)

Conclusion

Section titled “Conclusion”

daily-blog-sharing-check is essentially a “content discovery engine” — leveraging OpenClaw’s multi-Agent architecture and Cron scheduling to automatically aggregate, evaluate, and deduplicate technical output scattered everywhere. It won’t write articles for you, but it tells you “what’s worth writing about today.”

For teams or individuals maintaining a tech blog, this kind of automated material discovery is far more efficient than the “write whatever comes to mind” approach.

Let OpenClaw Configure Its Own Ollama Local Model: Gemma 4 31B in One Conversation

Date: 2026-04-04 Environment: macOS 26.3.1 (Apple Silicon) · OpenClaw 2026.4.2 · Ollama running locally Model: gemma4:31b-it-bf16 (62GB, BF16 full precision)

Background

Section titled “Background”

OpenClaw supports multiple model providers (Anthropic, OpenAI, Ollama, vLLM, etc.), but configuring a local model typically requires manually editing JSON config files. This time we tried something different: having the agent complete the entire process directly in OpenClaw chat — from confirming Ollama status, editing configuration, to running an end-to-end test.

All it took was one sentence:

“Add the local ollama run gemma4:31b-it-bf16 model to the local OpenClaw model list and test it”

The Process

Section titled “The Process”

Step 1: Environment Detection

Section titled “Step 1: Environment Detection”

The agent executed two groups of commands in parallel:

  1. Check OpenClaw status — openclaw status, confirming the gateway was running normally (local ws://127.0.0.1:18789)
  2. Check Ollama local models — ollama list + curl http://127.0.0.1:11434/api/tags

Results confirmed:

  • Ollama was running, gemma4:31b-it-bf16 already pulled (62GB)
  • OpenClaw gateway healthy, but no Ollama provider configured yet

Step 2: Documentation Lookup

Section titled “Step 2: Documentation Lookup”

The agent automatically searched OpenClaw’s Ollama provider documentation (/providers/ollama) and found two integration methods:

MethodDescription
Auto-discoverySet OLLAMA_API_KEY but don’t define models.providers.ollama, and OpenClaw automatically discovers models from local Ollama
Explicit configurationManually define baseUrl, apiKey, and models list in models.providers.ollama

Since we needed precise control over model IDs and aliases, the agent chose explicit configuration.

Step 3: Check Existing Configuration

Section titled “Step 3: Check Existing Configuration”

Found that models.providers already had 3 custom providers, but no ollama.

Step 4: CLI Configuration Attempt (Hit a Snag)

Section titled “Step 4: CLI Configuration Attempt (Hit a Snag)”

The agent first tried using openclaw config set to set fields one by one:

The gotcha: OpenClaw’s config schema requires all mandatory provider fields (baseUrl, models) to be present simultaneously — you can’t set them one at a time. The config set command writing fields individually triggers intermediate state validation failures.

Step 5: Direct JSON Config Editing

Section titled “Step 5: Direct JSON Config Editing”

The agent switched to a Python script to edit ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json directly:

Then validated:

Step 6: Confirm Model Visibility

Section titled “Step 6: Confirm Model Visibility”

Output:

✅ Model appeared in the list — 195k context window, local auth verified.

Step 7: End-to-End Test

Section titled “Step 7: End-to-End Test”

The agent spawned a subagent with model: ollama/gemma4:31b-it-bf16 and sent a test prompt:

“Reply with only: OK_GEMMA4”

5 seconds later:

Test passed. 🎉

Final Configuration

Section titled “Final Configuration”

Key configuration written to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json:

Usage

Section titled “Usage”

After configuration, in any OpenClaw session:

You can also specify the model in cron jobs:

Key Takeaways

Section titled “Key Takeaways”

1. api: "ollama" vs OpenAI Compatible Mode

Section titled “1. api: "ollama" vs OpenAI Compatible Mode”

OpenClaw supports two Ollama integration methods:

ConfigbaseUrlapiDescription
Native modehttp://host:11434ollamaUses Ollama’s native /api/chat, full tool calling support
Compatible modehttp://host:11434/v1openai-completionsUses OpenAI-compatible endpoint, some features limited

Recommended: native mode (api: "ollama") for better tool calling support.

2. Limitations of config set

Section titled “2. Limitations of config set”

openclaw config set doesn’t currently support atomic writes for nested provider objects. When creating a new provider with multiple required fields at once, directly editing the JSON file is more reliable.

3. Auto-discovery vs Explicit Configuration

Section titled “3. Auto-discovery vs Explicit Configuration”
  • Auto-discovery: Set the OLLAMA_API_KEY=ollama-local environment variable and don’t define models.providers.ollama — OpenClaw will automatically list all local Ollama models
  • Explicit configuration: Define in models.providers.ollama for precise control over model IDs, aliases, context windows, and other parameters

If you just want quick access to all local models, auto-discovery is easier. For customization (aliases, parameter overrides, etc.), use explicit configuration.

4. The Cost of BF16 Full Precision

Section titled “4. The Cost of BF16 Full Precision”

gemma4:31b-it-bf16 weighs in at 62GB and requires sufficient GPU/unified memory. On Apple Silicon (M-series) chips, the unified memory architecture handles it reasonably well, but expect cold-start latency on first inference. In testing, a single simple response took about 5 seconds.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

From issuing the command to passing the test, the entire process took under 5 minutes, all within the OpenClaw chat window:

  1. Agent auto-detected environment → looked up docs → edited config → validated → confirmed visibility → end-to-end test
  2. The human said exactly one sentence
  3. The agent hit one snag (config set atomicity issue) and independently found an alternative

This is OpenClaw’s self-ops capability: the agent understands its own configuration system and uses its toolchain to configure itself. Next time a new model is added, you might not even need to say anything — just let heartbeat auto-discover newly pulled Ollama models.

This article was auto-generated by an OpenClaw agent after completing the configuration.

OpenClaw Cron Delivery to WeChat: Configuring Multi-Channel Environments

Apr 4, 2026
Vibe Sparking

The Problem: 17 Cron Jobs, Most Failing to Deliver

Section titled “The Problem: 17 Cron Jobs, Most Failing to Deliver”

Our OpenClaw cluster runs 17 cron jobs across 5 different Agents — meeting reminders, expense reminders, GitLab monitoring, data backups, blog content scanning, and more.

They executed fine, but delivery was entirely broken — or not configured at all. Two typical errors:

One GitLab monitoring job had 10 consecutive failures before anyone noticed.

Root Cause: Incomplete Delivery Config in Multi-Channel Environments

Section titled “Root Cause: Incomplete Delivery Config in Multi-Channel Environments”

The issue is that our OpenClaw instance has multiple messaging channels configured simultaneously (Telegram, Discord, Feishu, WeChat). When a Cron Job’s delivery only specifies channel: "openclaw-weixin" without a to (target chat ID), the system doesn’t know who to deliver to.

Single-channel setups don’t have this problem — the system infers the target automatically. But in multi-channel environments, three fields are required:

FieldPurposeExample
channelWhich messaging pluginopenclaw-weixin
toDeliver to whom (chat ID)oXXX@im.wechat
accountIdWhich bot sends it7dca...im-bot

The Fix

Section titled “The Fix”

Step 1: Find the WeChat Bot’s Target Info

Section titled “Step 1: Find the WeChat Bot’s Target Info”

Use sessions_list to find active WeChat sessions and extract the complete delivery triple from deliveryContext:

Step 2: Batch Update All Jobs

Section titled “Step 2: Batch Update All Jobs”

Use the Cron tool’s update action to update each job’s delivery config:

17 jobs updated total:

  • 12 had WeChat delivery configured but missing to/accountId → filled in
  • 5 were running silently (delivery: none) → switched to announce

Results

Section titled “Results”

After the fix:

  • GitLab monitoring delivered successfully twice in a row (was failing 10 times straight)
  • Jobs outputting NO_REPLY are automatically suppressed — no noise for the user
  • All reminder jobs awaiting their next trigger cycle for validation

Key Takeaways

Section titled “Key Takeaways”

1. Multi-Channel Requires Complete Config

Section titled “1. Multi-Channel Requires Complete Config”

All three fields are mandatory in multi-channel setups. Single-channel environments can omit to and accountId.

2. How to Find Your to Value

Section titled “2. How to Find Your to Value”

3. The NO_REPLY Pattern

Section titled “3. The NO_REPLY Pattern”

If a cron job decides there’s nothing worth pushing, output NO_REPLY — OpenClaw automatically skips delivery. Essential for high-frequency monitoring jobs.

4. Silent vs Push: Choose Wisely

Section titled “4. Silent vs Push: Choose Wisely”

Not every job needs delivery. Hourly data backups might be too noisy. Consider:

  • Push only on failure (add logic in the prompt)
  • Reduce push frequency (daily summary only)
  • Stay silent (delivery: none), check manually when needed

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

Multi-channel is one of OpenClaw’s strengths — one instance connecting WeChat, Telegram, Discord, and Feishu simultaneously. But it means Cron Job delivery config needs to be explicit. Remember the triple: channel + to + accountId, and you won’t hit this pitfall again.
