OpenClaw: Your Digital Operating System for Work & Life — The P.D.C.A.S Framework in Practice

Apr 4, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw: Your Digital Operating System for Work & Life

Section titled “OpenClaw: Your Digital Operating System for Work & Life”

Use AI as a tool, and you get a fancy search engine. Use AI as an operating system, and you get a tireless digital twin.

We’re at a subtle inflection point: AI is no longer just a “ask and answer” dialog box. It’s becoming something that can run continuously, execute proactively, and collaborate across contexts. OpenClaw was built for exactly this moment — it’s not another ChatBot wrapper, but an Agent-centric digital operating system.

This article takes you deep into OpenClaw’s core architecture and demonstrates how a P.D.C.A.S closed-loop workflow I use every day transforms fragmented digital life into a self-driving system.

What Is OpenClaw?

Section titled “What Is OpenClaw?”

In one sentence: OpenClaw is a multi-agent, multi-session, multi-channel AI operating system.

Let me unpack that.

Multi-Channel Access: Chat Anywhere, Anytime

Section titled “Multi-Channel Access: Chat Anywhere, Anytime”

OpenClaw isn’t locked to a single entry point. You can talk to your Agent through:

  • WebUI — Open a browser tab, start working. Great for long-form editing and complex tasks
  • TUI (Terminal UI) — For command-line enthusiasts: openclaw chat and you’re in
  • IM Integration — WeChat, Telegram, Discord, WhatsApp, Signal… send a message, Agent handles it

This means you can fire off a WeChat message on the subway, and by the time you’re at your desk opening the WebUI, the task is already done. Not science fiction — just my Tuesday.

SOTA Model-Driven: No Compromises

Section titled “SOTA Model-Driven: No Compromises”

OpenClaw supports flexible model configuration:

  • Claude Opus 4 as the primary model for complex reasoning and long-form writing
  • GPT-5.4 as an alternative, the best choice for certain scenarios
  • Gemini, DeepSeek and more, switchable on demand
  • Automatic model failover ensures the service never goes down

Each Agent can independently configure its model and thinking level, choosing the most appropriate “brain” for each task.

Multi-Agent Isolation & Collaboration

Section titled “Multi-Agent Isolation & Collaboration”

This is one of OpenClaw’s most powerful design choices. You can create multiple Agents, each with independent:

  • Workspace — Its own files, memory, configuration
  • Identity (SOUL.md) — Defining personality and behavioral guidelines
  • Skills — Each Agent excels at different things
  • Permission boundaries — Agents don’t interfere with each other

For example, my system has these Agents, each with its own role:

  • vs-sites-astro — Blog content creation and publishing
  • vs-openclaw-mgr — OpenClaw system management and maintenance
  • vs-wechat — WeChat message processing and content decryption
  • vs-ops-mgr — Team operations, meeting reminders, administrative tasks

They share the same OpenClaw Gateway but are logically fully isolated. vs-ops-mgr can’t see vs-sites-astro’s blog drafts, and vs-wechat won’t touch operations data.

Sessions: More Powerful Than Conversations

Section titled “Sessions: More Powerful Than Conversations”

In OpenClaw, a Session isn’t just “a chat log” — it’s a stateful execution environment:

  • Main Session — Your daily conversation with the Agent, maintaining full context
  • Isolated Session — Independent runtime for cron jobs and background tasks, keeping your main conversation clean
  • Sub-agents — The main Session can spawn child tasks that auto-report when complete

Each Session has its own context window management, memory injection, and tool permissions. This lets OpenClaw handle multiple tasks simultaneously without interference.

P.D.C.A.S: The Complete Loop from Idea to Share

Section titled “P.D.C.A.S: The Complete Loop from Idea to Share”

The classic PDCA (Plan-Do-Check-Act) cycle is well-established. But in an AI-driven workflow, I’ve added an S — Share, forming the P.D.C.A.S closed loop:

Let me walk through each stage with real OpenClaw workflows.

P — Plan: Communicate Ideas, Thoughts, Questions

Section titled “P — Plan: Communicate Ideas, Thoughts, Questions”

Scenario: You have an idea for an article about how engineers transition to engineering managers in the AI era.

You send your Agent a WeChat message:

“I want to write an article about how engineers can transition to engineering managers in the AI era”

The Agent doesn’t just say “OK.” Instead, it:

  1. Searches memory — Checks MEMORY.md and memory/ for prior related discussions
  2. Understands context — Combines your USER.md (who you are, what you care about) with SOUL.md (Agent’s behavioral guidelines)
  3. Proposes structure — Suggests an outline with title, core arguments, target audience
  4. Confirms direction — Waits for your go-ahead before executing

The key here: the Agent is your thinking partner, not an execution machine. It challenges your ideas, raises angles you hadn’t considered, and might even tell you “someone wrote something similar last week.”

D — Do: Drive OpenClaw to Execute

Section titled “D — Do: Drive OpenClaw to Execute”

Once direction is confirmed, the Agent starts executing. This is where OpenClaw’s architecture shines:

Immediate Execution:

Scheduled Execution (Cron Jobs):

OpenClaw’s cron system is the backbone of background automation. Two key examples from my setup:

daily-session-workspace-audit (Daily at 11:00 AM)

Section titled “daily-session-workspace-audit (Daily at 11:00 AM)”

Executed by the vs-openclaw-mgr Agent:

  • Scans all Agent workspaces for health status
  • Checks for uncommitted code changes
  • Cleans up expired temporary files
  • Validates critical configuration file integrity
  • Generates audit reports

Think of it as having a DevOps engineer patrol your system every day, ensuring everything runs smoothly.

daily-blog-sharing-check (Daily at 12:00 PM)

Section titled “daily-blog-sharing-check (Daily at 12:00 PM)”

Executed by the vs-sites-astro Agent:

  • Checks whether recently published blog posts have been pushed to WeChat Official Account
  • Verifies bilingual versions (Chinese + English) are complete
  • Checks that cover images and illustrations have been generated
  • Creates todo reminders for any gaps found

Both cron jobs run in isolated Sessions, never polluting your daily conversation. Results are pushed to your chat channel when complete.

Cross-Agent Collaboration:

Writing a blog post seems simple, but it actually involves multiple steps:

  1. vs-sites-astro handles content creation and Astro blog publishing
  2. Calls info-card-designer Skill to generate cover and illustration images
  3. Calls wenyan CLI to push to WeChat Official Account draft box
  4. Content is simultaneously generated in both Chinese and English

These steps can run sequentially, or the Agent can spawn sub-tasks for parallel processing.

C — Check: Test and Verify Results

Section titled “C — Check: Test and Verify Results”

After execution, verification is essential:

Immediate Verification:

  • Is the article correctly saved to src/content/docs/?
  • Is the frontmatter format correct (date, slug, tags, image)?
  • Does the cover image meet size requirements (900x383 px)?
  • Was the WeChat draft successfully created (returns Media ID)?

Scheduled Verification (daily-blog-sharing-check):

  • Automatic daily check: have recent articles completed the full publishing pipeline?
  • Any “written but not pushed to WeChat” omissions?
  • Any “Chinese done but English not translated” half-finished work?

This dual verification (immediate + scheduled) ensures nothing falls through the cracks. Like CI/CD + monitoring alerts in software development — checks at every layer.

A — Act: Review, Summarize, Commit to Memory

Section titled “A — Act: Review, Summarize, Commit to Memory”

This is OpenClaw’s most “soulful” feature — the memory system.

Each Agent maintains two layers of memory:

Daily Notes: memory/YYYY-MM-DD.md

  • What happened today
  • Which tasks were completed
  • What problems were encountered
  • Raw, unprocessed records

Long-term Memory: MEMORY.md

  • Lessons distilled from daily notes
  • User preferences and habits
  • Important decisions and their reasoning
  • A continuously updated “cognitive model”

The Agent periodically reviews daily notes during heartbeat checks, writing what’s worth keeping long-term into MEMORY.md. This isn’t copy-paste — it’s distillation — keeping the essence, discarding noise.

For example:

Daily note: “2026-04-03, user requested analysis of Claude Code Changelog 2.1.91, covering all 13 items.”

Long-term memory distilled: “User is highly interested in Claude Code updates, prefers detailed technical analysis over simple changelog translations.”

This memory mechanism means the Agent understands you better over time. The first time you might need to explain “I like this style.” By the tenth time, the Agent already knows.

S — Share: Publish to WeChat Official Account / Blog

Section titled “S — Share: Publish to WeChat Official Account / Blog”

The final step — and the most exciting — one-click sharing.

The wechat-official-account-article Skill is a custom publishing pipeline with a complete workflow:

Phase 0: Preflight

  • Verify Astro project directory
  • Confirm wenyan CLI is installed
  • Check info-card-designer Skill availability

Phase 1: Create Astro Blog Post

  • Adapt content to Astro Starlight format
  • Generate standardized frontmatter (including source_url pointing to the blog original)
  • Auto-categorize to appropriate directory

Phase 1.5: Generate Bilingual Version

  • Chinese source -> automatically translate to English
  • Preserve Markdown structure, code blocks, tables
  • Adapt language-prefix slug

Phase 2: Generate Cover & Illustration

  • Call info-card-designer to generate 900x383 px cover image
  • Generate matching illustration
  • Embed in article body

Phase 3: Push to WeChat

  • Publish to WeChat draft box via wenyan CLI
  • Format with lapis theme
  • Return Media ID for confirmation

Phase 4: Update Issue Tracking

  • Create work ticket in engineering/00-issues/
  • Mark completed checklist items
  • Enable future tracking

The entire flow from “I want to publish an article” to “it’s sitting in the WeChat draft box” is fully automated by the Agent. You only need to set the original content flag and comment settings in the WeChat backend at the end.

System Architecture Overview

Section titled “System Architecture Overview”

Cron Jobs: The System’s Heartbeat

Section titled “Cron Jobs: The System’s Heartbeat”

OpenClaw’s scheduling system operates in two modes:

Cron Jobs: Precision Timing

Section titled “Cron Jobs: Precision Timing”

For tasks that need exact triggers:

  • daily-session-workspace-audit — 11:00 AM daily, system health check
  • daily-blog-sharing-check — 12:00 PM daily, content publishing completeness check
  • wechat-decrypt-daytime — Hourly during daytime, WeChat message decryption
  • Various reminders — Meeting advance notices, expense reminders, weekly report reminders

Heartbeat: Flexible Patrol

Section titled “Heartbeat: Flexible Patrol”

For checks that don’t need exact timing but should happen regularly:

  • Email inbox patrol
  • Calendar reminders
  • Social media notifications
  • Memory maintenance

The two modes complement each other: Cron guarantees precision, Heartbeat guarantees coverage.

Skills System: The Agent’s Capability Matrix

Section titled “Skills System: The Agent’s Capability Matrix”

OpenClaw’s Skills system gives Agents “professional skills.” My current system has 80+ ready skills covering:

  • Content Creation — wechat-official-account-article, info-card-designer, summarize
  • Software Development — coding-agent, github, gh-issues
  • Communication — himalaya (email), imsg, wacli (WhatsApp)
  • Knowledge Management — obsidian, apple-notes, bear-notes
  • System Operations — healthcheck, node-connect, tmux
  • Life Assistance — weather, apple-reminders, openhue (smart lighting)
  • Information Retrieval — web-search, web-fetch, blogwatcher

Each Skill is a standalone SKILL.md file defining inputs, execution steps, output specs, and error handling. The Agent loads the relevant Skill on demand — just like a human consulting an operations manual.

Real-World Case Study: How This Article Was Written

Section titled “Real-World Case Study: How This Article Was Written”

That’s right — the article you’re reading is itself a product of the P.D.C.A.S loop:

  1. Plan — Proposed the idea in WebUI: “Write a long article about OpenClaw as a digital operating system”
  2. Do — Agent analyzed requirements, organized structure, pulled cron job and skill info from memory, wrote the full article
  3. Check — Verified article structural completeness, checked technical accuracy, confirmed frontmatter format
  4. Act — Recorded this writing experience in today’s memory file
  5. Share — Published to blog and WeChat Official Account via the wechat-official-account-article Skill

Meta-recursion: Using OpenClaw to write an article about OpenClaw, then using OpenClaw to publish it. That’s the best proof there is.

Why “Operating System” and Not “Tool”?

Section titled “Why “Operating System” and Not “Tool”?”

A tool is something you pick up and use. An operating system is always running.

OpenClaw doesn’t need you to open an app to work. Its Gateway runs continuously, cron jobs execute on schedule, message routing distributes automatically. While you sleep, it’s patrolling. While you’re in meetings, it’s processing messages. While you’re coding, it’s auditing your Workspace.

This is “operating system”-level AI — not passively waiting for commands, but actively maintaining your digital life.

Final Thoughts

Section titled “Final Thoughts”

We’re experiencing a paradigm shift from “AI tools” to “AI operating systems.” OpenClaw represents one practice of this direction:

  • Not replacing humans, but augmenting them — Agents handle repetitive work; humans focus on creative thinking
  • Not a point tool, but a system architecture — Multi-agent, multi-session, multi-channel, forming a complete ecosystem
  • Not one-off conversations, but continuous operation — Cron jobs, heartbeat checks, memory systems build long-term relationships
  • Not a closed platform, but an open framework — Skills are customizable, models are switchable, channels are extensible

The P.D.C.A.S loop isn’t a new concept, but with AI Agent support, it’s become frictionless for the first time. From idea to share, no more switching between ten apps, no more manually checking every step — OpenClaw weaves it all into a smooth workflow.

In the future, your digital life won’t need you to “operate” it. You just need to think, decide, and create — the rest is for your Agent operating system to handle.

This article was written by OpenClaw Agent vs-sites-astro and auto-published via the wechat-official-account-article Skill.

Tags:
  • OpenClaw
  • AI Agent
  • Productivity
  • Workflow Automation
  • PDCAS

Managing Schedules, Time, and Reminders with OpenClaw

Apr 3, 2026
Vibe Sparking

How an AI assistant builds a structured calendar management system from scratch

Background

Section titled “Background”

As a team lead, you deal with a constant stream of meetings, recurring tasks, and deadlines every day. Traditional calendar tools like Google Calendar and Outlook are mature, but they lack deep integration with AI assistants — you can’t tell your calendar “organize my to-dos for this week,” and it can’t figure out “which day is the last business day of the first week this month.”

OpenClaw offers a different approach: AI assistant + structured data + scheduled tasks to build a conversational, automatable calendar management system.

Architecture Overview

Section titled “Architecture Overview”

Three layers working together:

  • Event data layer: JSON files storing event information
  • Reminder execution layer: OpenClaw Cron triggers on schedule
  • Delivery layer: Messages pushed to your preferred IM

Step 1: Design the Event Data Structure

Section titled “Step 1: Design the Event Data Structure”

Why Not Just Use Cron?

Section titled “Why Not Just Use Cron?”

OpenClaw’s Cron can set timed reminders, but it only handles “when to remind” — not “the full context of the event.” When you ask “what meetings do I have this week” or “did we process last month’s expenses,” Cron alone can’t answer that.

That’s why we need a layer of structured event data to capture complete event information.

Inspired by Google Calendar, but Lighter

Section titled “Inspired by Google Calendar, but Lighter”

Google Calendar’s event model (based on iCalendar RFC 5545) is battle-tested. We borrow its best ideas:

Three Key Fields Explained

Section titled “Three Key Fields Explained”
FieldPurposeWho sees it
summaryTitle — what is this eventEveryone
descriptionFormal description: agenda, goals, contextParticipants
notesPrivate notes: execution details, lessons learnedOnly you

We use summary (following the iCalendar standard) rather than title to maintain compatibility with Google Calendar.

Events Track the Past, Not Just the Future

Section titled “Events Track the Past, Not Just the Future”

Traditional calendars only look ahead. But in practice, “did we have that meeting last week” and “was this month’s expense processed” matter just as much.

We differentiate with the status field:

  • confirmed — Confirmed, pending execution
  • tentative — Tentative
  • completed — Done
  • cancelled — Cancelled

Completed events with result (outcome) and followUp (next steps) become an event ledger — both a schedule and a record.

Step 2: File Structure Design

Section titled “Step 2: File Structure Design”

Single File vs Date-Based Split

Section titled “Single File vs Date-Based Split”

Initially we put all events in one events.json, but quickly hit problems:

  • The file kept growing
  • Concurrent updates caused conflicts
  • Archiving was painful

We settled on a three-tier structure:

recurring.json: Recurring Event Templates

Section titled “recurring.json: Recurring Event Templates”

Extract repeating events into templates, defined once:

events/YYYY-MM-DD.json: Daily Event Instances

Section titled “events/YYYY-MM-DD.json: Daily Event Instances”

Concrete instances generated from templates, or one-off events:

Linked to the template via recurringId for traceability.

Benefits

Section titled “Benefits”
  1. Concurrency-safe — Different days edit different files
  2. Natural archiving — Past dates are inherently ordered
  3. Small files — A few events per day, fast reads/writes
  4. Template reuse — Define recurring events once

Step 3: Set Up Cron Reminders

Section titled “Step 3: Set Up Cron Reminders”

OpenClaw’s Cron system is the execution engine for reminders. Each reminder maps to a Cron Job.

Creating Reminders

Section titled “Creating Reminders”

The AI assistant automatically:

  1. Creates an event template in recurring.json
  2. Creates the corresponding Cron Job
  3. Links them via cronJobId

Multiple Reminders

Section titled “Multiple Reminders”

A single event can have multiple reminders:

For example, a weekly dev standup:

  • 1 day ahead (Sunday 9:30): Prepare
  • 30 minutes ahead (Monday 9:00): Starting soon

Smart Date Logic

Section titled “Smart Date Logic”

Some reminders need logical evaluation. For instance, “last business day of the first week each month” can’t be expressed with a simple cron expression.

Solution: Cron triggers every business day from the 1st to the 7th, and the AI Agent determines whether today qualifies. If not, it stays silent (NO_REPLY).

This is the power of AI + Cron — Cron handles scheduling, AI handles judgment.

Delivery Channels

Section titled “Delivery Channels”

Reminders need to reach you. OpenClaw supports multi-channel delivery:

Options include WeChat, Telegram, Discord, Feishu, and more. Stick to one primary channel to avoid scattered notifications.

Step 4: Daily Usage

Section titled “Step 4: Daily Usage”

Viewing Your Schedule

Section titled “Viewing Your Schedule”

Just ask in natural language:

  • “What do I need to do today?” → AI reads today’s events + tasks, sorted by priority
  • “What’s left undone this week?” → AI scans the week’s events, filters incomplete ones
  • “Did we process last month’s outsourcing costs?” → AI looks up the event’s status and result

Recording Completion

Section titled “Recording Completion”

AI automatically updates the event’s status to completed and records the result.

Adding Events

Section titled “Adding Events”

AI handles it all in one go: create template → create 2 Cron Jobs → link cronJobIds → Git commit.

Working with Memory

Section titled “Working with Memory”

The calendar system manages structured events; memory manages natural language records. They’re linked via memoryRef:

Check event status in the calendar, check detailed notes in memory — each does what it’s best at.

Real-World Results

Section titled “Real-World Results”

Here’s what the system currently manages in practice:

9 recurring event templates:

  • 3 weekly meetings (dev standup, client dev sync, client meeting)
  • 1 weekly task (project report)
  • 1 weekly session (AI seminar)
  • 3 monthly tasks (payroll review, invoice reimbursement, outsourced labor costs)

12 Cron reminder jobs:

  • All delivered via WeChat
  • Some events configured with multiple reminders (1 day + 30 minutes)
  • Complex date logic handled by AI

Daily archived event records:

  • Completed events auto-tagged with status + result
  • Bidirectional links to memory logs
  • Git version control for full traceability

Comparison with Traditional Calendar Tools

Section titled “Comparison with Traditional Calendar Tools”
DimensionGoogle CalendarOpenClaw Approach
CreationManual form fillingNatural language conversation
RemindersFixed-time popups/emailsAI-judged + multi-channel push
Completion trackingNot supportedStructured status + result
QueriesCalendar viewNatural language Q&A
Complex datesNot supported (e.g., “last business day of first week”)AI dynamic evaluation
Notes integrationNonememoryRef bidirectional links
Version controlNoneGit-managed, fully traceable
ExtensibilityLimited by APIJSON + code, fully flexible

Best Practices

Section titled “Best Practices”
  1. Unify your delivery channel — Send all reminders to one IM, don’t scatter them
  2. Use templates for recurring events — Define once, apply everywhere
  3. Record results for completed events — Don’t just check the box; note the outcome
  4. Let AI handle complex logic — Cron schedules, Agent judges
  5. Git version control — Auto-commit every change for traceability and rollback
  6. Calendar + memory collaboration — Structured data and natural language records, each doing what it does best
  7. Regular maintenance — Use the heartbeat mechanism to auto-archive and clean up stale data

Conclusion

Section titled “Conclusion”

OpenClaw’s calendar management isn’t meant to replace Google Calendar. It offers an AI-native approach:

  • Natural language to create and query events
  • Structured data to keep information complete
  • Cron + AI for smart reminders
  • Git for data traceability
  • Multi-channel push for reliable delivery

The core idea: Make AI your steward, not just your alarm clock.

Based on real-world team operations and management practices. Calendar management system runs on the OpenClaw platform.

Tags:
  • OpenClaw
  • Calendar Management
  • AI
  • Productivity
  • Cron

OpenClaw 2026.4.2 逐项调研报告

Apr 3, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw 2026.4.2 逐项调研报告

Section titled “OpenClaw 2026.4.2 逐项调研报告”

生成时间：2026-04-03 10:30 CST 版本：v2026.4.2 (d74a122) 发布者：@steipete，2026-04-02

总体判断

Section titled “总体判断”

这是一个典型的 “架构收束 + 插件边界重划 + 安全补强 + 多渠道修复” 版本。

不是”功能炫技版”，而是：

  • 把原来散在 core 里的能力往 plugin-owned boundary 收
  • 把 background orchestration 正式拉回 Task Flow substrate
  • 把 provider transport / routing / auth / TLS / header 统一
  • 把 exec approval / host exec / node exec 的默认行为重新定型
  • 修复上一批版本里因为作用域、配对、路由、审批、流式输出带来的回归

2026.4.2 的主线，是 OpenClaw 从”能跑很多事”继续往”边界更清晰、可运维、可恢复、可插件化”演进。

一、Breaking Changes

Section titled “一、Breaking Changes”

1) Plugins/xAI：x_search 配置迁移

Section titled “1) Plugins/xAI：x_search 配置迁移”

背景问题

Section titled “背景问题”

以前 x_search 走的是 core 配置路径：tools.web.x_search.*

这意味着：

  • 搜索能力虽然由 xAI 插件提供，但配置却还挂在 core 里
  • 配置归属不清
  • 后续插件自治、插件安装/禁用/迁移都不够干净

2026.4.2 具体变化

Section titled “2026.4.2 具体变化”

迁移到插件自有配置路径：

  • plugins.entries.xai.config.xSearch.*
  • 鉴权统一到：
    • plugins.entries.xai.config.webSearch.apiKey
    • 或环境变量 XAI_API_KEY

使用场景

Section titled “使用场景”
  • 用 xAI 提供的 x_search
  • 多 provider 搜索并存
  • 希望插件配置与插件生命周期一致

例子

Section titled “例子”

以前：

现在应迁到类似：

注意事项

Section titled “注意事项”
  • 这是 breaking，老路径不会是长期兼容路径
  • 最稳妥迁移方式：openclaw doctor --fix
  • 如果你有自定义部署模板、集群配置分发器、示例配置仓库，需要一起更新

历次版本脉络

Section titled “历次版本脉络”
  • 早期：很多工具配置混在 core
  • 近几版：越来越强调 plugin-owned config
  • 这一版：把 x_search 正式从 legacy core path 剥离

竞品对比

Section titled “竞品对比”
产品搜索配置方式
OpenClaw插件自有路径 plugins.entries.xai.config.*
NanoClaw代码级修改，无配置分层
IronClawplugin manifest 内声明
PicoClaw单一 config 文件，无分层
ZeroClawRust trait-based provider config
NanobotMCP server 级别配置

判断

Section titled “判断”

这是插件自治化的必经步骤。后续更多 web / provider / channel 配置大概率都会做同类收口。

2) Plugins/web fetch：Firecrawl web_fetch 配置迁移

Section titled “2) Plugins/web fetch：Firecrawl web_fetch 配置迁移”

背景问题

Section titled “背景问题”

以前 Firecrawl 的 web_fetch 配置也走 core：tools.web.fetch.firecrawl.*

这会导致：

  • core 对某个具体 provider（Firecrawl）耦合太深
  • fallback 路径带有 Firecrawl 特判
  • 后续引入别的 fetch provider 不优雅

2026.4.2 具体变化

Section titled “2026.4.2 具体变化”

迁移到插件自有路径：plugins.entries.firecrawl.config.webFetch.*

同时 web_fetch fallback 不再走 “Firecrawl-only core branch”，而是通过新的 fetch-provider boundary

使用场景

Section titled “使用场景”
  • 使用 Firecrawl 做网页提取
  • 同时支持多种 fetch provider
  • 要求插件替换/禁用更可控

注意事项

Section titled “注意事项”
  • 同样建议 openclaw doctor --fix
  • 如果你有自动化脚本 grep 旧路径，会全部失效
  • 这也意味着后续 web_fetch 会成为 provider-agnostic 抽象

历次版本脉络

Section titled “历次版本脉络”
  • 之前：web fetch 在 core 里有大量 provider 特判
  • 现在：开始形成 fetch provider seam
  • 未来：可能出现更多 fetch providers 并存、路由、优先级链

竞品对比

Section titled “竞品对比”
产品Web Fetch 抽象
OpenClaw新 fetch-provider boundary，插件可替换
NanoClaw直接调 Anthropic SDK 内置能力
IronClawHTTP client + endpoint allowlist
PicoClaw内置 HTTP + 可选 provider
ZeroClawtrait-based fetch provider
NanobotMCP server 提供 fetch 能力

判断

Section titled “判断”

这条很重要。它不是单纯改路径，而是在说：

web_fetch 以后不再是 “Firecrawl 的别名”，而是 OpenClaw 的一个可插拔抓取抽象层。

二、Changes：逐项解析

Section titled “二、Changes：逐项解析”

3) Task Flow substrate 回归：managed / mirrored，同步模式、持久状态、revision、openclaw flows

Section titled “3) Task Flow substrate 回归：managed / mirrored，同步模式、持久状态、revision、openclaw flows”

背景问题

Section titled “背景问题”

OpenClaw 的后台任务、分布式编排、插件作者层逻辑，之前有点”上层花活很多，底层 substrate 不够强”。

常见痛点：

  • 后台任务状态丢失
  • orchestrator 和 runtime 状态不同步
  • 崩了以后难恢复
  • 任务流 inspection / recovery 工具不够

这次解决了什么

Section titled “这次解决了什么”

恢复 core Task Flow substrate，并支持：

  • managed vs mirrored sync modes
  • durable flow state
  • revision tracking
  • openclaw flows inspection/recovery

使用场景

Section titled “使用场景”
  • 背景任务编排
  • 长链路自动化
  • cron 触发后衍生多个子任务
  • 插件 authoring layer 想基于稳定底座构建流程

例子

Section titled “例子”

收到 Feishu 评论 → 创建任务流 → 拉文档上下文 → 生成答复 → 回帖 → 记录状态。中途 gateway 重启后仍能恢复 flow 状态。

注意事项

Section titled “注意事项”
  • 这标志着”流程”成为真正一等对象
  • 如果你自己写插件/authoring layer，应该尽量挂靠 taskFlow seam，而不是自己造状态机

版本脉络

Section titled “版本脉络”
  • 中间一些版本更偏”上层 authoring runtime”
  • 这版把 core substrate 重新做厚
  • 说明团队认识到：没有 durable orchestration substrate，agent 编排迟早变脆

竞品对比

Section titled “竞品对比”
产品后台编排能力
OpenClawTask Flow substrate (managed/mirrored, durable, revision, CLI inspection)
NanoClaw基础 cron/scheduled jobs，无 flow 抽象
IronClawRoutines (cron + event triggers + webhooks)
PicoClawSubTurn + Hooks + EventBus (v0.2.4+)
ZeroClaw不详，可能较轻量
Nanobot无内置 flow，靠 MCP server 外挂

判断

Section titled “判断”

这是本版最核心的架构演进之一。

4) Task Flow：managed child task spawning + sticky cancel intent

Section titled “4) Task Flow：managed child task spawning + sticky cancel intent”

背景问题

Section titled “背景问题”

父任务取消时，子任务可能已经在跑。常见两种糟糕状态：

  • 直接硬杀，导致系统不一致
  • 不硬杀，父任务却继续调度新任务

这次变化

Section titled “这次变化”
  • managed child task spawning
  • sticky cancel intent
  • 一旦决定取消，调度器立即停止继续排新活
  • 但已运行的 child task 可以收尾
  • 最后 parent flow 再 settle 到 cancelled

场景

Section titled “场景”
  • 多阶段流程
  • 有副作用的子任务（发消息、写文档、同步状态）
  • 需要”优雅取消”

例子

Section titled “例子”

一个 flow 已经发起 3 个子任务（拉上下文、调模型、写回渠道）。取消时不再调度第 4、5 个子任务，让已在跑的完成，然后整体标 cancelled。

注意

Section titled “注意”
  • sticky cancel 更接近工作流引擎语义，而不是”立即 SIGKILL”
  • 写插件时要区分：scheduler stop / child completion / parent settle

竞品对比

Section titled “竞品对比”
  • IronClaw 有 self-repair / stuck detection，但不明确有 parent-child cancel 语义
  • PicoClaw 的 SubTurn 有 steering 但非 durable flow cancel
  • 其他竞品无此级别编排

5) Plugins/Task Flow：api.runtime.taskFlow bound seam

Section titled “5) Plugins/Task Flow：api.runtime.taskFlow bound seam”

背景问题

Section titled “背景问题”

插件或 trusted authoring layer 之前如果想操作 flow，可能要显式传 owner id、host context 等，易错、啰嗦、边界不安全。

新变化

Section titled “新变化”

提供 bound seam api.runtime.taskFlow，由 host-resolved OpenClaw context 绑定，不必每次传 owner identifiers。

场景

Section titled “场景”
  • 插件内部发起/控制 flow
  • 受信 authoring layer 编排任务

例子

Section titled “例子”

Feishu 插件收到评论事件后，可直接在当前宿主上下文下开 flow，而不是拼一堆 owner/session 参数。

注意

Section titled “注意”
  • 这是插件作者福音
  • 也意味着 runtime boundary 更标准化
  • 不建议继续用旁门左道直接操宿主内部状态

6) Android/assistant：Assistant role + Google Assistant App Actions metadata

Section titled “6) Android/assistant：Assistant role + Google Assistant App Actions metadata”

背景问题

Section titled “背景问题”

Android 上 OpenClaw 作为”被系统语音助手触发”的入口不完整。

新变化

Section titled “新变化”
  • assistant-role entrypoints
  • Google Assistant App Actions metadata
  • Android 可从 assistant trigger 启 OpenClaw，并把 prompt 交给 composer

场景

Section titled “场景”

“Hey Google, ask OpenClaw to …”，手机侧快速唤起 agent。

注意

Section titled “注意”
  • 这不是完整 agent automation，只是系统入口打通
  • 真正体验还取决于 Android intent / app actions / OEM 行为

竞品对比

Section titled “竞品对比”
产品移动端入口
OpenClawAndroid Assistant + iOS companion
NanoClaw无原生移动端
IronClaw无原生移动端
PicoClawAndroid APK (v0.2.4+)
ZeroClaw无原生移动端
NanobotWeb UI 为主

判断

Section titled “判断”

移动端入口正在增强，但生态成熟度仍明显低于桌面/CLI/聊天渠道。

7) Exec defaults：gateway/node host exec 默认 YOLO（security=full, ask=off）

Section titled “7) Exec defaults：gateway/node host exec 默认 YOLO（security=full, ask=off）”

背景问题

Section titled “背景问题”

以前 host exec 的默认行为在不同 host/gateway/node、approval fallback、doctor/reporting 之间不一致，用户容易误判”到底会不会弹审批”。

新变化

Section titled “新变化”

默认请求 security=full + ask=off，并让 approval-file fallback、docs、doctor 报告都对齐这个”默认无提示”语义。

这是什么意思

Section titled “这是什么意思”

不是更安全，而是默认更直接执行。强调的是”host exec 的默认姿势是 YOLO”。

场景

Section titled “场景”
  • 本机自动化
  • 已高度信任的受控环境
  • 需要减少 approval friction

注意事项

Section titled “注意事项”

这是一个运维上必须重视的改动：

  • 对高信任单用户机器：更顺手
  • 对共享环境/远端节点/高风险宿主：风险升高
  • 必须结合你自己的 exec-approvals policy、sandbox、tool policy 使用

竞品对比

Section titled “竞品对比”
产品Exec 默认安全模型
OpenClaw默认 YOLO（security=full, ask=off），靠 policy 约束
NanoClaw容器隔离，bash 在容器内执行
IronClawWASM sandbox + endpoint allowlist
PicoClawCron security gating (v0.2.3+)
ZeroClawpolicy-based security
Nanobot无内置 exec，走 MCP server

版本脉络

Section titled “版本脉络”

最近几版一直在整理 exec approvals、host routing、node exec 行为；这版属于默认值定型。

判断

Section titled “判断”

这是本版另一个关键变化。OpenClaw 正在把默认执行体验做得更”像一个真正会动手的 agent”，代价是必须靠更强的边界和策略约束兜底。

8) Providers/runtime：provider-owned replay hooks

Section titled “8) Providers/runtime：provider-owned replay hooks”

背景问题

Section titled “背景问题”

不同 provider 的 transcript replay、cleanup、reasoning dispatch 逻辑不完全一样，统一放 core 很快会变得臃肿。

新变化

Section titled “新变化”

把 replay 相关表面开放给 provider 自己实现：transcript policy / replay cleanup / reasoning-mode dispatch。

场景

Section titled “场景”
  • 不同 provider 有不同 transcript/reasoning 格式
  • 恢复历史会话、转发上下文、处理 reasoning tokens

判断

Section titled “判断”

说明 OpenClaw 正从”统一 adapter”往”provider 主权更高的 runtime seam”演化。

9) Plugins/hooks：before_agent_reply

Section titled “9) Plugins/hooks：before_agent_reply”

背景问题

Section titled “背景问题”

插件做完 inline action 后，有时已经知道最终该回什么，没必要再走 LLM，省钱、省时、减少不可控性。

新变化

Section titled “新变化”

新增 hook before_agent_reply，允许插件生成 synthetic reply，直接 short-circuit LLM。

场景

Section titled “场景”
  • 明确型动作：审批结果、工具确认、固定模板回复
  • 渠道级动作回执
  • 自动化流程完成通知

例子

Section titled “例子”

用户点了”批准”，插件可直接回”已批准并执行”，无需再调模型生成自然语言。

注意

Section titled “注意”
  • 插件返回 synthetic reply 时，要保证口径、权限和上下文正确
  • 用过度了会让系统看起来”到处 bypass LLM”

竞品对比

Section titled “竞品对比”
  • NanoClaw 无插件 hook 体系
  • IronClaw 有 plugin architecture 但未见同等 hook
  • PicoClaw 有 Hooks (v0.2.4+)，可能有类似能力
  • Nanobot 通过 MCP server 可间接实现

判断

Section titled “判断”

这是插件化体系变强的标志，尤其适合 workflow-heavy 场景。

10) Channels/session routing：provider-specific session grammar 下放到插件

Section titled “10) Channels/session routing：provider-specific session grammar 下放到插件”

背景问题

Section titled “背景问题”

Telegram topic、Feishu scoped inheritance、不同 provider 的 session-key 规则以前更偏 core 内部逻辑。

新变化

Section titled “新变化”

把这些 conversation grammar / session-key surfaces 下放到 plugin-owned surfaces。

场景

Section titled “场景”
  • 多渠道 session 路由
  • topic/thread/scoped inheritance
  • 重启和 bootstrap 后 session 连续性

判断

Section titled “判断”

这是”渠道插件真正拥有自己的会话模型”的一步。

11) Feishu/comments：Drive comment-event flow

Section titled “11) Feishu/comments：Drive comment-event flow”

背景问题

Section titled “背景问题”

Feishu 文档协作的评论流不是普通聊天消息流。需要评论线程上下文、文档节点上下文、原线程内回复、文档协作动作。

新变化

Section titled “新变化”

增加专用 Drive comment-event flow，支持：

  • comment-thread context resolution
  • in-thread replies
  • feishu_drive comment actions

场景

Section titled “场景”
  • 文档审阅
  • 协作文档批注处理
  • 文档型工作流 agent

例子

Section titled “例子”

有人在文档某段评论”这里能否补数据来源？“，OpenClaw 可以读上下文并直接在线程里答复。

注意

Section titled “注意”
  • 文档评论和 IM 会话不是一回事
  • 权限、上下文粒度、对象 ID 都不一样

竞品对比

Section titled “竞品对比”
产品企业协作文档集成
OpenClawFeishu Drive comments + IM
NanoClaw无
IronClaw无
PicoClawWeChat/WeCom (v0.2.4+)，无文档级
ZeroClaw无
Nanobot无

判断

Section titled “判断”

这很适合企业协作场景，意味着 OpenClaw 正朝”工作协作入口”扩。

12) Matrix：m.mentions 规范支持

Section titled “12) Matrix：m.mentions 规范支持”

背景问题

Section titled “背景问题”

Matrix 客户端（如 Element）对 mention 通知依赖规范字段，而不是只看纯文本 @user。

新变化

Section titled “新变化”

在文本发送、媒体 caption、编辑、poll fallback、action-driven edits 中都发 spec-compliant m.mentions。

判断

Section titled “判断”

渠道适配走向”协议级合规”，不是停留在字符串 hack。

13) Diffs：plugin-owned viewerBaseUrl

Section titled “13) Diffs：plugin-owned viewerBaseUrl”

背景问题

Section titled “背景问题”

diff viewer 链接如果每次工具调用都传 baseUrl，不稳定且繁琐。

新变化

Section titled “新变化”

插件侧支持稳定的 viewerBaseUrl。

场景

Section titled “场景”

反向代理、公网查看器、多环境统一 viewer 域名。

14) Agents/compaction：agents.defaults.compaction.model 一致化

Section titled “14) Agents/compaction：agents.defaults.compaction.model 一致化”

背景问题

Section titled “背景问题”

/compact 手动触发与其他 context-engine compaction 路径，对 model override 的使用不一致。

新变化

Section titled “新变化”

统一让 engine-owned compaction 使用配置的 override model。

场景

Section titled “场景”

主模型贵，但压缩上下文想用便宜模型。

判断

Section titled “判断”

典型的”配置语义一致性修复”，对长期运维很重要。

15) Agents/compaction：notifyUser 变 opt-in

Section titled “15) Agents/compaction：notifyUser 变 opt-in”

背景问题

Section titled “背景问题”

🧹 Compacting context... 总是提示，很多渠道上很吵。

新变化

Section titled “新变化”

Section titled “七、多实例集群管理者重点关注”
  1. xAI / Firecrawl 配置路径迁移 — 先跑 openclaw doctor --fix，再检查模板/部署文档/自动化脚本
  2. host exec 默认 YOLO — 重新审视各实例的 exec policy，尤其远端 node / gateway host
  3. 2026.3.31 pairing / loopback 回归修复 — 如果最近遇到本地 exec / spawn pairing-required，这版值得升
  4. Task Flow substrate — 如果要做后台编排、跨实例工作流，这是大好事
  5. provider transport 收口 — 自定义 base URL / proxy / 私网访问策略用户应重点回归测试
  6. workspace/plugin/.env 安全补丁 — 对多仓库、多工作区、第三方插件环境很关键
  7. 渠道细节修复 — Telegram approvals / Feishu comments / Slack-Matrix-Teams streaming / WhatsApp presence-media

八、结论

Section titled “八、结论”

值得升级，但不是”无脑升”的版本。

  • 如果依赖插件配置、host exec、审批、Feishu/Telegram/Slack/Matrix、provider base URL、自定义 transport → 非常值得升
  • 如果配置很多 legacy path、自定义模板很多、对 exec 安全边界要求高 → 升级前必须做一轮配置审计

2026.4.2 = 一次把 OpenClaw 往”可运营的 agent runtime 平台”推进的基础设施版本。

OpenClaw Daily Session-Workspace Documentation Audit Cron Job

Apr 3, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Background

Section titled “Background”

In an OpenClaw multi-agent environment, each agent generates a large volume of session conversation records daily, containing important information such as configuration changes, deployment operations, troubleshooting, and architectural decisions. However, this information often stays in session records without being distilled into the workspace’s memory/ documentation.

Taking a local OpenClaw instance running multiple agents as an example, over 100 sessions were generated in 3 days, but the first audit found that 73% of important keypoints were undocumented (only 7 out of 26 keypoints had corresponding memory records).

Core requirement: Establish an automated audit mechanism to daily check all agent session records, extract key information, and compare with workspace documentation to find content that “exists in conversations but not in documents.”

Technical Approach

Section titled “Technical Approach”

Data Sources

Section titled “Data Sources”

OpenClaw session records are stored in ~/.openclaw/agents/<agent-id>/sessions/, with each session being a .jsonl file (JSON Lines format), one event per line:

Key fields:

  • type: "message" — user and assistant conversation messages
  • role: "user" | "assistant" — message role
  • content — can be a string or array ([{type: "text", text: "..."}])

Approach Evolution

Section titled “Approach Evolution”

Approach 1: Parallel Subagents (❌ Not Recommended)

Section titled “Approach 1: Parallel Subagents (❌ Not Recommended)”

The initial design spawned one subagent per agent for parallel processing, using sessions_yield to wait for all results.

Problem: In isolated cron sessions, each yield wake-up only receives one subagent’s result. Multiple subagents mean multiple yield cycles, and the main session can be prematurely terminated.

In actual testing, all subagents completed successfully (60-100 seconds each), but the main session was marked finished after receiving only partial results.

Approach 2: Single Session + exec Data Extraction (✅ Recommended)

Section titled “Approach 2: Single Session + exec Data Extraction (✅ Recommended)”

Complete all work within a single isolated session:

  1. Use exec to run a Python script for batch extraction of all agent session data
  2. Use exec to read each workspace’s memory files
  3. The agent analyzes and generates the report
  4. Use the write tool to save the report file

Advantages: No subagent coordination overhead, no yield dependency, reliable workflow.

Deployment Steps

Section titled “Deployment Steps”

Prerequisites

Section titled “Prerequisites”
  • OpenClaw instance running with at least one agent configured
  • Agent has exec tool permissions
  • Python3 available

Creating the Cron Job

Section titled “Creating the Cron Job”

Create via OpenClaw cron tool:

Data Extraction Script

Section titled “Data Extraction Script”

Sample Report

Section titled “Sample Report”
AgentSessionKey PointDocumentNotes
ops-agent-Asession-1Created calendar event management system✅ calendar/schema.json
ops-agent-Asession-1Reminder cron time adjusted from 9:00 to 11:00❌Change only in cron config
mainsession-2New agent added to config file❌Agent registration undocumented
agent-Bsession-3Automated weekly report update❌No memory files at all
agent-Csession-4Provider failover error storm, 8+ retries❌Serious reliability issue
agent-Dsession-5Version upgrade, plugin security scan blocked components❌Upgrade undocumented

Statistics: 26 keypoints, 7 documented (27%), 19 undocumented (73%).

Lessons Learned

Section titled “Lessons Learned”

1. sessions_yield + Subagents Unreliable in Isolated Sessions

Section titled “1. sessions_yield + Subagents Unreliable in Isolated Sessions”

Symptom: After spawning multiple subagents, the main session is marked finished after receiving only partial results.

Solution: Don’t use subagent + yield in isolated cron sessions. Use single-session exec instead.

2. Session JSONL Files Can Be Large

Section titled “2. Session JSONL Files Can Be Large”

Individual session files can reach several MB. Use exec + python3 for line-by-line parsing, extracting only the first 300 characters of message content. Process at most 5 recent sessions per agent.

3. Inconsistent content Field Format

Section titled “3. Inconsistent content Field Format”

User message content is typically a string, while assistant content is typically an array. Both formats must be handled.

4. Filtering Heartbeat and System Messages

Section titled “4. Filtering Heartbeat and System Messages”

Filter heartbeat messages by checking if content starts with HEARTBEAT or heartbeat.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

This cron job solves the “knowledge sedimentation gap” in OpenClaw multi-agent environments. Through daily automated audits, you can:

  1. Discover undocumented important decisions and operations
  2. Quantify documentation coverage (first audit: only 27%)
  3. Identify specific content that needs supplementation
  4. Track each agent’s memory maintenance health

Recommended to use alongside AGENTS.md Memory Maintenance rules, letting agents proactively fill in missing documentation records during heartbeats.

OpenClaw Sandbox Restriction Error: Causes and Solutions

Apr 3, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Symptoms

Section titled “Symptoms”

When an agent tries to read or write a file, it returns an error like:

Or you see this in tool call results:

Root Cause

Section titled “Root Cause”

This is not a Docker container sandbox issue — it’s OpenClaw’s filesystem security boundary (the fs-safe module) at work.

OpenClaw assigns each agent a workspace root directory, and all file I/O tools (read, write, edit) are restricted to this directory. The logic works as follows:

  1. Resolve the file’s absolute path
  2. Check whether it falls within the workspace root (isPathInside check)
  3. If not → throw SafeOpenError("outside-workspace")

This is a hardcoded security mechanism, not a configuration option. There are no allowedPaths or extraReadPaths whitelist settings to bypass it.

Where Is the Workspace Root?

Section titled “Where Is the Workspace Root?”

By default, the workspace root is the path specified in the agent configuration, typically:

You can configure it via workspace.path in openclaw.yaml:

Solutions

Section titled “Solutions”

Solution 1: Copy or Symlink Files into the Workspace (Recommended)

Section titled “Solution 1: Copy or Symlink Files into the Workspace (Recommended)”

The simplest and safest approach. Bring the files the agent needs into the workspace:

⚠️ The actual target path of a symlink must still be within the workspace root, or it will be blocked just the same. Symlinks cannot be used to “escape” the sandbox.

Solution 2: Expand the Workspace Scope

Section titled “Solution 2: Expand the Workspace Scope”

If the agent needs to access files spread across a larger directory tree, point the workspace to a higher-level directory:

This gives the agent access to everything under /Volumes/data/my-project/.

Considerations:

  • A larger workspace means more files accessible to the agent, widening the security boundary
  • All agents share the same workspace configuration (unless different agent config files specify different paths)

Solution 3: Use the exec Tool for Indirect Access

Section titled “Solution 3: Use the exec Tool for Indirect Access”

The read/write/edit tools are subject to fs-safe restrictions, but the exec tool takes a shell command execution path with different constraints:

This depends on the exec security policy (tools.exec.security) configuration. By default, exec may require user approval.

Solution 4: Provide Content Directly in the Conversation

Section titled “Solution 4: Provide Content Directly in the Conversation”

If you only need a file’s contents temporarily, the simplest approach is to paste it directly into the conversation — no need for the agent to read the file itself.

Common Trigger Scenarios

Section titled “Common Trigger Scenarios”
ScenarioCauseRecommended Solution
Agent wants to read source repo filesRepo is outside workspaceSolution 2: Expand workspace
Agent wants to read system config files/etc/ is outside workspaceSolution 3: exec cat
Agent wants to read files in user home~/ is outside workspaceSolution 1: Copy in, or Solution 3
Skill references an absolute pathPath is outside workspaceSolution 1: Symlink or copy

Non-Solutions

Section titled “Non-Solutions”

The following approaches are not available in the current version:

  • ❌ sandbox.enabled: false — This config option doesn’t exist (fs-safe is not a toggleable feature)
  • ❌ sandbox.allowedPaths — There is no path whitelist mechanism
  • ❌ Per-agent sandbox rules — Workspace is a gateway-level configuration

Design Intent

Section titled “Design Intent”

This restriction is intentional security design:

  1. Prevent file leaks from prompt injection — Malicious prompts cannot make the agent read sensitive files outside the workspace
  2. Limit blast radius — Even if the agent behaves unexpectedly, the impact is contained within the workspace
  3. Multi-agent isolation — Agents with different workspaces don’t interfere with each other

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
SolutionSecurityUse Case
Copy/symlink into workspace✅ HighA few external files
Expand workspace scope⚠️ MediumNeed access to entire project tree
exec indirect read⚠️ Medium (requires approval)Occasional system file reads
Paste content in conversation✅ HighTemporary, one-time needs

Recommended approach: Plan your workspace scope to cover all files the agent routinely needs, without making it excessively broad. For occasional external files, use exec or paste manually.

Upgrading OpenClaw to 2026.4.2: Pitfalls and Lessons Learned

Apr 3, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Upgrade Overview

Section titled “Upgrade Overview”
  • Pre-upgrade version: 2026.3.28
  • Post-upgrade version: 2026.4.2

The upgrade command itself is straightforward:

The core update took about 82 seconds (60s for npm global update + 21s for openclaw doctor checks).

However, several issues came up along the way.

Issues Encountered

Section titled “Issues Encountered”

1. Plugin Security Scan Blocking

Section titled “1. Plugin Security Scan Blocking”

The new version introduced stricter plugin security checks. Some plugins were blocked during auto-update with errors like:

  • Environment variable access combined with network send — possible credential harvesting
  • Shell command execution detected (child_process)

This is a new security scanning mechanism in 2026.4.2 that applies equally to all plugins. Any code containing child_process calls or patterns that combine environment variable reads with network sends gets flagged as potentially dangerous.

Fix: Force install with the unsafe flag:

2. Duplicate Plugin Installation Conflict

Section titled “2. Duplicate Plugin Installation Conflict”

After force-installing a plugin, plugins list showed multiple entries for the same plugin:

EntryVersionSourceStatus
Built-in2026.4.2stockloaded
Force-installed global1.6.5globalloaded
Older global install1.5.5globaldisabled

Root cause: Version 2026.4.2 had already bundled this plugin into the core package (stock source), with a newer version than the third-party npm package. Force-installing the third-party version actually introduced an older version and triggered duplicate plugin id warnings.

Fix: Uninstall the redundant global installs and keep the built-in version:

Lesson: When a plugin update fails after upgrading, check plugins list first to see if it’s already built in before force-installing.

3. ClawHub vs npm Type Mismatch

Section titled “3. ClawHub vs npm Type Mismatch”

When trying to install a plugin via openclaw plugins install, the CLI routed through ClawHub and returned:

But the package on npm was a standard channel plugin.

Cause: openclaw plugins install <slug> defaults to ClawHub resolution, where the package was registered as a skill type. npm and ClawHub are independent distribution channels, and type labels can differ.

To install the npm version explicitly, use the full package name:

Mistake to avoid: Following the suggestion to run openclaw skills install created an unwanted skill copy in workspace/skills/ that had to be manually removed.

4. Plugin Version Number Mismatch

Section titled “4. Plugin Version Number Mismatch”

plugins list showed a plugin at version 2.0.0, but the on-disk package.json read 2.0.1.

Root cause: plugins list reads the version field from openclaw.plugin.json (the plugin manifest), not from package.json. The upstream package bumped the npm version but forgot to sync the manifest — a minor upstream bug.

Temporary fix: Manually update the version in the manifest file.

5. Gateway Service Not Loaded

Section titled “5. Gateway Service Not Loaded”

After upgrading, openclaw gateway restart reported “service not loaded.”

Fix: Run openclaw config → select Daemon to reinstall the LaunchAgent:

Upgrade Takeaways

Section titled “Upgrade Takeaways”
  1. Check before installing: When plugin updates fail, run openclaw plugins list to see if it’s already built in — avoid overwriting a newer version with an older one
  2. Security scanning is the new normal: Starting with 2026.4.2, all plugins are scanned. For trusted plugins, use --dangerously-force-unsafe-install
  3. ClawHub ≠ npm: The same package may have different type labels across the two channels — watch for plugin vs skill install command differences
  4. Version numbers come from the manifest: plugins list reads from openclaw.plugin.json, not package.json
  5. Restart Gateway after upgrading: Run openclaw gateway restart — if the service is missing, reinstall the Daemon via openclaw config

WeChat Chat Auto-Decrypt & Markdown Export Guide

Apr 3, 2026
Vibe Sparking

WeChat Chat Auto-Decrypt & Markdown Export Guide

Section titled “WeChat Chat Auto-Decrypt & Markdown Export Guide”

Auto-decrypt WeChat 4.0 databases and incrementally export chat history to Markdown files every 10 minutes using OpenClaw cron jobs.

Background

Section titled “Background”

WeChat 4.0 for macOS encrypts its local databases with SQLCipher 4 (AES-256-CBC + HMAC-SHA512). The wechat-decrypt project can extract the encryption key from the WeChat process memory and decrypt the databases, but the resulting SQLite data is still structured and not easy to read or search.

This solution builds on wechat-decrypt by adding:

  1. Incremental Markdown export script — organizes chat history into readable .md files by contact/group and date
  2. OpenClaw cron job — automates the decrypt + export workflow

Prerequisites

Section titled “Prerequisites”
  • macOS with WeChat 4.0 logged in and running
  • wechat-decrypt configured and ready (config.json and all_keys.json in place)
  • python decrypt_db.py runs successfully
  • Python dependencies: pycryptodome, zstandard
  • OpenClaw installed and running

Database Structure Overview

Section titled “Database Structure Overview”

Key databases after decryption:

DatabasePurpose
contact/contact.dbContact info (username, remark, nick_name)
session/session.dbSession list (group chat names, last message)
message/message_0~6.dbChat messages (sharded across multiple DBs)

Message Table Schema

Section titled “Message Table Schema”

Each contact/group chat maps to a Msg_<md5(username)> table:

  • local_type & 0xFFFF = base message type (1=text, 3=image, 34=voice, 43=video, 49=link/app message, 10000=system message)
  • WCDB_CT_message_content = 4 indicates the content is zstd-compressed
  • Group chat text messages have message_content prefixed with wxid_xxx:\n to identify the sender
  • The rowid in the Name2Id table corresponds to real_sender_id

Export Script

Section titled “Export Script”

export_markdown.py

Section titled “export_markdown.py”

Place this in the wechat-decrypt/ directory, alongside decrypt_db.py.

Core logic:

  1. Load contact remark names / nicknames from contact.db
  2. Load group chat display names from session.db
  3. Iterate through message_0~6.db, for each Msg_<hash> table:
    • Match the corresponding username via MD5 lookup in Name2Id
    • Filter incremental messages using create_time >= 3 days ago and server_id > last exported
    • Decompress zstd content, parse sender info, extract text
    • Group by date and write to markdown_export/<contact_name>/<YYYY-MM-DD>.md
  4. Update .export_state.json to track export progress

Incremental mechanism: Each (db_file:table_name) pair records the maximum exported server_id. On subsequent runs, only newer messages are queried and appended to the corresponding date file.

Output Structure

Section titled “Output Structure”

Markdown Format Example

Section titled “Markdown Format Example”

Deployment Steps

Section titled “Deployment Steps”

Step 1: Create the Export Script

Section titled “Step 1: Create the Export Script”

Place the complete export_markdown.py in the wechat-decrypt/ directory. You can have OpenClaw generate it for you:

Prompt:

Step 2: Test Run

Section titled “Step 2: Test Run”

The first run exports all messages from the last 3 days. Subsequent runs only append new messages.

Step 3: Create an OpenClaw Cron Job

Section titled “Step 3: Create an OpenClaw Cron Job”

Prompt:

OpenClaw will create an isolated cron job with an equivalent configuration:

Managing the Cron Job

Section titled “Managing the Cron Job”

NeedWhere to Modify

Why Does OpenClaw Still Require Approval for Long Commands Even with Default Allow?

Apr 3, 2026
Vibe Sparking

A source code investigation into OpenClaw’s exec approval mechanism

The Problem: Default Allow Set, but Long File Writes Still Need Approval

Section titled “The Problem: Default Allow Set, but Long File Writes Still Need Approval”

While using OpenClaw to auto-generate bilingual blog posts, I hit a counterintuitive issue.

The ~/.openclaw/exec-approvals.json default policy was already set to:

This should mean most exec commands run without approval prompts.

Yet in practice, the Chinese article wrote successfully, but the English version triggered an approval prompt:

If the default is already “allow,” why would a “command too long” error still require approval?

To find out, I dug into OpenClaw’s installation directory and latest source code.

The Trigger

Section titled “The Trigger”

The command in question was a heredoc writing an entire English article to a file:

The command itself isn’t dangerous — it’s just writing heredoc content to a file. But because the entire article was embedded in the command string, the total command length was very long. OpenClaw flagged it as:

  • Command too long
  • Potential obfuscation risk
  • Requires explicit approval

This wasn’t the regular exec permission policy — it was a higher-priority security interception.

The Investigation

Section titled “The Investigation”

Step 1: Verify Configuration

Section titled “Step 1: Verify Configuration”

Confirmed OpenClaw version (2026.4.2) and the approval config file. The defaults were indeed security: "full" + ask: "off" + askFallback: "full".

The regular exec allow configuration was correct.

Step 2: Locate the Error Source

Section titled “Step 2: Locate the Error Source”

Searched the OpenClaw installation directory for the error message, which led to the obfuscation detection module exec-obfuscation-detect.ts.

Key finding — a hardcoded constant:

And the detection logic:

Any command longer than 10,000 characters gets flagged as obfuscation detected.

Step 3: Check if Default Allow Can Override

Section titled “Step 3: Check if Default Allow Can Override”

Traced the gateway execution logic:

Once obfuscation is detected, the command enters the requiresAsk branch regardless of ask: "off".

Step 4: Search for a Skip Switch

Section titled “Step 4: Search for a Skip Switch”

Searched the source code for skipObfuscation, bypassObfuscation, disableObfuscation, and similar terms.

Result: No skip, disable, or exemption configuration exists.

  • MAX_COMMAND_CHARS = 10_000 is hardcoded
  • obfuscation.detected unconditionally forces approval
  • No public config can disable this rule

Step 5: Confirm Timeout Fallback Behavior

Section titled “Step 5: Confirm Timeout Fallback Behavior”

Normally, askFallback: "full" auto-approves on timeout. But obfuscation detection is an exception:

Obfuscated commands are denied even on approval timeout — no fallback.

Full Detection Rules

Section titled “Full Detection Rules”

Beyond command length, OpenClaw checks for these obfuscation patterns:

RuleDescription
command-too-longCommand exceeds 10,000 characters
base64-pipe-execBase64 decode piped to shell
hex-pipe-execxxd decode piped to shell
printf-pipe-execprintf escape sequences piped to shell
eval-decodeeval with encoded/decoded input
pipe-to-shellContent piped directly to shell interpreter
shell-heredoc-execShell heredoc execution
curl-pipe-shellRemote content piped to shell (has safe URL allowlist)
octal-escapeBash octal escape sequences
hex-escapeBash hex escape sequences
python-exec-encodedPython/Perl/Ruby encoded execution
var-expansion-obfuscationVariable assignment chain with expansion

These rules form OpenClaw’s command security layer, operating independently from the permission management layer.

Conclusion

Section titled “Conclusion”

Two-Layer Control

Section titled “Two-Layer Control”

OpenClaw implements two distinct control dimensions at the exec layer:

  1. Approval Policy Layer — Managed by exec-approvals.json: default allow, ask behavior, fallback
  2. Security Detection Layer — Intercepts suspicious command patterns, takes priority over the policy layer

Even with permissions wide open, the security layer can still block suspicious commands.

The Right Workaround

Section titled “The Right Workaround”

Since this rule can’t be disabled, the solution is to change how you write files:

Option 1: write + cp Use OpenClaw’s write tool to create the file in the workspace (bypasses shell entirely), then use a short cp command to move it to the target path.

Option 2: Split writes Don’t stuff an entire article into one heredoc. Split into multiple cat >> appends, each under 10KB.

Option 3: Core principle Let shell handle file transport, not file content.

One-Line Summary

Section titled “One-Line Summary”

OpenClaw’s default allow only affects regular exec approvals — it doesn’t bypass obfuscation detection. For long text file writes, use tool-based file creation + short shell commands for copying.

Making OpenClaw Cluster Commands Work Over Non-Interactive SSH: A PATH Troubleshooting Guide

Apr 2, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Making OpenClaw Cluster Commands Work Over Non-Interactive SSH

Section titled “Making OpenClaw Cluster Commands Work Over Non-Interactive SSH”

Date: 2026-04-02 Topic: Fixing openclaw / node / npm not found over non-interactive SSH across multiple hosts Scope: Mixed macOS (zsh) + Linux (bash) clusters

Background

Section titled “Background”

When managing an OpenClaw cluster, you frequently run remote commands via non-interactive SSH:

The problem: A command that works in an interactive login shell may not be found over non-interactive SSH.

While upgrading a Mac Mini node, this issue was fully exposed:

This led to a cluster-wide audit and fix.

Root Cause: Non-Interactive SSH Doesn’t Load the Config Files You Think It Does

Section titled “Root Cause: Non-Interactive SSH Doesn’t Load the Config Files You Think It Does”

zsh Behavior

Section titled “zsh Behavior”

zsh loads different files depending on the mode:

FileInteractive LoginInteractive Non-LoginNon-Interactive SSH
~/.zshenv✅✅✅
~/.zprofile✅❌❌
~/.zshrc✅✅❌
~/.zlogin✅❌❌

Key insight: For zsh, ~/.zshenv is the only file reliably loaded in non-interactive SSH.

If PATH is only in ~/.zprofile or ~/.zshrc, ssh host "openclaw --version" will fail.

bash Behavior

Section titled “bash Behavior”

bash is trickier. Non-interactive SSH commands typically don’t read ~/.bashrc / ~/.profile PATH modifications — especially when .bashrc starts with the common guard:

This means PATH augmentation logic simply doesn’t execute in non-interactive mode.

Common symptom:

Cluster Audit Results

Section titled “Cluster Audit Results”

Testing ssh host "openclaw --version" across all nodes:

Host TypeShellStatusIssue
Mac Mini M1 (Homebrew)zsh❌/opt/homebrew/bin not in non-interactive PATH
MacBook Pro (asdf)zsh❌asdf Node bin not in non-interactive PATH
MacBook Pro (manual install)zsh✅~/.zshenv already configured
Linux VPS (npm-global)bash❌openclaw in ~/.npm-global/bin, not in PATH
Linux VPS (AWS)bash❌Same

3 out of 5 machines broken.

Fix Strategy: Fix the Exposure Layer, Not the Installation Layer

Section titled “Fix Strategy: Fix the Exposure Layer, Not the Installation Layer”

We chose the minimal-impact approach: fix command discoverability, don’t change installation layouts.

Why not change npm global install paths?

  • Creates old/new path inconsistencies
  • Complicates future upgrades and debugging
  • Fragments installation strategies across machines

Minimal fix:

  • zsh machines → Add PATH to ~/.zshenv
  • bash machines → Symlink to /usr/local/bin

The Fixes

Section titled “The Fixes”

zsh Machines: ~/.zshenv

Section titled “zsh Machines: ~/.zshenv”

Homebrew installs:

asdf installs:

bash Machines: Symlink to /usr/local/bin

Section titled “bash Machines: Symlink to /usr/local/bin”

Direct, stable, no impact on existing install layout.

Final State

Section titled “Final State”

All nodes now work over non-interactive SSH:

Lessons Learned

Section titled “Lessons Learned”

1. zsh: Only Trust ~/.zshenv for Non-Interactive PATH

Section titled “1. zsh: Only Trust ~/.zshenv for Non-Interactive PATH”

Keep it minimal — only environment variables, no aliases, prompts, or completions.

2. bash: Don’t Rely on .bashrc for Non-Interactive PATH

Section titled “2. bash: Don’t Rely on .bashrc for Non-Interactive PATH”

Most default .bashrc files return in non-interactive mode. A symlink to /usr/local/bin is more reliable than modifying rc files.

3. “node/npm Found” ≠ “openclaw Found”

Section titled “3. “node/npm Found” ≠ “openclaw Found””

The easiest misdiagnosis:

  • node/npm in /usr/bin → works non-interactively
  • openclaw in ~/.npm-global/bin → doesn’t

Always test the actual target CLI:

4. Fix Exposure Before Installation

Section titled “4. Fix Exposure Before Installation”

The problem is “not found”, not “not installed.” Minimal changes are best for cluster environments.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
ShellFixRationale
zshPATH in ~/.zshenvOnly file reliably loaded non-interactively
bashSymlink to /usr/local/binMore stable than modifying rc files

After fixing: remote upgrades are smoother, non-interactive SSH is reliable, and batch operations are predictable.

Small issue, big impact on daily efficiency. Fix it once, save time forever.

Based on a real cluster audit. Applicable to any mixed macOS (zsh) + Linux (bash) environment with CLI remote-accessibility issues.

OpenClaw 2026.4.1-beta.1 Deep Dive: 14 New Features, 9 Key Fixes & Competitive Analysis

Part I: New Features

Section titled “Part I: New Features”

1. Tasks/Chat: /tasks — Native Background Task Panel

Section titled “1. Tasks/Chat: /tasks — Native Background Task Panel”

Background Previously, OpenClaw’s background tasks (sub-agent runs, cron jobs, long executions) lacked unified visibility. Users couldn’t check “what tasks are running and their status” directly from chat — they had to rely on /status or the Web UI separately. For complex multi-task scenarios, information was severely fragmented.

Use Cases

  • Type /tasks in chat to see all background tasks linked to the current session
  • While a sub-agent runs a PR review, monitor progress from the main session via /tasks
  • Agents can also query task counts via the session_status tool internally
  • Falls back to agent-local task counts when no linked tasks are visible

Notes

  • Only shows tasks linked to the current session — cross-session tasks require checking their respective sessions
  • Related #54226 — a long-standing issue reflecting strong community demand
  • Complements but doesn’t duplicate existing session_status output

Competitive Comparison

Trend: Chat-as-IDE direction — task panels are the first step, with task cancellation, retry, and dependency graphs potentially coming next.

2. Web Search/SearXNG: Built-in SearXNG Search Plugin

Section titled “2. Web Search/SearXNG: Built-in SearXNG Search Plugin”

Background OpenClaw previously supported DuckDuckGo, Brave, Tavily, and other search engines, but they either require API keys or are unreliable in certain network environments (e.g., China, intranets). SearXNG is an open-source metasearch engine that can be self-hosted — ideal for privacy-conscious and offline deployment scenarios.

Use Cases

  • Enterprise intranet: company prohibits external search API calls — self-host SearXNG to aggregate internal search engines
  • Privacy: avoid sending search queries to third-party commercial APIs
  • China deployment: DuckDuckGo is unstable in China — SearXNG can be configured with Baidu and other backends

Notes

  • Requires self-deploying a SearXNG instance (one-click Docker deployment)
  • host parameter is customizable, defaults to localhost
  • Ships as a bundled plugin — no additional plugins install needed

Section titled “3. Amazon Bedrock/Guardrails: Bedrock Guardrails Support”

Background AWS Bedrock offers Guardrails for API-level content filtering, PII detection, and topic restrictions on model input/output. Previously, OpenClaw’s Bedrock provider didn’t support passing Guardrails configuration, preventing enterprise users from leveraging AWS compliance capabilities.

Use Cases

  • Content safety: restrict models from discussing specific topics
  • Compliance auditing: integration with Guardrails logging and AWS audit trails

Background Talk Mode is the voice interaction mode in OpenClaw’s macOS client. Previously it could only be activated via UI buttons or keyboard shortcuts. Voice Wake allows activation through a wake word (similar to “Hey Siri”), enabling fully hands-free operation.

Tasks/Gateway: Task Maintenance Blocking Event Loop

Synchronous SQLite operations during task registration maintenance blocked the Node.js event loop, causing gateway freeze ~1 minute after startup. Now decoupled.

allow-always now persists to the user-level trust store, surviving restarts.

Refreshed tokens are now immediately persisted, preventing refresh_token_reused loops.

Memory/Session Indexing: Session Transcripts Preserved After Restart

Full reindexing now preserves session memory, making search results more complete.

Section titled “Plugins/Bundled Runtimes: Fixed Bundled Plugin Dependencies”

Restored dependency staging across packed install, Docker build, and local staging paths.

OpenClaw Exec Approval Bypass Guide: 4 Approvals to Turn Off Approvals

Apr 2, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw Exec Approval Bypass Guide: 4 Approvals to Turn Off Approvals

Section titled “OpenClaw Exec Approval Bypass Guide: 4 Approvals to Turn Off Approvals”

Every cat triggers an approval popup? From principles to config in one guide, plus a real Bootstrap Paradox story.

The Problem: Every Command Needs a Click

Section titled “The Problem: Every Command Needs a Click”

After upgrading to OpenClaw v2026.4.1, you may notice — every shell command the agent runs triggers “Exec approval needed”, requiring manual approval.

Reading a file? Popup. Running grep? Popup. Cat a config? Popup.

It’s not a bug, it’s a feature. OpenClaw’s Exec Approval mechanism is a safety guardrail preventing AI agents from running dangerous commands without your knowledge. Good intention, but for self-managed local instances, the interaction cost is too high.

How It Works: Three Layers Decide a Command’s Fate

Section titled “How It Works: Three Layers Decide a Command’s Fate”

Configured in ~/.openclaw/exec-approvals.json:

1. Security Level

Section titled “1. Security Level”
ValueBehavior
denyBlock everything
allowlistOnly allowlisted commands pass
fullAllow everything

2. Ask (Popup Behavior)

Section titled “2. Ask (Popup Behavior)”
ValueBehavior
alwaysAsk for every command
on-missAsk only when not allowlisted
offNever ask

3. Ask Fallback (When No UI Available)

Section titled “3. Ask Fallback (When No UI Available)”
ValueBehavior
denyReject
allowlistAllow if allowlisted
fullAllow everything

Default is roughly security: "deny" + ask: "on-miss" — nearly every command triggers a popup.

Three Approaches

Section titled “Three Approaches”

Option 1: Progressive Allowlist (For the Cautious)

Section titled “Option 1: Progressive Allowlist (For the Cautious)”

Choose “Always allow” instead of “Allow once” each time. After a few days, common commands pass silently.

autoAllowSkills: true auto-allows CLI tools referenced by installed skills.

Good for: Shared instances, production, audit-required environments.

Option 2: Full Bypass (For Self-Managed)

Section titled “Option 2: Full Bypass (For Self-Managed)”

Three words: never ask again.

Good for: Local dev machines, personal instances, you-are-the-admin scenarios.

Option 3: Visual Configuration via Control UI

Section titled “Option 3: Visual Configuration via Control UI”

Web UI → Nodes → Exec approvals card. Click to configure, no JSON editing needed.

How To

Section titled “How To”

Config file: ~/.openclaw/exec-approvals.json

For Option 2, change the "defaults" field to:

Takes effect immediately — no gateway restart needed.

Rolling Back

Section titled “Rolling Back”

Your allowlist is preserved.

Per-Agent Fine Control

Section titled “Per-Agent Fine Control”

For multi-agent setups, only unlock specific agents:

defaults covers agents without individual config. agents.<id> overrides defaults.

Appendix: The Bootstrap Paradox

Section titled “Appendix: The Bootstrap Paradox”

Here’s the actual process of turning off Exec Approval — note the recursive irony:

Approval #1: Search for exec-approvals docs

Approval #2: Read the official documentation

Approval #3: View current config

Approval #4: Modify config to disable approvals

“Last approval ever 🎉 After this one, exec approval will never bother you again.”

4 approvals to complete “turn off approvals.” Classic Bootstrap Paradox — you need the key to get the key. At least you only need to forge it once.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”
Who You AreRecommendedKey Config
Local dev / PersonalFull bypasssecurity: full + ask: off
Shared / ProductionProgressive allowlistsecurity: allowlist + ask: on-miss + autoAllowSkills
Maximum securityManual allowlistsecurity: allowlist + ask: always

Exec Approval is good design, but good design must match the use case. For self-managing admins, popups aren’t security — they’re friction.

Based on OpenClaw v2026.4.1, config file ~/.openclaw/exec-approvals.json.

OpenClaw Remote Upgrade Guide: Upgrading a Mac Mini Node via Tailscale + SSH

Apr 2, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw Remote Upgrade Guide: Upgrading a Mac Mini Node via Tailscale + SSH

Section titled “OpenClaw Remote Upgrade Guide: Upgrading a Mac Mini Node via Tailscale + SSH”

Date: 2026-04-02 Target: Mac Mini M1 node (macOS 26.3.1) Method: Tailscale + SSH tunnel Upgrade path: OpenClaw 2026.3.28 → 2026.4.1

Background

Section titled “Background”

We have a Mac Mini M1 running as an OpenClaw node, connected via Tailscale mesh networking. The admin manages it through a local SSH tunnel (localhost:<local-port> → <tailscale-ip>:<remote-port>).

Pre-upgrade state:

  • OS: macOS 26.3.1 (arm64)
  • Node.js: v25.8.2 (Homebrew, at /opt/homebrew/bin)
  • OpenClaw: 2026.3.28
  • Gateway service: LaunchDaemon (system-level plist)

Gotchas

Section titled “Gotchas”

Gotcha 1: Non-Interactive SSH Can’t Find Commands

Section titled “Gotcha 1: Non-Interactive SSH Can’t Find Commands”

Why: Non-interactive SSH doesn’t load .zshrc / .zprofile, so Homebrew-installed Node/npm isn’t in PATH.

Fix: Manually export PATH:

Gotcha 2: npm Install Timeout Kills SSH Session

Section titled “Gotcha 2: npm Install Timeout Kills SSH Session”

Running npm install -g openclaw@latest directly over SSH — the large package download gets killed by the local exec timeout mechanism (SIGKILL).

Attempted workarounds:

  • ServerAliveInterval=30 → Didn’t help (it’s a local exec timeout, not SSH keepalive)
  • nohup ... & → Log file was 0 bytes (zsh non-interactive nohup redirection is unreliable)

Gotcha 3: No Internet Connectivity

Section titled “Gotcha 3: No Internet Connectivity”

Mid-upgrade, discovered the node had no internet access:

  • registry.npmjs.org → curl timeout
  • registry.npmmirror.com → DNS failure (ENOTFOUND)
  • brew install tmux → Same timeout

Lesson: Always test connectivity before attempting upgrades.

Gotcha 4: nohup + zsh Non-Interactive Is Unreliable

Section titled “Gotcha 4: nohup + zsh Non-Interactive Is Unreliable”

zsh in non-interactive mode has inconsistent stdout/stderr redirection with nohup. Use tmux instead.

Gotcha 5: LaunchDaemon Requires sudo

Section titled “Gotcha 5: LaunchDaemon Requires sudo”

The gateway runs as a LaunchDaemon (system-level service), so restarts require sudo:

For non-interactive SSH, sudo needs password via stdin (production environments should use sudoers NOPASSWD or a secrets manager):

The Working Procedure

Section titled “The Working Procedure”

After network recovery, the complete upgrade steps:

1. Test Network Connectivity

Section titled “1. Test Network Connectivity”

2. Run Upgrade Inside tmux (Survives SSH Disconnects)

Section titled “2. Run Upgrade Inside tmux (Survives SSH Disconnects)”

3. Check Progress Periodically

Section titled “3. Check Progress Periodically”

Output:

4. Verify Version

Section titled “4. Verify Version”

5. Restart Gateway (LaunchDaemon)

Section titled “5. Restart Gateway (LaunchDaemon)”

6. Verify Gateway Is Running

Section titled “6. Verify Gateway Is Running”

Lessons Learned

Section titled “Lessons Learned”
IssueLesson
Non-interactive SSH has no PATHAlways manually export PATH for remote commands
Long npm installs get killedUse tmux — never run long commands over bare SSH
nohup logs emptyzsh non-interactive + nohup redirection is unreliable; tmux is more robust
No internetTest connectivity before upgrading — don’t wait for npm to hang
LaunchDaemon needs sudoThe cost of headless Mac with LaunchDaemon — remote restart requires sudo access
Plaintext passwordsUse sudoers NOPASSWD or a secrets manager in production

Before/After

Section titled “Before/After”
ItemBeforeAfter
OpenClaw2026.3.282026.4.1
Node.jsv25.8.2v25.8.2 (unchanged)
Upgrade time—~1 minute (once network was up)

Remote Upgrade Checklist

Section titled “Remote Upgrade Checklist”

For future remote OpenClaw node upgrades:

  • Test internet connectivity (curl registry.npmjs.org)
  • Confirm tmux is installed
  • Run npm install -g openclaw@latest inside tmux
  • Verify version with openclaw --version
  • Restart gateway (launchctl bootout + bootstrap)
  • Verify HTTP probe returns 200
  • Clean up tmux session
