Background

Section titled “Background”

Every week, I need to update an Excel weekly report. The process is fixed, but tedious:

  1. Copy last week’s file and update the date in the filename
  2. Move completed items from the “Recent Releases” sheet to the “Release History” sheet
  3. Add new feedback to the “Recent Plans” sheet
  4. Record this week’s release in the “Recent Releases” sheet
  5. Fix formatting issues such as text wrapping

This time, I did not open Excel at all. Instead, I used OpenClaw WebChat and let AI OpenClaw complete the entire workflow automatically.

Process

Section titled “Process”

1. Copy the weekly report and update the filename

Section titled “1. Copy the weekly report and update the filename”

I told OpenClaw to copy last week’s report and change the date in the filename from last week to this week.

OpenClaw automatically generated a Python script to copy and rename the file.

2. Archive completed items

Section titled “2. Archive completed items”

I told OpenClaw to move the four completed items from the “Recent Releases” sheet to the top of the “Release History” sheet, and then clear the data area in “Recent Releases.”

The moved items included:

  • Keep two decimal places
  • Fix multiple issue feedback items
  • Device log analysis

OpenClaw read the sheet data, inserted the rows into the target sheet, and cleaned the source data in one go.

3. Add new feedback to recent plans

Section titled “3. Add new feedback to recent plans”

I described two new issue feedback items in chat, and OpenClaw wrote them into the corresponding sheet:

TypeSummary
Issue feedbackUsers cannot see device details → optimize the design solution
Issue feedbackCountdown is not displayed → layout adjustment + message reminder

4. Add this week’s release record to recent releases

Section titled “4. Add this week’s release record to recent releases”

I described this week’s release content, and OpenClaw wrote it into the “Recent Releases” sheet:

Waiting time adjustment, calculator entry

Note: OpenClaw initially placed it in the release history sheet by mistake. After I pointed it out in chat, it immediately corrected it to the right place.

5. Fix formatting

Section titled “5. Fix formatting”

I asked OpenClaw to check all non-empty cells and ensure the Wrap Text property was set correctly.

Technical implementation

Section titled “Technical implementation”
ItemDescription
OpenClawOpenClaw
Excel libraryPython openpyxl
Interaction methodWebChat natural language conversation
WorkflowUser describes the task → OpenClaw generates a Python script → execute → feedback → user confirms/corrects → iterate

Why use AI OpenClaw to operate Excel?

Section titled “Why use AI OpenClaw to operate Excel?”

Good use cases

Section titled “Good use cases”
  • Repeated weekly reports: the structure is the same every week, only the content changes
  • Multi-sheet coordination: moving data across sheets is easy to get wrong manually
  • Consistent formatting: checking Wrap Text cell by cell is tedious
  • Remote operation: you can finish the task by chatting on your phone even when away from your computer

Less suitable scenarios

Section titled “Less suitable scenarios”
  • Complex formulas and chart operations
  • Tasks that require visual confirmation of layout
  • One-off tasks where manual work is faster

Key advantages

Section titled “Key advantages”

Correctable iteration: if OpenClaw makes a mistake, such as writing to the wrong sheet, I can correct it through chat. This is more intuitive than debugging a script manually.

Zero learning curve: there is no need to learn the openpyxl API or write code. I can simply describe the action in natural language, like “move these rows over there.”

Takeaways

Section titled “Takeaways”
  1. Be specific: do not say “update the weekly report”; say “move the four items from Recent Releases to the top of Release History”
  2. Work step by step: let OpenClaw do one thing at a time, then confirm before continuing
  3. Check promptly: after each step, ask OpenClaw to read back the result for verification
  4. Allow mistakes: OpenClaw may put something in the wrong place, but the cost of correction is very low—just say it

The entire process was completed without opening the Excel application. Through OpenClaw chat, I finished copying, archiving, adding updates, and fixing formatting in the weekly report.

Share Claude Code Skills with OpenClaw — A Complete Guide

Apr 1, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Let OpenClaw reuse Claude Code’s installed plugins/skills directly — no duplicate installs, auto-synced updates.

Background

Section titled “Background”

Claude Code (Anthropic’s official CLI) installs plugins via the /install command. Each plugin can contain multiple skills following the AgentSkills specification, with SKILL.md as the entry point.

OpenClaw also supports the AgentSkills format — the two skill structures are fully compatible. By creating symlinks, you can let OpenClaw directly reuse all skills installed through Claude Code.

How It Works

Section titled “How It Works”

Claude Code’s Skill Storage Structure

Section titled “Claude Code’s Skill Storage Structure”

Claude Code stores plugins under ~/.claude/plugins/cache/:

installed_plugins.json records each plugin’s installPath (the currently active version). The cache directory may retain historical versions — always refer to the path in installed_plugins.json.

OpenClaw’s Skill Loading Directories

Section titled “OpenClaw’s Skill Loading Directories”

OpenClaw loads skills from these directories (highest to lowest priority):

PriorityPathDescription
1 (highest)<workspace>/skillsCurrent workspace skills
2<workspace>/.agents/skillsWorkspace-level agent skills
3~/.agents/skillsPersonal global skills
4~/.openclaw/skillsManaged/local skills
5Bundled skillsBuilt-in with the install package
6 (lowest)skills.load.extraDirsExtra directories from config

Same-name skills at higher priority override lower ones.

The Sharing Strategy

Section titled “The Sharing Strategy”

Symlink Claude Code’s skill directories into ~/.agents/skills/ (layer 3):

  • ✅ All local OpenClaw agents can use them
  • ✅ Won’t override workspace-level custom skills
  • ✅ Will override bundled skills (reasonable — Claude Code’s are typically newer)
  • ✅ Symlinks don’t copy files — updates in Claude Code take effect automatically

Step-by-Step

Section titled “Step-by-Step”

Step 1: Verify Claude Code Has Plugins Installed

Section titled “Step 1: Verify Claude Code Has Plugins Installed”

Example output:

Step 2: List Skills in Plugins

Section titled “Step 2: List Skills in Plugins”

Step 3: Create Symlinks

Section titled “Step 3: Create Symlinks”

Manual approach (link individual skills):

Automated approach (batch-link all installed plugin skills):

Step 4: Verify

Section titled “Step 4: Verify”

Restart the OpenClaw session or wait for the skills watcher to auto-refresh. New skills will appear in the <available_skills> list.

Auto-Sync Script

Section titled “Auto-Sync Script”

Save the following as sync-claude-skills.py:

Script features:

  • Only processes currently active versions from installed_plugins.json
  • Won’t override non-symlink native OpenClaw skills
  • Automatically cleans up stale symlinks from uninstalled plugins
  • Detects path changes (version hash changes on plugin upgrade) and updates links
  • Idempotent — safe to run repeatedly

Scheduled Auto-Sync

Section titled “Scheduled Auto-Sync”

Option 1: OpenClaw Cron (Recommended)

Section titled “Option 1: OpenClaw Cron (Recommended)”

Create a cron job in OpenClaw to sync every 4 hours:

Option 2: System crontab

Section titled “Option 2: System crontab”

Important Notes

Section titled “Important Notes”

Name Conflicts

Section titled “Name Conflicts”

Different Claude Code plugins may contain same-named skills (e.g., skill-creator appearing in both anthropic-agent-skills and claude-plugins-official). The script uses a first-come-first-served strategy — later discoveries of the same name are skipped.

To specify priority, manually create symlinks to override.

Security

Section titled “Security”
  • Third-party Claude Code plugins should be treated as untrusted code
  • Review SKILL.md contents before enabling
  • Some skills may depend on specific environment variables (e.g., API keys) — configure these in OpenClaw’s skills.entries

Remote Instances

Section titled “Remote Instances”

Symlinks only work locally. To share these skills with remote OpenClaw instances:

  1. Copy skills to the remote machine (rsync or scp)
  2. Or install Claude Code on the remote machine and run the sync script there

Plugin Updates

Section titled “Plugin Updates”

After Claude Code updates a plugin (/install upgrade), the installPath in installed_plugins.json points to the new version directory. Simply re-run the sync script to update symlinks.

Real-World Results

Section titled “Real-World Results”

On a machine with 28 Claude Code plugins installed, the sync script created 135 skill symlinks, covering:

SourceCountExamples
Anthropic Official (document-skills)15+pdf, docx, pptx, xlsx, frontend-design, claude-api
PM Skills40+lean-canvas, SWOT, PRD, OKR, competitor-analysis
Superpowers12TDD, code review, git worktrees, parallel agents
Everything Claude Code25+Django/Spring Boot/Go patterns, security scan
OthersVariousbeads, planning-with-files, episodic-memory

All skills become available in the next OpenClaw session — no additional configuration required.

The Complete Guide to OpenClaw Slash Commands

Apr 1, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Compatible with OpenClaw 2026.3.x+

OpenClaw slash commands are your direct shortcut to the Gateway — no model involved, zero tokens consumed, instant execution. Master them, and you’ve mastered OpenClaw’s control panel.

1. Command System Overview

Section titled “1. Command System Overview”

OpenClaw commands come in three tiers:

TypeBehaviorExamples
CommandsStandalone messages, handled by Gateway/help, /stop, /kill
DirectivesCan be inlined in messages, invisible to model/think, /model, /fast
Text-onlyOnly available in text chat! ls -la, /compact

Key distinction: When sent alone, directives persist to the session; when embedded in a message, they only apply to that single turn. This matters — it comes up repeatedly.

Permission Model

Section titled “Permission Model”

Not everyone can use commands. Authorization chain:

  1. If commands.allowFrom is configured → only this matters, everything else ignored
  2. Otherwise → channel allowlist + pairing + commands.useAccessGroups
  3. Unauthorized sender’s commands → silently dropped, inline /... treated as plain text

Fast Path

Section titled “Fast Path”

Command-only messages (entire message is just the command) take the fast path: no queue, no model, no @mention required (in group chats). This means /stop always works immediately, even while the model is generating.

2. Everyday Commands

Section titled “2. Everyday Commands”

Section titled “/status — Your Dashboard”

Returns complete session state: model, provider usage/quota, thinking level, elevated status, etc.

Use cases:

  • Check quota: After a heavy task, /status to see remaining Claude credits
  • Confirm config: After switching models, /status to verify
  • Debug slowness: Agent responding slowly? /status to check if thinking got bumped up

Tip: /status is an inline shortcut — write me a script /status returns status first, then processes the message.

/help and /commands

Section titled “/help and /commands”

Forgot a command? Ask anytime. Both support inline usage.

/whoami — Identity Check

Section titled “/whoami — Identity Check”

Alias: /id. Returns your sender id (provider + user identifier).

Section titled “/model — Model Switching”

Section titled “/fast — Quick Mode”

Section titled “/reasoning — Expose Reasoning”

Aborts all ongoing operations. Takes fast path — always works immediately.

The Complete Guide to OpenClaw Tools

1. File Operations

Section titled “1. File Operations”

Read — Read Files

Section titled “Read — Read Files”

Read file contents. Supports text files and images (jpg, png, gif, webp).

ParameterTypeRequiredDescription
pathstring✅File path (relative or absolute)
offsetnumber❌Start line (1-based)

Note: Text output truncated at 2000 lines or 50KB (whichever first). Images returned as attachments for vision model analysis.

Write — Write Files

Section titled “Write — Write Files”

Create or overwrite files. Auto-creates parent directories.

ParameterTypeRequiredDescription
pathstring✅File path
contentstring✅Content to write

⚠️ Completely overwrites the target file. For small changes to large files, use Edit instead.

Edit — Precise File Editing

Section titled “Edit — Precise File Editing”

Exact text replacement in files. Two modes:

Single replacement: oldText + newText

Multiple replacements: edits array with {oldText, newText} objects

Note: oldText must uniquely match; edits must not overlap; modes cannot be mixed.

2. Command Execution

Section titled “2. Command Execution”

Exec — Run Shell Commands

Section titled “Exec — Run Shell Commands”

Execute shell commands with foreground, background, and PTY support.

ParameterTypeRequiredDescription
commandstring✅Shell command
workdirstring❌Working directory
yieldMsnumber❌Auto-background after ms (default 10000)
backgroundboolean❌Run in background immediately
timeoutnumber❌Timeout in seconds (default 1800)
ptyboolean❌Pseudo-terminal for TTY commands
hoststring❌sandbox/gateway/node
elevatedboolean❌Request elevated permissions

Use cases:

  • Run scripts: exec("python3 train.py")
  • Long builds: exec("npm run build", yieldMs=1000) — auto-backgrounds
  • Interactive CLIs: exec("htop", pty=true)
  • Remote execution: exec("uptime", host="node", node="my-server")

Process — Manage Background Processes

Section titled “Process — Manage Background Processes”

Manage exec sessions started in the background.

ActionPurpose
listList all background sessions
pollWait for updates (use timeout)
logView process output
writeWrite to stdin
send-keysSend keystrokes (Enter, Ctrl+C, etc.)
killTerminate process

Tip: Avoid rapid poll loops — use poll with timeout parameter.

3. Web & Search

Section titled “3. Web & Search”

Web Search — Internet Search

Section titled “Web Search — Internet Search”

Search the web using DuckDuckGo. Returns titles, URLs, and snippets.

ParameterTypeRequiredDescription
querystring✅Search query
countnumber❌Results (1-10)
regionstring❌Region code (e.g., us-en)

Note: No API key needed. Results cached 15 minutes. Returns snippets only — use Web Fetch for full pages.

Web Fetch — Extract Web Content

Section titled “Web Fetch — Extract Web Content”

Fetch and extract readable content from URLs (HTML → Markdown/Text).

ParameterTypeRequiredDescription
urlstring✅URL to fetch
extractModestring❌markdown (default) or text
maxCharsnumber❌Max characters to return

⚠️ Does not execute JavaScript — SPAs may return empty shells.

4. Multimedia

Section titled “4. Multimedia”

Image — Image Analysis

Section titled “Image — Image Analysis”

Analyze images with a vision model.

ParameterTypeRequiredDescription
imagestring❌Single image path or URL
imagesarray❌Multiple images (up to 20)
promptstring❌Analysis prompt

5. Sessions & Multi-Agent

Section titled “5. Sessions & Multi-Agent”

Sessions Spawn — Create Sub-Agents

Section titled “Sessions Spawn — Create Sub-Agents”

Spawn isolated sub-agent sessions for background task execution.

ParameterTypeRequiredDescription
taskstring✅Task description
modelstring❌Model override
modestring❌run (one-shot) or session (persistent)
runtimestring❌subagent or acp
threadboolean❌Bind to channel thread

Note: Non-blocking; sub-agent auto-announces results; max 8 concurrent by default.

Sessions List / History / Send / Yield

Section titled “Sessions List / History / Send / Yield”
ToolPurpose
Sessions ListList active sessions
Sessions HistoryView message history for a session
Sessions SendSend message to another session
Sessions YieldEnd current turn, wait for sub-agent results

Subagents — Manage Sub-Agents

Section titled “Subagents — Manage Sub-Agents”
ActionPurpose
listList running sub-agents
killTerminate a sub-agent
steerRedirect a sub-agent mid-run

Cron — Task Scheduling

Schedule types:

TypeDescriptionExample
atOne-shot{kind: "at", at: "2026-04-01T10:00:00+08:00"}
everyFixed interval{kind: "every", everyMs: 3600000}

TL;DR

Section titled “TL;DR”

Installing OpenClaw in China comes down to three things:

  1. Use the Tsinghua mirror for Homebrew (USTC mirror has issues)
  2. Re-login to your terminal after installing Homebrew (source ~/.zshrc isn’t enough)

Nail these three, and one command gets you there.

Step 1: Run the Install Script (Failed)

OpenClaw provides a one-liner install script:

But in China, the first run will almost certainly fail. Here’s what I hit:

Pitfall 1: sudo Access

Section titled “Pitfall 1: sudo Access”

Homebrew needs sudo to create /opt/homebrew. If your user isn’t an admin, fix that first:

Pitfall 2: Homebrew Mirror

Section titled “Pitfall 2: Homebrew Mirror”

Connecting directly to GitHub from China to install Homebrew is basically impossible. The install script tries to use mirrors from your environment variables, but picking the wrong mirror is just as bad.

I first tried the USTC mirror (mirrors.ustc.edu.cn) and got:

Solution: Use the Tsinghua mirror. Set these environment variables before running the install script:

Then install Homebrew manually:

Pitfall 3: brew: command not found

Section titled “Pitfall 3: brew: command not found”

Homebrew installed successfully, but brew can’t be found. This is the easiest step to overlook.

Homebrew tells you to add itself to PATH, but it writes to .zprofile:

Key point: If you’re logged in via SSH, source ~/.zshrc won’t load .zprofile. You need to log out and back in, or manually run eval "$(/opt/homebrew/bin/brew shellenv zsh)".

Also persist the Tsinghua mirror config in .zprofile:

DeepSeek is ideal for users in China — no proxy needed, API works directly.

After setup, OpenClaw runs as a macOS LaunchAgent and auto-starts on boot.

Three Ways to Connect OpenClaw to Claude — Which One Fits You?

Mar 31, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Each integration method has trade-offs. The smart move is combining them.

TL;DR

Section titled “TL;DR”
  • OpenClaw connects to Claude three ways: API Key, CLI Backend, setup-token
  • API Key has full features but uncapped costs — heavy users can hit $2,000-5,000/month
  • CLI Backend saves money but is slow and feature-limited
  • setup-token is being blocked by Anthropic — stop relying on it
  • Best approach: Reverse Proxy API + CLI Fallback — capped monthly cost, full features

The Problem

Section titled “The Problem”

You’ve set up your OpenClaw Gateway and want to connect Claude Opus 4.6. Open the docs — three auth methods stare back at you.

Which one?

This isn’t a “whatever works” decision. Pick wrong and you could spend thousands extra per month. Pick right and you get the same features for a flat subscription fee.

The overview:

MethodAuth SourceBillingContextSpeedStability
Anthropic API KeyAPI ConsolePay-per-token1M (beta)FastHigh
Claude CLI BackendClaude subscriptionFixed monthly1M (beta)SlowMedium
setup-tokenClaude Code CLIFixed monthly200KFastBeing blocked

Method 1: Anthropic API Key

Section titled “Method 1: Anthropic API Key”

Straight from Anthropic’s official API, billed per token.

This is the “proper” way. Official support, complete documentation, every feature available — streaming, tool calling, Prompt Caching, 1M context. All of it.

Configuration is straightforward:

Multi-key rotation is supported — auto-switches on 429 rate limits:

The catch is cost. Opus 4.6 tokens aren’t cheap. Run dozens of long conversations daily and your monthly bill could land between $2,000 and $5,000. No ceiling.

Best for: Well-funded teams, or individual developers with light usage who prioritize stability.

Method 2: Claude CLI Backend

Section titled “Method 2: Claude CLI Backend”

Reuses your locally logged-in claude CLI. OpenClaw calls claude -p to get responses.

The upside is simple: it uses your subscription quota. Pro at $20, Max at $100 or $200 — predictable monthly spend.

The downside is equally clear. Every call spawns a CLI subprocess. No streaming. Noticeably slower than the API. Gateway restarts break the session and lose context. Tool calling isn’t supported — text in, text out only.

Best for: Personal use on a local gateway, where response time isn’t critical.

Method 3: setup-token (Stop Using This)

Section titled “Method 3: setup-token (Stop Using This)”

Grab an OAuth token via claude setup-token and hit the Anthropic API directly.

Sounds ideal — fixed monthly cost, API-speed responses, streaming and tool calling included.

But Anthropic is shutting this down. Users are already hitting HTTP 401: authentication_error: OAuth authentication is currently not supported. The 1M context beta header rejects sk-ant-oat-* tokens. Tokens expire and need constant regeneration.

This path has no future.

The Real Answer: Reverse Proxy API + CLI Fallback

Section titled “The Real Answer: Reverse Proxy API + CLI Fallback”

claude-cli backendReuse local claude CLI OAuth sessionUses subscription quota (Max/Pro)Personal users with Claude subscription

FAQ

Q: What’s the difference between claude-cli auth and API Key auth?

Section titled “Q: What’s the difference between claude-cli auth and API Key auth?”

Billing model. claude-cli uses your Claude subscription (Max/Pro) quota — there’s a daily/monthly usage cap but no per-token charge. API Key billing is per actual token usage with no hard cap, but costs can be higher.

Q: What if my local claude CLI session expires?

Section titled “Q: What if my local claude CLI session expires?”

OpenClaw auto-detects session expiry and attempts refresh. If refresh fails, you need to log in again manually:

OpenClaw will automatically pick up the new session — no Gateway restart needed.

Q: Can a remote Gateway use claude-cli?

Section titled “Q: Can a remote Gateway use claude-cli?”

Yes, but claude CLI must be installed and logged in on the remote host. The CLI backend is called locally by the Gateway process — it doesn’t forward CLI calls through SSH tunnels.

For remote instances (e.g., vns8-aws-tokyo), SSH into the remote host to install and log in:

Q: Why use Opus 4.6 [1M] over the standard window?

Section titled “Q: Why use Opus 4.6 [1M] over the standard window?”

The 1M context is transformative for these use cases:

  • Long-conversation agents: No frequent compaction needed, full context retained
  • Code analysis: Load entire project’s key files in a single context
  • Heartbeat tasks: HEARTBEAT.md instructions + conversation history + multi-channel messages eat through context fast

The tradeoff is slightly higher time-to-first-token. If your use case doesn’t need long context, standard claude-opus-4-6 (200K) is faster.

Q: What does “plugin auto-loading” mean?

Section titled “Q: What does “plugin auto-loading” mean?”

Since v2026.3.28, when you reference the claude-cli backend in your config, the corresponding bundled plugin is automatically enabled — no more manual declaration in plugins.allow. This is part of the “CLI Backend Pluginization” improvement.

claude-cli auth is the most effortless way for personal users to use Claude in OpenClaw:

  1. Zero API Key management — reuse claude CLI’s OAuth login
  2. Uses subscription quota — Max users get Opus 4.6 [1M] at no extra cost

One caveat: remote Gateways need the claude CLI installed and logged in separately on the remote host.

OpenClaw Multi-Agent Permissions ≠ User Isolation: A Dangerous Misconception

Mar 29, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Think assigning different Agents to different users makes you secure? The Gateway trust model says otherwise.

What the Misconception Looks Like

Section titled “What the Misconception Looks Like”

When people first encounter OpenClaw’s multi-agent configuration, a natural thought emerges:

“I’ll create 3 Agents—admin for myself, developer for colleagues, viewer for external users—each with separate permissions. That’s user isolation, right?”

The config looks clean enough:

Three Agents, three permission sets, each with a clear role. Perfect?

No. This is a dangerous security illusion.

Why It Doesn’t Work: The Gateway Trust Model

Section titled “Why It Doesn’t Work: The Gateway Trust Model”

Core Fact: One Gateway = One Trust Domain

Section titled “Core Fact: One Gateway = One Trust Domain”

The official OpenClaw documentation is explicit:

Inside one Gateway instance, authenticated operator access is a trusted control-plane role, not a per-user tenant role.

In plain English:

  • Anyone who can connect to the Gateway is an operator
  • Operators have no hierarchy—there’s no “super admin” vs “regular user”
  • All operators have equal access to the Gateway’s control plane

What This Means in Practice

Section titled “What This Means in Practice”

Anyone with Gateway authentication (token or password), regardless of which Agent they’re “assigned” to, can:

ActionPossible?Consequence
List all Agents’ sessions✅ YesKnow who’s using what
Read other Agents’ chat history✅ YesSee all of admin’s conversations
Send messages to admin Agent’s session✅ YesExecute tools with admin’s permissions
Access Gateway API endpoints✅ YesFull control-plane operations

You configured deny: ["*"] for the viewer, but they can send messages directly to admin’s session and execute anything through admin’s permissions.

It’s like giving an intern a keycard that only opens the conference room—while the building’s back door is wide open.

A More Visual Explanation

Section titled “A More Visual Explanation”

sessionKey Is Not an Auth Token

Section titled “sessionKey Is Not an Auth Token”

Another common misunderstanding:

“Different Agents use different sessionKeys—surely the other party can’t get in without knowing the key?”

The official docs are clear:

Session identifiers (sessionKey, session IDs, labels) are routing selectors, not authorization tokens.

A sessionKey tells the Gateway “which conversation context I want to interact with”—it’s an address, not a lock. Knowing your street address doesn’t mean having your house key, but in the Gateway trust model, all operators hold the same master key.

What Multi-Agent Permissions Actually “Separate”

Section titled “What Multi-Agent Permissions Actually “Separate””

Let’s clarify the capability boundary:

✅ What It Can Do

Section titled “✅ What It Can Do”
  • Restrict the AI’s tool invocation scope — The viewer Agent’s AI truly can only call read, not exec
  • Reduce accidental AI misuse — Different Agents stay in their lanes
  • Functional partitioning within a trust domain — Your development Agent and messaging Agent stay separate

❌ What It Cannot Do

Section titled “❌ What It Cannot Do”
  • Prevent people from accessing other Agents’ data — The control plane is shared
  • Block privilege escalation via other Agents’ sessions — You can send messages to high-privilege Agents
  • Provide OS-level or filesystem-level isolation — Same machine, same user
  • Serve as a multi-tenant security boundary — It was never designed for this

One-line summary:

Multi-agent permissions constrain what the AI can do, not what people can see. To isolate people, isolate Gateways.

When Multi-Agent Permissions Are Appropriate

Section titled “When Multi-Agent Permissions Are Appropriate”
ScenarioSecure?Notes
One person, multiple purposes✅ Perfectly fineDev Agent and support Agent separated, reducing AI overreach
Same trust-domain team⚠️ AcceptableColleagues trust each other; prevents accidents, not malice
Family members sharing⚠️ Depends on trustFine if you don’t mind family seeing your chat history
Untrusted collaborators❌ Not secureEither party can access the full control plane
Public-facing service❌ Not secureExternal users = operators, catastrophic consequences
Client / vendor separation❌ Not secureVendor can see all client data

The Right Way to Isolate Users

Section titled “The Right Way to Isolate Users”

Option 1: One Gateway Per Person (Recommended)

Section titled “Option 1: One Gateway Per Person (Recommended)”
  • Each trust boundary gets its own Gateway instance
  • Separate OS users (ideally separate hosts / VPS)
  • Independent credentials, filesystems, configurations
  • Physical isolation = real isolation

Option 2: Same Machine, Different OS Users (Minimum)

Section titled “Option 2: Same Machine, Different OS Users (Minimum)”
  • Multiple OS users on the same machine
  • Each with their own ~/.openclaw directory
  • File permission isolation (ensure 0700)
  • Different ports, different auth tokens

Option 3: Container Isolation

Section titled “Option 3: Container Isolation”
  • One container per user
  • Network and filesystem naturally isolated
  • Ideal for team deployments

If You’re Already Using Multi-Agent “Isolation”…

Section titled “If You’re Already Using Multi-Agent “Isolation”…”

Check Immediately

Section titled “Check Immediately”

  1. Run a security audit:

    Watch for security.trust_model.multi_user_heuristic — the audit tool detects “config looks like multi-user but is actually single Gateway” situations.

  2. Verify Gateway auth token distribution — Who has the token? If untrusted parties have it, your “viewer” permissions are meaningless.

  3. Review channel configuration — Who can trigger the bot in Telegram / Slack? Everyone who can trigger it is an operator.

Migration Path

Section titled “Migration Path”

If you find your current setup is insecure:

  1. Create independent Gateway configurations for each trust boundary
  2. Migrate respective Agent configs and credentials
  3. Update channel bindings (each Gateway binds to its own bot)
  4. Revoke the old shared token
  5. Run openclaw security audit again

Suggestions for the OpenClaw Team

Section titled “Suggestions for the OpenClaw Team”

The current trust model is clear, documented, and intentional—a personal assistant doesn’t need multi-tenancy. But as use cases expand, the community needs:

  1. Prominent warnings in Agent configuration docs — Currently, agent permission config and security docs are separate; it’s easy to read only the former and assume “this is enough”
  2. Enhanced multi-user detection in openclaw security audit — When multiple agents + multiple channel sources are detected, proactively warn about trust model limitations
  3. Long-term consideration for per-user permission layers — Supporting user-level access control without splitting Gateways, reducing operational overhead for multi-person scenarios

One-Line Takeaway

Section titled “One-Line Takeaway”

Multi-agent permissions govern what the AI can do, not what people can see. To isolate people, isolate Gateways.

Don’t let a tidy config file give you a false sense of security.

Based on analysis of official OpenClaw security documentation (docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/security). Last updated: 2026-03-29

  • OpenClaw

  • Multi-Agent
  • Trust Model
  • User Isolation

OpenClaw Permission Control Deep Dive: From 9-Layer Security to Production-Grade Hardening

Mar 29, 2026
Vibe Sparking

A comprehensive guide to OpenClaw’s tool permission system — combining official documentation and community best practices. Not just configuration templates, but a deep look at the trust model, audit mechanisms, and architecture trade-offs.

Why Permission Control Is OpenClaw’s Core Challenge

Section titled “Why Permission Control Is OpenClaw’s Core Challenge”

OpenClaw is not a chatbot — it’s an AI assistant platform with real system capabilities: file read/write, command execution, message sending, browser control, and more. A single prompt injection, if permissions aren’t locked down, could turn into an rm -rf or a bizarre email to your boss.

The fundamental question of permission control: How do you make AI powerful enough without letting it cross the line?

Part 1: Trust Model — The Foundation of All Configuration

Section titled “Part 1: Trust Model — The Foundation of All Configuration”

Personal Assistant Model, Not Multi-Tenant Platform

Section titled “Personal Assistant Model, Not Multi-Tenant Platform”

This is the most easily overlooked yet most important point:

OpenClaw’s security model is a personal assistant model — one Gateway instance = one trust boundary.

This means:

  • All users within a single Gateway share the same tool permissions. There’s no permission isolation between sessions; sessionKey is a routing selector, not an authentication token.
  • If multiple people share a bot (e.g., everyone in a Slack group can @it), every person can trigger all tool calls that agent is allowed to make.
  • Need real user isolation? Split your Gateways — use different Gateway instances for different trust boundaries, ideally running under different OS users or even different machines.

Real-World Consequences

Section titled “Real-World Consequences”
ScenarioRiskCorrect Approach
Company Slack group sharing one botAnyone can drive exec/file operations via promptsDedicated machine + dedicated OS user + minimal permissions
Personal multi-channel (Telegram + WhatsApp)Same trust domain, acceptableEnsure DM pairing + group requireMention
Family sharingFamily trust level determines configSensitive operations on separate Gateway

Part 2: The 9-Layer Permission Security Model

Section titled “Part 2: The 9-Layer Permission Security Model”

Every time AI calls a tool (read files, execute commands, send messages…), it must pass through 9 gates in sequence — blocked at any gate means termination. Layers go from coarse to fine:

Three Iron Rules

Section titled “Three Iron Rules”
  1. deny is irreversible — once any layer denies a tool, no subsequent layer can restore it
  2. Only tightening — later layers only get stricter, never re-enable what earlier layers disabled
  3. Fine overrides coarse — agent-level config overrides global; sender-level overrides group-level

⚠️ Common pitfall: Using deny: ["exec"] at Layer 1 to disable command execution, then allow: ["exec"] at Layer 5 for a specific agent — doesn’t work, exec is already dead. You can only fix it at Layer 1.

Part 3: Four Base Permission Tiers

Section titled “Part 3: Four Base Permission Tiers”

tools.profile is the starting point for permission configuration. OpenClaw provides 4 presets:

minimal — Minimum Permissions

Section titled “minimal — Minimum Permissions”
  • ✅ Status queries only, no file/command/message operations
  • Use case: Public services, demo environments, zero-trust scenarios

coding — Development Mode ⭐ Most Common

Section titled “coding — Development Mode ⭐ Most Common”
  • ✅ File read/write, command execution, session management, memory operations
  • Use case: Daily development, operations, project management

messaging — Messaging Mode

Section titled “messaging — Messaging Mode”
  • ✅ Chat session-related operations
  • ❌ No system files or commands
  • Use case: Customer service, message broadcasting, pure conversation bots

full — Full Access Mode

Section titled “full — Full Access Mode”
  • ⚠️ No restrictions whatsoever, admin use only
  • Official recommendation: Start with messaging or coding, open up as needed

Part 4: Fine-Grained Permission Configuration in Practice

Section titled “Part 4: Fine-Grained Permission Configuration in Practice”

4.1 Global Allow/Deny Lists

Section titled “4.1 Global Allow/Deny Lists”

Allow filesystem group tools but deny write operations = read-only filesystem

Tool Group Quick Reference:

  • group:fs — Filesystem (read/write/edit/apply_patch)
  • group:runtime — Runtime (exec/process)
  • group:automation — Automation (cron/gateway/browser)

4.2 Per-AI-Provider Differentiation

Section titled “4.2 Per-AI-Provider Differentiation”

Tighten permissions for cheaper/smaller models — smaller models are more susceptible to prompt injection, which is why the official audit checks models.small_params.

4.3 Multi-Agent Role Separation

Section titled “4.3 Multi-Agent Role Separation”

4.4 Sandbox Isolation

Section titled “4.4 Sandbox Isolation”

⚠️ Critical trap: Configuring sandbox.docker but not setting mode to "all" = sandbox is inactive. In this case, exec host=sandbox actually runs on the Gateway host! The official audit checks sandbox.docker_config_mode_off.

4.5 Sub-Agent Permissions

Section titled “4.5 Sub-Agent Permissions”

Sub-agents already have session operations disabled by default; this further locks down the control plane and automation tools.

4.6 Group / Channel / Sender-Level Control

Section titled “4.6 Group / Channel / Sender-Level Control”

All groups deny exec by default → specific group even stricter → but a specific user in that group gets exec back. This is the full capability of Layer 9.

Part 5: Security Auditing — Not Optional

Section titled “Part 5: Security Auditing — Not Optional”

Run Audits Regularly

Section titled “Run Audits Regularly”

Key Audit Items (Sorted by Severity)

Section titled “Key Audit Items (Sorted by Severity)”
SeverityCheckDescription
🔴 criticalgateway.bind_no_authRemote binding without authentication
🔴 criticalgateway.tailscale_funnelPublic internet exposure
🔴 criticalfs.state_dir.perms_world_writableState directory is world-writable
🔴 criticalsandbox.dangerous_network_modeDocker using host network mode
🔴 criticalsecurity.exposure.open_groups_with_elevatedOpen groups + elevated tools
🟡 warntools.exec.security_full_configuredexec bypasses approval
🟡 warntools.exec.auto_allow_skills_enabledSkills auto-trusted for exec
🟡 warnsandbox.docker_config_mode_offSandbox configured but not active
🟡 warntools.profile_minimal_overriddenAgent overrides global minimal

Selection Guide

Section titled “Selection Guide”
  • Need multi-channel + multi-agent + fine permissions → OpenClaw
  • Security compliance is a hard requirement → IronClaw (default-deny everything)
  • Embedded / resource-constrained → NanoClaw / PicoClaw
  • Quick idea validation → ZeroClaw / Nanobot
  • OpenClaw too complex but need core features → Start with ZeroClaw, migrate as needed

Part 8: Future Evolution

Section titled “Part 8: Future Evolution”

Near-Term

Section titled “Near-Term”

  1. Dynamic runtime approval expansion — Currently only exec has ask mode; future may extend to browser, gateway, cron, and more tools with runtime approval prompts.

  2. Continuous auditing — Evolving from manual openclaw security audit to background continuous monitoring + real-time alerts via webhooks.

  3. Hot permission policy updates — Permission config changes taking effect immediately without Gateway restart.

Mid-Term Trends

Section titled “Mid-Term Trends”

  1. Conditional policy engine — Evolving from static JSON allow/deny to a policy language supporting conditional expressions (time ranges, IP ranges, call frequency, etc.).

  2. Per-user permission boundaries — Implementing user-level permission isolation without splitting Gateways, reducing operational cost for multi-user scenarios.

  3. Cross-Gateway federation management — Unified policy distribution and compliance auditing for multi-instance cluster scenarios.

Long-Term Outlook

Section titled “Long-Term Outlook”

  1. RBAC / ABAC model — Evolving from tool-level allow/deny to role/attribute-based access control, integrating with enterprise IAM systems.

  2. Audit log compliance export — Supporting audit log formats required by compliance frameworks like SOC2 / ISO27001.

  3. AI behavior analysis — Detecting anomalous tool usage behavior based on historical call patterns (e.g., sudden surge in exec calls).

Conclusion

Section titled “Conclusion”

OpenClaw’s permission control system is the most comprehensive among similar products, with the 9-layer model covering everything from global scope to individual senders. Core takeaways:

  1. Understand the trust model first — Personal assistant ≠ multi-tenant; shared bot = shared permissions
  2. deny irreversibility is by design — Guarantees the security chain only tightens
  3. Start from the hardened baseline — Lock everything first, open up as needed, not the other way around
  4. Regular auditing is not optional — openclaw security audit --deep should be a routine ops habit
  5. Small model + big permissions = high risk — The weaker the model, the easier it is to inject; permissions must be tightened accordingly

Permission configuration may look complex, but it boils down to one sentence: From outside to inside, from coarse to fine, only tighten, never loosen.

Based on OpenClaw official security documentation (docs.openclaw.ai/gateway/security) and community practices. Last updated: 2026-03-29

1. Breaking Changes

Section titled “1. Breaking Changes”

1.1 Qwen Portal OAuth Removal (#52709)

Section titled “1.1 Qwen Portal OAuth Removal (#52709)”

Background: Qwen (Tongyi Qianwen) previously integrated with portal.qwen.ai via qwen-portal-auth OAuth — an early authentication method. Alibaba Cloud has since unified the Qwen API under the Model Studio platform, and the old OAuth flow is no longer maintained.

Use Case: Users running Qwen series models (qwen-turbo, qwen-plus, qwen-max, etc.) as OpenClaw inference backends.

Example: Previously, selecting Qwen during openclaw onboard would launch a browser-based OAuth authorization flow. Now it requires a direct Model Studio API Key input:

Notes:

  • ⚠️ Breaking — Existing Qwen users must reconfigure authentication after upgrading
  • You’ll need to obtain an API Key from dashscope.console.aliyun.com first
  • If any cluster instances use Qwen, prepare new keys before upgrading

Comparison with Similar Products:

ProductQwen SupportAuth Method
OpenClaw✅ Model Studio API KeyAPI Key
ZeroClaw✅ Via OpenRouter/direct configAPI Key
Nanobot✅ Native supportAPI Key
NanoClaw❌ No direct supportN/A
PicoClaw❌ NoneN/A
IronClaw✅ Via configAPI Key + encrypted storage

Trend: LLM providers standardizing on API Key authentication is the clear direction — OAuth flows are too heavyweight for CLI tools.

1.2 Doctor Auto-Migration Window Tightened

Section titled “1.2 Doctor Auto-Migration Window Tightened”

Background: openclaw doctor previously auto-fixed legacy config keys of any age. Now it only auto-migrates keys from within the last two months; older ones trigger an error instead.

Use Case: OpenClaw instances that haven’t been upgraded for a long time running openclaw doctor.

Example: If an instance hasn’t been upgraded for 3 months and its config contains old-format keys from late 2025, doctor will no longer silently fix them — it will report a validation error requiring manual intervention.

Notes:

  • ⚠️ Cluster instances may trigger this if they’ve been dormant for a while
  • Recommended: run openclaw doctor on the current version before upgrading to ensure config is up to date

Comparison: Most similar products are too new to have config migration issues. ZeroClaw has zeroclaw migrate openclaw but that’s a one-time import, not continuous migration.

Trend: A sound engineering decision — unlimited backward compatibility accumulates technical debt.

Section titled “2.1 xAI / Grok: Responses API + x_search (#56048)”

  • Search real-time trends, tweets, and public sentiment
  • Example: Ask “What are people discussing about AI Agents on X today?” → Grok uses x_search to pull real-time tweets

Notes:

  • The xAI plugin now auto-enables from web-search and tool config — no manual plugin activation needed
  • openclaw onboard and openclaw configure --section web now include x_search configuration options
  • x_search uses the shared xAI key — no additional API key required

2.2 MiniMax Image Generation + Model Cleanup (#54487)

Section titled “2.2 MiniMax Image Generation + Model Cleanup (#54487)”

Background: MiniMax is a Chinese AI company that launched the image-01 image generation model. Simultaneously, old models were cleaned up, retaining only M2.7.

Use Case:

  • Text-to-image: generate mode with aspect ratio control
  • Image-to-image: image-to-image editing mode
  • Example: Say “Generate a cyberpunk-style cat” in chat → calls MiniMax image-01

Notes:

  • Domestic API access may require specific network configuration

Comparison: Most similar products don’t natively support image generation providers, relying on users to configure MCP or external tools. OpenClaw pushes further on multimodal support.

Trend: Agents aren’t just text interaction anymore — image generation/understanding is becoming a standard capability.

2.3 OpenAI apply_patch Enabled by Default

Section titled “2.3 OpenAI apply_patch Enabled by Default”

Background: apply_patch is OpenAI Codex’s code editing tool, previously requiring manual activation.

Use Case: Now available by default when using OpenAI or Codex models for code editing tasks.

Notes:

  • Sandbox policy aligned with write permissions — apply_patch permissions match file write permissions
  • Good news for ACP tasks using Codex in our cluster

Comparison: ZeroClaw and IronClaw haven’t implemented apply_patch yet. NanoClaw handles code editing inside containers due to its container isolation approach.

2.4 Mistral Request Standardization Fix

Section titled “2.4 Mistral Request Standardization Fix”

Background: Subtle differences between Mistral’s official API and OpenAI-compatible API request formats were causing 422 errors.

Use Case: Users connecting directly to Mistral’s official API (not via OpenRouter relay).

Notes: If you previously abandoned Mistral direct connection due to 422 errors, it’s worth trying again.

2.5 Google/Gemini Model Resolution Fix (#56567)

Section titled “2.5 Google/Gemini Model Resolution Fix (#56567)”

Background: Gemini 3.1’s pro/flash/flash-lite variants failed to resolve under different provider aliases, and flash-lite had prefix-matching order issues.

Use Case: Users configured with Google AI Studio, Vertex AI, or other Gemini provider aliases.

Notes: Fixed provider ID passthrough issues and added template-provider fallback. If Gemini flash-lite model switching wasn’t working before, it should be fine now.

2.6 Ollama thinking=off Fix (#53200)

Section titled “2.6 Ollama thinking=off Fix (#53200)”

Background: When thinkingLevel=off was set, Ollama models would still generate hidden reasoning tokens in the background, wasting compute and adding latency.

Use Case: Locally deployed Ollama running thinking-capable models (e.g., DeepSeek-R1, QwQ) where reasoning isn’t needed.

Notes: The fix now sends the think: false parameter. Important for resource-constrained devices — avoids unnecessary reasoning tokens.

Comparison: PicoClaw and ZeroClaw both support Ollama, but their thinking parameter control granularity doesn’t match OpenClaw’s.

2.7 Anthropic Stop Reason Handling (#56639)

Section titled “2.7 Anthropic Stop Reason Handling (#56639)”

Background: The Anthropic API sometimes returns non-standard stop reasons (e.g., sensitive — content safety block), which previously caused OpenClaw to crash.

Use Case: Any scenario using Claude models, especially when touching sensitive topics.

Notes: Now returned as a structured error instead of a crash. Important for cluster stability.

2.8 OpenAI Codex Image Tool Fix (#54829)

Section titled “2.8 OpenAI Codex Image Tool Fix (#54829)”

Background: Codex models were missing media-understanding provider registration, causing image analysis to fail.

Use Case: Using ACP to have Codex analyze screenshots, UI images, etc.

Notes: Also fixed generic image-runtime fallback (#54858), affecting third-party providers like OpenRouter and MiniMax Portal.

2.9 OpenAI WebSocket Reasoning Preservation (#53856)

Section titled “2.9 OpenAI WebSocket Reasoning Preservation (#53856)”

Background: In WebSocket mode, tool turns would lose reasoning replay metadata and tool-call item IDs, causing subsequent reasoning to break.

Use Case: Real-time interaction scenarios using OpenAI Responses API + WebSocket.

Notes: Two fixes (reasoning blocks restored + metadata kept intact) suggest this was a deep-seated issue.

2.10 GitHub Copilot Auth Refresh (#55360)

Section titled “2.10 GitHub Copilot Auth Refresh (#55360)”

Background: The expires_at value was treated as milliseconds when it was actually a seconds-level epoch, causing setTimeout to overflow and enter an infinite hot loop.

Use Case: Users running GitHub Copilot as a provider.

Notes: This was a performance bug — it would max out CPU. If you previously experienced system sluggishness after configuring Copilot, this was the cause.

2.11 Agent Model-Level Rate Limit Isolation (#49834)

Section titled “2.11 Agent Model-Level Rate Limit Isolation (#49834)”

Background: Previously, one model hitting 429 would block all models under the same auth profile.

Use Case: Configurations with multiple model fallbacks (e.g., Claude → GPT → Gemini).

Example: Claude hits 429, GPT should continue working, but previously the entire profile got cooled down.

Notes:

  • Cooldown strategy changed from exponential (1min → 1h) to stepped (30s / 1min / 5min) — more reasonable
  • New user-visible countdown messages
  • Important for heavily-used cluster instances

ZeroClaw✅ Trait-driven✅Basic

2.13 Agent Model Hot-Switching

Section titled “2.13 Agent Model Hot-Switching”

Background: Switching models mid-embedded-run previously waited for the current run to finish before taking effect.

Use Case: Using /model to switch to another model when the current one is overloaded or stuck.

Notes: Now switches at the next safe retry boundary without waiting for the entire run to complete. Noticeably improves responsiveness.

4.3 Agent Compaction Multiple Fixes (#49479, #51072, #46417, #45493)

Section titled “4.3 Agent Compaction Multiple Fixes (#49479, #51072, #46417, #45493)”

Background: Compaction (context compression) is a critical feature for long conversations. This release includes four related fixes:

  1. Post-compaction AGENTS refresh maintained in stale-usage preflight and queued followups
  2. Cancellation reason refinement — safeguard-specific cancel vs. manual /compact no-op distinction
  3. Timeout recovery — compress before high-context LLM timeout instead of retrying
  4. Count coordination — embedded auto-compaction success updates sessions.json

Use Case: Long-running agent sessions, especially during complex coding tasks.

Notes: #46417 is particularly important — previously, high-context timeouts would infinitely retry the same oversized request. Now it compresses first, then retries.

OpenClaw Upgrade: Plugins Crashed? Just Run Update Twice

Mar 26, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw Upgrade: Plugins Crashed? Just Run Update Twice

Section titled “OpenClaw Upgrade: Plugins Crashed? Just Run Update Twice”

46 seconds. Core upgrade done. Logs clean. Version jumped from 2026.3.23-2 to 2026.3.24.

Then both plugins crashed.

QQ Bot and WeChat, same error. A hashed build artifact that no longer exists.

What happened

Section titled “What happened”

The DDmlaKdG in install.runtime-DDmlaKdG.js is a build-time hash. When the core upgraded from the old version to the new one, it repackaged everything — new hashes. But the first-round plugin update was still running from the old process, which held the old module map in memory. It tried to load a file that had already been replaced.

Classic update-order race condition. Core files swapped, installer still reading the old map.

The fix: run it again

Section titled “The fix: run it again”

Second round, the core version stayed the same (already latest), but the installer was now the new one. Paths resolved correctly. Both plugins installed:

  • @tencent-connect/openclaw-qqbot → v1.6.5
  • @tencent-weixin/openclaw-weixin → v2.0.1

38.4 seconds. Done.

Bonus: plugin security scanning

Section titled “Bonus: plugin security scanning”

The second update run printed a batch of WARNINGs I hadn’t paid attention to before. This time I read them.

OpenClaw runs static code analysis on every plugin, flagging two high-risk patterns:

Environment variable access + network send. Reading tokens from env, then sending data over the network. This is the textbook credential exfiltration pattern. For messaging platform plugins, it’s expected behavior (they need API keys to call platform APIs). The scanner doesn’t judge intent — it flags everything.

Shell command execution. Plugins calling child_process. Audio transcoding via ffmpeg, platform detection via uname — all reasonable. But malicious plugins could use the same mechanism to run arbitrary code.

QQ Bot plugin warnings

Section titled “QQ Bot plugin warnings”
LocationWhat it does
gateway.ts:49Env vars + network send
slash-commands.ts:37Shell command
audio-convert.ts:630Audio transcoding (ffmpeg)
platform.ts:305Platform detection
postinstall-link-sdk.js:43Post-install script
proactive-api-server.ts:37Env vars + network send

WeChat plugin warnings

Section titled “WeChat plugin warnings”
LocationWhat it does
log-upload.ts:76Shell command
process-message.ts:428Env vars + network send

For official Tencent-maintained plugins, these are false positives. But if you’re installing unknown third-party plugins and see these warnings, read the source code.

OpenClaw’s approach is right — better to over-report than to miss something.

Config backup

Section titled “Config backup”

Plugin updates modify the main config file. OpenClaw backs it up automatically:

If behavior changes after an upgrade, diff the two files to see what moved.

Manifest ID vs npm package name

Section titled “Manifest ID vs npm package name”

The npm package has a scope (@tencent-connect/), but the plugin’s internal manifest uses the short name (openclaw-qqbot). Config files use the short name. Keep this in mind when editing openclaw.json.

Upgrade checklist

Section titled “Upgrade checklist”
  1. Plugin throws ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND? Run openclaw update again
  2. Check plugin security warnings, especially for unofficial plugins
  3. Diff openclaw.json before and after upgrades
  4. Time budget: core ~40s, with plugins about a minute total

Recorded 2026-03-26, OpenClaw 2026.3.24, macOS arm64

OpenClaw v2026.3.24 Stable: Teams SDK Migration, Sandbox Security Fix, 27 Bug Fixes

Mar 26, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw v2026.3.24 Stable

Section titled “OpenClaw v2026.3.24 Stable”

Five days, four releases. v2026.3.22 broke records. v2026.3.23 patched 29 bugs in 48 hours. v2026.3.24-beta.1 landed 18 feature changes and 40+ fixes. Beta.2 ran a quick RC validation. Now the stable release is out, moving everything from beta.1 into the stable channel with 27 bug fixes.

This post won’t rehash beta.1 content. It focuses on fixes new to the stable release, the security change you need to know about, and how the beta-to-stable pipeline worked.

Reference: GitHub Release v2026.3.24

Beta to Stable: A 3-Day Convergence

Section titled “Beta to Stable: A 3-Day Convergence”

Beta.2 cherry-picked only 3 fixes for validation and shipped stable 2.5 hours later. The team was confident in beta.1’s quality. Beta.2 was a smoke test, not a regression sweep.

Feature Changes: Same as Beta.1

Section titled “Feature Changes: Same as Beta.1”

All 18 feature changes are identical to beta.1. Nothing added, nothing removed. If you read the beta.1 post, skip this section.

Key changes at a glance:

  • Gateway: /v1/models and /v1/embeddings endpoints, model parameter passthrough
  • Teams: Official SDK migration with streaming replies, welcome cards, AI labeling
  • Teams: Message edit and delete
  • Skills: Install metadata for 7 built-in skills with guided dependency setup
  • Control UI: Skills management overhaul with status filters and detail dialogs
  • Slack: Rich interactive reply consistency restored, Options: auto-renders as buttons
  • CLI: --container flag for Docker/Podman in-container execution
  • Discord: LLM-generated thread titles
  • Plugins: before_dispatch hook
  • Control UI/macOS: 6 UI improvements (file preview, tree navigation, model selector)
  • Runtime: Node 22 minimum lowered to 22.14
  • CLI: Node version preflight check before upgrade

Security Fix: Media Path Alias Sandbox Bypass

Section titled “Security Fix: Media Path Alias Sandbox Bypass”

This is the most important fix in this release.

Problem: Outbound tools and message actions could bypass media-root restrictions through mediaUrl or fileUrl alias fields, accessing files outside the sandbox. A malicious prompt injection could trick an agent into reading /etc/passwd via fileUrl and sending it externally.

Root cause: Security boundary checks only covered primary path fields. Alias fields were unchecked.

Impact: Multi-tenant OpenClaw deployments are at highest risk. Single-user setups are less exposed but should still upgrade.

Path traversal via alias fields is a classic web security issue. Jupyter Notebook and Code Server have both had similar vulnerabilities. This fix unifies all path fields under the same security check.

Bug Fixes: 16 Items in Stable Changelog

Section titled “Bug Fixes: 16 Items in Stable Changelog”

Outbound Media/Local Files: Policy Alignment

Section titled “Outbound Media/Local Files: Policy Alignment”

Sending host-machine local files failed when workspaceOnly was off. File sending used different permission logic than file reading. If you worked around this by copying files into the workspace, you can remove that workaround.

Gateway Restart Session Recovery

Section titled “Gateway Restart Session Recovery”

After a gateway restart, interrupted sessions got a best-effort restart notification but thread/topic routing information could be lost. Now uses heartbeat-based wakeup, preserves routing info, and retries failed outbound delivery once.

Docker First-Install Boot Loop

Section titled “Docker First-Install Boot Loop”

Fresh Docker installs got stuck in a loop: the CLI tried to connect to the gateway before it started, but the gateway needed config that the CLI was supposed to write. Classic chicken-and-egg. Fixed by writing config through the gateway process directly, bypassing network dependency.

Channel Startup Fault Isolation

Section titled “Channel Startup Fault Isolation”

An expired Telegram bot token would take down not just Telegram but Discord and WhatsApp too. Channels started serially with no try-catch isolation. Now each channel fails independently. This is the bulkhead pattern applied to channel startup.

WhatsApp Echo Suppression

Section titled “WhatsApp Echo Suppression”

In groups, gateway-sent messages were processed as new inbound messages, creating reply loops. The fix also stopped suppressing owner commands sent from linked accounts. Now tracks recently sent message IDs and only suppresses matching echoes.

WhatsApp Reply-to-Bot Detection

Section titled “WhatsApp Reply-to-Bot Detection”

Replying to a bot message in a group to trigger the bot stopped working. The bot’s selfLid was being read differently. WhatsApp’s linked account mode, where bot and owner share one number, is the root complexity here.

Telegram Forum #General Topic Routing

Section titled “Telegram Forum #General Topic Routing”

The #General topic (topic ID = 1) in Telegram forum mode failed to route when Telegram omitted forum metadata. If you use OpenClaw in Telegram forum groups, upgrade for this fix.

Discord Gateway Crash Elimination

Section titled “Discord Gateway Crash Elimination”

Discord server disconnects caused full process crashes instead of graceful reconnection. Lifecycle errors during startup, runtime, and teardown phases are now properly classified and handled.

Discord Timeout Visible Replies

Section titled “Discord Timeout Visible Replies”

When a Discord worker timed out (agent thinking too long), users saw nothing. Now sends a visible timeout message.

ACP Direct Chats TTS Empty Audio

Section titled “ACP Direct Chats TTS Empty Audio”

In voice conversation mode, if TTS synthesis failed, neither audio nor text was delivered. Now falls back to text delivery when TTS returns empty audio.

Telegram 403 Error Handling

Section titled “Telegram 403 Error Handling”

After a bot was kicked from a group, queued messages kept retrying forever. Now preserves specific 403 reasons (blocked/kicked/not a member) and marks “bot not a member” as permanent failure to stop retries.

Telegram Photo Size Preflight

Section titled “Telegram Photo Size Preflight”

Uploading photos that didn’t meet Telegram’s dimension requirements failed with PHOTO_INVALID_DIMENSIONS. Now checks dimensions before sending and falls back to document upload. Telegram rules: longest side under 1280px, aspect ratio under 20:1.

Slack DM Reply Optimization

Section titled “Slack DM Reply Optimization”

DM replies had unnecessary overhead, and web-search was triggered automatically when it shouldn’t have been. Streamlined reply logic, web-search changed to explicit opt-in.

Embedded Runs SecretRef Crash

Section titled “Embedded Runs SecretRef Crash”

Unresolved SecretRef configuration crashed embedded agent runs. Now falls back to the resolved runtime snapshot.

Hidden Fixes: In Beta.1 but Not Listed in Stable Changelog

Section titled “Hidden Fixes: In Beta.1 but Not Listed in Stable Changelog”

These shipped in beta.1, were validated through beta.2, and entered stable — but the stable changelog doesn’t list them individually.

  • Feishu SecretRef startup crash: Unresolved SecretRef treated as “not configured” instead of crashing
  • Feishu open group policy @mention filtering: Non-text messages in groupPolicy: open groups were blocked by implicit mention checks. After upgrade, bot receives all non-text messages in groups
  • Feishu @mention detection degradation: Bot identity fetch timeout raised to 30s with background recovery
  • Feishu/Teams card payload: Native card payload changed from required to optional
  • Feishu docx block ordering: Document block order scrambled when writing new documents
  • Google image model migration: openclaw doctor --fix didn’t set /v1beta path correctly
  • Custom Google provider paths: Custom-named providers lost /v1beta prefix
  • Telegram slash commands under SecretRef
  • Docker Compose port parsing: "8080:3000" format parsed incorrectly
  • LanceDB proxy environment embedding requests
  • Build stability: Hash chunk files or shell shims broken after local rebuilds
  • Skill installer security hardening: Regex whitelist, output sanitize, URL protocol restrictions, source warnings

Skill Installer Security Hardening Details

Section titled “Skill Installer Security Hardening Details”

Worth calling out separately:

  1. Install commands validated against a regex whitelist — only predefined package manager commands allowed
  2. Skill metadata sanitized before terminal output to prevent escape sequence injection
  3. URL fields restricted to http/https, blocking file:// and other protocols
  4. Non-built-in skill installs show source warnings
  5. Removed file:// workspace links

These hardening measures alongside the new /v1/models and other endpoints show the team taking security boundaries seriously while expanding functionality.

Upgrade Recommendations

Section titled “Upgrade Recommendations”

Must upgrade:

  • Multi-tenant OpenClaw (media path alias sandbox bypass)
  • Telegram forum groups (General topic routing fix)
  • Docker deployments that hit the first-install boot loop
  • WhatsApp groups with echo loops

Should upgrade:

  • Teams integration users (SDK migration is a full rewrite)
  • Gateway OpenAI compatibility needed
  • Slack rich interactive components

Can wait:

  • Single-channel, single-user deployments running stable

Upgrade:

If your Node.js version is below 22.14, the new version tells you before installing instead of crashing after.

Trends

Section titled “Trends”

Five days, four releases from v2026.3.22 to v2026.3.24. This pace reflects where OpenClaw is: alternating between feature expansion and stability convergence.

Directions to watch:

  • OpenAI compatibility layer is filling out. Assistants API and Realtime WebSocket proxy are likely next.
  • Plugin lifecycle hooks currently only have before_dispatch. A full message lifecycle hook system is coming.
  • Skill ecosystem moved from install metadata to security hardening, building toward a ClawHub marketplace.
  • Feishu got 5 bug fixes in one release, signaling growing adoption in China and active community feedback.

OpenClaw’s positioning in 2026 has shifted from “multi-channel bot” to “AI Agent platform.” Local-first, omnichannel delivery, programmable — that intersection has no direct competitor.

One Session, Idea to 57 Passing Tests: Building OpenClaw Fleet Manager with gstack

Mar 25, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Date: 2026-03-25 Project: OpenClaw Fleet Manager (vs-openclaw-ops) Tools: Claude Code + gstack (office-hours, plan-eng-review, plan-design-review)

Where I Started

Section titled “Where I Started”

I had a rough ideas document — a management solution for OpenClaw, the open-source AI agent platform with 247K+ GitHub stars. The core concept: help IT admins deploy and manage multiple OpenClaw instances through Docker container isolation, with a web admin panel. Three tiers (personal, team, enterprise), a pile of bullet points, zero code.

That was it. No architecture design. No UI design. No repository. Just a markdown file and a wishlist.

What gstack Did

Section titled “What gstack Did”

Act 1: /office-hours — From Idea to Design Document

Section titled “Act 1: /office-hours — From Idea to Design Document”

gstack’s /office-hours skill ran a structured brainstorming session that felt like actual YC office hours. It worked through five questions one by one:

  1. What’s the coolest version of this? → “One-click deployment”
  2. Who would you demo this to? → “Enterprise IT admins”
  3. What’s the fastest thing you could ship? → “A complete PoC”
  4. What’s the closest competitor, and what makes yours different? → “Portainer — too generic”
  5. What’s the 10x vision? → “AI-driven ops — a master OpenClaw managing the entire fleet”

Then it searched the competitive landscape. Found real competitors: ClawHost (single-instance deployment), NanoClaw (Docker Sandbox container isolation), Docker’s own cagent project. But nothing offered an “OpenClaw managing OpenClaw” fleet management model.

Codex second opinion: gstack called OpenAI’s Codex (GPT-5.4) for an independent cold-read analysis. Codex delivered the sharpest insight of the entire session: “What actually excites him isn’t the admin dashboard UI — it’s the infrastructure magic. If they lose sight of that and spend months on CRUD screens, they’ve drifted from their own north star.”

That reframed the entire build order: CLI first, magic first, UI second.

Output: a complete design document covering problem statement, three implementation options, assumptions, cross-model perspectives, and a recommended approach — all written to ~/.gstack/projects/ for downstream skills to consume automatically.

The spec review loop then ran 3 rounds of adversarial review (5/10 → 6/10 → 7/10), surfacing missing failure handling, undefined health-check intervals, and SQLite write contention — things I never would have caught myself.

Act 2: /plan-eng-review — Locking Down Architecture

Section titled “Act 2: /plan-eng-review — Locking Down Architecture”

The engineering review found 4 architectural divergences between my design document and the tech stack I actually wanted to use:

DecisionDesign Doc SaidWhat I WantedReview Conclusion
DatabaseSQLitePostgreSQLSQLite for PoC — Postgres adds deployment friction, contradicts “one-click magic”
AuthSimple API Keybcryptjs + JWTAPI Key — single-user PoC doesn’t need password hashing
DesktopOut of scopeInclude in monorepoDirectory placeholder only — don’t build it
Shared packages1 package3 packagesKeep 3 (I won this one)

Each decision came as an AskUserQuestion with effort estimates, completeness scores, and explicit recommendations. No hedging — concrete tradeoffs throughout.

The test review generated an ASCII coverage map across 40 code paths spanning server, CLI, and web, marking which paths needed unit tests and which needed E2E. It flagged two critical gaps: ocm create timeout handling and ocm upgrade failure rollback.

Act 3: /plan-design-review — From 3/10 to 7/10

Section titled “Act 3: /plan-design-review — From 3/10 to 7/10”

The design review was brutal. Codex and Claude evaluated independently, and the UI design scored near zero across all 7 criteria. Key findings:

  • Hard veto #1: The landing screen risked becoming a generic SaaS card grid
  • Hard veto #7: The app UI used stacked cards instead of a real layout
  • Every check failed — unclear branding, no visual anchor, page purpose not scannable from headings, unclear section responsibilities

The fix: a table-first operational workspace designed for IT admins. A fleet health summary bar across the top, table columns with OpenClaw-specific fields (channels, version, model, status), and a split-panel layout with tabs for instance details.

The interaction states table alone captured 6 unspecified states that would have shipped as “no data” without the review:

  • Empty state → guided CTA (“Create your first instance”)
  • Destroy confirmation → type instance name to confirm (like GitHub repo deletion)
  • Create progress → 60-second progress bar + live log output
  • SSE disconnect → low-profile banner + auto-reconnect

Act 4: YOLO Mode — Implementation

Section titled “Act 4: YOLO Mode — Implementation”

With architecture and design locked, I said “YOLO mode” and let Claude Code build without interruption.

Built in a single session:

Test results: 57/57 passing

Server tests use a mocked dockerode (no real Docker daemon required) and a fresh in-memory SQLite database per test. Every API test gets a fully isolated database — zero state leakage between tests.

Key implementation details that came directly from the review sessions:

  • Upgrade rollback: if the new container fails to start, the service automatically rebuilds using the previous version
  • Port allocation: sequential assignment starting from base port 3100, with exhaustion detection at base + 200
  • CLI auto-start: if the server isn’t running, the CLI automatically starts it in the background
  • Audit log: every create/destroy/upgrade/stop operation records a timestamp, action, instance name, and JSON details

What I Took Away from gstack

Section titled “What I Took Away from gstack”

The Review Pipeline Is the Product

Section titled “The Review Pipeline Is the Product”

The three skills — /office-hours, /plan-eng-review, /plan-design-review — form a pipeline where each skill consumes the output of the previous one. The office-hours design document feeds automatically into the engineering review. The engineering review’s architecture decisions feed into the design review. The design review’s state table feeds into the test plan.

Decisions are cumulative and nothing gets lost. When I said “SQLite for PoC” in the engineering review, that decision propagated into test configuration (in-memory SQLite), CLI behavior (no external database dependency), and the Docker service (no Postgres container in the compose file).

Cross-Model Tension Is Valuable

Section titled “Cross-Model Tension Is Valuable”

gstack called Codex (GPT-5.4) twice — once for a project cold-read during office-hours, once for independent UI critique during the design review. Both times Codex caught things Claude missed:

  • Office-hours: Codex introduced a “GitOps agent fleet” concept that became the innovation/lateral option
  • Design review: Codex flagged a copy model error — the UI was using emotional language (“infrastructure magic”) instead of operational language (“instances”, “health history”, “upgradeable”)

The cross-model synthesis section explicitly marked where the two models agreed and where they diverged. Agreement = higher confidence. Divergence = worth examining further.

The “Boil the Lake” Principle Actually Works

Section titled “The “Boil the Lake” Principle Actually Works”

gstack’s core premise: AI makes the marginal cost of completeness approach zero, so always do the complete thing. In practice:

  • The spec review ran 3 rounds rather than stopping at the first pass
  • The test coverage map traced all 40 code paths, not just the happy path
  • The design review covered all 7 dimensions, not just “looks okay”
  • The upgrade service implemented rollback rather than “rebuild and hope”

The marginal cost of doing complete work with AI really does approach zero. Writing 57 tests took roughly 10 minutes. The upgrade rollback logic took roughly 5 minutes. The name-confirmation destroy dialog would take roughly 5 minutes to implement in the UI. None of it is worth skipping.

By the Numbers

Section titled “By the Numbers”
MetricValue
Total session time~2 hours
Design doc review rounds3 (5→6→7/10)
Architecture decisions4 (all resolved)
Design decisions12 (all resolved)
Critical gaps found2 (create timeout, upgrade rollback)
Code files created18
Tests written57
Tests passing57
External AI calls2 (Codex for office-hours + design review)
Web panel completion0 (still to build)

What’s Next

Section titled “What’s Next”

The web panel (Next.js + shadcn/ui) is the remaining 40% of the PoC. The design review already specified it:

  • Table-first workspace + fleet health summary bar
  • Create wizard (2 steps: name + version, then optional channel)
  • Instance detail split-panel layout + tabs
  • Audit log + filtering by instance and action type
  • All interaction states (loading, empty, error, success, destroy confirmation)

The test plan is written. The API is built. Types are shared. All that’s left is the frontend.

Built with gstack v0.11.18.2 — full office-hours → eng-review → design-review → implementation pipeline.
