OpenClaw v2026.3.24-beta.1: Gateway Compat, Teams Rewrite, One-Click Skills, Container CLI

Mar 25, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw v2026.3.24-beta.1

Section titled “OpenClaw v2026.3.24-beta.1”

Three releases in four days. v2026.3.22 was the biggest release in OpenClaw history. v2026.3.23 cleaned up 29 bugs within 48 hours. Now v2026.3.24-beta.1 lands with gateway compatibility changes, a full Microsoft Teams SDK migration, one-click skill installs, container CLI support, a Control UI overhaul, and another 40+ fixes.

The beta tag is honest: this moves fast, test before you deploy.

Reference: GitHub Release v2026.3.24-beta.1

Gateway: OpenAI Compatibility for RAG and Custom Clients

Section titled “Gateway: OpenAI Compatibility for RAG and Custom Clients”

The gateway now speaks more of the OpenAI API surface. Three changes, all from @vincentkoc.

/v1/models and /v1/embeddings. Tools like LangChain, LlamaIndex, and custom RAG pipelines that probe /v1/models before sending requests used to get 404s from OpenClaw’s gateway. Now they get a model list. Embedding endpoints work too.

Explicit model overrides. If a client sends a specific model name through /v1/chat/completions or /v1/responses, the gateway now forwards it instead of silently replacing it with the agent’s default. RAG orchestrators that route different queries to different models can now pass through OpenClaw without losing that routing.

If you’re using OpenClaw as a gateway in front of a RAG stack, this is the change that makes it work without wrapper hacks.

Microsoft Teams: Full SDK Migration

Section titled “Microsoft Teams: Full SDK Migration”

This isn’t a patch. The entire Teams integration has been rewritten on the official Microsoft Teams SDK. Two PRs — #51808 and #49925 — cover the full scope.

Streaming 1:1 replies. DM responses now stream token-by-token instead of arriving as a single block after the model finishes.

Welcome cards with prompt starters. New conversations show a card with suggested prompts so users don’t stare at an empty chat wondering what to type.

Feedback and reflection. Users can rate responses. The bot can reflect on its own output.

Typing indicators and status updates. The bot shows “typing…” while processing and sends informative status updates for long-running operations.

Native AI labeling. Messages from the bot are labeled as AI-generated, following Microsoft’s AI-agent UX guidelines.

Message edit and delete. Sent messages can be edited or deleted, including in-thread fallbacks when no explicit target is provided.

If your organization runs Teams and has been waiting for OpenClaw’s Teams support to feel production-ready, this is it.

Skills: One-Click Install and Status Filters

Section titled “Skills: One-Click Install and Status Filters”

Skills used to require reading docs, checking dependencies, and manually configuring API keys. Two changes make this simpler.

Install recipes on bundled skills. Seven bundled skills — coding-agent, gh-issues, openai-whisper-api, session-logs, tmux, trello, weather — now include install metadata. The CLI and Control UI can detect missing requirements and offer to install them. Thanks @BunsDev. (#53411)

Control UI status-filter tabs. The skills page now shows tabs: All / Ready / Needs Setup / Disabled, each with counts. Clicking a skill opens a detail dialog with requirements, a toggle switch, install action, API key entry, source metadata, and homepage link. The old inline cards are gone. Thanks @BunsDev. (#53411)

CLI improvements. The missing-requirements label softened from “missing” to “needs setup.” openclaw skills info now surfaces where to get an API key, the CLI save command, and the storage path. The macOS app shows a “Get your key” link and storage-path hint in the API key editor. Thanks @BunsDev. (#53411)

CLI: Run Commands Inside Containers

Section titled “CLI: Run Commands Inside Containers”

New --container flag and OPENCLAW_CONTAINER env var. Point any openclaw command at a running Docker or Podman OpenClaw container and it executes inside that container. Thanks @sallyom. (#52651)

Before:

After:

Works with any openclaw subcommand. No more shell-into-container-then-run workflows.

Control UI: Visual Overhaul

Section titled “Control UI: Visual Overhaul”

Five changes from @BunsDev that collectively redesign the Control UI. (#53411)

Agent workspace files. File rows in the agent workspace are now expandable <details> elements with lazy-loaded inline markdown preview. Comprehensive .sidebar-markdown styles cover headings, lists, code blocks, tables, blockquotes, and details/summary.

Markdown preview dialog. Frosted backdrop, properly sized panel, styled header, and @create-markdown/preview v2 system theme. Headings, tables, code blocks, callouts, and blockquotes auto-adapt to light/dark mode.

macOS app navigation. The horizontal pill-based subsection navigation is replaced with a collapsible tree sidebar using disclosure chevrons and indented rows.

Agent model selector. The default agent model dropdown now shows a “Not set” placeholder instead of being blank.

Live tools view. The /tools endpoint now shows what tools the current agent can actually use right now, with a compact default view and optional detailed mode. The Control UI adds a live “Available Right Now” section.

Slack: Rich Reply Parity Restored

Section titled “Slack: Rich Reply Parity Restored”

Rich reply formatting was broken for direct deliveries. Trailing Options: lines in responses now auto-render as buttons/selects. Interactive setup defaults improved. Reply controls are isolated from plugin interactive handlers. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#53389)

Discord: Auto-Thread Naming

Section titled “Discord: Auto-Thread Naming”

New optional autoThreadName: "generated" config. Auto-created threads can be renamed asynchronously with LLM-generated titles. The existing message-based naming remains the default. Thanks @davidguttman. (#43366)

Plugins: before_dispatch Hook

Section titled “Plugins: before_dispatch Hook”

New before_dispatch hook with canonical inbound metadata. Handled replies route through the normal final-delivery path, preserving TTS and routed delivery semantics. Thanks @gfzhx. (#50444)

Security Fixes

Section titled “Security Fixes”

Sandbox media bypass closed. The mediaUrl/fileUrl alias was a way to escape media-root restrictions on outbound tool and message actions. Closed. (#54034)

Skill installer validation. Skill installer metadata is now validated against strict regex allowlists per package manager. Skill metadata is sanitized for terminal output. URL protocol allowlisting applies to markdown preview and skill homepage links. Non-bundled skill install sources get a warning. Unsafe file:// workspace links are removed. Thanks @BunsDev. (#53471)

Bug Fixes: The Full List

Section titled “Bug Fixes: The Full List”

Gateway and Runtime

Section titled “Gateway and Runtime”

Restart sentinel. After a restart, the interrupted agent session now wakes via heartbeat instead of a best-effort restart note. Outbound delivery retries once on transient failure. Explicit thread/topic routing is preserved through the wake path. Thanks @VACInc. (#53940)

Docker setup loop. Fresh Docker installs were failing because the pre-start openclaw-cli onboard/config writes tried to reach a gateway that wasn’t up yet — creating a namespace loop. Setup-time writes now route through openclaw-gateway. Thanks @amsminn. (#53385)

Channel boot isolation. Channel startup stays sequential, but per-channel boot failures are now isolated. One broken channel no longer blocks the rest. Thanks @JonathanJing. (#54215)

Embedded run secrets. Unresolved SecretRef config no longer crashes embedded agent runs — falls back to the resolved runtime snapshot. Fixes #45838.

Gateway ports. Docker Compose-style OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_PORT host publish values parse correctly without reviving the legacy CLAWDBOT_GATEWAY_PORT override. Thanks @bebule. (#44083)

Runtime build. Lazy dist runtime entry paths and bundled plugin npm staging stabilized so local rebuilds stop breaking. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#53855)

WhatsApp

Section titled “WhatsApp”

Group echo suppression. The bot now tracks recent gateway-sent message IDs and suppresses only matching group echoes. Owner /status, /new, and /activation commands from linked-account fromMe traffic are preserved. Thanks @w-sss. (#53624)

Reply-to-bot detection. Implicit group reply detection restored by unwrapping botInvokeMessage payloads and reading selfLid from creds.json. Reply-based mentions reach the bot again in linked-account group chats.

Telegram

Section titled “Telegram”

Forum topic recovery. #General topic 1 routing recovered when Telegram omits forum metadata. Covers native commands, interactive callbacks, inbound message context, and fallback error replies. Thanks @huntharo. (#53699)

Outbound error handling. Actionable 403 membership/block/kick details preserved. Bot-not-a-member treated as permanent delivery failure — Telegram sends stop retrying doomed chats. Thanks @w-sss. (#53635)

Photo validation. Telegram photo dimension and aspect-ratio rules are checked before sending. Invalid or unavailable image metadata falls back to document sends instead of failing with PHOTO_INVALID_DIMENSIONS. Thanks @hnshah. (#52545)

Pairing codes. Rendered as Telegram-only code blocks while keeping shared pairing replies plain text for other channels. Thanks @sumukhj1219. (#52784)

Native commands. Slash-command execution runs against the resolved runtime snapshot so DM commands reply even when fresh config reads surface unresolved SecretRefs. Thanks @nimbleenigma. (#53179)

Topic creation from CLI. Message thread create routes through Telegram topic-create with the required topic name field. Thanks @andyliu. (#54336)

Discord

Section titled “Discord”

Gateway supervision. Gateway error handling centralized behind a lifetime-owned supervisor. Early, active, and late-teardown Carbon gateway errors stay classified consistently and stop surfacing as process-killing teardown crashes.

Timeout replies. A visible timeout reply is sent when the inbound worker times out before a final reply starts. Includes auto-thread targets and queued-run ordering. Thanks @Kimbo7870. (#53823)

Config types. Missing autoArchiveDuration added to DiscordGuildChannelConfig so TypeScript definitions match schema and runtime. Thanks @davidguttman. (#43427)

Feishu

Section titled “Feishu”

Startup crashes. Unresolved SecretRef app credentials treated as not-configured during account resolution. CLI startup and read-only Feishu config surfaces stop crashing. Thanks @hpt. (#53675)

Group policy. When groupPolicy is open, image, file, audio, and non-text group messages reach the bot without requiring @mentions, unless operators explicitly enable mention gating. Thanks @byungsker. (#54058)

Mention enforcement. requireMention enforcement stays strict when bot identity probes fail. Startup timeout raised to 30s. Cancellable background identity recovery added. Thanks @lefarcen. (#43788)

Card payloads. Provider-native card payloads made optional in merged tool schemas. Media-only sends stop failing validation. Thanks @lndyzwdxhs. (#53715)

Docx block ordering. Document tree order from docx.document.convert is preserved when inserting blocks. Heading/paragraph/list misordering in Feishu documents fixed. Thanks @TaoXieSZ. (#40524)

Slack

Section titled “Slack”

Runtime defaults. Slack DM reply overhead trimmed. Codex auto transport restored. DM preview threading, cache scoping, warning dedupe, and explicit web-search opt-in tightened. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#53957)

ACP

Section titled “ACP”

Direct chat delivery. A terminal ACP result is always delivered when final TTS doesn’t yield audio, even if block text already streamed. Redundant empty-text final synthesis skipped. Thanks @w-sss. (#53692)

Models and Providers

Section titled “Models and Providers”

Doctor/image generation. Migrated legacy Nano Banana Google provider config seeded with the /v1beta API root and an empty model list so openclaw doctor --fix completes. Thanks @mahopan. (#53757)

Google model normalization. Bare Google Generative AI API roots normalized for custom provider names. Built-in Google model-id rewrites work when api is declared only on individual models. Thanks @Kathie-yu. (#44969)

DeepSeek pricing. Zero-cost DeepSeek catalog rates replaced with current DeepSeek V3.2 pricing. Usage totals stop showing $0.00. Thanks @arkyu2077. (#54143)

Memory and Plugins

Section titled “Memory and Plugins”

LanceDB proxy. The env-configured HTTP/HTTPS proxy dispatcher bootstraps before OpenAI embeddings requests. Memory capture and recall work in proxy-required environments again. Thanks @neeravmakwana. (#54119)

Builtin SQLite memory. Redundant sync and status query churn reduced by snapshotting file state once per source, reusing sync statements, and consolidating status reads. Thanks @vincentkoc.

Plugin hooks. Terminal hook decision semantics enforced for tool/message guards. Thanks @joshavant. (#54241)

Agents and Cron

Section titled “Agents and Cron”

Cron heartbeat suppression. The default heartbeat system prompt is suppressed for cron-triggered embedded runs, even when targeting non-cron session keys. Cron tasks stop reading HEARTBEAT.md and polluting unrelated threads. Thanks @Protocol-zero-0. (#53152)

Cron delivery. Best-effort announce runs marked as not-delivered when any payload fails. Partial delivery failures logged instead of silently reporting success. Thanks @MoerAI. (#42535)

CLI and Tooling

Section titled “CLI and Tooling”

Log timestamps. Pretty log timestamps always include an explicit timezone offset in both default UTC and --local-time modes. Thanks @sahilsatralkar. (#38904)

Browser detection. macOS LaunchServices Edge bundle IDs recognized so Chromium detection stops falling back to Chrome when Edge is the system default. Thanks @zoherghadyali. (#48561)

Marketplace

Section titled “Marketplace”

ClawHub skill URL. Corrected the ClawHub skill URL in agent docs. Marketplace archive downloads stream to disk so installs avoid excess memory use. Thanks @QuinnH496. (#54160)

TUI

Section titled “TUI”

Chat history. Pending user messages preserved when a slow local run emits an empty final event. History reload deferred and flushed after the newer active run finishes. Silent/tool-only runs no longer stay incomplete. Thanks @joelnishanth. (#53130)

Docs

Section titled “Docs”

IRC examples. Five json55 code-fence typos fixed so Mintlify applies JSON5 syntax highlighting correctly. Thanks @Hollychou924. (#50842)

Upgrade

Section titled “Upgrade”

This is a pre-release beta. Test in staging before production.

If you’re still on v2026.3.22, go through v2026.3.23 first — the v2026.3.23 fixes are included here, but the migration path is smoother in sequence.

Contributors

Section titled “Contributors”

25+ contributors in this release: @vincentkoc, @BunsDev, @sallyom, @davidguttman, @gfzhx, @VACInc, @amsminn, @JonathanJing, @w-sss, @huntharo, @hnshah, @sumukhj1219, @nimbleenigma, @bebule, @neeravmakwana, @joshavant, @Protocol-zero-0, @MoerAI, @sahilsatralkar, @zoherghadyali, @QuinnH496, @joelnishanth, @Hollychou924, @hpt, @byungsker, @lefarcen, @lndyzwdxhs, @TaoXieSZ, @Kimbo7870, @mahopan, @Kathie-yu, @arkyu2077, @andyliu, @07akioni.

OpenClaw WeChat Plugin Installed But Silent? Four Hidden Traps

Mar 25, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw WeChat Plugin Installed But Silent? Four Hidden Traps

Section titled “OpenClaw WeChat Plugin Installed But Silent? Four Hidden Traps”

Feng followed the openclaw-weixin npm docs, installed the WeChat plugin, and sent a test message in a WeChat group.

OpenClaw didn’t respond.

The gateway log showed the plugin loaded successfully. openclaw status reported no errors.

The problem lived in the gap between “looks fine” and “actually working.”

Trap 1: Old directory blocking reinstall

Section titled “Trap 1: Old directory blocking reinstall”

During reinstall via npx CLI, the installer printed:

Easy to miss in the scroll. The old directory wasn’t overwritten, so the new plugin never actually installed. The gateway log reported [plugins] openclaw-weixin failed to load — couldn’t find the openclaw/plugin-sdk/channel-config-schema module.

Fix: Delete the old directory manually before reinstalling.

Trap 2: QQ plugin missing axios

Section titled “Trap 2: QQ plugin missing axios”

Also installed openclaw-qqbot. Gateway reported:

The QQ plugin lists axios as a dependency, but the install process didn’t pull it in.

Fix: Install it manually in the plugin directory.

Trap 3: Version detection poisoned

Section titled “Trap 3: Version detection poisoned”

This one was the nastiest.

The QQ plugin’s node_modules/openclaw wasn’t a symlink — it was a full directory copy, version 1.6.5. When OpenClaw’s version checker scanned node_modules, it hit this copy first and treated 1.6.5 as the system version.

Result: the WeChat plugin rejected itself during registration:

The actual system installation was 2026.3.22. But the detection logic got fooled by the embedded copy inside the QQ plugin.

Fix: Delete the embedded copy and replace with a symlink to the real installation.

Trap 4: Plugin OK but no account wired

Section titled “Trap 4: Plugin OK but no account wired”

After fixing the first three issues, openclaw status showed openclaw-weixin status as OK.

Still no messages.

Checked the logs — no getUpdates polling happening. Looked at the config: channels.openclaw-weixin was {}. The plugin was installed and loaded, but no account was connected.

Tokens were stored in ~/.openclaw/openclaw-weixin/accounts/, but the config didn’t reference them.

Fix: Set the account config manually.

Both WeChat accounts started receiving and sending messages.

QQ plugin status

Section titled “QQ plugin status”

The QQ plugin still has an SDK compatibility issue — the applyAccountNameToChannelSection export doesn’t match. No accounts configured yet. Waiting for upstream fix.

Four lessons

Section titled “Four lessons”

1. Delete the old plugin directory before reinstalling. The installer won’t overwrite — it silently skips.

2. Third-party plugins with a full openclaw copy in node_modules will break other plugins. Replace with a symlink to the system installation. This isn’t in your config — it’s in how the plugin is packaged.

3. Plugin loaded successfully doesn’t mean messages are flowing. openclaw status checks plugin registration, not whether the channel has account config. Look for getUpdates polling in the logs.

4. When debugging “no response” issues, start from the logs. Four problems stacked on top of each other, each presenting as “no response.” Only the logs let you peel them apart.

Key file locations

Section titled “Key file locations”
FilePath
Plugin directory~/.openclaw/extensions/openclaw-weixin/
Token storage~/.openclaw/openclaw-weixin/accounts/
Config file~/.openclaw/openclaw.json → channels.openclaw-weixin
Logs/tmp/openclaw/openclaw-YYYY-MM-DD.log

Environment

Section titled “Environment”
  • OpenClaw 2026.3.22
  • openclaw-weixin@2.0.0
  • openclaw-qqbot@1.6.5
  • Node.js v24.9.0 (asdf)
  • macOS

Managing Multiple OpenClaw Instances from a Single Machine

Mar 24, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Managing Multiple OpenClaw Instances from a Single Machine

Section titled “Managing Multiple OpenClaw Instances from a Single Machine”

Three servers, three OpenClaw instances. One on AWS sh, one on a Mac mini at home, one on a dev machine at the office.

Every time I needed to check a cron job on one of them: open terminal, ssh admin@xxx, wait for connection, run openclaw cron list, read the output, exit. Switch to the next machine. Repeat.

This lasted three days. On day four, I went looking for a better approach.

The Problem

Section titled “The Problem”

It’s not that it’s technically impossible — it’s that the operational cost is too high.

Every SSH session requires remembering IPs, usernames, and ports. Three machines is manageable. Five gets confusing. Worse, once you SSH in, you’re operating in the remote environment where OpenClaw versions, Node versions, and config paths might differ from your local setup.

I had one incident: ran openclaw doctor --fix on a remote machine, and it “fixed” things based on that environment’s dependency graph, overwriting a working plugin configuration.

What I needed: operate remote instances using my local CLI tools, without logging into remote machines.

The Core Idea

Section titled “The Core Idea”

OpenClaw’s Gateway mode supports remote connections out of the box. Each instance exposes an HTTP/WebSocket interface on a local port (default 18789). If you can reach that port, you can use your local openclaw CLI with --url and --token flags to operate remotely.

Combine this with SSH tunnels and Tailscale networking, and you can manage all instances from a single machine.

The architecture is straightforward:

Each tunnel maps the remote 18789 port to a different local port. The local CLI uses --url ws://localhost:18800 for Instance A, 18801 for Instance B, and so on.

Step 1: SSH Tunnels with tmux

Section titled “Step 1: SSH Tunnels with tmux”

SSH tunnels break. Network hiccups, machine sleep, ISP issues — all can kill the connection. A bare ssh -N -L ... disappears when it drops, and you have to remember to reconnect.

Wrap tunnels in tmux:

Benefits:

  • Tunnel runs in the background, survives terminal closure
  • tmux ls shows all tunnel states at a glance
  • Easy to kill and recreate when broken

Use a consistent naming convention: tunnel-<host>-openclaw. Three months later, tmux ls output is still clear:

Step 2: Local CLI Remote Operations

Section titled “Step 2: Local CLI Remote Operations”

With tunnels in place, the local openclaw CLI can operate remote instances directly. The key flags are --url and --token:

Send messages to a remote instance with tui --message:

One gotcha: openclaw agent does not support --url and --token flags. For remote messaging, use openclaw tui --message only.

Step 3: Web UI Access

Section titled “Step 3: Web UI Access”

Each tunneled port also works in a browser:

Token authentication is required in the browser. Bookmark all three and switch between instances with a click.

Step 4: Instance Inventory

Section titled “Step 4: Instance Inventory”

Record all instance details in a central TOOLS.md:

Adding a new machine means copying the template and filling it in. Tunnel commands and Web UI URLs are ready to copy-paste.

Step 5: Health Checks

Section titled “Step 5: Health Checks”

A script that iterates over all tmux tunnel sessions and checks HTTP status codes:

Output:

ERR means the tunnel is down. Kill and rebuild:

Anti-Patterns

Section titled “Anti-Patterns”

Lessons from wrong turns:

AvoidPrefer
SSH into remote host to run openclawLocal CLI + --url/--token via tunnel
Raw WebSocket JSON-RPCopenclaw tui --message
Bare ssh without tmuxAlways tmux new-session -d -s ...
openclaw agent --urlopenclaw tui --message (agent doesn’t support —url)

Advanced: Using OpenClaw to Manage OpenClaw

Section titled “Advanced: Using OpenClaw to Manage OpenClaw”

Everything above is still manual management. The next step: dedicate an OpenClaw instance whose job is managing the others.

This is what vs-openclaw-mgr does. It’s an OpenClaw instance with all remote instance connection details stored in its workspace. This management instance can:

  • Periodically check health of all remote instances
  • Send instructions to remote instances via tui --message
  • Aggregate cron results across multiple instances
  • Provide a single view of all instance states

The management instance has its own identity (named Warden), its own memory system, and its own tool inventory. It never SSH-es into any remote machine — all operations go through SSH tunnels and the local CLI.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

Managing multiple OpenClaw instances comes down to three things:

  1. Tailscale networking — All machines can reach each other
  2. SSH tunnels + tmux — Map remote ports to local, keep them alive
  3. Local CLI + —url/—token — Operate remotely without logging in

If you have enough instances, dedicate one OpenClaw to manage the rest. Store the instance inventory and connection details in its workspace, and let the management instance look after the fleet.

Going from manual SSH to single-machine management took about an afternoon. Adding new machines afterward is just copying a template, creating a tunnel, and updating the inventory.

OpenClaw Upgrade War Story: Three Package Managers Walk Into a Bar

Mar 24, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw Upgrade War Story: Three Package Managers Walk Into a Bar

Section titled “OpenClaw Upgrade War Story: Three Package Managers Walk Into a Bar”

Eleven PM. Run openclaw doctor --fix. Expect a clean bill of health.

Three red errors stare back.

What Happened

Section titled “What Happened”

Starting state: OpenClaw 2026.3.22, installed via bun globally at /Users/vs/.bun/install/global/node_modules/openclaw, Node v25.8.1 managed by Homebrew. Nothing unusual.

openclaw doctor --fix reported three issues:

#ProblemSeverity
1openclaw-weixin v1.0.3 failed to load: Cannot find module 'openclaw/plugin-sdk'Blocking
2acpx plugin config residue: path doesn’t existBlocking
3Memory search has no embedding providerFeature gap

The first two caused config validation to fail outright. The third was a minor gap, but it confirmed the environment wasn’t clean.

Fixing Made It Worse

Section titled “Fixing Made It Worse”

Tried the obvious things first.

Visited http://localhost:18789/chat — 503. Error message: Control UI assets not found. The Web UI static assets simply weren’t part of the installed package.

Manually cleaned openclaw.json with Claude Code — removed acpx residues from plugins.allow, plugins.load.paths, plugins.entries.acpx, and plugins.installs.acpx. Four separate locations.

Gateway restarted and responded, but Web UI stayed at 503.

Tried pnpm ui:build — failed. scripts/ui.js isn’t included in the npm distribution. Dead end.

openclaw update — already on latest. No updates available.

At this point it became clear the problem wasn’t a config issue. It was deeper.

The Package Manager Graveyard

Section titled “The Package Manager Graveyard”

The uninstall process revealed the real mess.

Three package managers, each leaving behind different artifacts. Bun installed the binary and node_modules. An npm bin stub might still be sitting in /opt/homebrew/bin/. Homebrew managed Node itself but not OpenClaw. Path resolution in this environment was completely unpredictable.

After cleanup, which openclaw returned command not found. Clean slate.

Reinstall, Same Problems

Section titled “Reinstall, Same Problems”

Used the official install script:

This time it went through npm, installing to /opt/homebrew/lib/node_modules/openclaw, version 2026.3.22. The script auto-ran doctor and enabled ACP runtime.

But openclaw-weixin still reported Cannot find module 'openclaw/plugin-sdk'. Reinstalling the plugin, re-running the install script — same result.

The acpx config residue also reappeared. The doctor/update process apparently re-writes those entries.

Reinstalling the same version doesn’t fix compatibility issues. The plugin v1.0.3 and OpenClaw 2026.3.22 have an SDK resolution gap that no amount of config editing can bridge.

The Rollback: One Step Back, Two Steps Forward

Section titled “The Rollback: One Step Back, Two Steps Forward”

Different approach. Install a version known to work, stabilize, then upgrade.

This time npm resolved through asdf-managed Node v24.9.0, placing OpenClaw at /Users/vs/.asdf/installs/nodejs/24.9.0/lib/node_modules/openclaw.

Gateway started. One warning about the config file being written by a newer version, but it didn’t block operation.

2026.3.13 was up and running. Stable.

Jumping from Solid Ground

Section titled “Jumping from Solid Ground”

Next morning:

Upgraded from 2026.3.13 straight to 2026.3.23-1 in 28.89 seconds.

40+ plugin id mismatch warnings during the process (built-in plugin manifest IDs didn’t match), but the upgrade completed. Gateway didn’t auto-start, so:

Final state:

  • Version: 2026.3.23-1
  • Node: v24.9.0 (asdf)
  • Gateway: running
  • Plugins: 5 loaded, 76 disabled, 1 error (openclaw-weixin)

The weixin plugin still doesn’t work. That’s a plugin-level compatibility issue — waiting for an upstream fix. Everything else runs fine.

Five Lessons

Section titled “Five Lessons”

1. One global tool, one package manager. Bun, npm, and Homebrew installations interfered with each other. Path conflicts made error messages meaningless. After unifying on npm + asdf Node, everything became predictable.

2. Back up config before upgrading. openclaw.json gets rewritten by newer versions. If you need to roll back, a clean config backup saves hours.

3. “Rollback then upgrade” beats “install latest directly.” Install a known stable old version, verify it works, then run openclaw update. The update path handles version transitions better than a fresh install of the latest version.

4. Plugin ecosystems lag behind core releases. When the core ships a new release, plugins don’t always keep up. openclaw-weixin v1.0.3 has a known SDK resolution issue. Confirm core functionality first, wait on plugins.

5. openclaw doctor --fix is the first step, not the only step. It diagnoses and auto-fixes some problems, but package manager path conflicts and plugin SDK compatibility are outside its repair scope. The diagnostic output is valuable. The actual fix is manual.

Command Reference

Section titled “Command Reference”

Before your next upgrade, check where which openclaw points. If you’re not sure of the answer, this article might save you a late night.

  • OpenClaw
  • upgrade
  • package-manager
  • npm
  • bun
  • asdf

OpenClaw v2026.3.23: 29 Fixes in 48 Hours — The Community Cleanup After the Big One

Mar 24, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw v2026.3.23: 29 Fixes in 48 Hours

Section titled “OpenClaw v2026.3.23: 29 Fixes in 48 Hours”

You ship the biggest release in your project’s history. Ten breaking changes. Eighty-plus contributors. Then you wait.

The bug reports started within hours of v2026.3.22 landing. Browser tabs hanging on attach. ClawHub credentials invisible on macOS. Mistral models blowing past token limits. Gateway processes crash-looping under systemd. The community didn’t just report — they diagnosed, reproduced, and in many cases pointed straight at the root cause.

v2026.3.23 is the result: 29 targeted fixes, shipped 48 hours later. No new features. No breaking changes. Just repairs.

Reference: GitHub Issue #52808

Browser: Attach and Reuse Actually Work Now

Section titled “Browser: Attach and Reuse Actually Work Now”

Two fixes, both from @vincentkoc, both addressing the same root problem: the browser integration was too eager to declare success.

Chrome MCP attach timing. When you pointed OpenClaw at an already-running browser via Chrome MCP, the handshake completed before the tabs were actually usable. OpenClaw now waits for existing-session tabs to become interactive after attach instead of treating the initial protocol handshake as ready. (#52930)

CDP loopback reuse. If a loopback browser was already running but briefly unreachable — common during high CPU load or after wake from sleep — OpenClaw would skip it and fall back to relaunch detection. Now it retries the already-running instance through a short reachability window before giving up. (#53004)

Both fixes are invisible when things work. When they don’t, you get phantom browser launches and orphaned Chrome processes. That’s over.

ClawHub on macOS: Three Auth Paths, All Broken

Section titled “ClawHub on macOS: Three Auth Paths, All Broken”

v2026.3.22 made ClawHub the default plugin source. That means ClawHub auth is no longer optional — it’s load-bearing. On macOS, three separate auth resolution paths were silently failing.

macOS auth config. Saved ClawHub credentials stored via the macOS auth config path and XDG auth paths were being ignored. Fixed. (#53034)

Application Support path. The local ClawHub login stored under macOS Application Support wasn’t being read, even though XDG config was still honored. Now both paths work. Thanks @scoootscooob. (#52949)

Gateway skill browsing. The local ClawHub auth token wasn’t resolving for gateway-side skill browsing, and browse-all requests were hitting the wrong endpoint. Switched to search. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52949)

If you were on macOS and openclaw plugins install clawhub:<package> silently failed or prompted for credentials you’d already saved — this is why.

Plugins: Messaging, Memory, and Config

Section titled “Plugins: Messaging, Memory, and Config”

Six fixes spanning the plugin surface. The common thread: optional things that stopped being optional, and initialization that happened too late.

Discord and Slack messaging. The message tool started requiring Discord components and Slack blocks that used to be optional. They’re optional again. Separately, Feishu message(..., media=...) sends now route through the outbound media path instead of failing silently. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52970, #52962)

LanceDB memory plugin. First use of the memory-lancedb plugin would fail because LanceDB wasn’t bootstrapped into the plugin runtime state. Now it initializes on first access. (#26100)

Stale plugin config. If your plugins.allow list referenced a plugin id that no longer exists — renamed, removed, or typo — OpenClaw would refuse to start with a fatal config error. Now it warns and continues. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52992)

DeepSeek refactor. The bundled DeepSeek provider has been refactored onto the shared single-provider plugin entry point, aligning it with other bundled providers. Thanks @07akioni. (#48762)

Matrix duplicate exports. Under Jiti, the Matrix plugin was exporting duplicate resolveMatrixAccountStringValues runtime-api entries, causing load failures. Fixed. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52909, #52891)

Models and Providers: Token Limits, Pricing Loops, and Proxy Gaps

Section titled “Models and Providers: Token Limits, Pricing Loops, and Proxy Gaps”

Mistral token defaults. Bundled Mistral max-token defaults were set above safe output budgets, causing truncated or rejected completions. Lowered to safe values. openclaw doctor --fix now repairs old persisted Mistral provider configs automatically. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52599)

OpenRouter pricing recursion. The openrouter/auto pricing refresh was recursing indefinitely during bootstrap. If your gateway was slow to start or you saw stack overflow traces on launch — this was it. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#53035)

Web search provider. The web_search agent tool was using a stale or default provider selection instead of the active runtime provider. Thanks @jzakirov. (#53020)

OpenAI Codex OAuth proxy. Two related fixes. The env-configured HTTP/HTTPS proxy dispatcher wasn’t initialized before stored-credential token renewal, and separately, it wasn’t initialized before OAuth preflight and token exchange. If you run OpenClaw behind a corporate proxy and use Codex OAuth or MiniMax OAuth, both paths now bootstrap the proxy dispatcher first. Thanks @openperf. (#52228; fixes #51619, #51569)

Channels: Telegram, Discord, WhatsApp, Plivo

Section titled “Channels: Telegram, Discord, WhatsApp, Plivo”

Telegram message ordering. Same-chat inbound messages were losing debounce order, and stale busy-session followups were getting stranded — never delivered, never timed out. Both fixed. Thanks @osolmaz. (#52998)

Telegram asDocument alias. forceDocument on image and GIF sends now has a user-facing asDocument alias. Small quality-of-life addition. Thanks @bakhtiersizhaev. (#52461)

Discord privileged commands. Native slash commands that require elevated permissions were failing silently. Now they return an explicit unauthorized reply. Thanks @scoootscooob. (#53041)

WhatsApp auto-enable. openclaw doctor auto-enable was appending built-in channel ids like whatsapp to plugins.allow, cluttering your config with entries that don’t belong there. Stopped. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52931)

External channel catalogs. External channel catalogs can now override shipped fallback metadata, and overridden npm specs are honored during channel setup. (#52988)

Plivo voice replay. Plivo v2 replay keys were unstable — webhook retries collided with replay protection, causing dropped or duplicated voice call events. Keys are now stable. No more phantom replays.

Agents: Skills, Subagents, and Anthropic Transcripts

Section titled “Agents: Skills, Subagents, and Anthropic Transcripts”

Skill config resolution. Embedded skill config and env injection now prefer the active resolved runtime snapshot instead of a potentially stale one. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#53098)

Subagent timeouts. When a worker wait timed out, the completion event fired against a stale runtime snapshot. Now it rechecks the latest snapshot first. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#53106)

Anthropic transcript ordering. During transcript image sanitization, the ordering of assistant thinking and redacted-thinking blocks was getting shuffled. Preserved. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52961)

Gateway and Security

Section titled “Gateway and Security”

Gateway probe timeouts. Successful gateway handshakes were timing out as “unreachable” while post-connect detail RPCs were still loading. The probe now distinguishes between a failed connect and a slow post-connect phase. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52927)

Gateway crash loops. Lock conflicts were crash-looping the gateway under launchd and systemd. If you saw your gateway restart every few seconds in your service manager logs — fixed. Thanks @vincentkoc. (#52922)

Gateway auth hardening. Canvas routes now require auth. Agent session reset now requires admin scope. Both were unauthenticated before this fix.

Exec approval matching. Shell-wrapper positional-argv allowlist matching was incorrectly matching on non-direct carriers. Tightened to real direct carriers only. Thanks @vincentkoc.

Release packaging. Previously released bundled plugins and Control UI assets were missing from published openclaw npm installs. If you installed v2026.3.22 from npm and found missing UI assets or plugins — this is the fix. Thanks @vincentkoc.

Upgrade

Section titled “Upgrade”

Run openclaw doctor --fix after upgrading — it now repairs stale Mistral configs and cleans up spurious plugins.allow entries.

No breaking changes. No config migration needed. Drop-in replacement for v2026.3.22.

The Pattern

Section titled “The Pattern”

Massive releases produce massive surface area for bugs. That’s expected. What matters is the response time and the quality of community diagnostics.

@vincentkoc alone is credited on 18 of these 29 fixes. @scoootscooob, @osolmaz, @bakhtiersizhaev, @jzakirov, @openperf, and @07akioni each caught and helped resolve issues within hours of the release.

This is what a healthy open-source project looks like after a big ship: fast reports, fast fixes, no drama.

Full changelog: GitHub Release v2026.3.23

Twenty-nine fixes. Forty-eight hours. The biggest release needs the fastest follow-up.

OpenClaw v2026.3.22: Largest Release Ever — 10 Breaking Changes, 80+ Contributors, Full Security Overhaul

Mar 23, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw v2026.3.22: Largest Release Ever

Section titled “OpenClaw v2026.3.22: Largest Release Ever”

Ten breaking changes in one release tag. If you run OpenClaw in production, read this before you run npm update.

This isn’t a typical feature dump. v2026.3.22 is the release where OpenClaw cleans house. The old Chrome extension relay, CLAWDBOT_* env vars, .moltbot state directories, the monolithic extension-api — all gone, with no compatibility shims.

Over 80 contributors made this happen.

Breaking Changes: Read This First

Section titled “Breaking Changes: Read This First”

ClawHub-first installs. openclaw plugins install <package> now checks ClawHub before npm. Falls back to npm only when ClawHub doesn’t have that package or version.

Chrome extension relay removed. The legacy Chrome extension relay path, bundled extension assets, driver: "extension", and browser.relayBindHost are gone. Run openclaw doctor --fix to migrate. Docker, headless, sandbox, and remote browser flows are unaffected.

Image generation standardized. The image_generate tool now handles both create and edit paths. Old nano-banana-pro docs and examples are removed. Switch to agents.defaults.imageGenerationModel.

New plugin SDK surface. The public SDK is now openclaw/plugin-sdk/*. openclaw/extension-api is deleted with no compatibility shim. Bundled plugins must use injected runtime for host-side operations.

Message discovery API change. ChannelMessageActionAdapter.describeMessageTool(...) is now the only way to do shared message tool discovery. Legacy listActions, getCapabilities, and getToolSchema are removed.

Matrix plugin rewritten. New Matrix plugin built on the official matrix-js-sdk. If upgrading from the previous plugin, follow the migration guide.

Legacy env names removed. All CLAWDBOT_* and MOLTBOT_* env names are removed from runtime, installers, and test tooling. Use the matching OPENCLAW_* names.

Legacy state dir removed. .moltbot state-dir and moltbot.json auto-detection are gone. Move to ~/.openclaw or set OPENCLAW_STATE_DIR.

Exec env sandbox hardening. Build-tool JVM injection (MAVEN_OPTS, SBT_OPTS, GRADLE_OPTS, ANT_OPTS), glibc tunable exploitation (GLIBC_TUNABLES), and .NET dependency resolution hijack (DOTNET_ADDITIONAL_DEPS) are blocked from the host exec environment. Gradle init script redirect is restricted to override-only.

Discord Carbon reconcile. Native command deployment defaults to Carbon reconcile. Discord restarts no longer churn slash commands through OpenClaw’s local deploy path.

Plugin Ecosystem: ClawHub and Bundles

Section titled “Plugin Ecosystem: ClawHub and Bundles”

ClawHub is now first-class. Native openclaw skills search|install|update flows, openclaw plugins install clawhub:<package> with tracked update metadata, and gateway support for ClawHub-backed requests.

Marketplace support. Claude marketplace registry resolution, plugin@marketplace installs, marketplace listing, and update support are live.

Bundle compatibility. Codex, Claude, and Cursor bundle discovery and install. Bundle skills map into OpenClaw skills. Claude bundle settings.json defaults apply to embedded Pi with shell overrides sanitized.

Hook management. Hook-pack install and update route through openclaw plugins. openclaw hooks focuses on hook visibility and per-hook controls.

Plugin commands. Owner-gated /plugins and /plugin chat commands for plugin list/show and enable/disable flows.

Models and Providers

Section titled “Models and Providers”

OpenAI default switch. Default OpenAI setup model switches to openai/gpt-5.4. Codex stays on openai-codex/gpt-5.4. Chat, image, TTS, transcription, and embedding defaults are centralized in one shared module.

GPT-5.4 family. Native forward-compat support for gpt-5.4-mini and gpt-5.4-nano.

Anthropic Vertex. Core anthropic-vertex provider for Claude via Google Vertex AI, including GCP auth and discovery.

Chutes provider. Bundled Chutes provider with plugin-owned OAuth/API-key auth and dynamic model discovery.

Web search providers. Exa, Tavily, and Firecrawl join as bundled web-search plugins with dedicated tools and config paths.

MiniMax M2.7. Default model bumps from M2.5 to M2.7. M2.7-highspeed added. /fast maps to highspeed variants. MiniMax API and OAuth plugins merged into a single default-on plugin.

xAI Grok updates. Bundled Grok catalog synced to current Pi-backed IDs, limits, and pricing. /fast maps to xAI Grok fast model family.

Z.AI GLM updates. Bundled GLM catalog synced to current Pi metadata, including 4.5/4.6 model families and updated pricing.

Xiaomi MiMo V2. Xiaomi provider switches to /v1 OpenAI-compatible endpoint. MiMo V2 Pro and MiMo V2 Omni added.

Agents and Sessions

Section titled “Agents and Sessions”

Per-agent thinking defaults. Per-agent thinking/reasoning/fast defaults with auto-revert for disallowed model overrides.

/btw side questions. Quick tool-less answers about the current session without changing future context. Dismissible in-session TUI answers, explicit BTW replies on external channels.

Compaction improvements. Users get notified when followup auto-compaction starts and finishes. Optional post-compaction session JSONL truncation drops summarized transcript entries. Default agent timeout raised from 600s to 48h.

Sandbox and Browser

Section titled “Sandbox and Browser”

Pluggable sandbox backends. OpenShell backend with mirror and remote workspace modes. SSH sandbox backend with secret-backed key, certificate, and known_hosts inputs. sandbox list/recreate/prune is now backend-aware.

Browser profiles. browser.profiles.<name>.userDataDir lets Chrome DevTools MCP attach to Brave, Edge, and other Chromium-based browsers.

Security Hardening

Section titled “Security Hardening”

The security section of this release is longer than most projects’ entire changelogs.

Windows SMB credential leak. Remote-host file:// media URLs and UNC/network paths are blocked before local filesystem resolution in core media loading and adjacent prompt/sandbox attachment seams.

Exec approval hardening. time is treated as a transparent dispatch wrapper — approvals bind the inner executable. Blank Hangul filler code points are escaped in approval prompts to prevent visually empty Unicode from hiding command text. macOS allowlist resolution hardened against wrapper and env spoofing. jq removed from default safe-bin allowlist.

Network security. Explicit-proxy SSRF pinning hardened for HTTPS proxy tunnels. Voice-call webhooks reject missing provider signature headers before body reads. Pre-auth body budget dropped to 64 KB/5s. Concurrent pre-auth requests per source IP are capped.

Device pairing. iOS setup codes bound to intended node profile. First-use bootstrap redemption that asks for broader roles is rejected.

Nostr/Synology Chat. Nostr DM policy enforced before decrypt with pre-crypto rate and size guards. Synology Chat reply delivery bound to stable numeric user_id by default.

Media security. Remote-media error-body snippets bounded with streaming caps and idle timeouts matching successful downloads.

Messaging Platforms

Section titled “Messaging Platforms”

Telegram. Auto-rename DM forum topics, per-account custom Bot API endpoints, silent error replies setting, hard-timeout stuck polling. New setups default to requireMention=true.

Feishu. Structured interactive approval and quick-action launcher cards, current-conversation ACP and subagent session binding, streaming reasoning token rendering, identity-aware structured card headers and footers.

Discord. Strict DM component allowlist auth. allow_sending_without_reply on reply-targeted sends.

Mattermost. replyToMode: "off" honored for threaded posts. DM delivery retries with configurable backoff.

Mobile

Section titled “Mobile”

Android dark theme. System-aware dark theme across onboarding and chat flows. Talk speech synthesis moved behind gateway. Call log and SMS search support added.

Control UI

Section titled “Control UI”

Canvas expand. Expand-to-canvas button on assistant chat bubbles with in-app session navigation.

Appearance settings. Unified theme border radii with a Roundness slider to adjust corner radius from sharp to fully rounded.

Notable Fixes

Section titled “Notable Fixes”

Too many to list exhaustively. The ones with the biggest blast radius:

  • Gateway startup speed. Bundled channel plugins load from compiled dist entries. Cold starts drop from tens of seconds back to seconds. Primary model prewarmed before channel startup.
  • OpenAI-compatible tool calls. Duplicate tool_call_id values deduplicated. Third-party providers no longer reject with HTTP 400.
  • WhatsApp reconnect. Append recency filter restored. Protobuf Long timestamps handled correctly. Outbound listener state preserved across reconnects.
  • Compaction safety. Orphaned tool_result blocks repaired after session.compact(). Long tool loops trigger overflow recovery before next model call hard-fails.
  • Memory flush. Transcript-hash dedup stays active across memory-flush fallback retries. No more duplicate MEMORY.md entries.

Upgrade

Section titled “Upgrade”

Run openclaw doctor --fix after upgrading.

Breaking change checklist:

  1. Check plugin installs — ClawHub is now the default source
  2. Chrome extension relay users — removed, use existing-session or user driver
  3. nano-banana-pro users — switch to agents.defaults.imageGenerationModel
  4. Plugin developers — migrate to openclaw/plugin-sdk/*
  5. Matrix users — follow migration guide for the new plugin
  6. CLAWDBOT_* / MOLTBOT_* env vars — rename to OPENCLAW_*
  7. ~/.moltbot state dir — move to ~/.openclaw
  8. Java/Gradle projects using host exec env vars — check sandbox block list
  9. Discord slash command deployment changed — Carbon reconcile is the new default
  10. Message tool discovery API changed — migrate to describeMessageTool(...)

Full Changelog

Section titled “Full Changelog”

See the GitHub Release for the complete list of PRs and contributors.

Ten breaking changes. Eighty-plus contributors. One house-cleaning release. Some versions add features. This one defines direction.

Discord or Feishu? Platform Choice for Autonomous Coding with OpenClaw ACP and YOLO Mode

Mar 20, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Same AI model. Same codebase. Same OpenClaw configuration. I type a task description into Discord, and Claude Code runs autonomously for 40 minutes --- reading files, writing code, running tests, committing changes. I type the same task into Feishu, and it executes once then goes silent. No follow-up. No threading. No session.

The difference is not the model. It is the chat platform’s architecture.

The Platform Comparison

Section titled “The Platform Comparison”

I spent a week running identical ACP workflows on both platforms. Here is what actually works:

FeatureDiscordFeishu
mode=run single-shotSupportedSupported
Thread binding (persistent sessions)SupportedNot supported
Slash commands (/acp spawn, /acp status)WorkError: “Thread bindings unavailable for feishu”
Channel-level agent routingNative (peer binding)Works but confusing UX
Multiple agents on one BotNatural (channel separation)Awkward (same group chat)
YOLO mode compatibilityFull (thread = isolated context)Partial (run mode only)

The single-shot row looks identical. Everything below it diverges.

Why YOLO Mode Is Not Optional

Section titled “Why YOLO Mode Is Not Optional”

Before comparing platforms, I need to address the elephant in the room. Claude Code in its normal interactive mode asks for permission constantly. Edit this file? Run this shell command? Install this package? In a terminal session, you tap y and move on. From a chat message, there is no terminal. There is no interactive TUI. There is nobody sitting there to approve.

I measured it during a typical refactoring session: roughly 100 permission prompts per hour. That is almost two per minute. From a chat platform, each one would be a dead end.

--dangerously-skip-permissions --- what the community calls YOLO mode --- is not a shortcut for lazy developers. It is an architectural prerequisite. OpenClaw’s acpx spawns Claude Code as a subprocess. That subprocess must run unattended. If it stops to ask permission, the chat session hangs with no way to respond.

The actual flag is --permission-mode bypassPermissions. In your agent config:

Without this flag, ACP does not function. Not “works poorly” --- does not function. Every autonomous coding workflow through every chat platform requires it.

Safety Guardrails That Actually Work

Section titled “Safety Guardrails That Actually Work”

Running with bypassed permissions sounds reckless. It is not, if you layer the right constraints.

Docker containers. Run the agent workspace inside a container. The worst case is a trashed container, not a trashed host. OpenClaw’s workspace config supports container isolation natively.

Git as rollback. Every task starts from a clean commit. If the agent produces garbage, git reset --hard takes you back. This is not theoretical safety --- I use it weekly.

Hooks still fire. This is the critical detail most people miss. PreToolUse hooks execute even in bypass mode. You can block specific operations:

The hook script can inspect the command and return a non-zero exit code to block it. Bypass mode skips the interactive permission prompt. It does not skip hooks.

--disallowedTools works in bypass mode. If the agent should never touch the database directly:

Bounded tasks. “Refactor the auth module to use JWT” works. “Make the codebase better” does not. Specificity is a safety mechanism.

Discord’s Architecture Advantage

Section titled “Discord’s Architecture Advantage”

Discord was built for persistent, threaded conversations inside channel-scoped contexts. This maps perfectly onto autonomous coding sessions.

Channels are isolation boundaries. One bot token, three channels, three different agents. #backend runs a Python specialist. #frontend runs a React expert. #infra runs a Terraform agent. Each channel has its own peer binding in openclaw.json. Users interact with the right agent without thinking about routing.

Threads are coding sessions. When you /acp spawn in a Discord channel, OpenClaw creates a thread. That thread becomes an isolated context for the agent. All messages in the thread feed into the same Claude Code session. The agent can report progress, ask clarifying questions, and receive follow-up instructions --- all within the thread.

A typical 40-minute session looks like this:

  1. User types /acp spawn with a task description
  2. OpenClaw creates a thread, starts Claude Code with YOLO mode
  3. Claude Code reads files, plans changes, starts coding
  4. Progress messages appear in the thread every few minutes
  5. User notices something in the output, sends a correction in the thread
  6. Claude Code picks up the correction and adjusts
  7. Task completes, changes are committed

That step 5 is the key. It is not fire-and-forget. It is supervised autonomy. The thread is the supervision channel.

resumeSessionId for context chaining. When a session ends, OpenClaw stores the session ID. Starting a new task in the same thread can resume from where the previous session left off. The agent remembers what it already did.

This only works because Discord threads persist. The thread ID is the anchor.

Feishu’s Limitations

Section titled “Feishu’s Limitations”

Feishu is excellent team communication software. It is not built for persistent agent sessions.

Thread binding is not implemented. When I tried /acp spawn in a Feishu group chat, the error was immediate:

No workaround. The Feishu channel plugin in OpenClaw does not support thread creation or thread-scoped message routing. Every message lands in the flat group chat timeline.

No slash commands in group chats. Feishu’s bot command model does not map cleanly to OpenClaw’s ACP command structure. The /acp prefix either does not register or conflicts with Feishu’s own command handling. What works on Discord out of the box requires custom message parsing on Feishu.

Only mode: "run" works. You can send a message, OpenClaw dispatches it to Claude Code, Claude Code runs once, and the response comes back. Single request, single response. No session persistence. No follow-up in context. Every message is a fresh conversation.

This is still useful. “Generate a utility function that validates email addresses” works fine as a single-shot task. “Refactor the authentication module across 12 files” does not --- that needs iterative context.

groupPolicy allowlist drops messages silently. This one burned an hour of debugging. Feishu defaults to groupPolicy: "allowlist". If your group chat is not explicitly on the list, messages arrive at OpenClaw and get dropped. No error. No log. Nothing. The bot appears to ignore you.

This fixes it, but the silent failure mode is hostile to anyone setting things up for the first time.

The Real-World Decision

Section titled “The Real-World Decision”

I run both platforms simultaneously. Here is how I split the work:

Discord handles autonomous workflows. Multi-file refactoring. Feature implementation. Test generation. Bug investigation. Anything that takes more than one Claude Code turn. The thread-based session model means I can start a task, check back in 20 minutes, course-correct if needed, and let it continue.

Feishu handles task-driven single-shot execution. Quick code generation. Documentation lookups. Configuration file generation. One question, one answer. These work perfectly within Feishu’s message model, and the team is already there --- no need to move them to Discord for simple tasks.

The choice is not “which platform is better.” It is “which platform fits the task shape.”

If your team lives in Feishu and your tasks are bounded single-shot operations, Feishu works. You do not need Discord. Set up mode: "run", configure groupPolicy, and you have an AI coding assistant in your existing team chat.

If you want autonomous multi-step coding sessions --- the kind where Claude Code runs for 30 minutes across dozens of files --- you need Discord. Not because of preference. Because of threads.

Configuration Side by Side

Section titled “Configuration Side by Side”

Discord (full ACP with thread binding):

Feishu (single-shot only):

Same agent. Same YOLO mode flag in the agent config. Different mode value because Feishu cannot support spawn.

What I Expect to Change

Section titled “What I Expect to Change”

Feishu’s bot platform is evolving. Thread-like features exist in Feishu’s topic groups. OpenClaw’s Feishu plugin could eventually map topic replies to thread bindings. If that happens, the gap closes significantly.

For now, the gap is real. Plan accordingly.

YOLO mode is the prerequisite. The platform choice determines what you can do with it. Discord gives you supervised autonomy through threads. Feishu gives you fast single-shot execution through existing team infrastructure. Same agent, same config, different interaction shapes. Pick the one that matches your workflow.

One Bot Token, Multiple Agents: OpenClaw Discord Channel-Level Routing

Mar 18, 2026
Vibe Sparking

A Discord server with a dozen channels, one bot handling everything. The coding channel and the casual chat channel get the same responses. Technical questions get vague answers. Creative discussions get stuffed with code snippets.

The problem isn’t the agent. The problem is one agent doing everyone’s job.

OpenClaw has a routing system that maps different channels to different agents. Same bot token, but #code-help runs a code review specialist, #creative-writing runs a writing assistant, and #support runs a troubleshooting guide. No code required — five CLI commands and one JSON edit.

Prerequisites

Section titled “Prerequisites”
  • OpenClaw installed and running
  • Discord bot created with a valid token (if not, see the previous post: OpenClaw Discord Bot Setup)
  • At least two agent configurations ready (otherwise routing has no point)

How Routing Works

Section titled “How Routing Works”

OpenClaw’s bindings array matches in order. First match wins. Specificity from high to low:

PriorityMatch ScopeUse Case
1peer — specific channel or userPer-channel customization
2guildId — entire serverServer-level differentiation
3accountId — bot accountAccount-level default
4No match conditionGlobal fallback

Same logic as firewall rules: narrow rules must come before broad ones.

Step 1: Register the Discord Bot Account

Section titled “Step 1: Register the Discord Bot Account”

Skip if you’ve already connected Discord.

Step 2: Create Your Agents

Section titled “Step 2: Create Your Agents”

Each agent gets its own workspace and configuration directory. System prompts, model parameters, tool chains — all managed separately per agent config directory.

Want the coding channel agent to follow documentation strictly and the writing channel agent to run at higher temperature? Adjust each in their respective config directories.

Step 3: Open Group Message Permissions

Section titled “Step 3: Open Group Message Permissions”

Easy to miss. OpenClaw defaults groupPolicy to allowlist — whitelist mode. The effect: every channel message gets silently dropped. No errors, no warnings, no logs.

If the bot joins a channel and ignores every message, check this first. It’s almost always the cause.

Step 4: Edit Routing Bindings

Section titled “Step 4: Edit Routing Bindings”

Manually edit ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json and add channel-level rules to the bindings array:

One rule per channel. The id field takes the Discord channel ID.

Two ways to get a channel ID:

  • Turn on Developer Mode in Discord settings, right-click the channel, copy ID
  • CLI query: openclaw directory groups list --channel discord --account <accountId>

Ordering matters. Channel-level bindings must appear before account-level bindings for the same bot. If the account-level rule sits higher in the array, it matches first and the channel rule never fires. Same principle as CSS specificity or iptables.

Step 5: Restart the Gateway

Section titled “Step 5: Restart the Gateway”

Routing doesn’t hot-reload. After editing config, restart is required.

What It Looks Like in Practice

Section titled “What It Looks Like in Practice”

Three channels, three agents:

  • #code-help -> code-review-agent (low temperature, strict documentation adherence)
  • #creative-writing -> writing-assistant (high temperature, free style)
  • #support -> troubleshoot-agent (medium temperature, guided troubleshooting)

Three binding rules, one bot token. Whichever channel a user sends a message in, the corresponding agent handles it. Channels without specific bindings fall through to the account-level or global default agent.

Troubleshooting

Section titled “Troubleshooting”

Bot doesn’t respond in channels at all Check if groupPolicy is set to open. The default whitelist silently drops all channel messages.

Channel-level binding not working — all channels respond the same way Check the order in the bindings array. Channel rules must come before account rules.

How to get channel IDs Discord Settings > App Settings > Advanced > Developer Mode. Then right-click any channel to copy its ID.

Multi-server scenarios Use guildId for server-level routing. Channel-level peer rules have higher priority and can layer on top: a server defaults to Agent A, but a specific channel within it routes to Agent B.

Comparison with Feishu and QQ

Section titled “Comparison with Feishu and QQ”

OpenClaw’s routing isn’t Discord-specific. Feishu group chats and QQ group chats support the same peer-level binding. The differences:

  • Discord channels are naturally separate conversation spaces — routing them to different agents feels intuitive
  • In Feishu group chats, a bot that suddenly changes response style confuses users
  • QQ group binding uses the same logic, but permission configuration differs

Discord’s channel model and multi-agent routing are a natural fit.

Next Steps

Section titled “Next Steps”
  • Tune each agent’s system prompt to sharpen their role in each channel
  • Use guildId bindings for multi-server isolation
  • Combine with ACP Thread Binding to switch agents within the same channel via threads (see the previous post)

One bot token. Five configuration steps. Channel-level isolation. The routing priority table has four rows — remember it: peer > guildId > accountId > default.

QClaw via WeChat: Remote PC Control Sounds Great — Until You Hit the Limits

Mar 18, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Send a WeChat message, and your PC executes a command.

QClaw delivers on that promise. Scan a QR code to bind your WeChat account, and your chat window becomes a remote terminal. From the subway, from a restaurant, from anywhere you have WeChat open — your PC at home or the office follows instructions.

After a week of daily use, here’s what I found.

What QClaw Is

Section titled “What QClaw Is”

QClaw is Tencent’s one-click installer built on the OpenClaw open-source framework. Download, install, scan — three steps. No command line, no environment setup. Works on both Mac and Windows.

The core pitch: remote PC control through WeChat. After binding, QClaw appears in WeChat as a “customer service message” channel. You send text, it executes on your PC. File operations, browser control, script execution, scheduled tasks — the official claim is 5,000+ skills.

The default model is a domestic Chinese LLM (Kimi 2.5), with options to switch to other domestic models.

The first time it worked, I was genuinely impressed. Sent “list the files on my desktop” — got back a file listing in seconds. It runs. No complaints there.

The Problem Lives in WeChat

Section titled “The Problem Lives in WeChat”

QClaw is not a “contact” in WeChat. It’s an “application.”

That single distinction creates a chain of friction.

No group chats. You cannot add QClaw to any WeChat group. Want the AI to process something discussed in a work group? Not possible. QClaw only talks to you in a one-on-one “application message” thread.

No message forwarding. See some text or an image in a group chat that you want QClaw to handle? You can’t forward it. WeChat’s forwarding target list doesn’t include “applications.”

Copy-paste only. To send text to QClaw, long-press to copy, switch to the QClaw conversation, paste. Images are worse — save to your photo album first, then open QClaw and send from the album.

This isn’t a QClaw bug. It’s WeChat’s platform architecture. In WeChat’s world, “contacts” are first-class citizens. “Applications” are second-class. QClaw entered as an application, and the constraints follow.

In daily use, the friction is larger than you’d expect. Your instinct says “just forward this to QClaw.” Then you remember you can’t, and you start the manual relay. After a few rounds, it gets old.

Compared to OpenClaw, Clear Feature Gaps

Section titled “Compared to OpenClaw, Clear Feature Gaps”

QClaw is built on OpenClaw, but it’s not OpenClaw. Key differences:

Model Selection

Section titled “Model Selection”

QClaw only supports domestic Chinese LLMs. You can choose Kimi, MiniMax, or configure other domestic models. Claude, GPT, and other international models are not available.

For tasks that need specific model capabilities — complex code generation, multilingual translation, long-context reasoning — this limitation directly affects output quality.

PC Side Is Read-Only

Section titled “PC Side Is Read-Only”

On your PC, QClaw shows the message history from WeChat. But the reverse doesn’t work: you cannot send messages from the PC-side QClaw back to WeChat.

View only. No reply. Communication is one-directional.

This means all commands must originate from WeChat. When you’re sitting at your computer, this design feels redundant — you’re already at the PC, why not just use OpenClaw directly?

Relationship with OpenClaw

Section titled “Relationship with OpenClaw”

QClaw reads OpenClaw’s default workspace files, memory, and skills. They share these local resources.

But there’s no message channel between them. QClaw doesn’t sync execution results back to OpenClaw’s conversation history. OpenClaw doesn’t know what QClaw did. They share a filesystem, not a communication bus.

Where QClaw Fits

Section titled “Where QClaw Fits”

Complaints aside, QClaw has genuine use cases.

You’re away from your PC and need it to do something. Forgot to email a file, need to run a script, want to check local data. Pull out your phone, send a WeChat message. This is QClaw’s smoothest scenario.

Tasks where domestic LLMs are sufficient. File organization, simple copywriting, data summarization, format conversion. These don’t need the most powerful models. Domestic LLMs handle them fine.

Scheduled tasks and push notifications. Set up automated workflows, QClaw executes on schedule, and results arrive in your WeChat. This direction works well.

The unsuitable scenarios are equally clear: anything requiring group collaboration, frequent message forwarding for processing, Claude/GPT-level model capabilities, or bidirectional PC communication.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

QClaw lowers the deployment barrier for OpenClaw and makes WeChat an entry point for AI agents. The direction is right.

But WeChat treating it as an “application” creates daily friction that exceeds expectations. No group chats, no forwarding, mandatory manual relay — these aren’t minor issues. Combined with domestic-only model support, read-only PC side, and no message bridge to OpenClaw, the functional boundary is clear but narrow.

My recommendation: treat QClaw as a “WeChat trigger.” When you’re away from your PC and need something done remotely, send a WeChat message. Don’t try to use it as a complete AI assistant — that’s OpenClaw’s job.

Know where the boundary is, and it works fine within it.

  • Tencent QClaw Setup Tutorial - Tencent Cloud Community

Your AI Agent Belongs in WeChat: openclaw-wechat Bridges the Gap

Mar 18, 2026
Vibe Sparking

You have a brilliant AI agent. It reasons through complex questions, recognizes images, holds conversations with context. It lives on your server, behind OpenClaw’s web dashboard.

Nobody in your family will ever open that dashboard.

Your mom sends voice messages on WeChat at 7am. Your colleague drops PDFs in the work group. Your client photographs a defective part and wants an answer now. 1.3 billion people communicate through WeChat. They won’t switch to a web UI for your AI.

openclaw-wechat bridges this gap.

The WeCom bridge trick

Section titled “The WeCom bridge trick”

The plugin routes AI conversations through WeCom (enterprise WeChat). WeCom has a built-in “WeChat Plugin” feature in its admin console. Enable it, scan a QR code with your personal WeChat, and your AI agent shows up as a contact you can message directly.

No new app. No login page. Just WeChat, which is already open on every phone in China.

From text-only fork to five message types

Section titled “From text-only fork to five message types”

The plugin started as dingxiang-me’s OpenClaw-Wechat v0.1.0 — text messages in and out through the WeCom callback API. Xueheng-Li forked it and started expanding.

What v0.3.7 handles now:

TypeReceiveSendDetails
TextYesYesAuto-splits long messages at UTF-8 byte boundaries (2048-byte limit)
ImageYesYesAI Vision analysis on received images
VoiceYesNoThree-tier speech recognition fallback
VideoYesYesAuto-download and upload to WeCom media storage
FileYesYesReadable formats (.txt, .md, .json, .pdf) auto-extracted for AI

The Markdown-to-plaintext conversion runs automatically on outbound messages — WeCom doesn’t render Markdown, so the plugin strips it before sending.

Voice recognition: three fallback levels

Section titled “Voice recognition: three fallback levels”

Voice messages on WeChat are common. The plugin handles them with a degradation chain:

  1. WeCom built-in recognition — uses whatever Tencent provides in the Recognition field
  2. Remote Qwen3-ASR — if you have a GPU server, run asr_server.py with the 0.6B parameter model. Handles 52 languages and 22 Chinese dialects. Roughly 2-4 seconds per short clip on an RTX 4090D.
  3. Local FunASR — runs on CPU, Apple MPS, or CUDA. Slower but needs no remote server.

The audio pipeline: download AMR from WeCom, FFmpeg converts to 16kHz WAV, then whichever speech model is available takes over. If one level fails, the next picks up. No single point of failure.

Conversation memory

Section titled “Conversation memory”

Before v0.3.6, every message was a fresh conversation. The AI had no idea what you said 30 seconds ago.

The fix uses OpenClaw SDK’s own history methods — recordPendingHistoryEntry and buildPendingHistoryContextFromMap. The last 20 messages are rebuilt as context before each AI call. This is the same mechanism the official Telegram and Discord channels use.

/clear resets history. /status shows the current message count.

The “can send but can’t receive” debugging saga

Section titled “The “can send but can’t receive” debugging saga”

OpenClaw 2026.3 shipped with stricter channel plugin requirements. The WeCom plugin broke in a specific, frustrating way: outbound messages worked fine. Inbound was dead silent. No error. No log entry. The callback URL returned the Control UI’s HTML page instead of “wecom webhook ok”.

Three issues conspired:

Status reporting. The health monitor queries channel status periodically. Without proper reporting (running state, account snapshots, probe results), it assumed the channel was dead and restarted it in a loop.

Gateway lifecycle. startAccount was returning immediately instead of staying alive until its abortSignal fired. Each restart spawned a new instance while old routes lingered. Race conditions.

Route registration. registerHttpRoute() needed explicit auth: "plugin" and match: "exact" in the new version. Without them, the Gateway’s SPA fallback for the Control UI captured the callback URL first. The webhook hit the React app instead of the plugin handler.

v0.3.7 fixes all three.

The AgentId trap

Section titled “The AgentId trap”

Even after the code fix, some users hit the same symptom. The cause: WeCom lets you create multiple self-built apps. Each has its own AgentId, Secret, Token, and EncodingAESKey. These four values must all come from the same app.

One real case: a developer had agentId=1000002 in their config while the WeCom console had callbacks on agentId=1000003. Outbound worked (the API is more forgiving). Inbound went to the wrong app’s handler. Swapping the ID fixed it immediately.

Verify your config matches:

Quick setup

Section titled “Quick setup”

Prerequisites

Section titled “Prerequisites”
  • OpenClaw installed and running (openclaw doctor passes)
  • WeCom admin access
  • A public URL for callbacks (Cloudflare Tunnel works well)

Install

Section titled “Install”

Configure

Section titled “Configure”

Add to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json:

Verify

Section titled “Verify”

Then save the callback configuration in the WeCom admin console.

Connect personal WeChat

Section titled “Connect personal WeChat”

In the WeCom admin console: My Enterprise > WeChat Plugin. Scan the QR code with your personal WeChat. Done. Your AI agent is now a WeChat contact.

Dynamic IP workaround

Section titled “Dynamic IP workaround”

WeCom requires your server’s outbound IP on a whitelist. Home broadband in China usually means a dynamic IP. The fix: run a small proxy (tinyproxy) on a VPS with a fixed IP, set WECOM_PROXY in your config, and add the VPS IP to WeCom’s whitelist.

The plugin’s wecomFetch() routes all outbound WeCom API calls through this proxy. Inbound callbacks can still come through a Cloudflare Tunnel — the proxy only handles outbound.

Troubleshooting checklist

Section titled “Troubleshooting checklist”
SymptomCheck
Callback verification failscurl https://your-domain/wecom/callback — should return “wecom webhook ok”, not HTML
Can send but can’t receiveVerify all four values (AgentId, Secret, Token, AESKey) come from the same WeCom app
Error 60020 (IP not allowed)Add your server’s outbound IP to the app’s trusted IP list, or configure WECOM_PROXY
No AI responseCheck openclaw logs -f | grep wecom for inbound entries
Voice recognition failsVerify FFmpeg installed, check WECOM_STT_URL or local FunASR dependencies
Health monitor restart loopUpgrade to v0.3.7+ — status reporting and gateway lifecycle are fixed

Why this matters

Section titled “Why this matters”

There’s a pattern in how AI tools reach mainstream adoption. The technology itself is rarely the bottleneck. Distribution is. Building another chat interface doesn’t help when a billion people already have one they prefer.

openclaw-wechat is interesting not because of any single technical feat, but because of the approach: meet users where they are. Use the enterprise platform as a bridge to the consumer platform. Handle every message type people actually send. Remember the conversation. Survive platform upgrades. Document the traps so the next person doesn’t fall in.

If your users are in China and your AI is on OpenClaw, this is how you reach them.
