Chat-Driven Coding: How We Wired Claude Code into Feishu with OpenClaw ACP

Mar 17, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Last Tuesday, I typed a message in our Feishu group chat: “@dev-bot write Vitest unit tests for the Content and QaItem models, plus Playwright e2e tests.” Then I went to make coffee. When I came back, the tests were written, committed, and the bot had posted a summary in the same chat thread. I never opened a terminal.

This is what happens when you wire OpenClaw’s ACP protocol into your team’s messaging platform. Getting here involved a dead-end detour through tmux, a hard lesson about Feishu’s threading limitations, and a session chaining pattern that turned out better than what I originally wanted.

What is ACP

Section titled “What is ACP”

ACP (Agent Coding Protocol) is OpenClaw’s interface for controlling external coding tools. OpenClaw agents talk to a local process manager called acpx, which spawns and manages coding agent processes.

Supported coding tools:

agentIdTool
claudeClaude Code CLI
codexOpenAI Codex CLI
piPi agent
opencodeOpenCode CLI
geminiGemini CLI
kimiKimi CLI

The basic idea: your OpenClaw agent receives a message in a chat group, decides the task needs coding, and spawns a coding agent process to handle it.

Configuration

Section titled “Configuration”

Enabling ACP

Section titled “Enabling ACP”

In ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json:

defaultAgent: "claude" means Claude Code gets used when no specific agent is requested. backend: "acpx" points to the local process manager.

Multi-agent setup

Section titled “Multi-agent setup”

This is where it gets useful. Each OpenClaw agent gets its own identity:

Each agent has:

  • Its own workspace directory (with SOUL.md, MEMORY.md)
  • A separate Feishu bot account (independent AppID and AppSecret)
  • Isolated session storage under ~/.openclaw/agents/<id>/sessions/

Feishu channel configuration

Section titled “Feishu channel configuration”

requireMention: true means the bot only responds when @-mentioned in group chats. This prevents it from jumping into every conversation.

How it works

Section titled “How it works”

The workflow:

The sessions_spawn call looks like this:

The dead ends

Section titled “The dead ends”

tmux: don’t bother

Section titled “tmux: don’t bother”

Before confirming ACP’s run mode worked with Feishu, we tried driving Claude Code through tmux. Start a tmux session, launch Claude Code inside it, pipe commands through tmux send-keys, capture output with tmux capture-pane.

Three problems killed it:

  1. claude -p with a stdin pipe silently switches to non-interactive print mode. No TUI.
  2. Claude Code’s TUI uses alternate screen buffers. capture-pane returns empty output while Claude works in the alternate buffer.
  3. Chinese characters sent through tmux send-keys arrive garbled.

This approach was abandoned. ACP’s native protocol replaced it completely.

Thread binding: Feishu can’t do it

Section titled “Thread binding: Feishu can’t do it”

ACP supports persistent coding sessions. Spawn a session, bind it to a chat thread, and every message in that thread goes to the same Claude Code context. On Discord and Telegram, this works well.

On Feishu: “Thread bindings unavailable for feishu.”

This means:

  • /acp spawn, /acp status, and other slash commands don’t work in Feishu groups
  • Persistent mode: "session" fails
  • The agent must use internal tool calls (sessions_spawn, subagents(action="list")) instead of slash commands

Channel comparison:

Channelmode=runThread BindingPersistent session
DiscordYesYes (needs config)Yes
TelegramYesYes (forum topics)Yes
FeishuYesNoNo
SignalYesNoNo

The pattern that works

Section titled “The pattern that works”

One-shot runs with session chaining

Section titled “One-shot runs with session chaining”

Use mode: "run" for one-shot execution. No persistent session, no thread binding needed.

For context continuity, chain runs with resumeSessionId:

acpx compacts the old context (takes 1-2 minutes), then Claude Code resumes with full awareness of the previous session. This chained pattern works well for how development tasks actually flow. Each task is discrete. Context carries forward when needed.

Session lifecycle

Section titled “Session lifecycle”
StateMeaning
pendingInitializing
runningTask executing
idleTask complete, waiting

Session data lives in three layers:

Monitoring

Section titled “Monitoring”

Tail the ACP stream log during execution:

Or have the agent read the stream file and post updates to the Feishu group.

Troubleshooting

Section titled “Troubleshooting”

ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED

Section titled “ACP_SESSION_INIT_FAILED”

This happens when trying to run /acp slash commands in a Feishu group session. Feishu sessions aren’t ACP-enabled. Let the agent handle ACP through internal tool calls instead.

Session timeout

Section titled “Session timeout”

If an ACP session stops producing events:

If the main task (file writes) completed, treat it as success. If not, resume with resumeSessionId.

Best practices

Section titled “Best practices”

Do:

  • Always specify cwd when spawning sessions. Without it, Claude Code operates in the default directory.
  • Use mode: "run" on Feishu. Chain with resumeSessionId for continuity.
  • Split large tasks into multiple run sessions. Each picks up where the last left off.
  • Monitor through stream logs. Have the agent periodically read and report progress.
  • Use Discord or Telegram for persistent interactive coding sessions.

Don’t:

  • Use /acp spawn or /acp status slash commands in Feishu groups. They won’t work.
  • Try to drive Claude Code through tmux. ACP replaced that entirely.
  • Start new sessions for the same task without resuming. You waste tokens and lose context.
  • Skip cwd. Claude Code in the wrong directory creates files in the wrong place.

What’s next

Section titled “What’s next”

The setup runs daily. Developers trigger coding tasks from Feishu without thinking about the plumbing. The multi-agent architecture means each project gets its own bot identity, workspace, and session isolation.

If your team uses Feishu and you want AI coding agents integrated into your chat workflow, ACP with mode: "run" is the path. It’s not the persistent interactive session that Discord and Telegram support, but for task-driven development, the chained one-shot pattern works better than expected.

OpenClaw Discord Bot Setup: The Message Content Intent Trap and How to Fix It

Mar 17, 2026
Vibe Sparking

You already have an OpenClaw agent running on Feishu. It handles questions, routes to the right models, spawns Claude Code sessions. Someone asks: “Can we get this in Discord too?”

How hard can it be? Not hard. But there are traps.

This is the record of adding Discord to an OpenClaw agent setup, the bug that ate two hours, and the one configuration decision that makes Discord worth the effort.

Environment

Section titled “Environment”
  • macOS
  • OpenClaw 2026.3.13
  • Target agent: vs-dev
  • Already running on Feishu, adding Discord as second channel

Step 1: Create the Discord Bot

Section titled “Step 1: Create the Discord Bot”

Open the Discord Developer Portal at discord.com/developers/applications.

  1. Click New Application, name it (e.g. “vs-dev”)
  2. Go to Bot in the left sidebar, note the Bot Username
  3. Click Reset Token, copy the token immediately — it only shows once

Then the step that’s easy to skip and expensive to miss:

Enable Privileged Gateway Intents

Section titled “Enable Privileged Gateway Intents”

Still on the Bot page, scroll to Privileged Gateway Intents. Turn on all three:

  • Presence Intent
  • Server Members Intent
  • Message Content Intent — this one matters most

Save Changes.

Without Message Content Intent, the bot receives messages in group channels but can’t read their text. @mention detection fails because there’s no text to scan. The bot drops every group message silently. No error, no warning — just reason: no-mention in the logs.

Generate the Invite Link

Section titled “Generate the Invite Link”

Go to OAuth2 > OAuth2 URL Generator:

  • Scopes: bot + applications.commands
  • Bot Permissions: View Channels, Send Messages, Read Message History, Embed Links, Attach Files

Copy the generated URL, open it in a browser, select your target server, authorize.

Get Your IDs

Section titled “Get Your IDs”

Turn on Developer Mode (User Settings > Advanced > Developer Mode):

  • Server ID: right-click the server icon > Copy Server ID
  • User ID: right-click your avatar > Copy User ID

Step 2: Configure OpenClaw

Section titled “Step 2: Configure OpenClaw”

Add the Discord Channel

Section titled “Add the Discord Channel”

In ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json, add a Discord channel block:

What each field does:

FieldValueWhy
dmPolicy"pairing"DMs require pairing authorization first
groupPolicy"allowlist"Only respond in whitelisted servers
streaming"partial"Show streaming response previews
threadBindings.spawnAcpSessionstrueAllow Discord threads to bind ACP sessions
requireMentionfalseSkip @mention detection (see troubleshooting below)
users["<user-id>"]Only respond to these users

Add the Binding

Section titled “Add the Binding”

Route the Discord account to your agent:

Enable the Plugin

Section titled “Enable the Plugin”

Restart

Section titled “Restart”

Step 3: DM Pairing

Section titled “Step 3: DM Pairing”
  1. Open Discord, send a direct message to the bot
  2. The bot replies with a pairing code (e.g. 3YG9D95D)
  3. Approve it in terminal:
  1. The bot confirms in DM. Pairing complete.

Step 4: Verify

Section titled “Step 4: Verify”

You want to see:

Check for:

  • running — connection is live
  • in:Xs ago — recent incoming message
  • out:Xs ago — recent outgoing message
  • intents:content=limited — this means trouble (see below)

Troubleshooting

Section titled “Troubleshooting”

Bot doesn’t respond in group channels

Section titled “Bot doesn’t respond in group channels”

Symptom: Bot is connected, receives messages, but never replies. Logs show:

Root cause: intents:content=limited — the Message Content Intent isn’t active. The bot receives messages but the content field is empty. It can’t detect @mentions in text that doesn’t exist.

Fix (both tracks):

  1. Go to Discord Developer Portal > Bot > Privileged Gateway Intents. Make sure Message Content Intent is ON. Save. Wait up to 15 minutes for propagation.

  2. Set requireMention: false in the guild config. This is both a workaround and a design choice. Combined with the users whitelist, it gives precise control without depending on @mention parsing.

If content=limited persists after 15 minutes: Reset Token in the Developer Portal, update the token in openclaw.json, restart the gateway.

Bot reconnects frequently

Section titled “Bot reconnects frequently”

Symptom: Logs show repeated health-monitor: restarting (reason: disconnected).

Cause: Discord WebSocket instability. The health monitor reconnects automatically. This stabilizes after the Intent issue is resolved. Normal behavior — not a bug.

openclaw doctor keeps suggesting changes

Section titled “openclaw doctor keeps suggesting changes”

Symptom: Every restart triggers Moved channels.discord single-account top-level values into channels.discord.accounts.default.

Fix: Run openclaw doctor --fix to auto-correct the schema. Check afterward — it may create an extra accounts.default entry that needs cleanup.

109 commands exceeds limit

Section titled “109 commands exceeds limit”

Symptom: Log says discord: 109 commands exceeds limit; removing per-skill commands and keeping /skill.

Impact: None. Discord limits bots to 100 slash commands. OpenClaw automatically trims to stay under the limit, keeping the /skill entry point. All skills remain accessible through /skill.

Why Discord Over Other Channels

Section titled “Why Discord Over Other Channels”

Discord supports Thread Binding. Feishu doesn’t.

FeatureDiscordFeishu
ACP mode=run (oneshot)YesYes
ACP mode=session (persistent)YesNo
Thread-bound ACP sessionYesNo
/acp spawn slash commandYesNo
/acp statusYesNo

To spawn a persistent Claude Code session in a Discord thread:

Or through the agent’s tool calling (with spawnAcpSessions: true enabled):

The session lives in the thread. Send messages in the thread and they go to the same Claude Code session. Context persists across messages. For developers who work in Discord, this is the reason to set up the bot.

OpenClaw v2026.3.13-1: Recovery Release Ships 70+ Fixes Across Agents, Security, Mobile, and Messaging

Mar 17, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw v2026.3.13-1: Recovery Release Ships 70+ Fixes

Section titled “OpenClaw v2026.3.13-1: Recovery Release Ships 70+ Fixes”

GitHub won’t let you reuse a published release tag. When v2026.3.13 shipped broken, the team couldn’t just fix and re-push. So they tagged v2026.3.13-1, kept npm at 2026.3.13, and packed 70+ fixes into what became one of the most community-driven releases in the project’s history.

Why v2026.3.13-1?

Section titled “Why v2026.3.13-1?”

The original v2026.3.13 tag and GitHub Release broke. GitHub’s immutable release system prevents overwriting published tags. The solution:

  • Git tag / GitHub Release: v2026.3.13-1
  • npm package version: 2026.3.13 (unchanged)

The -1 suffix exists only for Git and GitHub. If you install via npm, nothing changes.

Agent fixes: the big ones

Section titled “Agent fixes: the big ones”

The agent layer received the most attention this cycle.

Thinking block replay. Anthropic thinking blocks were being replayed incorrectly during agent conversations. Fixed — they’re now dropped on replay (#44843).

Memory file double-injection. On case-insensitive file systems (macOS, Windows), memory files could get injected twice into agent context. Path comparison now handles case folding (#26054).

Session reset preservation. lastAccountId and lastThreadId were getting wiped on session reset. They’re preserved now (#44773). The reset prompt was also reworded to avoid triggering Azure content filters (#43403).

Cross-agent workspace resolution. When an agent spawned a subagent targeting a different agent’s workspace, the target path resolved incorrectly. Fixed (#40176).

Custom provider keys. Blank local API keys for custom providers were getting overwritten during onboarding. They’re preserved now (#45631).

Post-compaction sanity check. The compaction system now uses the full-session token count instead of a partial count for its sanity check (#28347).

Security hardening

Section titled “Security hardening”

Docker token leak. Gateway tokens could leak through the Docker build context. The Dockerfiles now prevent this (#44956). All Dockerfiles also add apt-get upgrade for base image security (#45384).

Control-UI auth. The auth bypass for insecure control-ui connections was accidentally removed. Restored, with proper connect failure classification (#45512).

macOS PortGuard. PortGuard was killing Docker Desktop processes when running in remote mode. It no longer does (#13798).

Shared auth on insecure connects. Shared auth state is now maintained on insecure control-ui connections (#45088).

Gateway token requests. Unanswered client requests are now bounded to prevent resource exhaustion (#45689).

Messaging platform fixes

Section titled “Messaging platform fixes”

Telegram. Inbound media downloads now retry over IPv4 fallback when IPv6 fails (#45327). Thread media transport policy is properly threaded into SSRF protection (#44639).

Feishu. Non-ASCII filenames are preserved in file uploads (#34262). An early event-level dedup layer prevents duplicate replies — if you’ve been seeing double messages, this is the fix (#43762).

Discord. Gateway metadata fetch failures no longer crash the handler (#44397).

Signal. Groups config is now part of the Signal channel schema (#27199).

Slack. Opt-in interactive reply directives let you build richer Slack integrations (#44607, #45463). The redundant ?? undefined in the Slack probe was cleaned up (#44775).

Mobile clients

Section titled “Mobile clients”

Android got a redesigned chat settings UI (#44894), a fix for HttpURLConnection leaks in TalkModeVoiceResolver (#43780), Google Code Scanner for onboarding QR codes (#45021), and a missing params field in the agent validation schema (#41171).

iOS ships an onboarding welcome pager (#45054).

Browser automation

Section titled “Browser automation”

The browser tool received three fixes for batch action dispatch. Selector and batch support are normalized (#45457). Batch failure and limit handling are hardened (#45506). Existing-session driver validation and session lifecycle management are tightened (#45682).

Build and UI

Section titled “Build and UI”

Memory regression. Plugin-sdk chunks were being duplicated, causing a roughly 2x memory regression. Fixed via deduplication (#45426).

Dashboard reload storm. Chat history was reloading in a loop on the dashboard. Stopped (#45541).

Chat rendering. Oversized chat replies stay readable (#45559). The scroll pill button got its chat-new-messages CSS class back (#44856). Chat context notice icon sizing was fixed (#45533).

Ollama. Native reasoning-only output is hidden for Ollama models (#45330).

Gemini. Model-id normalization now applies to the google-vertex provider too (#42435).

Other notable changes

Section titled “Other notable changes”
  • Cron deadlocks. Isolated cron nested lane deadlocks are prevented (#45459).
  • Plugin collisions. Plugins now fail fast on channel and binding collisions (#45628).
  • Timezone support. Docker containers support OPENCLAW_TZ for timezone configuration (#34119).
  • macOS exec approvals. exec-approvals.json settings are now respected in the gateway prompter (#13707).
  • Persona continuity. Compaction summaries preserve persona and language continuity (#10456).
  • Brave costs. Incorrect rendering of Brave costs in docs was fixed (#44989).
  • Sidebar polish. Sidebar status, agent skills, and chat rendering got a polish pass (#45451).
  • Updater refresh. The updater service refresh now guards against missing invocation cwd (#45486).
  • Default model update. Tests updated from openai-codex/gpt-5.3-codex to openai-codex/gpt-5.4 (#44367).
  • Gateway probe. Scope-limited probe RPC is treated as degraded reachability (#45622).
  • Session transcript. chat.inject now creates the transcript file when missing (#36645).
  • Discovery config. Missing domain added to wideArea Zod config schema (#35615).
  • Firecrawl config. Web fetch firecrawl config restored in runtime Zod schema (#42583).
  • Delivery dedup. Review follow-ups for delivery dedup were addressed (#44666).
  • Anthropic startup crash. A config-related crash on Anthropic startup was fixed (#45520).

Upgrade

Section titled “Upgrade”

Docker users: rebuild your images. The apt-get upgrade addition and token leak fix are worth it.

If you use Feishu and have been getting duplicate replies, this release fixes it. If you self-host behind a reverse proxy, the control-ui auth restore matters.

Full changelog

Section titled “Full changelog”

See the GitHub Release for the complete list of PRs and contributors.

70+ fixes. Dozens of contributors. One recovery tag. This is what open source looks like when the community shows up.

Connecting Feishu Bots to OpenClaw: Three Pitfalls That Cost Me an Hour

Mar 13, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Ran openclaw channels add --channel feishu. Nothing happened. Edited the config manually, restarted the gateway, sent “hi” to the bot in Feishu.

Nothing came back.

WebSocket was connected. Logs showed zero message events. Spent nearly an hour before finding the cause: a single permission toggle buried in the Feishu developer console.

This is the full record of connecting three Feishu enterprise apps to OpenClaw with independent agent routing, and the three pitfalls along the way.

Environment

Section titled “Environment”
  • macOS (FENG’s MacBook Pro)
  • OpenClaw 2026.3.11
  • Three Feishu enterprise apps: vs-po (production), vs-dev (development), vs-qa (testing)

Step 1: Create Feishu Enterprise Apps

Section titled “Step 1: Create Feishu Enterprise Apps”

Open the Feishu Developer Console at open.feishu.cn/app. Go to “Enterprise Apps” and create your applications.

App NamePurpose
vs-poProduction
vs-devDevelopment
vs-qaTesting

Get each app’s App ID and App Secret from the “Basic Information > Credentials” page.

Step 2: Configure OpenClaw Channels

Section titled “Step 2: Configure OpenClaw Channels”

Here’s the first pitfall.

openclaw channels add accepts a --token parameter — that’s what Telegram and Discord use. But Feishu doesn’t work with tokens. It needs an appId and appSecret pair, which must be written via config set:

After writing all three accounts, the Feishu section in ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json looks like:

Set dmPolicy to "open" if you want the bot to receive direct messages. The default "pairing" mode requires users to complete a pairing flow first.

Step 3: Create Agents and Bindings

Section titled “Step 3: Create Agents and Bindings”

Each Feishu account gets its own agent with an isolated workspace and agent directory:

Then configure bindings in openclaw.json to route each account’s messages to its agent:

The field name is agentId, not agent. Get it wrong and the gateway fails with Config invalid — the error message won’t tell you which field is the problem.

Step 4: Feishu Developer Console Configuration

Section titled “Step 4: Feishu Developer Console Configuration”

Each app needs three things configured in the console:

1. Add Bot Capability

Application Capabilities > Add Capability > Bot

2. Configure Event Subscription

Development Config > Events & Callbacks:

  • Subscription method: “Use long connection to receive events/callbacks”
  • Add event: im.message.receive_v1

3. Enable Permissions

Development Config > Permission Management. Enable at minimum:

  • im:message
  • im:message:send_as_bot
  • im:message.group_at_msg:readonly
  • im:message.group_msg
  • im:chat
  • im:message.p2p_msg:readonly (for receiving DMs — this is the critical one)

After changing permissions, create a new app version and publish it. Permission changes don’t take effect until published.

Pitfall 1: Plugin Loaded Three Times

Section titled “Pitfall 1: Plugin Loaded Three Times”

After restarting the gateway, the logs showed:

The Feishu plugin was loading from three sources:

  • OpenClaw’s built-in plugin
  • A local extension at ~/.openclaw/extensions/feishu/ (from a previous manual install)
  • A path auto-added to plugins.load.paths by the channels add command

Fix: remove the extra path from plugins.load.paths in openclaw.json, and rename the old local extension:

The built-in plugin is all you need.

Pitfall 2: Wrong Binding Field Name

Section titled “Pitfall 2: Wrong Binding Field Name”

Mentioned above. Writing agent instead of agentId causes a generic Config invalid error on startup. You’ll waste time checking whether your appId and appSecret values are correct, when the actual problem is the field name.

Pitfall 3: Messages Silently Disappear

Section titled “Pitfall 3: Messages Silently Disappear”

This one took the longest.

Configuration complete, gateway restarted, sent “hi” to the bot. No reply.

Logs showed:

WebSocket was connected. But zero im.message.receive_v1 events arrived.

The debug path:

  1. WebSocket connected — confirmed working
  2. Event log empty — messages weren’t being pushed at all, problem was on Feishu’s side
  3. Changed dmPolicy to open — still no messages
  4. Checked the Feishu developer console carefully — found it

im:message.p2p_msg:readonly was listed as “Not Enabled.”

This permission controls “read messages sent by users to the bot in DMs.” Without it, Feishu filters out the event at the server side. It doesn’t send it to the long connection, doesn’t return an error, doesn’t log a warning. The message just disappears.

Enabled the permission, published a new version, restarted the gateway. Messages started flowing immediately.

The worst part of this issue is the zero feedback. WebSocket is connected, config looks right, but messages vanish without a trace. If Feishu returned something like permission_denied when filtering events, it would save a lot of debugging time.

Configuration Checklist

Section titled “Configuration Checklist”

Run through this for every new Feishu app:

  • openclaw.json: Account appId / appSecret written correctly
  • bindings: Each accountId maps to correct agentId (not agent)
  • dmPolicy: "open" and allowFrom: ["*"] set (for receiving DMs)
  • Feishu console: Bot capability added
  • Feishu console: Subscription method is “long connection”, event im.message.receive_v1 added
  • Feishu console: im:message.p2p_msg:readonly permission enabled
  • Feishu console: Latest app version published
  • openclaw gateway restart executed

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

Feishu integration with OpenClaw is straightforward once you know where the traps are. Three things don’t work the way you’d expect: credentials go through config set instead of --token, local extensions can conflict with built-in plugins, and missing DM permissions cause messages to silently vanish. With the checklist above, the next setup takes a few minutes.

  • bot configuration
  • troubleshooting

OpenClaw + Feishu + Scrum: Running a Complete R&D Closed Loop with an AI Agent Team

Mar 13, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw + Feishu + Scrum: Running a Complete R&D Closed Loop with an AI Agent Team

Section titled “OpenClaw + Feishu + Scrum: Running a Complete R&D Closed Loop with an AI Agent Team”

This is not another article about AI helping you write code. Everyone’s done that. This is about something different: giving AI agents actual team roles — Product Owner, Developer, QA Engineer, Scrum Master — and letting them collaborate with each other and with humans in a Feishu group chat, running a real Sprint from backlog to release.

The gap nobody talks about

Section titled “The gap nobody talks about”

Most teams use AI as a personal productivity tool. You open a chat window, ask it to generate code or write tests, copy the result. The AI never talks to your teammates. It doesn’t know what the PO defined or what QA found broken. The moment cross-role collaboration starts, AI exits the room.

We wanted to change that.

The idea: create five AI agents on OpenClaw, each bound to a separate Feishu bot account, each assigned a specific Scrum role. Put them all in one Feishu group chat. Let them read each other’s messages, challenge each other’s work, and collaborate through shared workspace files.

Architecture overview

Section titled “Architecture overview”

Stack:

  • OpenClaw — local AI gateway, manages multi-agent + multi-Feishu-bot accounts
  • Feishu — IM collaboration platform, connected via enterprise custom apps
  • Scrum — development framework that constrains agent behavior boundaries

Role design: tension by intent

Section titled “Role design: tension by intent”

Adversarial roles

Section titled “Adversarial roles”

“Adversarial” is not a negative word here. These three roles have natural goal tension. They check each other and produce better outcomes.

RoleAgent IDFeishu BotCore Responsibility
POvs-po@vs-poRequirements, acceptance criteria, priority ranking, story splitting
Devvs-dev@vs-devTechnical design, implementation, unit tests, tech debt management
QAvs-qa@vs-qaTest case design, defect discovery, regression verification, quality gates

PO pushes for feature completeness and business value. Dev pushes for implementation simplicity and maintainability. QA pushes for system stability and edge coverage. The three naturally push against each other, driving requirements toward clarity and code toward robustness.

Facilitative roles

Section titled “Facilitative roles”
RoleAgent IDFeishu BotCore Responsibility
SMvs-sm@vs-smProcess guardian, blocker removal, team rhythm, ceremony facilitation
Projectproject-a@project-aProgress tracking, risk management, cross-team sync, release coordination

Workspace design

Section titled “Workspace design”

Each agent has a private workspace plus access to a shared workspace:

The shared workspace is the team’s single source of truth. Agents collaborate by reading and writing shared files. Private workspaces hold each agent’s task notes and context state.

OpenClaw configuration

Section titled “OpenClaw configuration”

Feishu account setup

Section titled “Feishu account setup”

In ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json:

Creating agents

Section titled “Creating agents”

Feishu group setup

Section titled “Feishu group setup”
  1. Create a Feishu group: “R&D Collaboration - Sprint #1”
  2. Add all five bots to the group
  3. In Feishu Developer Console, enable group chat permissions for each app:
    • im:message.group_at_msg:readonly
    • im:message:send_as_bot
  4. Subscribe to im.message.receive_v1 event, use long connection mode

Walkthrough: a User Story from backlog to release

Section titled “Walkthrough: a User Story from backlog to release”

Requirement: Add “Forgot Password” to the user center

Sprint Planning: story writing

Section titled “Sprint Planning: story writing”

Human initiates:

@vs-po responds:

Technical review

Section titled “Technical review”

Human initiates:

@vs-dev responds:

@vs-po clarifies:

QA joins: test case design

Section titled “QA joins: test case design”

@vs-qa responds after being asked to design test cases:

Scrum Master drives rhythm

Section titled “Scrum Master drives rhythm”

SM runs daily standup:

QA verification finds bugs

Section titled “QA verification finds bugs”

After Dev notifies completion, QA runs tests:

@vs-dev fixes and responds:

Project coordinates release

Section titled “Project coordinates release”

@project-a generates release note:

Collaboration pattern summary

Section titled “Collaboration pattern summary”
ScenarioInitiated by@WhoOutput
Sprint PlanningHuman@vs-poUser Story + AC
Technical ReviewHuman/PO@vs-devTechnical approach + risks
Test DesignHuman/Dev@vs-qaTest cases
Daily StandupScheduled/Human@vs-smStandup summary + blockers
Test HandoffDev@vs-qaTest execution + report
Bug ReportQA@vs-devFix confirmation
Release PrepHuman@project-aRelease note

Design principles

Section titled “Design principles”

1. Clear role boundaries, no overstepping

Section titled “1. Clear role boundaries, no overstepping”
  • PO does not write code — only defines “What”
  • Dev does not define requirements — only decides “How”
  • QA does not pass substandard features — regardless of schedule pressure

Each agent’s SOUL.md and AGENTS.md files define the role and refusal policies.

2. Shared workspace is the collaboration hub

Section titled “2. Shared workspace is the collaboration hub”

All agents collaborate by reading and writing the shared/ directory. Sprint Board, Bug list, and requirement documents all live there. Humans can inspect and edit at any time.

3. Humans are the final decision makers

Section titled “3. Humans are the final decision makers”

AI agents propose approaches, surface risks, and execute tasks, but critical decision points need human confirmation:

  • Requirement priority changes
  • Release timing windows
  • Security-related policy calls

4. Scrum Master guards the process

Section titled “4. Scrum Master guards the process”

The SM agent does no business work — only:

  • Detects blockers and escalates
  • Maintains Sprint rhythm
  • Facilitates ceremonies (standup, retrospective, review)

Why this pattern works

Section titled “Why this pattern works”

It’s not about replacing people. It’s about:

  1. Amplifying decisions — AI handles information gathering, drafting, test case generation, and status tracking. Humans focus on judgment and decisions.
  2. Enforcing process discipline — Agents don’t skip steps. Requirements always have acceptance criteria. Tests always have cases.
  3. 24/7 responsiveness — Code committed at 2 AM gets initial QA feedback from the QA agent immediately.
  4. Knowledge accumulation — Each agent’s workspace builds context over time. No dependency on individual memory.

What’s next

Section titled “What’s next”
  • Scheduled heartbeat for SM agent to auto-trigger daily standups
  • GitHub Webhook integration: auto-trigger @vs-qa verification on PR merge
  • Shared workspace synced with Git for Sprint Board versioning
  • Sprint Retrospective: SM facilitates agent team retrospective at Sprint end

OpenClaw provides the multi-agent infrastructure. Feishu provides the collaboration surface your team already uses. Scrum provides the framework that keeps AI agents focused, bounded, and accountable. Together, AI stops being your private assistant and starts being an actual working member of your team.

OpenClaw Enterprise Architecture: A CTO's Guide to Multi-Project AI Agent Management

Mar 13, 2026
Vibe Sparking

You’re a CTO. You have five projects, three Slack workspaces, two QQ groups, a Telegram channel, and a dozen engineers who keep asking the same deployment questions. You’ve been thinking about AI agents — not the demo kind, the kind that sits inside your team’s workflow and handles real work.

You spin up OpenClaw. Create one agent. Connect it to Slack. It works. Then someone asks: “Can we get one for Project B too?” And another: “Can it also respond in our QQ group?” Suddenly you’re facing the real question: how do you architect this for an entire engineering organization?

The wrong instinct

Section titled “The wrong instinct”

Most CTOs start the same way. They think in channels. One agent for Slack. One for QQ. One for Telegram. This feels intuitive but it’s wrong. Channels are just doors — entry points for messages. Organizing agents around doors means duplicated logic, inconsistent responses, and a maintenance headache that grows with every new platform you add.

Understanding the real architecture

Section titled “Understanding the real architecture”

OpenClaw has four components that matter:

  • Gateway — The control plane. Routes messages, manages sessions and memory, connects everything.
  • Agents — The brains. Each one is an LLM with its own prompt, tools, and memory.
  • Channels — The doors. Slack, QQ, Telegram, Web, CLI. Just input surfaces.
  • Bindings — The routing rules. They decide which door leads to which brain.

Once you see this separation clearly, the architecture designs itself.

The enterprise blueprint

Section titled “The enterprise blueprint”

For a CTO managing multiple projects with a team of engineers, the recommended pattern is: Platform + Project Isolation + Multi-Channel Access.

Platform Agents handle shared concerns. A DevOps Agent that knows your CI/CD pipelines. A Code Review Agent with your team’s coding standards loaded. A Documentation Agent. These serve everyone, regardless of project.

Project Agents are scoped. Project-carehealth gets an agent loaded with its PRD, codebase structure, and issue tracker. Project-ragLabs gets its own. Each project agent knows its domain deeply and doesn’t leak context to other projects.

Personal Agents serve roles. The CTO Agent generates cross-project daily reports — CI status, code churn, open risks, customer escalations. The PM Agent tracks feature progress. The QA Agent monitors test coverage trends.

One Gateway is enough

Section titled “One Gateway is enough”

For teams under 30 people with fewer than 10 projects: one Gateway. Simpler to operate, agents share tools, configuration is centralized.

You only split to a second Gateway when you need hard isolation — like separating internal team agents from customer-facing service agents. Different data boundaries, different prompt security, different tool permissions.

Channels stay flat, routing gets smart

Section titled “Channels stay flat, routing gets smart”

One Slack channel type. One QQ channel type. One Telegram channel type. Don’t multiply channels by agents.

Use Bindings to route:

  • Mention routing: Type @devops in any channel, message goes to DevOps Agent. Type @project-carehealth, it goes to Project-carehealth Agent.
  • Channel routing: Messages in #project-carehealth automatically go to Project-carehealth Agent. Messages in #devops go to DevOps Agent.

Mention routing is more flexible when multiple agents share a channel. Channel routing is cleaner when teams have dedicated spaces.

Security is not optional

Section titled “Security is not optional”

Enterprise deployment means controlling what agents can do:

  • Tool whitelists per agent. DevOps Agent gets kubectl and terraform. Coding Agent gets repo and PR access. No agent gets shell root.
  • No production deploys from agents. No exceptions.
  • No secret reading. Agents should not access credentials stores directly.
  • Gateway stays off the public internet. More security incidents come from exposed admin panels than from prompt injection.

The Coordinator pattern

Section titled “The Coordinator pattern”

When you’re ready for the next level, add a Coordinator Agent. It sits above the others. When a request comes in that spans multiple domains — “What’s the risk status across all projects?” — the Coordinator decomposes it, dispatches sub-tasks to Project Agents and the DevOps Agent, collects responses, and synthesizes a unified answer.

This is multi-agent orchestration. It turns OpenClaw from a collection of chatbots into an AI-native operations platform.

The CTO Super Agent

Section titled “The CTO Super Agent”

Build yourself a CTO Agent with one command: /cto report. Every morning, it pulls CI status from all projects, checks open blockers, summarizes code review velocity, flags security alerts, and delivers a single digest. No more checking five dashboards.

Team roles for OpenClaw

Section titled “Team roles for OpenClaw”
RoleResponsibility
CTOGateway strategy, Agent architecture decisions
AI EngineerAgent prompt maintenance, tool development
Project Agent OwnerPer-project agent knowledge base, prompt, tools
DevOpsGateway operations, logging, permissions, security

The complete picture

Section titled “The complete picture”

Start here. One Gateway. Role-based agents. Flat channels. Smart routing. Locked-down permissions. When you outgrow it, add the Coordinator.

This is your organization’s AI infrastructure. Treat it like one.

One curl command, an AI brain for QQ: openclaw-qqbot review and group chat gotchas

Mar 12, 2026
Vibe Sparking

One curl command, and QQ has an AI brain.

Not clickbait. openclaw-qqbot actually delivers on that promise. But the story doesn’t stop at installation.

Background

Section titled “Background”

I’ve been testing AI assistant channels for OpenClaw — WeChat, Telegram, Discord, QQ. Each has its tradeoffs. QQ Bot, through the openclaw-qqbot plugin from Tencent Connect, turned out to be the easiest to get running and the most surprising in what it does well.

Setup: suspiciously simple

Section titled “Setup: suspiciously simple”

Registration means scanning a QR code on the QQ Open Platform with your phone QQ. That creates a bot. Copy the AppID and AppSecret. Then one command:

That’s it. The script downloads, cleans up old plugins, installs the latest version, configures the channel, and restarts the service. Open QQ, find your bot, send a message. It replies.

No VPN. No proxy configuration. No Docker. No webhook URL setup. For anyone who’s fought with network restrictions while setting up other AI channels in China, this feels almost too good to be true.

Subsequent upgrades are even simpler — no need to re-enter AppID and Secret:

Voice-to-text: the real standout

Section titled “Voice-to-text: the real standout”

The killer feature isn’t image generation or file understanding — those depend on your AI model, not the plugin. It’s voice-to-text.

Send a voice message to your bot. The plugin automatically converts it (SILK to WAV), runs STT transcription, sends the text to your AI model, and returns the response. The user never has to think about the transcription step — talking to your AI assistant feels as natural as messaging a friend on QQ.

On mobile, voice input is often faster than typing, especially for Chinese. Configure an STT provider once, and forget about it.

Configuration:

Rich media and multi-bot

Section titled “Rich media and multi-bot”

The plugin handles bidirectional rich media: images, voice, files (up to 20MB), and video. AI sends via <qqimg>, <qqvoice>, <qqfile>, <qqvideo> tags. Incoming media gets processed automatically — images go to vision models, voice gets transcribed, files get read.

Running multiple bots? Add an accounts block to your config. Each bot gets its own WebSocket connection and token cache, completely isolated:

Quoted messages work properly too. QQ sends quote indices (REFIDX_xxx) instead of the actual quoted text. The plugin resolves these from a local persistent store and injects the quoted context into AI input. Your AI actually knows what message the user is replying to.

Group chat: where things get complicated

Section titled “Group chat: where things get complicated”

Private chat (C2C) is flawless. Group chat works too — the bot responds to @mentions — until QQ’s security system decides it doesn’t.

After a morning of debugging (bot2 reconnected about a dozen times due to network issues), QQ intervened:

Bot has security risk, group message API temporarily banned, estimated recovery time: 14:22:43

The trigger was likely a combination: frequent reconnections looked like automated abuse, and responses containing Markdown tables and long formatted text triggered content risk detection.

The ban lifted on schedule. But the lesson was clear: QQ’s security audit system is real, active, and not particularly transparent about its rules. Repeated triggers extend the ban duration.

Practical takeaways

Section titled “Practical takeaways”

Pros:

  • No network restrictions — works behind the Great Firewall without any proxy
  • Simplest configuration of any OpenClaw channel
  • Voice-to-text input is genuinely useful on mobile
  • Multi-bot support with isolated accounts
  • Quoted message context resolution

Cons:

  • Group chat message API gets temporarily banned when security detection triggers
  • Ban triggers are opaque: frequent reconnections, complex Markdown, high message volume
  • Repeated triggers increase ban duration

Recommendations:

  • Use it. It’s the fastest path to a working QQ AI assistant.
  • Keep group chat replies concise. Avoid tables and heavy Markdown formatting.
  • Don’t reconnect frequently during development — use stable network conditions.
  • If banned, wait it out. Don’t retry immediately — that makes it worse.
  • For critical group chat use cases, keep a fallback communication channel.

OpenClaw v2026.3.11: WebSocket Hijacking Patched, Ollama Gets First-Class Setup, Memory Goes Multimodal

Mar 12, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw v2026.3.11: WebSocket Hijacking Patched, Ollama Gets First-Class Setup, Memory Goes Multimodal

Section titled “OpenClaw v2026.3.11: WebSocket Hijacking Patched, Ollama Gets First-Class Setup, Memory Goes Multimodal”

A cross-site WebSocket hijacking path in trusted-proxy mode could hand operator.admin access to untrusted origins. That’s patched now. But the security fix is just the opener for one of OpenClaw’s largest releases — 56 commits touching nearly every subsystem.

Security: upgrade immediately

Section titled “Security: upgrade immediately”

GHSA-5wcw-8jjv-m286. The Gateway’s WebSocket handler now enforces browser origin validation for all browser-originated connections, regardless of whether proxy headers are present. Previously, in trusted-proxy mode, the origin check could be skipped. An attacker on an untrusted origin could establish a WebSocket connection and gain operator.admin scope.

If you run OpenClaw behind a reverse proxy, upgrade before doing anything else.

Ollama: proper onboarding at last

Section titled “Ollama: proper onboarding at last”

Setting up Ollama with OpenClaw used to mean editing config files and guessing which models to pull. That’s over.

The new onboarding flow offers two modes:

  • Local — everything runs on your machine
  • Cloud + Local — browser-based cloud sign-in paired with local model inference

You get curated model suggestions during setup. Cloud models skip unnecessary local pulls. The wizard handles it.

This also introduces the OpenCode Go provider — a new Go-based runtime. Zen and Go share one OpenCode key but keep their runtime providers separate. If you’re already using OpenCode Zen, the existing key works for Go too.

Memory goes multimodal

Section titled “Memory goes multimodal”

Memory search was text-only. Now it handles images and audio.

Enable opt-in multimodal indexing for memorySearch.extraPaths using Gemini’s gemini-embedding-2-preview. Configure output dimensions per your needs. When dimensions change, the index rebuilds automatically. Scope-based reindexing keeps things efficient — only changed scopes get re-embedded.

For the Gemini embedding backend specifically, gemini-embedding-2-preview support includes configurable output dimensions and automatic reindex on dimension changes. Two separate PRs landed for this, from different contributors, both now merged.

iOS: rebuilt from the home screen up

Section titled “iOS: rebuilt from the home screen up”

Three changes ship together:

  1. Welcome screen. A bundled home view with a live agent overview. Refreshes on connect, reconnect, and foreground return.
  2. Docked toolbar. Floating controls are gone. The compact connection pill moved off the top-left overlay.
  3. Chat opens in the right session. Chat now opens in the resolved main session instead of a synthetic ios session.

Also fixed: the app no longer stays disconnected after returning from background. Previous behavior required waiting for a later wake path — now it reconnects immediately when foreground returns after stale background sockets are torn down.

A local beta release flow with Fastlane support also landed, covering prepare, archive, and upload to TestFlight.

macOS: chat model picker

Section titled “macOS: chat model picker”

The macOS client adds a chat model picker in the shared chat composer. Explicit thinking-level selections persist across relaunch. Provider-aware session model sync is hardened for the shared composer path.

The onboarding flow now detects when remote gateways need a shared auth token and explains where to find it on the gateway host — including when a successful check used paired-device auth instead.

Breaking: cron job isolation

Section titled “Breaking: cron job isolation”

Cron jobs can no longer notify through ad hoc agent sends or fallback main-session summaries. This is deliberate tightening of isolated cron delivery.

Run openclaw doctor --fix to migrate legacy cron storage and legacy notify/webhook delivery metadata.

If you have cron jobs that relied on sending messages through agent sends as a side channel, they’ll stop working. The migration path is explicit.

Gateway auth hardening

Section titled “Gateway auth hardening”

Multiple security fixes landed across the auth stack:

  • SecretRef traversal rejection. Exec SecretRef traversal IDs rejected across schema, runtime, and gateway.
  • Fail closed on missing SecretRefs. Local gateway.auth.* SecretRefs that are unavailable now fail closed instead of silently falling back to gateway.remote.* credentials.
  • Config write scoping. /config and /allowlist edits now enforce configWrites against both originating and targeted account scopes, blocking sibling-account mutations.
  • Session reset auth split. Conversation /new and /reset split from the admin-only sessions.reset control-plane RPC.
  • Plugin runtime auth. Unauthenticated plugin HTTP routes no longer inherit synthetic admin gateway scopes.
  • Sandbox session-tree visibility. Session-tree visibility and agent-to-agent access guards enforced before reading or mutating target session state.

Model and agent fixes

Section titled “Model and agent fixes”

Leaked model control tokens stripped. GLM-5 and DeepSeek internal delimiters (<|...|> and full-width variants) no longer reach end users.

Fallback improvements. HTTP 499 (Anthropic client-closed overload), Venice 402 (insufficient balance), Poe 402 (used up points), and Gemini MALFORMED_RESPONSE stop reasons all now trigger model fallback correctly.

Cooldown fix. Expired auth-profile cooldown counters reset properly instead of re-escalating into long loops. Default cooldown windows with no failure history report as unknown instead of rate_limit.

Kimi Coding fix. Tools sent in native Anthropic format again — kimi-coding was degrading tool calls into XML/plain-text pseudo invocations.

Telegram: four delivery fixes

Section titled “Telegram: four delivery fixes”
  1. Final preview delivery. Split active preview lifecycle from cleanup retention to avoid duplicate fallback sends.
  2. First-preview edge case. Ambiguous missing-message_id finals handled correctly for first-preview/no-id cases.
  3. Stale cleanup-retain. Archived-preview retains no longer leave stale partial bubbles beside fallback-sent finals.
  4. Outbound HTML chunking. Long HTML messages chunk correctly, with plain-text fallback when HTML chunk planning can’t safely preserve the full message.

ACP: ten patches

Section titled “ACP: ten patches”

The Agent Communication Protocol got heavy attention:

  • resumeSessionId for spawned ACP sessions
  • Main session alias canonicalization (main before lookup)
  • Image attachment forwarding into ACP runtime turns
  • Session restore and prompt completion degrade gracefully on failures
  • Tool streaming with text content and file-location hints
  • Gateway-backed session controls and metadata exposure
  • Stop reason mapping: error completions resolve as end_turn instead of refusal
  • Mode change rejections propagated instead of silent success
  • Implicit streaming for mode="run" spawns to eligible parent sessions
  • ACPX pin bumped to 0.1.16

Everything else

Section titled “Everything else”

Discord. autoArchiveDuration channel config for auto-created threads. Runtime config threading for SecretRef-based credentials.

Mattermost. First-line indentation preserved when stripping bot mentions. Native table rendering instead of fenced-code fallback.

MS Teams. General channel conversation ID used as resolved team key for allowlist matching.

Signal. channels.signal.accountUuid accepted in strict config validation.

Feishu. Local image paths upload as Feishu images again via mediaLocalRoots.

CLI. ANSI/C1 control bytes stripped from skills list --json. ASCII table borders default on legacy Windows consoles. Memory search/index managers closed in one-shot CLI shutdown.

Sandbox. Staged writes pinned to verified parent directories. TAR extraction hardened against symlink escapes.

Upgrade

Section titled “Upgrade”

Run openclaw doctor --fix after upgrade to migrate legacy cron storage if you use cron jobs.

The security fix alone makes this a mandatory upgrade for anyone running OpenClaw with browser access behind a reverse proxy.

Two Macs, One LAN, Endless 'Allow device to connect?' — Fix It in Four Commands

Mar 12, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Two Macs, one LAN, same OpenClaw setup.

One runs as Gateway, the other connects as a node. After connecting, the Gateway pops up:

Allow device to connect?

Click Allow. A few minutes later, it pops up again. And again. Close the window, reopen, still there.

This isn’t a bug.

Why the prompt appears

Section titled “Why the prompt appears”

OpenClaw has a device pairing mechanism. The rule is straightforward:

  • 127.0.0.1 / localhost → local loopback, trusted, no prompt
  • Everything else → external device, pairing required

Two Macs on the same LAN have IPs like 192.168.x.x. To the Gateway, that’s indistinguishable from a random machine on the internet — not localhost, so pairing kicks in.

Multiple GitHub issues confirm this behavior: non-localhost connections always trigger pairing. There’s no “same subnet = auto-trust” logic.

Why it keeps coming back after clicking Allow

Section titled “Why it keeps coming back after clicking Allow”

Common reasons:

  1. Device identity changed. Gateway token rotation, network switch, macOS update — any of these can alter the node’s device fingerprint. Changed fingerprint means the Gateway sees a new device or a device needing repair, retriggering pairing.
  2. Pending repair not cleared. When a device is stuck in “awaiting repair confirmation,” the UI Allow button doesn’t always resolve it fully. Many scenarios require CLI approval.
  3. Token churn loop. Recent macOS reports show tokens refreshing repeatedly, causing a pairing-required cycle.

The UI Allow button sometimes grants temporary passage without completing the full device lifecycle.

The correct fix: four CLI commands

Section titled “The correct fix: four CLI commands”

Run these on the Mac acting as Gateway:

Step 1: List devices and pending requests

Section titled “Step 1: List devices and pending requests”

Find entries with pending repair or pending pairing status. Note the requestId.

Step 2: Approve (or reject) the pending request

Section titled “Step 2: Approve (or reject) the pending request”

You can use reject instead of approve — the point is to clear the pending state. Don’t leave it hanging.

If pending isn’t cleared, the remove in step 4 will fail.

Step 3: Get the real device ID

Section titled “Step 3: Get the real device ID”

Output is JSON with each device’s hex device ID. The remove command needs this ID, not the display name (e.g., “FENG’s MacBook Pro”).

Step 4: Remove the device

Section titled “Step 4: Remove the device”

Run devices list again to confirm the list is clean.

Order matters. Clear pending first, get ID second, remove last.

Three topology options

Section titled “Three topology options”

Pick based on your use case:

Option A: Each Mac uses localhost only (recommended)

Section titled “Option A: Each Mac uses localhost only (recommended)”

Each Mac runs its own OpenClaw instance. Channels, apps, and UI connect only to local localhost. No LAN node-to-gateway cross-connection.

Benefit: localhost connections don’t trigger pairing. The prompt disappears at the source.

Best for: two Macs as independent work environments with no need to share a Gateway.

Option B: Keep LAN setup, approve once via CLI

Section titled “Option B: Keep LAN setup, approve once via CLI”

Keep one Mac as Gateway with the other as a node. Use the four-step CLI process above to properly approve or clean up devices on the Gateway side.

Benefit: retains centralized management flexibility.

Caveat: if device identity changes frequently (token churn), you may need to repeat the process occasionally. Pin your Gateway token to reduce identity drift.

Option C: Force-disable pairing checks (not recommended)

Section titled “Option C: Force-disable pairing checks (not recommended)”

You may have found these config options:

Or dangerouslyDisableDeviceAuth: true.

Two problems:

  1. allowInsecureAuth weakens device identity verification. Official security advisories flag this.
  2. dangerouslyDisableDeviceAuth has regression bugs in recent versions. Multiple reports show it doesn’t reliably bypass device checks.

Unless you fully understand the consequences and are in an isolated test environment, avoid these flags.

Quick reference

Section titled “Quick reference”

Lessons learned

Section titled “Lessons learned”
  • openclaw devices remove requires the hex device ID, not the display name. Use --json to get it.
  • Devices with pending repairs can’t be removed directly. Approve or reject first.
  • The UI Allow button isn’t equivalent to CLI approve in all scenarios. When the prompt loops, go straight to CLI.

Bottom line

Section titled “Bottom line”

You can’t fix this by “turning off the prompt.” You need to clear pending repairs and remove stale paired devices. Otherwise it comes back. The simplest path: skip LAN cross-connection entirely, use localhost on each Mac.

Two plugins, one bridge: sliverp/qqbot vs tencent-connect/openclaw-qqbot

Mar 12, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Search GitHub for “QQ Bot OpenClaw plugin” and you get two results that look almost identical. Same feature tables. Same demo screenshots. Same QQ group invite code.

Behind the parallel READMEs is a story about how open source works in China’s developer ecosystem.

The two repos

Section titled “The two repos”

sliverp/qqbot — the community version. Built by a developer named sliverp. 241 commits, version 1.5.4. MIT license. Package name: @sliverp/qqbot.

tencent-connect/openclaw-qqbot — the official version under Tencent Connect. 299 commits, version 1.5.7. MIT license. Package name: @tencent-connect/openclaw-qqbot.

Both connect OpenClaw to QQ. Both handle private chat, group @messages, channel messages, rich media (images, voice, video, files up to 20MB), STT/TTS, scheduled push, typing indicators, Markdown, and multi-account bots.

The shared features make sense once you realize the official version forked from the community one.

Where they diverge

Section titled “Where they diverge”

The differences tell you about each project’s priorities.

sliverp/qqbot adds developer tooling

Section titled “sliverp/qqbot adds developer tooling”
  • GitHub Actions E2E test workflow — automated testing baked into CI
  • CLI plugin management tool (bin/ directory)
  • Lean README: features, config, done

This is a project built by someone who ships fast and tests properly. The E2E pipeline and CLI tooling suggest a developer who plans to maintain this long-term.

tencent-connect/openclaw-qqbot adds production hardening

Section titled “tencent-connect/openclaw-qqbot adds production hardening”
  • Quoted message context — When a user quotes a previous message in QQ, the platform sends only a cryptic REFIDX_xxx key. The official plugin resolves these from a persistent local store (~/.openclaw/qqbot/data/ref-index.jsonl) and injects the full quoted body into AI context. The AI actually understands what the user is replying to.
  • Remote one-liner install — curl | bash with --appid and --secret flags. Zero-clone setup.
  • 30+ tag variant auto-correction — Write <qq-img> instead of <qqimg> and it still works.
  • Upload dedup caching — Same file sent twice doesn’t get uploaded twice.
  • Ordered queue delivery — Messages arrive in sequence.
  • Dedicated upgrade guide and structured changelogs in both English and Chinese.

These are features born from supporting a larger user base. The quoted context feature alone changes the conversation quality for group chats where users frequently reply to specific messages.

Side-by-side comparison

Section titled “Side-by-side comparison”
Aspectsliverp/qqbottencent-connect/openclaw-qqbot
Commits241299
Version1.5.41.5.7
Quoted contextNoYes (REFIDX resolution)
Install optionsCLI / npm / git cloneCLI / npm / git clone / curl one-liner
E2E testing CIYesNot documented
CLI plugin managerYesNot documented
Tag auto-correctionNot mentioned30+ variants
Upload dedupNot mentionedYes
Persistent ref storeNoYes (survives restarts)
Upgrade guideInline READMEDedicated doc
Changelog formatDirectory-basedSingle file (EN + ZH)
LicenseMITMIT
npm package@sliverp/qqbot@tencent-connect/openclaw-qqbot

What they share

Section titled “What they share”

Both plugins:

  • Use the same openclaw.json config schema
  • Support multi-account bot configuration with isolated WebSocket connections and token caches
  • Handle the same media formats with the same tag syntax (<qqimg>, <qqvoice>, <qqfile>, <qqvideo>)
  • Support STT/TTS with two-level priority config (plugin-specific overrides framework-level)
  • Share the same QQ community group

The config compatibility means switching between them is straightforward. Uninstall one, install the other, keep your openclaw.json.

The pattern worth noticing

Section titled “The pattern worth noticing”

The community version validated the demand. sliverp built the first bridge, proved it works, attracted users. The official version inherited that momentum and added enterprise polish.

Neither killed the other. Both repos remain active. They share the same community chat. This is the open source pattern working as designed: a developer scratches an itch, the platform notices, and builds on that foundation.

Which one should you use

Section titled “Which one should you use”

Pick sliverp/qqbot if:

  • You want to contribute code upstream
  • You value having E2E tests in CI
  • You prefer a leaner package
  • You’re running a personal AI assistant

Pick tencent-connect/openclaw-qqbot if:

  • You’re deploying for a team or business
  • You need quoted message context for natural group conversations
  • You want one-command setup with no git clone
  • You prefer official Tencent backing for long-term maintenance

Either way: the setup is nearly identical. Register at QQ Open Platform, create a bot, grab AppID and AppSecret, configure OpenClaw, start chatting. The intelligence comes from the AI model and skills you configure in OpenClaw, not from the channel plugin.

The bridge is built. Both lanes work. Pick the one that matches how you drive.

  • tencent-connect/openclaw-qqbot on GitHub

Three Walls Installing OpenClaw on macOS (and How to Break Through Each)

Mar 11, 2026
Vibe Sparking

One command. Three walls.

Looks simple enough. In practice, macOS finds three different ways to say no. I hit all of them in sequence. Here’s what happened and how to fix each one.

Wall 1: npm cache permission denied

Section titled “Wall 1: npm cache permission denied”

The install fails immediately with EACCES:

At some point in the past, sudo npm install changed the ownership of the cache directory to root. Now regular npm can’t write to it.

npm suggests sudo chown -R 501:20 "~/.npm". That works. I went with the simpler option:

npm recreates the cache on next run. Problem gone.

Wall 2: Sharp falls back to source compilation

Section titled “Wall 2: Sharp falls back to source compilation”

Next attempt, Sharp fails to install. The key lines:

Sharp is an image processing library backed by libvips (C++). Normally npm downloads a prebuilt binary. When the prebuilt doesn’t match your system — wrong Node version, CPU architecture, or macOS version — it falls back to compiling from source.

Source compilation needs libvips and node-gyp. macOS has neither by default.

Sharp passes this time.

Wall 3: Git SSH permission denied

Section titled “Wall 3: Git SSH permission denied”

Another failure. This time it’s Git:

npm is pulling a transitive dependency from GitHub via SSH:

The machine has no GitHub SSH key configured. The fix: tell Git to rewrite SSH URLs to HTTPS globally.

For broader coverage, edit ~/.gitconfig to catch all SSH URL variants:

Then retry:

It installs.

Summary

Section titled “Summary”

Three problems, three unrelated root causes:

ErrorCauseFix
EACCES on ~/.npmPast sudo poisoned cache ownershiprm -fr ~/.npm
Sharp build from sourceMissing libvips and node-gypbrew install vips && npm i -g node-gyp
SSH permission deniedTransitive dep uses SSH for GitHubgit config --global SSH-to-HTTPS rewrite

npm global installs on macOS look like a one-liner. In practice, they depend on cache state, native build toolchains, and Git protocol configuration. These three cover most of what goes wrong.

Installing OpenClaw-CN on macOS: Native Setup with QQ Bot in 10 Minutes

Mar 10, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Installing OpenClaw-CN on macOS: Native Setup with QQ Bot in 10 Minutes

Section titled “Installing OpenClaw-CN on macOS: Native Setup with QQ Bot in 10 Minutes”

Yesterday’s blog covered the Docker path. Today: bare metal. No containers, no compose files. Just a curl pipe, 676 npm packages, and a lobster that greets you at the end.

The OpenClaw Chinese community fork (openclaw-cn) adds a few things the upstream version doesn’t have: npm mirror support for users behind the Great Firewall, QQ Bot integration, and a fully localized onboarding wizard in Chinese.

What you need before starting

Section titled “What you need before starting”
  • macOS (tested on Darwin 25.3.0)
  • Node.js v22+ (v25.8.0 in my case)
  • Git 2.x
  • An Anthropic API key or a claude setup-token
  • A QQ Bot AppID and ClientSecret from QQ Open Platform

No Docker, no Homebrew packages beyond Node and Git.

The one-liner

Section titled “The one-liner”

The --registry flag routes npm through the China mirror. Without it, npm install can take forever or time out entirely from mainland China.

The installer shows a lobster box and a random quip:

System checks run first:

The locale warning is worth noting. If your terminal runs US-ASCII, the installer switches to en_US.UTF-8 automatically. No action needed, but it explains why some terminal apps might behave differently after the install.

Then npm pulls 676 packages. A few deprecation warnings for gauge, are-we-there-yet, npmlog, and node-domexception. Harmless. 36 seconds on a fast connection.

The setup wizard

Section titled “The setup wizard”

The installer launches an interactive setup. Here’s what each section does.

Security warning

Section titled “Security warning”

A box warns you that OpenClaw is beta, can read files and execute operations if tools are enabled, and bad prompts can trick it into unsafe actions. It recommends pairing/allowlist gating, sandbox with minimal privileges, and keeping secrets out of the agent’s file system reach. Read it. These are real risks.

Quick start config

Section titled “Quick start config”

Defaults are sensible:

SettingValue
Gateway port18789
Gateway bindLoopback (127.0.0.1)
Gateway authToken (default)
Tailscale exposureOff

Model provider

Section titled “Model provider”

I picked Anthropic and pasted a setup token from claude setup-token. The wizard validated it and set the default model to anthropic/claude-opus-4-6.

One catch: the model check said Model not found: anthropic/claude-opus-4-6. This happens when the model name format doesn’t match the provider’s expected format. It’s a non-blocking warning. Run /models list in the TUI later to pick a model the provider recognizes.

Channel selection: QQ Bot

Section titled “Channel selection: QQ Bot”

The wizard lists every supported channel:

  • DingTalk, WeCom, QQ, Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, Google Chat, Feishu, Slack, Signal, iMessage

I picked QQ (Community Edition). The wizard installed the @sliverp/qqbot plugin.

Then came the interesting part.

The plugin security warning

Section titled “The plugin security warning”

The installer flagged four suspicious patterns in the QQ Bot plugin. Let me break them down:

Environment variable access + network send (gateway.ts:140) — The plugin reads environment variables and sends data over the network. That’s the normal operation of a bot that needs API credentials. But the scanner can’t tell the difference between “reads QQBOT_APP_ID to authenticate” and “reads SSH_KEY to exfiltrate.” The warning is correct to flag it.

Shell command execution (audio-convert.ts, platform.ts, qqbot-cli.js) — The plugin spawns child processes for audio conversion (likely ffmpeg) and platform detection. This is common in media-handling plugins. The risk is real but the use case is legitimate.

The installer installed it anyway, into ~/.openclaw/extensions/qqbot. If you’re uncomfortable with these patterns, audit the source code before enabling the plugin. The file paths are in the warning.

QQ Bot configuration

Section titled “QQ Bot configuration”

I pasted my AppID and ClientSecret. The wizard wrote the config to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json.

Hooks and gateway service

Section titled “Hooks and gateway service”

The wizard offered three hooks:

  • boot-md — Loads markdown context at startup
  • command-logger — Logs all commands
  • session-memory — Persists conversation context across sessions

I enabled all three.

The gateway installed as a macOS LaunchAgent:

This means the gateway starts automatically on login and survives reboots. The plist file is a standard launchd job. Unload it with launchctl unload ~/Library/LaunchAgents/com.clawdbot.gateway.plist if you want to stop it.

The TUI

Section titled “The TUI”

The final step launches the terminal UI:

ASCII art spells out “CLAWBOT” with lobster emojis. The TUI connects to the local gateway via WebSocket. Type /quit to exit.

The Control UI is also available at:

Native vs Docker: when to use which

Section titled “Native vs Docker: when to use which”
FactorNative (this guide)Docker (previous guide)
Setup speedFaster, fewer moving partsSlower, but isolated
PersistenceLaunchAgent, survives rebootsDocker restart policy
Plugin ecosystemFull access to Homebrew/system toolsLimited, some skills fail
IsolationNone — agent runs as your userContainer sandbox available
China mirrorBuilt-in --registry flagManual npm config
QQ BotFirst-class community supportSame plugin, different install path

Use native if you want full plugin compatibility and don’t mind the agent running with your user privileges. Use Docker if you want isolation or are deploying on a server.

Troubleshooting

Section titled “Troubleshooting”

Model not found after setup — Run /models list in the TUI. Pick a model the provider recognizes. Common Anthropic models: claude-sonnet-4-6, claude-haiku-4-5.

Plugin security warnings — Read the flagged file paths. Audit the source if concerned. The warnings are informational, not blocking.

Locale warning on macOS — The installer handles it. If you still see encoding issues, add export LANG=en_US.UTF-8 to your .zshrc.

Gateway not starting — Check ~/.openclaw/logs/gateway.log. Common issues: port 18789 already in use, token file missing, or config JSON syntax error.

QQ Bot not responding — Verify AppID and ClientSecret. Check that sandbox members are added in QQ Open Platform. Run openclaw-cn security audit --deep for a full diagnostic.

Installing OpenClaw-CN on Windows 11: PowerShell, DeepSeek, and QQ Bot

Mar 10, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Installing OpenClaw-CN on Windows 11: PowerShell, DeepSeek, and QQ Bot

Section titled “Installing OpenClaw-CN on Windows 11: PowerShell, DeepSeek, and QQ Bot”

Docker was first. macOS native was second. Now: Windows 11, no WSL2, no containers. Just PowerShell, an npm mirror, and some faith.

OpenClaw-CN is the Chinese community fork of OpenClaw. It adds npm mirror support (essential behind the Great Firewall), QQ Bot integration, and a fully localized onboarding wizard. Today we install it on bare Windows.

Before you start

Section titled “Before you start”
  • Windows 11
  • Node.js v22+ (v24.14.0 in this run)
  • PowerShell (built-in)
  • A DeepSeek API key from platform.deepseek.com
  • QQ Bot AppID and ClientSecret from QQ Open Platform

No WSL2, no Docker Desktop. Node and PowerShell are enough.

Set execution policy

Section titled “Set execution policy”

PowerShell blocks unsigned scripts by default. Open PowerShell as Administrator and run:

This allows locally-created scripts and signed remote scripts to run. Without this, the installer won’t execute.

Run the installer

Section titled “Run the installer”

iwr downloads the install script. -Registry routes npm through npmmirror so packages actually arrive in China.

The output:

544 packages, 6 minutes. Three deprecated dependency warnings. Nothing broken.

Onboarding wizard

Section titled “Onboarding wizard”

The wizard starts automatically. A lobster greets you:

Security acknowledgment

Section titled “Security acknowledgment”

First screen is a security warning. OpenClaw can read files and execute actions on your machine. Bad prompts can trick it into unsafe operations. The warning recommends:

  • Pair/whitelist + @mention gating
  • Sandbox + least privilege tools
  • Keep secrets outside the agent’s file system
  • Use the strongest model available for tool-using bots

Read it. Acknowledge it. Move on.

Quick start configuration

Section titled “Quick start configuration”

The wizard offers Quick Start mode. Defaults:

Loopback binding means the gateway only listens on localhost. Good for testing.

Model configuration: DeepSeek

Section titled “Model configuration: DeepSeek”

Choose DeepSeek as the model provider. Enter your API key when prompted.

DeepSeek is a domestic Chinese AI model. No need for Anthropic or OpenAI keys, no proxy configuration, no VPN.

QQ Bot plugin

Section titled “QQ Bot plugin”

The wizard shows channel status - everything starts as “needs credentials” or “not configured.” Select QQ (community edition).

Plugin installation

Section titled “Plugin installation”

The community QQ plugin (@sliverp/qqbot@latest) downloads and installs. Then the security scanner fires:

This deserves a pause. The scanner flagged four patterns:

  1. Env variable access + network send - The plugin reads environment variables and sends data over the network. This is how most bot plugins work (reading API keys, sending messages), but the scanner correctly flags it as a credential harvesting risk.
  2. child_process calls - Three files use shell execution. Audio conversion and platform detection are legitimate use cases. The CLI script is expected.

This is a community plugin, not official. The source code is readable. If you’re cautious, review the flagged files before proceeding.

QQ Bot credentials

Section titled “QQ Bot credentials”

Get these from QQ Open Platform. Create a bot application, add sandbox members for testing.

Skills and hooks

Section titled “Skills and hooks”

The wizard finds 53 eligible skills. Install them when prompted.

Three hooks get enabled by default:

  • boot-md - loads context on startup
  • command-logger - logs commands
  • session-memory - saves session context

Gateway service

Section titled “Gateway service”

On Windows, the gateway installs as a Scheduled Task instead of a LaunchAgent (macOS) or systemd service (Linux).

Then the health check runs. And fails:

1006 is a WebSocket abnormal closure. The gateway process started but the WebSocket connection dropped without a proper close frame. On native Windows, this is a known rough edge. The onboarding wizard even warns at the start: “Native Windows is untested and problematic. WSL2 is strongly recommended.”

The gateway may need a manual restart, or you might need to check if the Scheduled Task actually launched the process.

Dashboard

Section titled “Dashboard”

Despite the health check warning, the dashboard URL is generated:

Open it in a browser. If the gateway process is running, you’ll see the control panel. If not, start it manually:

What’s different from macOS

Section titled “What’s different from macOS”
ItemmacOSWindows 11
Install commandcurl | bashiwr -OutFile; ./install.ps1
PrerequisiteNoneSet-ExecutionPolicy RemoteSigned
Packages676544
PersistenceLaunchAgentScheduled Task
Health checkPassedFailed (1006)
Official supportTested”Untested and problematic”

The honest summary

Section titled “The honest summary”

It installs. It configures. The QQ Bot credentials go in. DeepSeek connects. But the gateway health check fails on native Windows, and the project itself tells you to use WSL2.

If you need this running on Windows for real work, consider WSL2. If you’re testing or exploring, native Windows gets you far enough to see the dashboard and understand the architecture.

Next in this series: actually using the bot, sending messages through QQ, and seeing what DeepSeek does with them.
