Installing OpenClaw with Docker: One Script, Three Bugs, and a Working AI Agent

Mar 9, 2026
Vibe Sparking

Installing OpenClaw with Docker: One Script, Three Bugs, and a Working AI Agent

Section titled “Installing OpenClaw with Docker: One Script, Three Bugs, and a Working AI Agent”

A single shell command — ./docker-setup.sh — promises to spin up a personal AI agent that talks to Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, and a dozen other messaging platforms. The official docs make it sound like a three-minute job.

It took me an evening. Here’s what actually happened.

What is OpenClaw?

Section titled “What is OpenClaw?”

OpenClaw is a self-hosted AI agent platform. You give it API keys (Anthropic, OpenAI, etc.), connect messaging channels (Telegram, WhatsApp, Discord, Slack, Signal, IRC, LINE, and more), and it runs as your personal AI assistant across all of them. It has a web-based Control UI, supports skills/plugins, and can sandbox agent tool execution inside Docker containers.

Version 2026.3.8 is what I installed. It’s still beta. The startup message says so: “I read logs so you can keep pretending you don’t have to.”

Prerequisites

Section titled “Prerequisites”
  • Docker Desktop or Docker Engine with Compose v2
  • At least 2 GB RAM (1 GB hosts risk OOM during builds)
  • An Anthropic API key (or other supported provider)
  • A Telegram bot token from @BotFather (if you want Telegram)

Step 1: Clone and run the setup script

Section titled “Step 1: Clone and run the setup script”

The script builds a multi-stage Docker image from node:22-bookworm. My run completed with all 39 build steps cached:

Clean. No errors. The image weighs in with pnpm, Bun (for skills), and a full Node.js runtime.

Step 2: Interactive onboarding

Section titled “Step 2: Interactive onboarding”

The setup script launches an interactive wizard inside the container. It walks through:

  1. Security warning — OpenClaw is a personal-by-default system. Multi-user setups need additional hardening. Fair warning.

  2. QuickStart config — Gateway port 18789, loopback bind, token auth.

  3. Model provider — I picked Anthropic and pasted a setup token generated by claude setup-token.

  4. Channel selection — I chose Telegram and pasted my bot token from @BotFather.

  5. Skills installation — The wizard tried to install 27 skill dependencies. Most failed because the Docker container doesn’t have Homebrew or Go. Expected. You can install them later.

  6. Hooks — Enabled boot-md, bootstrap-extra-files, command-logger, and session-memory.

The onboarding flow is polished. Clear prompts, informative boxes, sensible defaults.

Then it broke.

Bug 1: Gateway crash-loop (the race condition)

Section titled “Bug 1: Gateway crash-loop (the race condition)”

After onboarding, the gateway container started crash-looping:

The gateway log told the real story:

Root cause: docker-setup.sh defaults OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_BIND to lan. The gateway starts, sees a non-loopback bind, and requires controlUi.allowedOrigins to be configured. But that config step happens later in the setup script. The gateway crashes before the script gets there. Since openclaw-cli uses network_mode: "service:openclaw-gateway", it can’t start either. Everything is deadlocked.

Fix:

Edit ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json and add:

Then re-run:

Bug 2: localhost vs 127.0.0.1

Section titled “Bug 2: localhost vs 127.0.0.1”

With the gateway finally running, I opened http://localhost:18789/chat in my browser. Connection refused — well, not refused, but blocked:

The onboarding wizard only added http://127.0.0.1:18789 to the allowlist. Browsers treat localhost and 127.0.0.1 as different origins per the same-origin policy.

Fix: Add both origins to ~/.openclaw/openclaw.json:

Restart the gateway:

Bug 3: Token and device pairing

Section titled “Bug 3: Token and device pairing”

The Control UI loaded but the WebSocket connection failed:

The Control UI needs the gateway auth token. Append it to the URL:

The token is in your .env file or was shown during onboarding. Then came one more wall:

The browser device needs explicit pairing approval:

The request ID shows up in the gateway logs or the Control UI error message.

Bonus: Telegram pairing

Section titled “Bonus: Telegram pairing”

If your Telegram bot responds with “access not configured,” it also needs pairing:

The pairing code appears when you first message the bot.

Note: groupPolicy: "allowlist" with an empty groupAllowFrom silently drops all group messages. If you want group chat support, configure the allowlist.

What you get after all that

Section titled “What you get after all that”

Once past the three-bug gauntlet:

  • Control UI at http://localhost:18789/chat — a clean web interface for chatting with your agent
  • Telegram bot responding to DMs with Claude Sonnet 4.6 (or whatever model you configured)
  • 20+ channel support — WhatsApp, Discord, Slack, Signal, IRC, LINE, Feishu, Matrix, and more
  • Skills system with installable plugins
  • Sandbox mode for isolating agent tool execution in separate containers
  • Health endpoints at /healthz and /readyz for monitoring

The platform is genuinely useful once it’s running. The gateway handles message routing, session management, and tool execution. The architecture is sound.

Quick reference: environment variables

Section titled “Quick reference: environment variables”
VariableWhat it does
OPENCLAW_IMAGEUse a pre-built remote image instead of building locally
OPENCLAW_GATEWAY_BINDlan (default), loopback, or custom binding
OPENCLAW_SANDBOX1 to enable Docker sandbox for agent tools
OPENCLAW_EXTRA_MOUNTSBind-mount host directories into the container
OPENCLAW_HOME_VOLUMENamed volume for persistent /home/node
OPENCLAW_DOCKER_APT_PACKAGESSystem packages to bake into the image

What should be fixed upstream

Section titled “What should be fixed upstream”

Three suggestions for the OpenClaw Docker setup:

  1. Set allowedOrigins before starting the gateway. The race condition is the biggest pain point. The setup script should write the config before the first docker compose up.

  2. Include both localhost and 127.0.0.1 in the default allowlist. Developers use both interchangeably. Blocking one is a paper cut.

  3. Auto-approve the first Control UI device pairing. If the user just completed onboarding, the first browser connection is clearly legitimate.

OpenClaw Telegram Topics: Run Parallel Task Flows in One Group

Feb 1, 2026
Vibe Sparking

OpenClaw Telegram Topics: Run Parallel Task Flows in One Group

Section titled “OpenClaw Telegram Topics: Run Parallel Task Flows in One Group”

OpenClaw is an open-source AI assistant that connects to Telegram, Discord, and other platforms. Its “concurrent task engine” capability shines when paired with Telegram’s Topics feature. This guide walks through setting up multiple isolated task flows in a single group.

Understanding OpenClaw’s Concurrency Model

Section titled “Understanding OpenClaw’s Concurrency Model”

OpenClaw processes tasks through Sessions:

  • One Session = one independent task flow with its own context
  • Multiple Sessions = OpenClaw handling concurrent tasks without cross-contamination

In Telegram, each Topic becomes a Session. One group can contain Chat, Work, and Feed Topics—each maintaining separate conversations and contexts.

Session Key Architecture

Section titled “Session Key Architecture”

OpenClaw generates session keys based on chat location:

LocationSession Key Pattern
DMsShared main session
Groupsagent:<agentId>:telegram:group:<chatId>
Topicsagent:<agentId>:telegram:group:<chatId>:topic:<threadId>

The :topic:<threadId> suffix isolates each Topic’s context. Messages in Topic A never bleed into Topic B.

Setting Up Parallel Task Lanes

Section titled “Setting Up Parallel Task Lanes”

Recommended Topic Structure

Section titled “Recommended Topic Structure”

Start with three Topics for common workflows:

TopicPurposeUse Case
ChatDaily conversationCasual questions, quick answers
WorkBusiness tasksDocument processing, data analysis
FeedInformation patrolNews aggregation, monitoring

Step 1: Enable Bot Group Visibility

Section titled “Step 1: Enable Bot Group Visibility”

Telegram’s Privacy Mode blocks bots from seeing group messages by default. Fix this:

  1. Open @BotFather
  2. Send /setprivacy
  3. Select your bot
  4. Choose Disable
  5. Remove and re-add the bot to your group
  6. Grant admin permissions

Admin status guarantees message visibility regardless of privacy settings.

Step 2: Enable Topics in Your Group

Section titled “Step 2: Enable Topics in Your Group”
  1. Open group settings
  2. Find Topics or Forum mode
  3. Toggle it on
  4. Create your Chat, Work, and Feed Topics

Step 3: Configure Per-Topic Behavior

Section titled “Step 3: Configure Per-Topic Behavior”

Edit your openclaw.json configuration:

Replace -1001234567890 with your group ID (forward any message to @userinfobot to get it). Replace 123 and 456 with your Topic thread IDs.

Configuration Options Explained

Section titled “Configuration Options Explained”
OptionValuesEffect
requireMentiontrue/falseWhether bot needs @mention to respond
systemPromptstringAdditional instructions for this Topic
skillsarrayLimit available skills per Topic
allowFromarrayRestrict senders in this Topic

Topics inherit parent group settings unless explicitly overridden.

Testing Your Setup

Section titled “Testing Your Setup”

Quick validation checklist:

  1. Send in Chat Topic: Bot should respond only when @mentioned (if requireMention: true)
  2. Send in Work Topic: Bot should respond to all messages (if requireMention: false)
  3. Check isolation: Reset one Topic’s session with /new—other Topics should retain their context

Common Issues and Fixes

Section titled “Common Issues and Fixes”

Bot Not Responding in Group

Section titled “Bot Not Responding in Group”

Cause: Privacy Mode still enabled or bot lacks admin status.

Fix: Re-run /setprivacy → Disable in @BotFather. Ensure bot is group admin.

DMs Work But Group Doesn’t

Section titled “DMs Work But Group Doesn’t”

Cause: Combination of privacy settings and requireMention misconfiguration.

Fix:

  1. Verify admin status
  2. Check requireMention value matches your intent
  3. Try explicit @mention first to confirm bot sees messages

Responses Appearing in Wrong Topic

Section titled “Responses Appearing in Wrong Topic”

Cause: Topic ID misconfigured in JSON.

Fix: Use @userinfobot to verify exact Topic thread IDs. Update config with correct values.

Session Reset Affecting Multiple Topics

Section titled “Session Reset Affecting Multiple Topics”

Known Issue: In multi-agent setups, /new on a non-default agent may reset both its session and the default agent’s session.

Workaround: Use single-agent setup per group or track this GitHub issue for patches.

Advanced: Multi-Agent with Separate Bots

Section titled “Advanced: Multi-Agent with Separate Bots”

For complex workflows, run multiple OpenClaw instances:

Each account maintains completely separate sessions and configurations.

Best Practices

Section titled “Best Practices”
  1. Start simple: Use three Topics maximum until workflow patterns stabilize
  2. Topic naming: Clear names help both humans and the bot understand context
  3. Selective mentions: Keep requireMention: true for high-traffic Topics to avoid spam
  4. History limits: Adjust historyLimit per Topic for context-heavy workflows
